The Starship spacecraft completed its first orbital flight, deploying Starlink satellites into orbit
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
22:50:07 EEST
04:50:07 KST

The Starship spacecraft completed its first orbital flight, deploying Starlink satellites into orbit
Kyiv • UNN
Starship reached orbit for the first time and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites despite an engine failure. The mission was shortened from 10 hours to 3.
On Monday, SpaceX's giant Starship rocket reached orbit for the first time and deployed new Starlink satellites into orbit, achieving important milestones despite an engine malfunction early in the flight and the decision to shorten the mission by seven hours, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
The mission was supposed to last 10 hours, but after engine problems arose, it was shortened to three hours. This flight from the Texas launch site was the rocket's fourteenth since 2023; Elon Musk's company plans to begin regular operations with it this year.
Unlike previous Starship flights, Monday's mission was not merely a test of a next-generation rocket but also an operational task involving the deployment into orbit of Starlink satellites worth millions of dollars. This made it the first revenue-generating Starship mission, although the spacecraft's final design is still under development.
SpaceX shares, which had previously risen by nearly 9% from their IPO price, fell by about 1% on Monday. A significant portion of SpaceX's market value and investors' confidence in the company—which was valued at $2 trillion as of Friday's market close—depends on the success of Starship, the world's first fully reusable spacecraft.
The unmanned vehicle, as tall as a 40-story building and consisting of the Super Heavy booster and the main upper stage mounted on it (the Starship spacecraft itself), lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase complex on the Gulf Coast near the city of Brownsville.
The Super Heavy booster carried Starship's upper stage into space, after which it returned to the waters of the Gulf of Mexico, making a controlled splashdown (the booster's previous two landing attempts ended in hard impacts with the surface). According to SpaceX, some of the booster's engines shut down during its descent.
SpaceX conducted a classified launch for the U.S. Space Force11.09.26, 02:55 • 4293 views
After reaching space, one of Starship's three main engines shut down prematurely; as a result, SpaceX representative Dan Huot announced during the mission's livestream that the spacecraft would not be able to reach orbit.
"The team has decided not to go to orbit," Huot said. However, a few minutes later, Huot changed the decision after engineers reported that the vehicle could still try to ignite the other onboard engines to reach orbit—which Starship successfully did shortly afterward.
We would add
Once in orbit, Starship deployed 26 next-generation Starlink satellites one after another at an altitude of approximately 269 km (161 miles), marking the first time the spacecraft had deployed a payload in orbit.
"All 26 operational Starlink V3 satellites have been deployed, and they are functioning nominally," Musk wrote on the social media platform X.
"Deploying all 26 Starlink V3 satellites into their target orbit is a huge achievement, especially given that this is the first commercial Starship flight to generate revenue," said Dean Slayden, a quality control manager and aerospace engineer at Accu Components. "But from an engineering perspective, the most interesting moment was how the team handled the engine failure during ascent."
The publication notes that engine problems also occurred during some of Starship's previous suborbital flights; this is a longstanding issue for the program involving a critically important aspect—the rocket's ability to maneuver in space. Although this capability is less important for deploying Starlink satellites into low Earth orbit, it is crucial for Starship's future missions, including delivering NASA astronauts to the Moon.
Jared Isaacman congratulated SpaceX on the social media platform X for managing "to get the ship to orbit and complete every phase of the flight safely, responsibly, and, most importantly, inspiringly."
The controlled descent of Starship into the waters of the Pacific Ocean—seven hours earlier than scheduled—ended with an engine maneuver that turned the vehicle into a vertical position for a nose-up splashdown. At the moment it touched the ocean’s surface, flames engulfed the rocket’s base; it subsequently tipped onto its side, followed by a powerful explosion that produced a large fireball. The company had not planned to recover and reuse the spacecraft after the mission.
Context
Starship was created to enable more frequent launches of SpaceX’s Starlink satellites and to carry out future NASA missions to the Moon. Reaching orbit—a key measure of the success of any new rocket intended to deliver payloads into space—was a long-awaited achievement for Starship. Musk once predicted that this would happen as early as 2022, with satellite launches following in 2023.
All 13 previous Starship test flights, conducted since 2023, had been limited to suborbital space as part of a development campaign that has lasted nearly a decade and cost SpaceX more than $15 billion. Musk said that in the future he plans to conduct hundreds or even thousands of Starship flights per year—launch rates unprecedented in the space industry.
"We are 2–3 years away from Starship flights at one-hour intervals," Musk wrote on the social network X on Sunday.

This TikTok home remedy could cause botulism—here’s what to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
19:47:33 UTC
04:47:33 KST

As flu season approaches, TikTokers are spreading a homemade elixir to supposedly boost the immune system that experts warn could in fact cause the fatal disease botulism.
In dozens of videos, some of which have hundreds of thousands of “likes” and “favorites,” wellness and herbalist influencers tout the benefits of garlic fermented in honey as an all-natural antibiotic and antimicrobial treatment and detoxifying potion. While both honey and garlic do have some antimicrobial benefits, the recipes used can promote the growth of Clostridium botulinum. This bacterium causes deadly botulism and is commonly found in both ingredients.
“Fermenting garlic in unpasteurized honey at room temperature can pose a risk of botulism,” says Karine LeBlanc, a spokesperson for Health Canada, the country’s national health policy organization. “Storing the mixture at room temperature may further increase the risk.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The number of foods that carry C. botulinum bacteria is small. The microorganisms grow best in low-oxygen conditions and require specific pH conditions. Both honey and garlic fall into the category of foods in which the bacteria can live, but under normal circumstances, the growth of spores would be inhibited, says Joy Gail Waite-Cusic, a professor of food safety at Oregon State University.
“There’s not enough available water in the honey for any bacteria to grow, and so it keeps, and it doesn’t mold either,” she says.
Combining the two ingredients is where trouble lies. Bacteria in the honey can pull water out of the garlic and then begin to multiply. If the fermentation process doesn’t decrease the mixture’s pH fast enough, this can also accelerate the bacteria’s growth further.
When ingested, the mixture could lead to infection with a bacterium that carries the nerve-attacking toxins that botulism is known for. Depending on how it enters the body, botulism can cause muscle weakness, slurred speech, difficulty breathing, stomach pain, diarrhea, nausea and vomiting. In extreme cases, the infection can cause death.
“If you consume that toxin, then it will exhibit its paralytic effects on you,” Waite-Cusic says. Among the most common targets, she says, are “your diaphragm, and so you stop breathing.”
The disease is rare, with only 243 confirmed cases and 30 additional probable cases recorded in 2021, the most recent year for which data is available, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Of the confirmed and probable cases, 181 were in infants, the highest incidence since 1976, when data started being collected.
The reason why the disease is so deadly for babies is that their gut microbiome is yet to develop the defense mechanisms needed to fight off the bacteria—by contrast, an adult’s gut biome and immune system is generally effective in fighting the bacteria when ingested.
“There are a few documented adult intestinal colonization botulism cases (mostly from Canada), where peanut butter was implicated and one infant in 2024” in the UK, says Haydee Dabritz, an epidemiologist with the California Department of Public Health’s Infant Botulism Treatment and Prevention Program.
Still, on rare occasions, it can continue to grow in an adult. While the disease is curable if the infected person seeks medical attention, it can be lethal if left untreated.
“The issue we're always facing with botulism discussions is it can kill you,” says Waite-Cusic. “It’s not ‘I’m gonna vomit for a few hours and get better.’ It’s ‘No, if you don’t get to a hospital and get the antidote, you’re dead.’”
While nobody wants to get sick during flu season, LeBlanc warns against relying on homemade remedies as a substitute for approved medications.
“If you think you may need an antibiotic or other antimicrobial medication, speak with a health care professional,” she says. “Antimicrobial medications, including antibiotics and antivirals, should only be used when prescribed.”
Waite-Cusic adds that you could see more benefit from garlic and honey by avoiding fermentation and eating them as they are. (Notably, raw honey cannot be given to babies under one year of age because of the potential for botulism.)
“You actually have the best antioxidant potential if they’re both raw," she says, referring to honey and garlic. “So you just want to eat the clove of garlic that’s now sweeter.”

CIA restores helicopter that took first Americans to Afghanistan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
19:40:40 UTC
04:40:40 KST

- The CIA restored the helicopter that flew its JAWBREAKER team into Afghanistan on Sept. 26, 2001, returning it to its 2001 paint scheme.
- Ronald Moeller, a self-described retired CIA paramilitary officer, noted on X that the aircraft is technically an Mi-8MTV, not an Mi-17.
The CIA has restored the helicopter that carried the first American team into Afghanistan after the Sept. 11 attacks, repainting it in the camouflage it wore in 2001 to mark the 25th anniversary of the mission.
The Russian-designed helicopter sits on the grounds of CIA headquarters in Langley, Virginia. It flew a seven-man CIA team, code-named JAWBREAKER, into Afghanistan’s Panjshir Valley on Sept. 26, 2001, just 15 days after the attacks. The agency calls the aircraft an Mi-17, but a retired CIA officer who says he was part of its history publicly corrected that.
“Actually an Mi-8 MTV. Nevertheless, she is a tremendous platform, performing flawlessly no matter the mission. Proud to have been part of her history,” wrote Ronald Moeller, who describes himself on X as a retired CIA paramilitary operations officer and former deputy assistant secretary of war for strategic readiness, in reply to the CIA’s anniversary post.
The two names describe closely related aircraft. The Mi-17 is the export designation for Russia’s Mi-8MTV family of medium transport helicopters, and the two are often used interchangeably. The CIA did not respond publicly to the correction.
The CIA bought the helicopter in the 1990s, reasoning that a Soviet-designed aircraft would draw little attention in Afghanistan, where both the Northern Alliance and the Taliban flew the same type. It could also handle the altitude. On the way to the Panjshir Valley, the crew had to cross the Anjuman Pass, which rises about 4,400 m (14,500 feet) above sea level.
The first flight carried the seven CIA officers, a three-member aircrew and two Afghan partners, according to the agency. Led by veteran officer Gary Schroen, the team brought millions of dollars in cash to recruit and equip Afghan fighters and prepared the ground for the U.S. military campaign against al-Qaeda and the Taliban. Their main partner was the Northern Alliance, whose leader, Ahmad Shah Massoud, had been assassinated by al-Qaeda operatives two days before the Sept. 11 attacks.
The helicopter went on to fly more than 300 missions in Afghanistan before its last operational flight in 2012. It was moved to CIA headquarters in 2018 and dedicated there on Sept. 26, 2019, exactly 18 years after the JAWBREAKER landing. Its fuel lines and other components were removed, and it was placed among rocks meant to resemble the Afghan landscape. It carries the tail number 91101, a reference to the date of the attacks.
Years outdoors took a toll. CIA Museum director Robert Byer told CBS News that the paint had badly faded in the sun and that animals had been getting inside. Over the past year, restorers sealed holes in the fuselage and repainted the aircraft to match its 2001 appearance. They also brought back “607,” the call sign of the Afghan pilot who flew the first mission.

Senate is set to vote on a sweeping college sports bill. Here's what it would do
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
19:37:01 UTC
04:37:01 KST

Senate is set to vote on a sweeping college sports bill. Here’s what it would do
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Proponents say the bill would allow smaller programs to compete with larger schools.
- Some critics argue that the bill would prevent highly sought-after college athletes from participating in their own negotiation process.
WASHINGTON — The Senate on Monday is expected to approve a bipartisan bill that would give the NCAA and its member conferences the authority to enforce uniform national rules on college athletics.
If the bill is passed by the Senate, it would move to the House and, if approved, on to President Trump for his signature.
What the Protect College Sports Act would do
Under the Protect College Sports Act — co-authored by Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Tex.) — the NCAA would be granted a limited antitrust exemption that would allow the organization to create standardized rules around athlete eligibility, limit conference realignment and prevent the creation of a super league — a private-equity model for college sports that would replace NCAA subdivisions.
The bill is also an attempt to codify the $2.8-billion antitrust settlement reached last year in House vs. NCAA, which allowed Division 1 schools to share revenue with their current players and compensate past players. The new bill would increase the revenue sharing cap to around $50 million per school from $21.5 million, albeit with a more strict and enforceable model.
Under Name, Image and Likeness deals, wealthier schools were able to circumvent the “soft” $21.5-million cap by lining up lucrative corporate sponsorships and endorsements for prospective athletes. The bill would allow the NCAA to crack down on attempts to bypass the limit by incorporating booster or affiliated-entity money into total revenue-sharing calculations, while also giving schools an additional $27 million in the funding cap to retain current athletes.
Potential boost for smaller schools
A potential consequence of the bill could be that big-name programs lose their ability to draw the best college athletes with promises of massive compensation, allowing smaller programs to compete under NCAA regulations.
The NCAA and its affiliates have spent tens of millions of dollars lobbying for congressional intervention on its rule-making power over the last seven years. Supporters of the bill, including Cruz, have said the bill would bring order and consistent regulation to college sports.
“If we’re going to be having a national competition … it is only Congress that can establish a clear and enforceable legal rule book,” Cruz said on the Senate floor last week.
Influential figures in college sports, including former Alabama head football coach Nick Saban and ESPN analyst Pat McAfee, have publicly called on Congress to pass the measure. It has also drawn support from 24 of the NCAA’s athletic conferences.
“Congress does need to fix the mess in the courts and create a national framework so the people inside college sports can enforce fair rules,” Saban said during a Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation committee hearing in June. “Without that legal certainty, every rule becomes another lawsuit, every standard becomes another risk, and the system keeps drifting toward a professional model.”
What the opponents say
The legislation is not without its opponents. Some players, labor organizations and members of Congress argue that the bill would prevent highly sought-after college athletes from participating in their own negotiation process.
“What this bill does, at its core, is protect a system of exploitation,” Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) said in an AFL-CIO trade union press release. “This bill protects the billions of dollars that coaches and executives are making by suppressing compensation for some of the most highly valued athletes in the world.”
The Congressional Black Caucus and the NAACP have also brought forward concerns that the bill does not allow Black athletes — who make up a majority of players in the football and basketball programs — into the collective bargaining process.
The NCAA plans to enforce a five-year eligibility rule, cap agent fees at 5%, put penalties on second transfers and codify student-athlete protections, such as 10-year degree completion assistance and post-eligibility healthcare. If the bill passes, all challenges to these rules would have to be handled in federal court.
Some senior Republican officials in the House, including Rep. Tim Walberg (R-Mich.) and Rep. Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.), have expressed some hesitance in passing the legislation without clarity as to whether student-athletes will be considered employees and if further limits should be placed on international student-athletes. If changes are made in the House, the bill would be returned to the Senate for another vote.
Support from Trump
Trump, on the other hand, has expressed strong support for the bill.
“THE PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT is a great Bill, and the Senate will hopefully stay in D.C. until it passes,” he wrote on Truth Social last month. “Without this Bill, millions of young Athletes will be hurt, programs will be canceled ... the fans will be robbed, and Universities will go broke.”

Apprenticeship money arrives as defence hunts for welders
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
20:32:44 BST
04:32:44 KST

Mayors are to be handed a £100 million fund to expand apprenticeships in their areas, an announcement John Healey made in his first Labour Party conference speech as Chancellor of the Exchequer and set within an argument about young people out of work.
The money lands at a moment when the defence industry is short of exactly the trades apprenticeships produce. Wes Streeting told the same conference that there is neither an economic nor a moral justification for the sector hiring thousands of workers from abroad while a million young people are out of work at home, and committed the department he leads to what he called the Prime Minister’s mission to reindustrialise Britain.
“After Covid, and before the election, the Tories let the number of young people in this country not in employment, in education, or training rise to nearly one million,” he said. “Two thirds have never worked.” He credited the review being carried out for government by Alan Milburn with laying bare the challenge, and said the best thing that can be offered to a young person is not a benefit payment but a first job.
“So when I was first elected, I had as my first top three priorities jobs, jobs, and jobs,” he said, describing the closure of the last pit in his area at Silverwood in 1994 and a period when one in three men locally were out of work. “The jobs went away. Hope and opportunity went too.” He set his own first job, washing pots and glasses in a North Yorkshire pub, against the position young people are in now. “But every person, every young person should know the pride of getting their first job, and taking home their first pay check.”
Whether any of it reaches defence depends on where the apprenticeships are created, and the shortages the industry reports are specific. Welders, fabricators, electrical trades and nuclear-qualified roles all take years to train rather than months, and shipbuilders and submarine builders compete for the same people as construction and the energy sector. Yards have brought welders in from overseas while domestic training catches up with order books that now run for decades.
That gap has been raised repeatedly over recent weeks, and Graeme Downie, the Labour MP for Dunfermline and Dollar, told the ADS Skills Conference this month that the country’s real deterrent is not its weapons but the people who build, maintain and operate them, while the Scottish Affairs Committee reported that Scotland is well placed to benefit from rising defence spending yet risks missing out unless persistent skills shortages are addressed.
GMB made the same argument when the Programme Euston docks were confirmed for British yards, with Robert Deavy, the union’s Scotland senior organiser in engineering, saying: “We urge the Scottish Government to work with UK ministers to deliver the investment needed to support the necessary apprenticeships and training to secure this contract.”
Healey also announced £300 million of investment by Rolls-Royce across factories at Derby, Bristol, Glasgow and Rotherham, and repeated the six billion pound figure for shipbuilding contracts. The Local Apprenticeship Service fund will run through mayors rather than through departments, which puts the decisions about which trades to back with the combined authorities in places where shipbuilding, aerospace and nuclear work is concentrated. His first Budget comes in a month, and he told delegates that fiscal discipline would run through the core of it.

Nvidia unveils safety product after rogue AI incidents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
19:31:19 UTC
04:31:19 KST

Nvidia unveils safety product after rogue AI incidents
SAN FRANCISCO - Nvidia on Sept 28 unveiled a system designed to stop autonomous AI programmes from straying beyond what they were instructed to do, after a wave of incidents raised alarm about the technology’s risks.
AI “agents” are designed to act on their own – browsing the web, writing and running code or handling files – rather than simply answering questions like a chatbot.
The technology has been hailed as the next stage of the AI revolution, but several leading companies have recently reported cases of agents breaking out of the test environments meant to contain them.
According to ChatGPT-maker OpenAI, websites accessed by its agents include those of US federal agencies, an Australian government health statistics portal and Hugging Face, a repository of AI models.
Amid the alarm, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang insisted that the problems can be solved.
“I believe it’s an engineering problem ... and we all need to hope that’s an engineering problem,” Huang told CNBC on Sept 28.
“If it’s not an engineering problem, it’s not solvable,” he added.
In Huang’s view, tech firms would not keep pushing the technology forward if they did not believe the risks could be managed.
Nvidia has a lot riding on that bet: its graphics processing units, or GPUs, power much of the AI boom, and the company’s fortunes are closely tied to the revolution continuing at full speed.
Huang likened the challenge to the early days of the internet, when websites could load programs onto people’s computers and spread viruses.
The answer then, he said, was to turn the web browser into a “containment system” that limited access.
Nvidia’s system similarly places each agent in a sealed-off digital space, or “sandbox,” and lets companies spell out exactly which files, networks and tools it may use.
A separate monitor, running on Nvidia hardware beyond the agent’s reach, watches its behaviour and can cut it off if it goes astray.
Nvidia said the system could have prevented the Hugging Face breach, in which the platform reported more than 17,000 agents attacking its infrastructure over days and weeks.
More than 100 organisations are working with Nvidia’s platform at launch, the company said, including Microsoft, Cisco, Salesforce and SAP.
Anthropic has connected its Claude agents to the system and SpaceXAI is applying it to its Grok models. AFP

Boox Announces the Picco, Its Smallest E-Reader Ever (2026)

04:30:00 KST

While smartphones won't stop getting bigger, e-readers seem to be getting smaller. Boox has been at the forefront with one of the most popular small e-readers, the Boox Palma, and now it is adding an even smaller model.
Boox announced the Picco, with preorders opening today. Its screen is just under 4 inches (3.97 to be exact), making it about the size of a playing card. It's even smaller than the Xteink X4 Pro I tested earlier this year, which has a 4.3-inch screen (but just slightly larger than the 3.7-inch Xteink X3), and considerably smaller than the upcoming Boox Palma 3's 6.19-inch screen. I liked the size of the Xteink in my hand, but navigating the interface and getting books were challenging, so I'm excited to see another option in that smaller size from a maker with more accessible ebooks (though still not as convenient as a Kindle or Kobo with their built-in stores).
The Picco will cost $100 and is expected to ship in November. I'll be testing it soon, but in the meantime, here are the details if you've been eyeing a tiny e-reader.
An E-Reader for Productivity
The Boox Picco has a monochrome screen with a resolution of 235 pixels per inch and an adjustable front light that switches between warm- and cool-toned lighting. The microSD card slot supports up to 2 TB of flash memory storage (a 16 GB card is included). There are both a touchscreen and physical page-turning controls, thanks to the buttons on the side of the device. The case has a magnetic ring so you can attach it to the back of a smartphone, though I'll have to see how well it fits when I test it, as I had mixed results attaching an Xteink to my phone due to both fit and magnet strength.
Boox says the Picco will have a streamlined operating system focused on reading and digital utility tools. It's also the first in what Boox calls its Tiles lineup, which is how you'll access ebooks on this device. You can also use web and USB-C file transfers (the Picco has Wi-Fi and Bluetooth connectivity) to get ebooks onto the Picco. The Picco also has the Pomodoro, Todo, and Countdown apps, so you can use it as both an e-reader and a productivity gadget—handy, and a bigger motivation to keep it attached to the back of your phone even when you aren't reading.
I'm intrigued to see it in action. Boox's most popular e-reader could become the Picco over the Palma 3, but we'll have to wait for both devices to become available to see which is the better buy. Stay tuned for my reviews of both when they come out.

A SpaceX Starship Rocket Officially Reached Orbit. Why That's So Significant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
19:22:46 UTC
04:22:46 KST

For three and a half years, ever since the spring of 2023, when SpaceX launched the first of its massive Starship rockets, the company has been promising that before too long the towering, stainless steel machine would get to orbit. This morning, on the 14th such launch, it made good on that boast.
“Starship performs its orbital insertion burn and enters orbit of Earth for the first time,” SpaceX announced on X at 9:15 a.m. ET, along with a video of that engine maneuver. It took just 25 minutes and 17 seconds for the spacecraft to travel from its launch pad in Starbase, Texas, to its circular orbit 170 miles high.
There is no overstating how important today’s success was to SpaceX’s—and NASA’s—long-term plans. Starship is pivotal to getting human beings to the moon and Mars, and SpaceX sees it as an ultimate replacement for its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket, which accounted for nearly 51% of the global total of commercial launches—including 85% of all satellites—in 2025. Starship’s far larger payload bay can carry a cargo equivalent of nearly five Falcon 9s, ultimately consolidating launches and cutting costs.
Starship is a two-part rocket. Standing 407 ft. on the launch pad, it is equipped with 33 first stage engines, which produce 16.7 million lbs. of thrust, making it far and away the most powerful rocket ever successfully launched—easily eclipsing NASA’s Space Launch System (SLS) and its 8.8 million lbs. Starship’s first stage represents 236 ft. of the overall stack. Atop it is the 171-ft. spacecraft—also dubbed Starship—a six-engine machine intended for satellite deployment and for crew travel.
In 2021, NASA selected Starship as one of two spacecraft that will land astronauts on the moon as early as 2028. (Blue Origin, the aerospace company founded by Amazon boss Jeff Bezos, will provide the other.) In 2027, NASA is planning a crewed test of either or both spacecraft in Earth orbit during the mission of Artemis III.
“Congrats @SpaceX!” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman posted on X after SpaceX confirmed this morning’s orbital success. “Gorgeous launch, getting Ship to orbit and managing every step in a safe, responsible, and especially inspirational way. @NASA, along with the rest of the interested public, is excited to help where we can and for Starship missions to become routine!”
Early on, routine was not remotely how Starship launches were being described. Four minutes into the rocket’s inaugural launch on April 20, 2023, it exploded spectacularly. Concrete and steel debris rained down in a near-400-acre footprint in the surrounding Boca Chica State Park, and a 3.85-acre fire burned south of the launch site. Environmental organizations mounted multiple legal challenges to slow or halt the launches until hazards could be eliminated. But the flights proceeded apace at a rate of once every three months, none achieving stable orbit—until today.
The launch this morning was both imperfect and stripped down to its orbital essentials. On the way up, one of the Starship’s six engines failed to burn properly, requiring the other engines to compensate for the missing thrust to get the ship in orbit.
In addition, the return to Earth was simplified. SpaceX has made itself famous for safely landing the first stage of its Falcon 9 and Starship boosters—with 641 out of 688 Falcon 9 launches featuring this kind of recovery, allowing the boosters to be reused and make flying cheaper. Starship’s first stage, meantime, performs what has become known as a chopstick recovery, with the booster navigating its way back to the launch tower where two giant metal arms pluck it from the sky. For the current mission, the chopstick recovery was done away with to simplify the flight objectives; instead the first stage made a soft, engine-assisted splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico. The Starship spacecraft was planned for a six-orbit, 10-hour mission, with the ship’s engines set to fire around the dinner hour Monday to bring the spacecraft down for a similar gentle, watery landing.
Today’s launch was not just a test flight; it was also an operational mission designed to deliver 26 Starlink satellites to orbit, adding to the whopping 11,000 that already comprise the Starlink constellation—with an eventual goal of 100,000. SpaceX released footage of Starship deploying the satellites with what it has dubbed its Pez dispenser system, because that’s exactly what the spacecraft resembles as it releases its payload one satellite at a time. Ultimately, the spacecraft was brought down early, after just three orbits, since its satellites had all been deployed and the ship proved its flight worthiness quickly.
The launch of Starship 14 is in many ways only a very small—if critical—step. Even the biggest SpaceX supporters don’t pretend that Starship is anywhere near ready to land astronauts on the moon in 2028. The spacecraft—which is now essentially a giant, flying, cargo truck—has to be adapted to carry crew, with all of the environmental and habitat modifications that implies. It will also have to solve a stubborn refueling problem: before heading out for the moon, Starship will need to enter a parking orbit around the Earth where up to a dozen other Starship-sized tankers will top off its tanks. It will have to fly its Artemis III test flight in 2027, and later, an uncrewed landing on—and liftoff from—the moon before it will be trusted to carry astronauts in as little as two years’ time.
Still, SpaceX promises that an Earth-orbital launch that today is headline-making could become almost as commonplace as the takeoff of a commercial airliner. Elon Musk, the company’s founder and CEO, has spoken openly about Starships launching as frequently as once a day—or even once an hour. Maybe. For now the company is celebrating one launch on one day, on a mission that didn’t even last past east coast lunchtime. But spaceflight is iterative and incremental. And today SpaceX moved one big increment indeed.

Debt costs more than defence, policing and justice combined
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
20:19:13 BST
04:19:13 KST

Britain is spending more servicing its national debt than it spends on the Home Office, defence and justice put together, John Healey told the Labour Party conference.
The Chancellor of the Exchequer used the comparison to attack the previous government’s record, telling delegates that Conservative decisions had left “a legacy of sky-high debt costs, for families and for government.” Turning to the opposition front bench, he said: “Your reckless actions are still causing pain for people today. You left crumbling public services. And you left Britain spending more on debt than the Home Office, Defence and Justice put together. And people won’t forget, people won’t forgive.”
He set out what that means for departmental budgets in terms defence readers will recognise. “The cost of the nation’s debt is not just a number in a Chancellor’s Budget,” he said. “It’s the money that we can’t spend on the NHS, on schools, on housing, on social care. On policing our streets, on controlling our borders, on defending our country. And I tell you these levels of debt are an assault on our common sense, they are an affront to our values.”
Healey attributed the position to three episodes, naming austerity under David Cameron, the effect of Brexit on exports under Boris Johnson, and the mini Budget of Liz Truss, which he said crashed the economy and collapsed confidence in Britain’s fiscal strength. He noted that the shadow chancellor appointed by Kemi Badenoch had helped write that mini Budget and still maintains there were good things in it.
The comparison carries weight because debt interest has grown into one of the largest single items in public spending, competing directly with the departments the Chancellor listed. Defence spending is committed to rise to 3.5 per cent of GDP on core defence by 2035 under the promise made to NATO allies, which Wes Streeting restated from the same platform as a cast iron guarantee, and the Defence Investment Plan has committed an additional £15 billion between 2026-27 and 2029-30, taking planned investment to around £298 billion across the four years.
Against that, the Chancellor made fiscal discipline the condition for everything else. “On day one as Chancellor, I said my first duty is fiscal discipline,” he said. “And I’ll tell you why. It underwrites every promise this Government makes. On growth, on jobs, on national security, and on public services. We can’t succeed without it.” He committed to balancing the books with a buffer against uncertainty, controlling borrowing to bring down inflation and reducing long-term pressures on the public finances.
His Budget is a month away, and he told delegates that fiscal discipline would run through the core of it. The tension that argument sets up for defence is a familiar one, since the department’s own investment plan runs over the same period in which the Chancellor has undertaken to bring borrowing under control, and Streeting acknowledged from the same stage that more spending on defence comes with choices and trade-offs.
Healey quoted his own predecessor as Defence Secretary on where those trade-offs lead, reaching back to Denis Healey’s warning from 1969 that cutting defence expenditure to the extent that security is imperilled leaves a country with no houses, no hospitals and no schools, only a heap of cinders.

Russia is ‘far from isolated’ – Richard Sakwa to RT (VIDEO)
The collective West’s efforts to isolate Russia have failed, as shown by the international turnout at this year’s Valdai Discussion Club, University of Kent professor emeritus of politics Richard Sakwa has told RT.
The 23rd annual session of the Valdai Discussion Club opened outside of Moscow on Monday, bringing together 120 participants from 40 countries. They include representatives from China, Brazil, Argentina, Algeria, Egypt, India, Iran, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and Türkiye, as well as the US, UK, Germany, Italy, France, and Canada.
Panel discussions will run through Thursday, October 1.

“Russia remains far from isolated” despite Western governments’ efforts to sideline it on the global stage since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, he said.
Russia continues to play an active role in the G20 and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and is a founding member of BRICS, which has expanded to 11 countries representing “nearly half the world’s population [and] about half the world’s GDP,” Sakwa explained.
Forums such as the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum, Primakov Readings, and the Valdai Discussion Club also continue to attract international interest, including from Western expert communities.
“If anyone is isolated, it’s more and more the West… and the world is getting on with trying to establish an agenda for peace and development,” the British political scientist told RT.
Describing the broader global shift, Sakwa argued that while the world remains within the post-WWII framework, “the institutions and patterns which have emerged after 1945 are changing,” along with the roles of major powers such as the US and Russia.

Iran nearing completion of key rail link key for India’s gateway to Eurasia

Iran nearing completion of key rail link key for India’s gateway to Eurasia
Iran has completed laying track on the southern stretch of the Chabahar-Zahedan railway, closing a key gap in a route designed to connect the port of Chabahar on the Gulf of Oman to Zahedan near the Afghan border. 
Iranian railway official Abbas Khatibi said last week that tracks had been laid for the crucial 480km stretch between Chabahar and Khash, and currently the priority is to complete the stations on the route, Tasnim news agency reported. 
The Chabahar–Zahedan link stretches 630 km, or 735 km including branch lines. With the northern sections already linked to the existing rail network, the Iranian authorities are now preparing it for operation. 
The Chabahar–Zahedan link is an extension of the larger International North–South Transport Corridor (INSTC), backed by India, Iran and Russia. The project has been in the making for decades because of its huge infrastructure requirements and has also been slowed by Western sanctions on both Iran and Russia. 
The milestone comes as the Middle East conflict has disrupted traditional transport and energy routes across the region. Chabahar has direct access to the Indian Ocean without requiring ships to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, a major chokepoint affected by the conflict.
Strategic Step: Iran Completes Chabahar-Zahedan Rail Link – Connecting Central Asia to Indian Ocean
The major infrastructure project looks set to become fully operational within 3-4 months with final safety checks for the route underway. (Economic Times)
The route connects… pic.twitter.com/pUKsSzJEJq
For India, the Chabahar-Zahedan link strengthens a trade route that reaches Afghanistan and Central Asia without transiting Pakistan. Cargo arriving by sea at Chabahar would be able to move inland through Iran’s rail and road network toward landlocked regional markets. 
India’s role in Chabahar is complicated by US sanctions. A conditional waiver covering the project, in which India invested around $120 million, expired in April. New Delhi maintained it was discussing the issue with both Tehran and Washington, describing the regional conflict as a “complicating factor.” 
In July, the conflict touched Chabahar itself, when US forces struck a surveillance tower at the neighboring Shahid Kalantari terminal linked to the project. India said the terminal was not damaged.

Pope Leo draws massive crowds in France. Is Catholicism making a comeback?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
19:08:17 UTC
04:08:17 KST

Pope Leo draws massive crowds in France. Is Catholicism making a comeback?
For a few days, France — one of Europe's most secular countries — looked like it was in the throes of a Catholic revival.
An estimated 800,000 people filled the streets for Pope Leo XIV's outdoor Mass in Paris on Saturday, according to the Vatican. Priests there were seen hearing confessions out in the open, no confessional required.
The night before, roughly 80,000 young people gathered for a lively prayer vigil full of singing and dancing at the Stade de France, the national football and rugby stadium.
In Lourdes, where believers say a famous Catholic shrine gushes with healing waters, streets were crowded with pilgrims waving flags and holding babies aloft as the pope passed in his popemobile. More than 150,000 people attended Sunday Mass there.
This, all in a country where hundreds of clergy were publicly executed during the French Revolution — many by guillotine.
A Catholic revival?
French Ambassador to the Holy See Charles Personnaz described the pope's visit as a "very living exchange between the pope and the people of France" and said it allowed an "appeal to the young people to engage themselves for peace, not to be afraid of the future."
"And that is a wondrous sign for the youth of France and everywhere in Europe, in fact," he said.
The crowds offered a striking welcome for the first American pope. They also raised a question: Is faith making a comeback in France?
Some evidence suggests renewed interest. The French bishops conference counted 21,386 adult and adolescent baptisms at Easter this year. That number included 13,234 adults, up 28% from last year and more than triple the number a decade ago.
Leo made a point to publicly visit some of the newly baptized during his visit.
Still, France has a population of nearly 70 million, and in the latest broad survey from the national statistics agency, 51% of people aged 18 to 59 said they had no religion. Just 29% identified as Catholic.
The same survey showed the fastest-growing religious category was Christians who did not identify as Catholic. Their share rose in the last decade from 2.5% to 9% among 18- to 49-year-olds. Islam rose from 8% to 11% in the same age range.
A number of French laws reflect the gaps between Catholic teaching and public policies and civic values. In 2024, France added a guaranteed freedom to seek an abortion to its constitution. Last month, it enacted a law allowing assisted dying under specified conditions for people with serious, incurable illnesses. Both measures conflict with the Catholic Church's position on the sanctity of life, and Leo spoke out against both on this trip.
Catholic affiliation also has been falling across much of the West. In the U.S., the share of adults identifying as Catholic dropped from 24% in 2007 to 19% in 2023-24, according to Pew Research's Religious Landscape Study.
The scenes in Paris and Lourdes have visibly inspired Pope Leo and clergy across France. But whether they signal a lasting change in church attendance or religious affiliation remains to be seen.

Aleksandar Vučić resigns as Serbia’s president eight months early to run for prime minister instead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
19:02:54 UTC
04:02:54 KST

Aleksandar Vučić resigns as Serbia’s president eight months early to run for prime minister instead
Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić has announced his resignation. His opponents have demanded it for nearly two years, since 16 people died when a railway station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in November 2024. But Vučić appears to be leaving the presidency to try to stay in power, rather than to give in to protesters. Meduza briefly explains how it came to this.
Who is Aleksandar Vučić?
Vučić has dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade. He began his career in the 1990s as a lawmaker for the Serbian Radical Party and served as information minister under Slobodan Milošević. In 2008, he broke with the far right and co-founded the more moderate Serbian Progressive Party.
The party first came to power as part of a coalition in 2012. Two years later, it won a majority in parliament, and Vučić became prime minister. He became president three years after that. He served almost two terms, resigning eight months before his second term was due to end. The resignation was expected: Vučić said in June that he was in his “final weeks” in office.
His longtime ally Ana Brnabić, speaker of Serbia’s parliament, the National Assembly, has become acting president. A new presidential election must be held within three months.
What was Serbian politics like under Vučić?
Serbia is a parliamentary republic in which the prime minister has more authority and responsibility than the president. But Vučić retained control of his party even after becoming president in 2017, despite the presidency being the formally weaker office. His party has governed Serbia for 14 consecutive years.
Freedom House, a U.S. organization that studies rights and freedoms around the world, rates Serbia as “partly free” under Vučić. It says he has sought to suppress the opposition and concentrate power at home, while balancing Serbia’s pursuit of EU membership with its ties to Moscow and Beijing abroad.
That balance became harder to maintain after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Serbia condemned the war and refused to recognize Russia’s annexation of Ukrainian regions, but it still has not joined EU sanctions against Russia. Since 2022, Serbia has also become one of the main destinations for Russians leaving because of the war: tens of thousands of Russian citizens have settled there over the past four years.
Why is Vučić leaving?
By his own account, he is leaving to take part in snap parliamentary elections on October 25. Vučić called the elections himself amid protests that have continued for nearly two years. They began after a canopy collapsed over the entrance to the recently renovated railway station in Novi Sad, Serbia’s second-largest city, in November 2024, killing 16 people. Gatherings to remember the dead grew into political rallies, with protesters accusing the government of negligence and demanding that those responsible be put on trial.
The protests peaked in spring 2025. On March 15, an estimated 150,000 to 300,000 people joined a demonstration in Belgrade, where authorities may have used an acoustic weapon against protesters. Soon afterward, students — the core of the protest movement — called for early parliamentary elections. “Corruption has taken root too deeply in state institutions,” the protesters said.
Vučić ignored that demand for 16 months, until early September 2026. Analysts believe he was counting on the student protests to lose momentum. Instead, the demonstrators gained experience in local elections and drew up their own slate of parliamentary candidates. Other opposition groups backed it, too.
What happens next?
Vučić cannot become Serbia’s president again: the country limits presidents to two five-year terms, and he has exhausted his eligibility. That is why, some believe, he decided to leave office early and take part in the parliamentary elections. If his Serbian Progressive Party wins, he could hold on to power as prime minister: fellow party members have already nominated him for the post.
But victory is far from certain. Polls in recent months suggest the Student List could pose a serious challenge to the ruling party’s slate, at the very least. Serbia’s coming election looks set to be its most interesting in years.

Korper said he had not been in touch with Van der Stap since the arrest. Attempts by Reuters to reach Van der Stap or identify a lawyer or representative were not immediately successful.

Burnham to announce government-backed body to invest in electricity grid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
19:00:42 UTC
04:00:42 KST

Andy Burnham will take his first major step to putting Britain’s utility companies into public control when, at the Labour conference, he announces a new government-backed body to invest in the electricity grid.
The prime minister will use his first speech as party leader to announce the creation of GB Grid, which will use money previously allocated to Great British Energy to compete with privately owned companies such as National Grid.
The announcement marks the first significant move towards delivering on his promise to put “the essentials of life” under public control – even as ministers wrestle with how to deliver on more radical policies such as nationalising Thames Water.
Burnham will tell the conference on Tuesday: “We have a cost crisis. We all know it. The price of energy is crippling for businesses, and British billpayers pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe.
“We have an energy system where prices are dictated in markets miles away, while families and businesses here shoulder the costs. Once again, the British public has lost control.”
He will add: “Within 10 years, I want our energy costs to be in line with other nations in Europe. That means we must reform a broken energy market so it serves the public interest.”
Burnham’s first conference speech as leader and prime minister caps a remarkable turnaround in his political fortunes since this time last year, when he was criticised by many in the party for talking openly about his desire to replace Keir Starmer.
Having now ousted Starmer from office, Burnham has spent much of his first few weeks promising to undo what he calls “40 years of neoliberalism”.
The creation of GB Grid is his first significant step to challenging the power of private companies to run Britain’s infrastructure.
The organisation will be given access to a pot of £4bn that has already been allocated to the government-backed Great British Energy – although it is not expected to use all of that money.
With businesses complaining about how long it takes to get a grid connection for new buildings and projects, GB Grid will use the funding to build more connections, as well as to maximise and speed up the rollout of renewables across the UK. It will be the first publicly owned player in electricity networks since privatisation.
Officials said the government would also expand the rights of businesses to build their own connections, allowing them to tap GB Grid’s funding to help pay for it – a move which they said helped speed up connections in Ireland by 11 months.
Speaking to the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast on Monday, the energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: “One of my frustrations with the last government is that they didn’t recognise the need to invest in the system, and so we’re having to do that at record pace over the course of the next decade.
“It is incumbent on all of us to make sure we’re doing it in the most cost-effective way.”

Govt deploys AI tool to cut delays in rural road project approvals
NEW DELHI: In a bid to cut down delays and improve quality, the government has deployed an AI-based detailed project report (DPR) scrutiny tool that aims at strengthening and streamlining the technical appraisal of rural road projects under Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana.Rolled out by rural development ministry’s National Rural Infrastructure Development Agency, last week, the tool, Parakh, has been implemented on a pilot basis in all states and UTs to assess its applicability and effectiveness. DPR preparation is a critical stage in rural road development, involving assessment of alignment, geometry, pavement design, traffic, soil and subgrade conditions, drainage, cross-drainage structures, quantities and cost estimates.With thousands of DPRs requiring multi-level technical scrutiny, the govt is hoping that this AI-enabled tool will substantially reduce repetitive scrutiny time, identify deficiencies at an early stage and facilitate faster processing of DPRs, thereby accelerating sanction, execution and timely completion of PMGSY works.As of now the same parameters are often checked repeatedly at different scrutiny levels, resulting in duplication of effort and longer processing time.
Consequently, sanction of works gets delayed, affecting subsequent execution and completion.Rural development secretary Rohit Kansal said, “Transparent and consistent technical scrutiny is essential for better planning and timely implementation of PMGSY projects. Through Parakh, AI is being used to make the scrutiny of DPRs simpler, more systematic and more evidence-based.”
“This will help technical experts identify key areas requiring attention and focus more on complex cases. At the same time, it will make the technical evaluation process more effective and transparent, further strengthening the quality of rural road projects,” he added.Since the scale of the rural road projects involved is vast — around 63,914 km of road length completed in past four years, inlcuding the ongoing fiscal year — officials said Parakh is designed to assist technical experts by using Al to analyse DPR data, undertake standardised checks and flag inconsistencies in the DPR during the scrutiny process.

Trump Insists Canada Has 'Big Unemployment.' Here's What the Data Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
18:48:28 UTC
03:48:28 KST

President Donald Trump has repeatedly stated that Canada has an issue with its unemployment rate as he criticizes America’s northern neighbor amid the ongoing trade war.
Revisiting the claims last week, Trump insisted Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government was “destroying” Canada with its immigration policies that he said were “causing problems.” It’s “already showing up in their numbers,” he said on Sept. 23. “Big unemployment.” Trump had made similar claims in August, amid the collapse of U.S.-Canada trade negotiations. “Canada’s unemployment rate is now at 10%, and rapidly rising. Their businesses are fleeing for the U.S., and it’s all because of their failed policies, and inept leadership,” he falsely argued.
Trump’s focus on Canada’s unemployment figures comes amid a prolonged trade standoff between his Administration and Carney’s government. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods took effect earlier this month, with Carney matching the economic pressure imposed by the U.S. Trump, who has repeatedly threatened to annex Canada, stoked tensions by signing an Executive Order renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America.” The U.S. import bans on certain Canadian products, largely centered on alcohol and dairy, are due to take effect Tuesday. Carney, meanwhile, is focusing on strengthening international alliances, including pursuing efforts for Canada to become the E.U.’s first “associate member,” in a bid to reduce the country’s economic reliance on the U.S.
As Trump targets Canada’s unemployment rate, here’s what the data says about how the Canadian economy is currently faring.
What is Canada’s unemployment rate—and is it rising?
Canada’s economy lost 42,000 jobs in August, a decrease of 0.2%, according to the country’s Labor Force Survey released on Sept. 4. The figure came in well below reported consensus expectations for a 15k gain.
The losses were concentrated in areas such as business, building, other support services, natural resources, and utilities. The number of public sector employees fell by 20,000 (0.4%), down for the third consecutive month.
Joseph Steinberg, a professor of economics at the University of Toronto, says several factors could be contributing to the job losses, including Canada’s slowing population growth.
Data from Statistics Canada shows the population of Canada reached an estimated 41,798,407 people on July 1, 2026, an increase of 189,425 people from July 1, 2025. This marked the “lowest annual July-to-July (or June to June before 1946) growth in the total size of the population since 1944/1945.”
Despite the job losses, Canada’s unemployment rate in August remained steady at 6.4%, following three consecutive monthly declines from May through July. The unemployment rate is lower in comparison to August 2025, when it stood at 7.1%.
Meanwhile, the employment rate in Canada—the proportion of the population aged 15 and older who are employed—decreased slightly, from 60.9% to 60.8%.
Canada “does not currently have an unemployment problem,” says Steinberg, reflecting on the data.
“Broadly speaking, the labor market in Canada is doing just fine. The unemployment rate is relatively stable,” he adds. “Trump is [also] ranting about immigration as a big problem, but right now Canada's immigration rate is actually quite low.”
Canada revised its immigration policy in late 2024, in an effort to curb rapid population growth that outpaced job creation. According to federal figures compiled by Office of the Parliamentary Budget Officer, the number of permanent residents admitted in 2025 was around 328,000, compared to 419,000 the year before.
Meanwhile, in the U.S., the unemployment rate in August also remained unchanged at 4.1%, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, slightly below the 4.3% recorded in August 2025.
But anyone looking to compare figures from the U.S. and Canada should be aware they have different ways of calculating headline unemployment rates, experts tell TIME.
The surveys cover slightly different populations: Canada’s unemployment figures include people as young as 15, while the U.S. begins counting once people are 16.
“To be measured as unemployed, you also have to indicate in the survey that you are searching somehow for a job. In the U.S., that requirement for 'search' is much more active than in Canada,” says Skuterud.
Trump has frequently touted U.S. unemployment rates and job growth. In April, he celebrated March job and unemployment figures, and again in September he called the addition of 162,000 jobs in August “great news” for a “thriving economy.”
However, late last year, U.S. unemployment had risen to a four-year high and it still remains above the 3.7% average recorded in 2019 before the pandemic.
Trade uncertainty amid the U.S.-Canada standoff
Formal trade negotiations between the U.S. and Canada halted at the end of August, and while officials have remained in contact with their counterparts, neither side has voiced any significant progress.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on Sept. 25 said there was “no urgency” on the U.S. side to reach an agreement.
“President Trump is comfortable where we are on Canada,” he insisted. “The Canadians, again, periodically, they come and they want to have a deal. When they do, we talk. As we saw before, we gave them a deal. They left. They call us now and then, and we have good conversations about potential deals. But no urgency on our side.”
In response, Canadian Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said Canada is “always ready to talk to the Americans about trying to find the right agreement," but stressed the country is not “desperate” to reach a trade deal with the U.S. if it has to come at “any cost.”
For businesses, the prolonged uncertainty surrounding the trade standoff can weigh on investment and, in turn, the creation of jobs, experts tell TIME.
“If you're a business, especially in one of these tariff-exposed industries, in an industry where the customer base is in large part in the U.S. this is not a time where you want to invest in a lot of new capital, and so that affects actual job creation, the labor demand side of the economy is impacted,” says Skuterud.
“The most important thing for businesses is certainty, predictability. They've got to know where their customer base is going to be, where their sales are going to be, and there's a lot of uncertainty in those industries right now.”

Putin orders fourth expansion of Russia’s armed forces this year

Meta-Led Anti-Terrorism Group Faces Mass Resignation of Expert Advisers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
18:47:54 UTC
03:47:54 KST

Six of the nine independent experts on the advisory board of the Global Internet Forum to Counter Terrorism—a consortium run by several of the biggest US tech companies—resigned on Monday, according to a letter seen by WIRED and interviews with four of the people.
The tensions between the independent advisory committee and the GIFCT date back to an email the counterterrorism and free speech experts received in July from Meta’s Nell McCarthy, a vice president overseeing content policy. For years, the group had advised the GIFCT on how to prevent platforms from becoming havens for the radical organizations and individuals blamed for some of the world’s worst mass violence.
But McCarthy wrote that while the consortium welcomed the experts’ insights on violent trends, it no longer desired their scrutiny on the effectiveness of Big Tech’s efforts to curtail violence. Meta and other leaders wanted to “refresh” the 6-year-old independent advisory committee the experts sat on, she wrote. Meta serves as chair of GIFCT’s operating board this year, giving it outsized influence over policy changes, though other companies on the panel must ultimately approve.
New additions to the rotating advisory committee had previously been elected by current members; under the plan laid out in July, they would instead be picked by tech companies. The committee would be barred from weighing in on key topics such as the consortium’s performance and making recommendations together as a group. Its role as a watchdog would be neutered, advisers believed.
In their resignation letter, the departing members of the committee wrote that their appeals against the plan had been “ignored” and that, in turn, they had “lost confidence in the GIFCT’s ability to deliver effectively on its founding mission” to prevent terrorists from exploiting online services. “We all know that a body that cannot scrutinise, take a position, or evaluate is not an advisory body at all,” the letter stated. “It is decoration and accountability theatre.”
Meta deferred comment on the resignations to the GIFCT. An unsigned statement sent to WIRED by a GIFCT spokesperson on behalf of the consortium’s leadership and the Meta-chaired operating board says the proposed changes have been “informed by several rounds of feedback” and are not yet final. They came out of discussions on “how to more effectively engage civil society and governments for substantive input” as “multi-stakeholderism is a core principle” for the GIFCT.
The consortium has about 35 members; other long-time board members include Microsoft and YouTube. A small staff alerts members to violent content, helps them exchange threat intelligence, and commissions research on countering extremism. While the coordination has helped some platforms combat problematic content, critics believe the group isn’t living up to its potential.
A WIRED investigation in 2024 uncovered several issues with GIFCT, including Meta delaying TikTok’s membership bid and poor relations between the companies at the helm and the unpaid independent advisory body. It also revealed failures in the tip-sharing database the consortium oversees to coordinate takedowns of problematic content.
The dismantling of the advisory group threatens to deteriorate the organization’s work further at a time when balancing free expression and online safety has become more challenging. Generative AI tools have simplified content creation but imposed limited guardrails.
Extremist content, including some that is now AI-generated, that promotes organizations such as Islamic State remains a persistent issue. Newer nihilistic collectives have turned to AI-supported scams such as sexploitation to coerce young victims into carrying out violence and abuse. Several AI chatbots have been accused of facilitating violence.
“A Shame”
The experts who resigned include university researchers and representatives of civil society organizations. They had agreed with McCarthy on the need for changes to improve the results of the decade-old anti-terrorism consortium. But they believe the proposal, which could be finalized soon, amounts to a step backward.
“There won’t be critical voices raising concerns about what GIFCT is doing or is not doing,” one of the departing experts says. “It may seem politically convenient for them to abolish the independent advisory committee, but they are going to regret it in the longer term.”
Another calls it “a shame” that the tech companies “instead of engaging and building better evaluation and transparency are pursuing a rollback of independence that was already weak to begin with.”
Both of the people spoke on the condition of anonymity out of fear of retaliation from the Trump administration, which has denied visas to people it believes are working to unfairly censor online content, and Republicans in Congress, who have been investigating supposed censorship groups. While the GIFCT hasn’t been targeted, both it and an adviser’s organization were mentioned in a February report from the House Judiciary Committee.
In a meeting soon after, the advisory committee questioned consortium leaders, including from Meta, about their plans to operate in what appeared to be a fraught political environment for content moderation, according to two of the advisers present. The committee didn’t get clear answers, the people say, but got pushback for raising questions considered beyond its purview. About three months later came McCarthy’s July email.
WIRED couldn’t immediately learn why four of the expert advisers did not join the others in resigning. The committee also includes representatives from the UN and a handful of governments such as Canada and the EU, and it’s unclear whether any of them will also exit. But last Friday, the entire panel of 17 members sent a letter, seen by WIRED, to McCarthy disagreeing with her plan to curtail their group’s independence and input.
When the consortium formed the advisory committee in 2020, its then-executive director Nick Rasmussen said he had encouraged many of the inaugural members to be “the conscience of the organization” and “if necessary, to call bullshit.”
In public reports, the committee has credited its input for helping grow the consortium, expand the types of tips shared, and increase the transparency of its work. But the people who resigned believe they were often consulted too late to meaningfully influence most of the consortium’s projects.
The proposal calls for transitioning the body’s name from “committee” to “community” and forbidding it from evaluating the consortium’s governance, budget, operations, and the work of individual member companies, according to the resignation letter.
New experts recruited to the “community,” regardless of who appoints them, will quickly come to the same conclusion as those who resigned, one of the people says. “We will be on a merry-go round. It may just be that the GIFCT model has run its course.”

2026-09-28
18:42:52 UTC

Family in Russia’s Irkutsk region accuses police of plying a 54-year-old man with alcohol and forcing him to sign papers for military service in Ukraine
The family of Vladimir Shch., a 54-year-old businessman from Ust-Kut in Russia’s Irkutsk region, complained to prosecutors that police had forcibly taken him to a military enlistment office, the news outlet Lyudi Baikala reported.
According to his relatives, a district police officer came to an apartment where Vladimir was visiting on the evening of September 20 in response to a complaint from neighbors. The officer then took him home to get his passport. The family says police kept Vladimir at the station all night, plied him with alcohol, and forced him to sign papers for a military service contract.
The next day, Vladimir was taken to a military enlistment office, where he spent about two hours signing papers. He was given alcohol again on the way there. His relatives believe Vladimir, who has poor eyesight, was denied his glasses at the office to keep him from reading exactly what he was signing. He was then sent for a medical examination.
Vladimir’s wife came to the enlistment office to get him, but the district officer refused to let him go, saying she was “preventing him from signing a contract for the special military operation.” After his medical examination, Vladimir was allowed outside for a cigarette. His wife met him outside and drove him home. His documents were returned, but the family says the officer later waited for him outside his home and told his relatives that Vladimir was now “on the hook.”
Vladimir’s daughter said at least 17 men may have been forcibly taken to the Ust-Kut military enlistment office over the past two weeks. She had also heard that police receive cash payments for helping sign people up for military service. She provided no evidence for either claim but asked prosecutors to investigate them.
In June, the outlet Ust-Kut24 reported cases in which people wearing military uniforms rounded up men with criminal records or disabilities in Ust-Kut and forcibly took them to military enlistment offices.

UNFPA report: Migrant workers cite livelihood insecurity, low wages, poverty and debt as reasons for moving out for better life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
18:40:51 UTC
03:40:51 KST

For migrant workers, moving brings better livelihoods—but little job security
NEW DELHI: Nearly 72% of migrant workers surveyed in three south Indian states felt that moving for work has improved their standard of living and more than half (around 57%) intended to continue working in their destination state, as per a new report.At the same time, it turns out that over 86% of workers have no signed employment contracts and many face difficulties ranging from accessing welfare and essential services to experiencing language, communication and social barriers.Clearly migration decisions are shaped strongly by livelihood insecurity and limited employment opportunities. Migrants cited low wages at origin, lack of jobs, better opportunities, irregular employment, poverty and debt among the principal reasons for moving.These findings are part of the South India Interstate Migration Survey (SIIMS) 2026, that offers first-of-its-kind data on the changing nature of migration within India and on how migrant workers from other states (primarily from northern and eastern) live and work in Karnataka, Keralam and Tamil Nadu.The study surveyed 1,824 migrant workers and covered sectors including agriculture, fishing and marine work, and daily labour in all three states.
It also covered hospitality in Keralam, textile and garment work in Tamil Nadu, and scrap collection in Karnataka.Over 92% of the migrants came from West Bengal (26.2%), Bihar (21.8%), Assam (17.1%), Odisha (12%), UP (9.6%) and Jharkhand (5.6%).Conducted by the International Institute of Migration and Development (IIMAD), the study was supported by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) in collaboration with the International Organization for Migration (IOM).It comes through that over 77% of the surveyed workers were recruited through non-contractor channels, nearly 58% are paid in cash with Rs 17640 the average monthly wage and the average working day being 9.87 hours. The report also brings into focus the gender disparity as it came through that women workers earned about Rs 3,313 less per month than men.The data shows that just a little over 19% of migrant workers can easily use their welfare benefits when they move between states; 35% can do so partly and around 45% can barely do so.It also comes through that over 73% face problems accessing welfare and 69% face problems accessing healthcare.The survey found that while 88.2% of migrant workers are included in formal financial services, exclusion was higher in Karnataka (26.8%) and among scrap collection workers (31.3%).
The study recommends building on One Nation One Ration Card so that welfare benefits follow the worker, multilingual help desks and helplines, stronger labour inspection and closer coordination between states.Andrea M Wojnar, UNFPA India Representative and Country Director Bhutan said, “By highlighting critical gaps in welfare portability, healthcare access, and workplace protections, this study provides a clear roadmap for stakeholders to turn data into targeted action.”

Russia’s mass drone attacks on Ukraine have a goal—likely Ukraine’s capitulation by spring 2027, ISW says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
18:40:00 UTC
03:40:00 KST

Russia is likely attempting to force Ukraine to capitulate by spring 2027 through a large-scale campaign of long-range strikes, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said in its 27 September report. Russian President Vladimir Putin's new theory of victory relies heavily on the mass use of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles against Ukraine, the institute assesses.
Russia keeps shifting to faster jet-powered drones that Ukraine's defenses struggle to stop, forcing it to spend scarce missiles on them. Russia's use of jet-powered drones rose eightfold from June to August, with Moscow launching around 7,700 such drones since their initial deployment, Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on 23 September. But Putin likely does not expect the campaign to last indefinitely, and he may hold off on a new mobilization until he sees whether the strikes work, ISW assesses.
Putin's modified theory of victory
Putin's modified theory of victory largely depends on Russia's ability to mass-launch cheap jet-powered Gerans that get through Ukrainian defenses often enough, the institute notes.
Even a Kremlin-linked Russian milblogger claimed on 27 September that the Russian strategy, which relies heavily on long-range strikes, is costly and cannot continue indefinitely, not least because Ukraine is hitting Russia harder too, according to the analysis.
At the same time, Putin stated on 25 September that Ukraine "must feel" Russia's "retaliatory" strikes. ISW assesses that this suggests he intends to intensify Russia's strike campaign in winter, as he has in previous winters.
If Putin is counting on Ukraine to break and capitulate this winter, he may be ignoring what the campaign will cost Russia over time, the institute notes. This strategy also counts on Ukraine's shortage of Patriot interceptors against ballistic missiles, and on the country's power grid and other vital systems giving way under months of strikes.
Until that approach runs out, Putin is unlikely to back down on his demands or agree to real ceasefire talks, ISW assesses.
Ukrainian interceptors could disrupt Russia's plan
A Kremlin-linked Russian milblogger claimed on 27 September that Russian forces launched predominantly jet-powered Geran-5 drones at Odesa, Mykolaiv, and Kyiv during the night of 26–27 September. According to the blogger, Russia's diverse arsenal of strike weapons and Ukraine's shortage of air defense assets allow Russian forces to maintain the current pace of strikes and expand the range of targets, ISW writes in its analysis.
At the same time, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 26 September that Ukraine's interception rate for jet-powered Shahed drones currently stands at 55%. Of more than 2,730 such drones Russia had launched in September by then, Ukrainian forces had downed or suppressed more than 1,500, he added.
Ukraine is testing interceptor drone prototypes in combat conditions, Ukrainian Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov told Novyny.LIVE on 27 September. The mass deployment of interceptors capable of shooting down jet-powered Gerans could begin within several months, he added. Ukrainian companies have already successfully tested several interceptor drones capable of intercepting Russian jet-powered drones in field conditions, the institute notes.
At the same time, it remains unclear whether Ukraine will be able to scale up its interceptor program quickly enough and achieve sufficient success to disrupt the intensification of Russia's campaign during the winter, ISW notes.
Why Putin may hold off on a new mobilization
Expanding Russia's arsenal of strike weapons is cheaper than carrying out a second mobilization economically, militarily, and socially, a Kremlin-linked Russian milblogger cited by the institute claimed.
Putin may put off large-scale forced mobilization until he sees whether the strikes deliver, ISW assesses, though his officials have been laying the groundwork for it despite Kremlin denials. Still, the need to replace Russia's enormous battlefield losses could push him to order such a mobilization as early as this fall, ISW notes, as Ukrainian and other sources have repeatedly reported he is preparing to do.
