N Ireland march fuels anger, concern
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:48 UTC
01:40:48 KST

UK leaders called for calm as a tense standoff with residents seeking to halt a pro-British Protestant march through a primarily Catholic area stretched into the night on Sunday, in one of the worst crises for Northern Ireland in the past few years.
The tensions were triggered after a Belfast appeal court overturned a High Court injunction in the early hours of Sunday to clear the march by the Orange Order to go ahead for the first time since 1997.
The Parades Commission, Northern Ireland’s independent body regulating contentious processions, had authorized 35 Orangemen to march silently along Garvaghy Road in Portadown, without bands or supporters on Sunday.
Photo: AFP
But as night fell on Sunday, the Orangemen were still trying to carry out their march. About 2,000 protesters including Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O’Neill and Claire Hanna, the leader of Irish nationalist party SDLP, blocked the route on Sunday.
This led to a standoff, with both sides declining to disperse and police between them, with marchers blocked from proceeding.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham appealed for “calm on all sides,” saying that “big gains” had been made in Northern Ireland “and we don’t want to see things go backwards.”
Northern Ireland was blighted for three decades by conflict between largely Catholic, pro-Irish republicans and Protestant, pro-UK unionists.
During the late 1990s, the Garvaghy Road became a major flashpoint.
The Orange Order is a pro-British organization that takes its name from William of Orange, the Protestant Dutchman who seized the English, Scottish and Ireland throne from Catholic King James II in 1689.
The head of the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition told protesters late on Sunday that he would meet Northern Ireland Minister Chris Bryant and the chief of police after receiving commitments that the march would not proceed overnight.
He asked that a small number of volunteers remain on the road through the night to ensure the commitments were not broken, the BBC reported.
“We’ve stopped them once, the process now is to stop them permanently,” Breandan Mac Cionnaith told the protesters.
SECURITY PRESENCE
There was a heavy security presence on Sunday in the Portadown area, 40km southwest of Belfast, with armored police vehicles and a helicopter overhead.
O’Neill, of the Irish republican Sinn Fein party, condemned the late-night court ruling.
She said she supported “the right of the Garvaghy Road residents to protest against this unwanted sectarian march.”
Sinn Fein President Mary Lou McDonald told reporters as she walked with the counterprotesters that the “residents and community have come out to defend their right to live free from sectarian harassment.”
Since the 1998 Good Friday peace accords ending the so-called Troubles in Northern Ireland “there has been lots of progress ... it has been transformational. People’s lives have been changed fundamentally,” McDonald said. “We are not going back.”
LEGAL CHALLENGES
Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson called for “unanimous condemnation” of O’Neill, accusing her of “breaking the law” by ignoring the will of the courts.
“Our party is maintaining the dignity of the Portadown Orangemen — as they have shown determination and patience so will we,” he told reporters.
On Saturday evening, a group of Orangemen left the church and walked down the hill, where they were met by a line of police who refused to let them pass.
Bryant flew in from the Labour Party conference in Liverpool to try to ease the situation through talks.
He said he wanted to meet “face to face” with political leaders and community leaders “to see if we can get to a settled position”.
A Belfast High Court judge had temporarily blocked the parade on Saturday, saying the long-running dispute could escalate across Northern Ireland.
Just before midnight on Saturday, a three-judge Court of Appeal panel overturned the injunction.
Carla Lockhart, a local MP from the pro-British Democratic Unionist Party, called the ruling “seismic.” She said residents had nothing to worry about.
“Thirty-five men walking down a road silently with no bands in an orderly fashion; there is nothing to fear,” she said.
The Parades Commission was established in 1998, the year the Good Friday Agreement largely ended three decades of conflict over British rule known as the Troubles.
It barred the Orange Order from completing the route that year and has consistently rejected subsequent applications.

A ceremony was held yesterday morning for the opening of the Shengji Tunnel, which is expected to ease traffic congestion during peak hours on Zhongxiao E Road Sec 7 and Academia Road, while also cutting travel time between Nangang and New Taipei City’s Sijhih District (汐止), Deputy Minister of the Interior Wu Tang-an (吳堂安) said in the statement.
The research park’s development has led to business and employment growth in Nangang, generating greater demand for transportation infrastructure in the area, including the construction of the central-government funded NT$1.878 billion (US$59.07 million) tunnel, Wu said.
Photo: Taipei Times
The new route removes a traffic bottleneck between Zhongxiao E Road Sec 7 and Lane 130, Academia Road Sec 1, and connects the biotechnology park with Taiwan Railway’s and Taipei Metro’s Nangang stations and surrounding residential areas, he said.
Aside from reducing travel time for local residents and commuters, the tunnel provides an alternative route if Academia Road is closed due to flooding or other emergencies, he said, adding that it includes a separate pedestrian and bicycle path.
The research park covers 14.19 hectares and houses several institutions, including Academia Sinica’s Biomedical Translation Research Center and the Food and Drug Administration.
Academia Sinica said in a statement that the new route is about 824m long, including a tunnel section of about 716m.
Academia Sinica President Chen Chien-jen (陳建仁), who attended the opening ceremony, said that the tunnel would not only ease traffic around the park, but further support the development of a biomedical research and biotechnology corridor in Nangang.
More than 2,600 researchers and other professionals are based at the park, which opened in October 2018, Academia Sinica said.
The new tunnel provides a more convenient route between the research park and the area around Nangang Station, reducing travel time from about 15 to 20 minutes during peak hours to less than 10 minutes, it said.

The baby bust could dent Australia’s lucky streak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:42 UTC
01:40:42 KST

The past four decades have been good for Australia. It rode a resources boom, enjoyed the glory days of China’s expansion and benefitted from the dismantling of trade barriers.
Yet population growth, a vital contributor, has been downplayed, despite its crucial role in the record 29-year stretch without a recession until the COVID-19 pandemic. Now, the government is flagging a change in the demographic picture that could help Canberra get ahead of a shift that is buffeting every major economy. Low fertility — and restrained immigration — would be a big feature over the next 40 years, the government said in an intergenerational report that attempts to sketch the world of 2060. The studies, published every few years, act as a kind of road map for where the country is going.
The latest edition, released last week, touched on some familiar themes: greater competition among the world powers and the perils and promise of artificial intelligence. However, more importantly, it also paid heed to falling birthrates and the expanding ranks of elderly people.
To its credit, Canberra is trying to get ahead of this really big shift. The hope is that by highlighting the changes early, businesses, consumers and officials across a range of institutions can make adjustments before drastic measures have to be implemented. There is already much anxiety around the world about the transition to much smaller families or households with no children. The baby bust that is already challenging growth models in China, South Korea and Western Europe is coming for Australia.
If anything, the changes would be more pronounced than leaders are prepared to countenance. That has been the experience of countries that thought the real impact of the baby bust was still a way off — and are now scrambling to steady the slide in fertility. Behind the sober analysis in the Australian report lurks a confronting question: Does a world where deaths outnumber births and a tight rein on new arrivals mean the best of times would be left behind?
The economy would grow more slowly, as would the labor force. The drivers of expansion would evolve. The healthcare industry would continue its ascent and services would become more dominant.
Whatever the nation looks like mid-century, there would be fewer Australians than previously forecast to experience it — and those who are there would be more elderly. Caps on immigration would play a role, but lower fertility is the main feature of the demographic transition. The fertility rate would probably drop to 1.34 by 2065, less than the 1.62 that the prior paper in 2023 anticipated. (A reading of 2.1 in the total fertility rate, a measure of the average number of children a woman has during childbearing years, is widely regarded as the level at which society can replenish itself.)
Could these predictions be off? If so, they are likely to lowball the outlook. The UN caused waves a few years ago when it projected that the number of Earth’s inhabitants would peak in the 2080s and then retreat. A recent paper put it in the mid-2050s.
Australia is still a long way from panicking. Officials rightly point out that even at that diminished level, fertility is still comfortably above the levels of South Korea, Singapore, China and Taiwan. There is also no effort to curry support for steps such as creating a ministry for low birthrates, as Seoul proposed a few years ago. The report puts Australia’s population at about 39 million by the mid-2060s. It is about 28 million now.
The assessment chimes with the center-left Labor government’s political priorities. Canberra wants to reduce the number of new arrivals, which surged in the aftermath of the pandemic, without indulging in the anti-foreigner rhetoric that has propelled the far-right One Nation party in opinion polls. Earlier this month, the government announced it would clamp down on people who have overstayed visas, as well restrict most student-visa holders from bringing family members.
The passing of high rates of fertility is not to be mourned. Women are more educated and seek fulfilling careers — often without males stepping up at home. Children risk becoming prohibitively expensive. Research from the US National Bureau of Economic Research attributed at least part of the accelerated birth decline to the iPhone. Banning smartphones is not a practical approach. Nor can any single policy lever alter the course we are on.
Australia has managed wrenching transitions before. Paul Keating, Australia’s treasurer and prime minister in the 1980s and 1990s, embarked on a modernization that earlier leaders had thought out of reach. Current Treasurer Jim Chalmers, who was in charge of the report, wrote his doctoral thesis on Keating. Now that he has put the issue on the agenda, Chalmers should show conviction in tackling the challenges to an economy long considered the envy of the world.
Daniel Moss is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asian economies. Previously, he was executive editor for economics at Bloomberg News. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Lin Chung-wei’s finish gave Taiwan a track and field medal for the second straight day, following Fu Chao-hsuan’s gold in the men’s high jump on Sunday.
Lin Chung-wei entered the final with a time of 49.10 seconds, the second-fastest time in the heats. He stayed among the leaders and was level for second after clearing the last hurdle, before finishing third in a personal-best 48.74 seconds.
Photo: Reuters
Qatar’s Bassem Hemeida won in 47.82 seconds, and Japan’s Taiju Goto took silver with a personal-best 47.93. Taiwan’s Chen Jian-rong placed fourth, also setting a personal best of 49.25 seconds.
Lin Chung-wei’s previous best was 48.77 seconds, set at a meet in Japan in May.
Taiwan’s other bronzes came in badminton mixed doubles, table tennis men’s singles and the women’s 25m pistol team event.
Photo courtesy of the Taiwanese delegation

Shooters Cheng Yen-ching, Tien Chia-chen and Chen Yu-ju combined for 1,734 points to place third in the women’s 25m pistol team event, behind China and South Korea.

Man City’s rise clouded by dark shadows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:40 UTC
01:40:40 KST

Manchester City’s fate is yet to be sealed, but reports they have been found guilty of widespread financial impropriety cast a new light on a meteoric rise from mid-table mediocrity to English Premier League domination since a transformative Abu Dhabi takeover in 2008.
In the 18 years since United Arab Emirates Vice President and Deputy Prime Minister Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan took charge, City have become the Premier League’s dominant force and also won a UEFA Champions League crown.
Their success has been even sweeter for generations of City fans who saw the club live in the shadow of local rivals Manchester United and even sink into the third tier of English soccer in the late 1990s.
Photo: Action Images via Reuters
In their 128-year history, prior to a takeover by the Abu Dhabi United Group, City had won just nine major trophies, including only two top-flight league titles.
However, the billions of pounds invested into east Manchester from the Middle East have yielded eight Premier League crowns, four FA Cups, seven League Cups and the club’s first Champions League title.
However, in November 2018, German news magazine Der Spiegel published a series of bombshell articles accusing City of flouting financial fair play rules.
City were found guilty by UEFA in February 2020 of breaking financial fair play (FFP) rules and given a two-year European ban and a fine. The ban was later overturned by the Court of Arbitration for Sport.
In February 2023, the Premier League charged City with 115 breaches of FFP play rules from 2009 to 2018. On Friday, reports said the club had been found guilty on all but one of the counts.
The Premier League charges included artificially inflating the value of sponsorship deals from companies in Abu Dhabi linked to City’s ownership, and disguising the true salaries of some players and managers with off-the-books payments.
City were also charged with failing to cooperate with the Premier League in its investigations.
All the while, money was pouring in to make the club a global superpower.
In 2022, City topped the Deloitte Money League for the first time as the world’s highest revenue-generating club, and they have just splashed out a record ￡460 million (US$523 million) on new players in one transfer window.
Manchester United’s former manager Alex Ferguson once dismissed his new challengers as “noisy neighbours.”
However, City did not waste time in making waves with their newfound wealth following the takeover, even if it took some time for the on-pitch success to follow.
Robinho’s arrival from Real Madrid in the final hours of the 2008 summer transfer window was the first of a flurry of superstar signings, and City enjoyed some local bragging rights by snatching Carlos Tevez from United the following year.
It was the arrivals of Yaya Toure, David Silva and Sergio Aguero that built the bedrock of City’s first title-winning side for 44 years.
In the most dramatic finale to a season the Premier League has ever seen, Aguero scored a 94th-minute goal to beat Queens Park Rangers on the final day of the 2011-2012 campaign, snatching the title from United’s grasp.
That sparked a run of eight Premier League titles in 13 seasons.
Roberto Mancini and Manuel Pellegrini were title winners in Manchester, but the arrival of Pep Guardiola in 2016 took City to a different level.
Guardiola had spent just four years in charge of his beloved Barcelona, before leaving citing exhaustion after winning three Spanish La Liga titles and two Champions Leagues, and three seasons at German giants Bayern Munich.
City managed to persuade Guardiola to extend his stay for a decade.
He rewarded them by overseeing arguably the most dominant period of sustained success in English soccer history, with six English top-flight titles in seven seasons between 2017-2018 and 2023-2024, including an unprecedented four in a row.
Europe was finally conquered in 2023 as City matched United’s previously unique achievement as the only side to win the Champions League, Premier League and FA Cup in the same season.
In the past few years, the financial charges have cast a shadow over the Etihad, even while trophies continued to be won.
In May, Guardiola was given a glorious send off, with a stand named in his honor.
The club’s detractors, who have long argued the whole era should be qualified by an asterisk, might yet be proved right should City be found guilty.

Trump ‘jokes’ aside, US stance unchanged: Perdue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:39 UTC
01:40:39 KST

US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) discuss arms sales to Taiwan every time they get together but the US stance on Taiwan remains unchanged following the Chinese leader’s state visit to Washington last week, the US president’s top envoy to Beijing said.
“We don’t support independence, and we don’t support coercion,” US Ambassador to China David Perdue said during an interview on Sunday in response to a question about Taiwan.
Xi pressured Trump to limit support for Taiwan during his trip. The Chinese leader pressed the US to outright “oppose” Taiwanese independence, his first public call for the US to change its decades-old position on the nation.
Photo: REUTERS
Asked whether the US is denying what Taiwan needs to defend itself to appease Xi, Perdue said that was “absolutely not the case.”
The Trump administration has already approved US$11 billion in sales of US arms to Taiwan and there are continuing conversations about other sales, he said.
“He actually asked President Xi would he like to buy some at one point,” Perdue said.
With Xi heading toward an expected fourth term in office, Beijing has renewed diplomatic pressure to isolate Taiwan. China has vowed to bring Taiwan under its control by force if necessary.
On Saturday, Trump said he did not spend a lot of time talking about Taiwan with Xi, and that the Chinese leader “understands very much” how he feels about the issue.
The US’ official position is that it does not support Taiwanese independence and opposes any unilateral changes to the “status quo” by Beijing or Taipei.
Trump delayed a planned US$14 billion arms package for Taiwan for months. After his last meeting with Xi in Beijing, Trump described that deal as “a very good negotiating chip.”
Taiwan’s role as a key chip supplier to meet artificial intelligence demands means the nation has a “symbiotic relationship” with the US, which is “why it should be protected,” Representative to the US Alexander Yui (俞大?) said on Sunday in a television interview.

Taiwanese developers are delaying new housing projects as tight credit, high prices and weak demand weigh on the market, with the transaction value of new-home and presale launches in northern Taiwan falling 17.6 percent in the first nine months of the year, the Chinese-language My Housing Monthly (住展雜誌) reported.
The value of residential projects launched in the region totaled about NT$766.7 billion (US$24.13 billion) through this month, down NT$163.4 billion from a year earlier, the magazine said.
The decline marks a further pullback from the market. Projects launched in the first three quarters of the year topped NT$1 trillion in the past few years, and it exceeded NT$900 billion last year.
Photo: CNA
“Developers are reluctant to add to the supply pressure and are choosing to delay new projects where possible,” magazine spokesman Chen Ping-cheng (陳炳辰) said.
Developers are also facing competition for investment funds from Taiwan’s stock market, which attracted substantial capital in the first half, Chen said.
Tighter mortgage conditions have further constrained buyers’ ability to finance home purchases, he said.
The central bank’s decision to raise the loan-to-value cap for second-home buyers to 70 percent, along with signals that it would not further tighten property curbs, has yet to generate a meaningful pickup in demand, Chen said.
A stock market pullback in July also failed to send significant funds into the property sector, as some investors remained stuck in losing equity positions, while others held back in expectation of a recovery in stocks, he said.
The slowdown was broad across northern Taiwan, the magazine said. Project launches in Taoyuan fell 32.2 percent to NT$195.1 billion, while in Taipei they dropped 30.7 percent to NT$143.1 billion, it said.
New Taipei City declined 19.8 percent to NT$280.2 billion, as developers become increasingly selective, the magazine said.
Hsinchu County was an exception, with the value of new projects more than doubling to NT$118.5 billion. Several large developments in the county’s Jhubei City (竹北) and Jhudong Township (竹東) helped drive the increase, as developers brought forward projects delayed during an earlier period of consolidation, it said.
Northern Taiwan would need about NT$233.3 billion of new launches in the fourth quarter to push the full-year total above NT$1 trillion, Chen said.
However, that target could be difficult to reach, as the central bank’s latest easing of property restrictions has yet to materially improve market sentiment, with some buyers likely to defer purchases toward the end of this year, while some large projects could be pushed into next year, he added.

Nvidia debuts system designed to control AI agents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:35 UTC
01:40:35 KST

Nvidia Corp introduced a new double-layered artificial intelligence (AI) security system that it says would have prevented the recent high-profile breach of Hugging Face by OpenAI’s AI models.
The semiconductor giant, which has been rapidly expanding its product lineup beyond chips, is rolling out two open-source software security tools that can be run on its hardware. They are designed to control what AI agents can access in real time and shut them down when they break the rules.
If cutting-edge labs had been using this technology to evaluate their AI models early on, it the Hugging Face attack could have been averted, Nvidia vice president of enterprise AI Justin Boitano said during a briefing with reporters ahead of yesterday’s announcement.
Photo: AFP
“From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach,” he said.
Misconduct by autonomous agents, including the Hugging Face incident in July, has roiled the AI industry and led to calls to slow down work on the technology. With the new product — dubbed the Open Agent Safety Platform — Nvidia is offering a way to prevent breaches without curbing AI development.
Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) has repeatedly downplayed the risk of AI slipping out of human control.
In the past few days, Huang has cast safety concerns as an engineering challenge, rather than something that requires more regulation or global coordination. His engineering solution to the AI safety problem has two parts. OpenShell, a software product that Nvidia already previewed at its hallmark technology-focused conference in March, can run on Nvidia’s Vera central processing units. It enables users to set rules for what AI agents can access and enforce them in real time. The software is open source, meaning it can be used and adapted freely.
Meanwhile, Nvidia Sentry is a new product that can run on the chipmaker’s BlueField data processing units. It is designed to provide an extra layer of AI monitoring that polices agents and intervenes to isolate any that act suspiciously, the company said.
“We believe this added security layer will allow the industry to test even the most advanced AI systems safely,” Boitano said of the Sentry product. “It can quarantine a suspicious agent in milliseconds.”
OpenAI’s recent incidents — including a breach of an Australian government system, as well as attempts to access dozens of US government and university Web sites — happened when its models escaped testing environments that were supposed to be secure.
As the problems proliferated, OpenAI on Friday said that it would pause training of its most capable AI models. In July, Anthropic PBC also disclosed that its agents broke out of what was supposed to be an isolated testing space.

EDITORIAL: Central bank walking tightrope
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:32 UTC
01:40:32 KST

Taiwan’s financial market has undergone a significant liquidity squeeze, with many banks raising loan rates to new highs, and local media reporting that several banks were extending approval periods, reducing loan amounts or rejecting loan applications. Where did the money go? Are monetary authorities ensuring that banks maintain adequate liquidity? Some experts attributed the changes to large-scale foreign fund outflows as overseas investors repatriated stock gains and dividends, while others cited the widening interest rate differential between the US and Taiwan, making some exporters more willing to hold US dollars than convert to New Taiwan dollars.
However, some analysts pointed to the artificial intelligence (AI)-driven economic boom as the reason it has become more difficult for individuals and businesses to apply for mortgages, loans and corporate financing. As large technology companies have an urgent need for capital expenditures and financing for AI projects, they are borrowing from banks or raising funds in the open market, leading to tighter liquidity and higher funding costs in the financial system, which has in turn caused banks to prioritize funding for tech firms over traditional industries and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).
Of course, booming stock market investment also absorbed market liquidity to a certain degree, as official data showed margin financing and securities account balances continued to hit new highs in the past few months. That explained why a key consideration in the central bank’s decision to keep policy interest rates unchanged at its quarterly board meeting on Sept. 17 was signs of tighter liquidity in the financial system; it would not want to make the situation worse by raising rates. While policymakers say market liquidity remains sufficient, analysts see the liquidity issue as an ongoing trend following a “death cross” between two major money supply gauges for two consecutive months.
In July, the M1B, a narrow measure of money in circulation, including cash and savings deposits, rose 7.34 percent from the previous year, while the broader M2 measure, which includes M1B, time deposits, foreign currency deposits and mutual funds, increased 7.42 percent year-on-year, resulting in the first “death cross” in four years, central bank data showed. M1B last month rose 6.65 percent from a year earlier, which was again smaller than M2’s 6.79 percent annual increase, the central bank reported on Wednesday last week. The death cross between the two money supply gauges occurs when people put cash away and choose the safety of time deposits, which signaled tighter liquidity in the market, experts said.
Loan rates have climbed steadily as deposit growth at banks fails to keep up with the pace of lending demand, and banks have become more stringent in extending credit as they prioritize larger or high-asset clients. For businesses, cash flow is key to building factories, purchasing equipment and raw materials, and paying their employees. Once banks raise rates and reduce credit lines amid a shrinking liquidity pool, it would affect firms’ product prices and profits. If businesses postpone factory expansion, reduce investment, slow recruitment or even re-evaluate bonuses and workforce allocation, what initially appears to be a funding issue between banks and businesses would trickle down to employees and customers.
Given uneven economic development and uneven capital allocation among local industries, the central bank has continued to use quantitative tools and monetary operations rather than interest rates to manage money supply conditions and contain liquidity expansion, while avoiding greater harm to interest-sensitive industries and vulnerable mortgage borrowers. If the central bank keeps rates unchanged longer than expected, it could create market expectations that it is in no hurry to raise rates.
However, if such expectations take hold and inflation rises again, the cost for the central bank to unwind the situation could be much greater. That puts the central bank in an awkward position.
As businesses and individuals face higher funding costs and tighter credit standards, the central bank must exercise monetary policy to control inflation while addressing the liquidity issue.
In the short term, foreign fund flows and local exporters’ US dollar holdings are the two main factors in determining whether market liquidity would become more ample. In the long term, it requires interagency coordination within the government to facilitate funding access for companies in need, especially traditional industries and SMEs.
When Panama severed diplomatic relations with Taiwan and recognized China in 2017, Beijing achieved one of its most important diplomatic victories in Central America. However, nearly a decade later, Panama is demonstrating that diplomatic recognition does not necessarily eliminate Taiwan from a country’s political system. Panama and Taiwan had diplomatic relations for more than 100 years and the goodwill between the countries was displayed last week when Panama’s National Assembly established an interparliamentary exchange group with the Legislative Yuan. Forty-five of the assembly’s 71 lawmakers joined the group, representing more than 60 percent of the legislature. Its members include National Assembly President Shirley
If Taiwan falls, the true battle moves from the beaches into the concrete streets. Western analysts fixate on the invasion phase. They end wargames when missiles stop flying and submit policy papers after the fate of a beachhead is decided. This narrow focus ignores the grim reality of “the day after.” To address this blind spot, the Irregular Warfare Center (IWC) published a seminal study on March 5, 2026, titled China’s Way of Occupation: Implications for Taiwan. Authored by Jan K. Gleiman and others, the report analyzes Beijing’s actions in Tibet, Xinjiang (East Turkestan), and Hong Kong to expose a chilling playbook

Today, I am filled with emotion at seeing students at Soochow University democratically remove their own statue of Chiang, a figure of authoritarian rule, after it was on display for 48 years The timing is noteworthy, with the nine-in-one local elections approaching.

‘Taiwan Review’ closes after 75 years. What happens to its archives?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:31 UTC
01:40:31 KST

In 1951, the Central Propaganda Department of the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) Central Reform Committee launched an English-language magazine, which, for the next 75 years, would serve as a mouthpiece for Taiwan’s government.
Initially titled the Free China Review, and later rechristened as the Taiwan Review, the magazine published its final issue in March.
Former editor Richard Vuylsteke has described the magazine as Taiwan’s “landmark foreign language publication going abroad.”
Photo: David Frazier
The magazine was not universally respected. Some international scholars, including a few contacted for this article, dismissed it as a “propaganda rag.” But others, including Shelley Rigger, a top US researcher at Davidson College, told the Taipei Times that the magazine “gave voice to Taiwan through an era of extraordinary change,” especially in the 1980s and 1990s, when “sources on Taiwan were rare.”
Though the Review’s termination is generally accepted as part of a general decline of print media, the disappearance of various digital archives, which began going offline in July, have distressed current and former staffers.
The Web site removals have come as a result of budget cuts by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), which manages the Review along with a range of other publications. The cuts extend to Taiwan Today, a daily news platform in nine languages — English, French, Spanish, German, Russian, Japanese, Vietnamese, Indonesian and Thai. Some of these language sections date back to the early 1970s.
MOFA has also discontinued the print edition of Taiwan Panorama, a bilingual English-and-Chinese cultural magazine launched in 1976 as Sinorama, which since July has continued only as an online version.
In all, the ministry has cut a total of NT$57 million in annual publication budgets and laid off at least 25 full-time workers.
MOFA has attributed the downsizing to declining readership and a changing media environment — print media has been declining since the 2010s. Ministry staffers have further said that the multiple language portals are no longer necessary given the prevalence of AI translation.
Ministry personnel have also spoken of redundancy with other government-supported news platforms. A separate ministry — the Ministry of Culture — currently funds the Central News Agency for print media, Radio Taiwan International for radio and TaiwanPlus for streaming video and TV, creating significant overlap.
While critics recognize these as good reasons, it has not mitigated their distress over the disappearance of a digital archive holding decades of content in multiple languages.
“We all have a terrible sense of waste and, in my case at least, anger for seeing 20 years of work being erased,” said Laurence Marcout, an editor and translator who worked in the government’s French language information department from 1992 to 2016.
When asked about the fate of these digital archives, MOFA told the Taipei Times it has no specific plans, saying that they “have been fully backed up and preserved and have not been deleted.” Physical archives exist in at least one national library, and any future actions will depend on budgets, needs and priorities, a ministry statement said.
For Marcout, this still does not address years of online-only content, which she says is falling into a “black hole.”
“The whole story says something about the lack of interest of the government for archives,” she said. “For me, it’s like when people here leave their old furniture by the side of the road.”
THE FREE CHINA REVIEW
The cover of the Free China Review’s first issue, dated April 1, 1951, featured a publicity photo of Chiang Kai-shek (蔣介石) with his wife Song Mei-ling (宋美齡).
Chiang’s KMT had only two years previously arrived in Taiwan to reestablish their government, and they urgently needed a channel to broadcast their views to the West.
In that inaugural issue, founding publisher and editor WY Tsao (曹文彥), a Zhejiang native with a Doctor of Laws from the University of California, boldly set forth a statement of purpose, declaring, “we, a group of intellectuals of Free China…shall endeavor to bring home to the world a true picture of Free China.”
The magazine’s mission, Tsao continued, would be to document the nation’s development “socially, economically, militarily and politically.”
Almost half a century later, that same mission still rang true to the Review’s staff, who, in a February 2000 editorial, affirmed, “That has been the policy of ‘the FCR’ ever since.”
Early articles were stridently hawkish. One from the first issue was titled, “Why Not Bomb Manchuria?” It argued that in the then ongoing Korean War, the US should attack military staging grounds inside China. (Washington would have considered such a move disastrous, as it would have brought the superpowers into direct and open conflict.)
Another welcomed the arrival of US Major-General William Chase to Taiwan, who had just arrived to set up American military bases that would remain until 1979.
FOREIGN EDITORS
In its first decades, the Free China Review was written and edited exclusively by Republic of China nationals, many of whom had studied in the West. The first foreign editor to appear on the masthead was an American, Richard Vuylsteke, who served as senior editor from 1986 to 1998.
Holding a PhD in political philosophy and Chinese history from the University of Hawaii, Vuylsteke was a transformative figure at the Review and would later go on to top positions at AmCham Taipei and Hawaii’s East-West Center.
But when he first stepped into the magazine’s offices in the mid-1980s, he described the situation as “pretty grim.”
Though the Review was then running on state-of-the-art, green-screen Wang computers, “it was a propaganda rag,” said Vuylsteke, now 81, via a call from his home in Hawaii.
“One of the first things I had to edit was on Chiang Kai-shek’s international medals and honors.”
“And the captions were just terrible,” he said. One of them simply read: “See the pretty bird.”
In his second year, 1987, Vuylsteke got a new boss in Shaw Yu-ming (邵玉銘), who’d just been named director-general of the Government Information Office (GIO), the agency that had published the Review since 1954.
Shaw called Vuylsteke into his office, saying he’d been scolded by a former professor at Columbia University, who told him, “I received this thing [Free China Review] free in the mail every month. Either turn it into a magazine, or stop publishing! It’s an embarrassment!” Vuylsteke said.
Shaw then asked his American editor, “Can you make this a magazine? All I want you to do is, don’t get me in trouble with the secret police or the military,” Vuylsteke recalled.
Vuylsteke told Shaw he’d try. Then under Shaw’s protection, he attracted respected contributors, including Far Eastern Review editor Philip Bowring and American diplomat Richard Bush. His office produced a beautifully designed, glossy magazine with features on everything from Beijing’s 1989 Tiananmen Square protests to the emergence of Taipei’s discotheque culture.
Another in-house editor during Vuylsteke’s tenure was Briton John Trenhaile, who also wrote popular spy novels set in Russia and China.
“I think it is probably one of the most satisfying jobs I’ve ever had,” Vuylsteke said.
THE ‘TAIWAN REVIEW’
The Review’s final 25 years were beset by instability, including two name changes, seesawing between ruling parties, the reorganization of the national bureaucracy and the rise of the Internet.
Former editor Lloyd Roberts recalled that the Monday following the 2000 election of Taiwan’s first president from the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), Chen Shui-bian (陳水扁), Trenhaile, who had by then become senior editor, “took a green marker and drew a gigantic smiley face in green on the whiteboard.”
Green is the color of the DPP.
“I think some of my colleagues weren’t happy with that,” Roberts recalled.
Earlier that month, the magazine had just changed its name from Free China Review — by then long considered an anachronism — to Taipei Review. Then three years later, it became the Taiwan Review.
According to Roberts, the changes “just made sense at the time, because Taiwan was changing so much.”
A 2003 editorial explained: “The name Taiwan unambiguously refers to the democratic, self-governing country that has become a model for political and economic progress in Asia.”
Marcout, the French editor, had also joined the GIO by this time and similarly experienced Taiwan’s democratization “from within.”
“When I started at the GIO in 1992, the propaganda element was still strong, but we tried our best to keep it at minimum,” she said.
Producing French versions of magazines, booklets, leaflets, adverts and documentaries, she said, “In the French department we were really trying to make French people understand the real Taiwan.”
END OF THE GIO
Looking back on the Taiwan Review’s final decades, multiple former staff identify 2012 as the beginning of the end. That was the year the government dissolved the GIO and reassigned several of its publishing departments to MOFA.
“MOFA didn’t know what to do with us!” said Marcout, describing the immediate aftermath of the move.
But as the new ministry firmed its grip, Marcout saw publications bending “more and more to the government’s priorities.” Though “the original aim was to show Taiwan,” the focus slowly drifted “back to propaganda,” she said. Under MOFA, the publications just “got worse and worse.”
One current staffer, who requested anonymity, pointed to a further disconnect in MOFA’s understanding of its non-English foreign language publications.
“These language editions all have developed their own unique communities of readers, and now there is nothing to replace them. It was actually the English version that was the most redundant,” the staffer said.
As for the fate of the digital archive, the editors and scholars interviewed for this article have various ideas. They range from an offline digital archive as part of Taiwan’s National Archives to a full restoration of the contents to the Internet. One thing they all hope to avoid is that the journals survive only in a handful of Taiwanese libraries.
“I do realize how futile it sounds today to hang on to the memory of these rags, but it seems to me that they are a testimony to Taiwan’s political evolution, and, if only for this reason, should be archived properly,” Marcout said.

Chi wasn’t even supposed to be there. He had accompanied his girlfriend, pop singer Shang Kuan Ping (上官萍), to negotiations with Wisma’s agent.

Thailand, Myanmar flood deaths increasing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:30 UTC
01:40:30 KST

AFP
At least eight people have died in flooding in Thailand since Sept. 16, although none in the capital, Bangkok, which declared a disaster this weekend following heavy rains, the Thai government said yesterday.
The eight died in eastern provinces — five in Sa Kaeo, two in Chanthaburi and one in Saraburi — according to the Thai Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation (DDPM), which did not give further details.
Photo: Bloomberg
Excluding Bangkok, more than 500,000 households and 1.7 million people across 27 provinces in Thailand have been affected by flooding, the DDPM said.
About 52,000 households were impacted in the capital, which on Saturday declared a city-wide disaster after almost 48 hours of heavy rain swelled canals and flooded roads.
No deaths have been reported in Bangkok, and the DDPM said water levels had stabilized.
However, heavy rain and flooding were visible in at least one eastern neighborhood, with residents wading through thigh-high waters.
Schools have been closed, and people urged to work from home –- a call that many heeded, with streets and public transport networks noticeably quieter yesterday morning.
“Some areas in Bangkok are still facing high water levels,” government spokesman Ekkapob Pianpises told a news briefing.
Drainage systems had reduced water levels to the point that more people could travel, he added.
Thailand is used to wet weather and September is the peak of the rainy season, but many residents said this year seemed worse than past ones.
Heavy floods and landslides in southern Myanmar have also killed at least 10 people, with up to 30 still missing, a local rescue worker said yesterday.
Myanmar’s southernmost Tanintharyi region has been hit by heavy rains since Friday night, part of an intense weather system hammering the region.
“We have recovered eight bodies, while between 20 to 30 people are missing” in Tanintharyi’s Launglon township, said Hein Htet of volunteer group People’s Administration Team.
He said three of the recovered bodies were teenagers who had gathered at a local monastery on Sunday but were swept away by a landslide that hit their village, burying 18 buildings.
“There are still people and villages in the danger zone with continued rainfall,” he said.
Authorities have not yet released any official toll in a country where a civil war complicates aid efforts.
The conflict often makes even the scale of natural disasters hard for humanitarian organizations to judge.
“We are inundated not only with the scale of the flood but also with the lack of resources,” Hein Htet said. “This is a natural disaster in the conflict area.”
Myo Min, chair of the volunteer Dawei Zabuthiri Emergency Medical Service, said some villages were rendered accessible only by foot, and aid teams had found hundreds of residents displaced from homes to monastery shelters.
“Rescue workers have not yet been able to fully manage the entire disaster area,” he said in a phone interview.
He said he expected a death toll between seven and 10 people, with 20 to 30 missing.
Myanmar, a country of 51 million people, ranks among the 10 nations most vulnerable to climate change, according to non-profit Germanwatch.
It has suffered from severe aid cutbacks following US President Donald Trump’s decision to slash Washington’s humanitarian assistance budget.

More than 70,000 fake Beyblades seized: police

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:29 UTC

The National Police Agency’s Third Special Police Corps yesterday said that from May to July, it intercepted five smuggling operations from China, seizing more than 70,000 counterfeit Beyblades with an estimated infringement value of NT$34.45 million (US$1.08 million).
It added that any bootleg unit that reached the local market could present hidden health hazards to players.
Beyblades, a line of spinning toy tops used in competitive gaming and developed in Japan by toy company Takara Tomy, have become popular in Taiwan, making them a target for fraudsters.
Photo copied by Lu Yun-feng, Taipei Times
The Third Special Police Corps, dedicated to safeguarding maritime borders and trade lines, said it seized 720 counterfeit Beyblades in New Taipei City, followed by 64,000 in New Taipei City and Taoyuan in June, and 4,176 in Tainan and Keelung in July.
The police corps said that its frontline officers are professional experts who are well versed in distinguishing between authentic and counterfeit Beyblades.
Upon opening the shipment boxes at the scene, the inspectors checked if the top-right corner of the outer packaging carried the blue “Takara Tomy” logo and the Beyblade mark in Japanese, it said.
Although the product design and overall look of the counterfeit goods resembled the genuine product, the poor print quality, color and lack of fine details were dead giveaways, it said.
The officers used reverse image searches to cross-reference product model numbers and determine whether they are authentic, it said, adding that importers of suspect products are asked to produce authorization documents.
The officers then contacted the authorized distributor in Taiwan, Lih Yen Co, to examine photographs and videos of the seized items, while they carried out sampling procedures and completed on-site identification, it said.
The Third Special Police Corps advised parents to accompany their children when purchasing Beyblades and make sure to look for the official certification mark and avoid buying from unverified retailers.
Counterfeit Beyblades have poor workmanship, are made of brittle plastic and are structurally unsound, it said.
During high-speed spinning and intense collisions, they are prone to shatter and send sharp debris flying, which could cause eye or facial injuries, it said.
The paint on counterfeit Beyblades might also contain toxic heavy metals and plasticizers, it said.
The police corps also cautioned consumers to be vigilant to avoid falling for online shopping scams.
Data from the New Taipei City Police Department listed 122 cases of Beyblade-related online shopping scams in the past seven months: one in March, 17 in April, 29 in May, 25 each in June and July, 19 in August and six so far this month.
The common methods used by scammers include requests for ATM cash transfers, payment app deductions, physical game point cards or even asking victims to mail their bank cards, the data showed.
The department warned that fraudsters usually draw in buyers by offering “ultra-low prices” or impersonate popular shopping Web sites to trick users into believing they are legitimate platforms, but victims never receive the goods after transferring money.
It reminded people that if they receive any messages requesting private transactions, off-platform payments, personal information, verification codes or ATM transactions, they should immediately stop following the instructions and verify with the platform’s official customer service.
The Third Special Police Corps said it would continue to closely monitor maritime borders and would not tolerate any products that compromise the health and safety of young Taiwanese.

Drone strategy beyond production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:26 UTC
01:40:26 KST

Over the past two weeks, the Taipei Security Dialogue and the Whole-of-Society Defense Resilience International Forum brought together leading figures working on Taiwan’s defense and resilience, with discussions ranging from higher defense spending and asymmetric capabilities to societal preparedness.
At the Taipei Security Dialogue, Stanford University Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies fellow Oriana Skylar Mastro made an interesting observation that many of Taiwan’s defense initiatives are intended to influence the audience in Washington. Taiwan faces an adversary considerably larger in military and economic terms, hence continued US support is an important element of deterrence.
Former chief of the general staff admiral Lee Hsi-min (李喜明) has in the past made a related point in discussing Taiwan’s ability to show it can resist aggression. Signaling commitment to partners is understandable, but it is most convincing when accompanied by credible capabilities at home.
At the resilience forum, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey praised Taiwan’s pace in developing asymmetric capabilities, particularly autonomous systems. Taiwan has indeed made considerable progress over the past few years. Yet the discussion raises a more difficult question: What exactly does Taiwan mean by asymmetric capability?
The term appears often in conferences, policy papers and public statements, but the definition is often less clear. Ukraine, Iran and other countries have all employed forms of asymmetric warfare, but under different circumstances, force structures and strategic objectives. Taiwan cannot simply acquire large numbers of relatively inexpensive systems and assume that asymmetry would follow.
This is particularly relevant to drones. The appearance of Chinese civilian drones over military positions in Kinmen County in 2022 provided an early indication of how inexpensive drones could create disproportionate operational problems. Taiwan subsequently accelerated drone and counterdrone development, while the “Drone National Team” and strong government support helped bring together manufacturers and technology companies.
At the same time, concepts that had long existed on the margins of Taiwan’s defense debate received attention. US Naval War College professor William Murray’s “porcupine strategy” and Lee’s “overall defense concept” became increasingly relevant to discussions about how Taiwan could use smaller, mobile and survivable systems against a much larger adversary. For a period, industrial development and strategic discussions about integrating uncrewed systems appeared to advance together.
However, the balance seems to have shifted. Much of the attention surrounding Taiwan’s drones now concerns manufacturing capacity, export growth, international partnerships and procurement targets. These are genuine achievements. Taiwanese manufacturers have expanded overseas relationships, while efforts to establish trusted, China-free supply chains have given the industry a potentially valuable position in international markets.
However, Taiwan’s original interest in drones was not primarily about exports. It emerged from a defense problem. A successful drone industry does not automatically produce an effective asymmetric military capability. Thousands of drones contribute little if the armed forces lack the command-and-control architecture, training, maintenance capacity, communications networks, force structure and operational concepts required to employ them effectively. Procurement increases inventory quickly, but institutional adaptation is considerably harder.
That point has repeatedly emerged in interviews with defense practitioners, strategists and policymakers. They disagree on many issues, but there is notable concern about the need for doctrine and organizational structures that integrate new technologies into Taiwan’s particular geography and defense requirements. Their perspective is often more cautious than the enthusiasm surrounding export figures and procurement announcements.
Other major drone users offer useful context. Ukraine and Russia have reorganized units, training and operational concepts during the war. Iran has spent years adapting uncrewed systems into a broader doctrine designed around its military limitations and regional objectives. Their models cannot simply be transferred to Taiwan, but they demonstrate a common principle: Hardware becomes strategically meaningful only when institutions adapt around it.
That does not mean Taiwan should slow its industrial ambitions. A self-sustaining drone industry, secure supply chains and access to international markets can bolster economic and national security. Export success can also support production capacity that Taiwan might need during a crisis.
The concern is the balance. If Taiwan’s objective is primarily to become a globally competitive drone manufacturing hub, current industrial progress is encouraging. If the objective is also to make uncrewed systems a central component of asymmetric defense, manufacturing and procurement must be accompanied by less visible work on doctrine, command and control, training, maintenance and force integration.
Those developments rarely produce impressive export statistics or headlines, but they determine whether drones are simply products Taiwan manufactures or capabilities Taiwan can actually rely on. Taiwan’s drone industry has gained considerable momentum. The strategic task now is to ensure that its military adaptation does not fall behind it.
Harun Talha Ayanoglu is a visiting research fellow at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research.

Photo: Lin Yi-chang, Taipei Times
The industrial park is expected to accommodate about 100 companies, create 1,200 jobs and generate NT$8 billion (US$251.73 million) in annual output. It is intended to attract drone manufacturers and suppliers, connecting them with the NCSIST’s research, development and manufacturing capabilities at the campus and expanding Chiayi’s drone industry cluster.
The event included a tour of a facility for integrated testing of medium and large drone systems, where President William Lai (賴清德) and other officials were briefed on the nation’s drone research, testing and manufacturing capabilities.
Construction of the 5.12 hectare campus began on Dec. 5, 2023, with an investment of NT$1.11 billion.
Photo: REUTERS
The industrial park has received NT$6.859 billion in public infrastructure funding approved by the Executive Yuan. It is to include production facilities, testing equipment, a flight-testing field and research and development space.
Lai said the campus opening shows that national-level research and manufacturing capabilities have taken root in Chiayi, while the industrial park would help spread those technological capabilities to the private sector and move Taiwan’s drone industry toward greater scale.
Chiayi is ripe for evolution from a research and testing base into an important hub for the nation’s drone industry, he said, adding that Taiwan has the capabilities to become an Asian center of the democratic drone supply chain.
Lai praised Weng and the county government for acting rapidly to develop the drone industry, including by repurposing unused school facilities to establish the Asia UAV AI Innovation Research Center (亞洲無人機AI創新應用研發中心) and seeking central government funding.
Lai said the site’s significance has become even more prominent with changes in the international situation.
“From the Ukrainian battlefield to Indo-Pacific regional security, uncrewed systems have become important to combat strength in modern defense,” Lai said. “At the same time, we must deepen cooperation with democratic partners and jointly build a safer and more resilient uncrewed aircraft supply chain, providing solid support for Indo-Pacific regional peace and stability.”
The Ministry of Economic Affairs last year launched a program that would invest NT$44.2 billion through 2030 to strengthen Taiwan’s drone industry and promote its development.
Taiwan’s drone industry output reached NT$12.9 billion last year, more than 2.5 times the previous year’s figure, while more than 267 companies are involved in systems integration and the manufacture of key components, Lai said.
Weng said the NCSIST selected Minsyong in 2019 as the site of an aerospace research and development base.
The county government subsequently repurposed unused facilities at the former National Taiwan Sport University campus in Taibao to establish a drone research center, he said.
While talking about how the Asia UAV AI Innovation Research Center was inaugurated in August 2022, Weng said Chiayi’s drone industry is gradually taking shape, with research, development and testing in Taibao complemented by research, manufacturing and an industrial cluster in Minsyong.

Chiang and much ado about nothing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:24 UTC
01:40:24 KST

Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) this month toured the city’s Shida (師大) neighborhood to inspect the area’s pedestrian-friendly zones and the city’s YouBike system. The mayor posed for a photo-op crouching by the side of the road with a group of people, reaching out to touch the pavement.
The problem is that revamping the pedestrian area on Shida Road was completed in the second half of last year, and given that Chiang already made a hoo-ha about it earlier this year, making another spectacle out of a second road inspection seems rather superfluous.
Seeking repeated recognition for his municipal achievements, Chiang is again playing to the gallery for political gain. Naturally, his behavior attracts scrutiny. Residents are not interested in how many times the mayor touches the ground; they are concerned about the problems in Taipei that have yet to be addressed seriously.
It comes as no surprise that the public might feeling that way, especially after a string of controversies in the city.
First, the public art bus shelter next to Muzha Park (木柵公園) in Taipei’s Wenshan District (文山) cost NT$4.13 million (US$129,956). Yet before it even opened, part of the structure showed rust stains and it was surrounded by withered plants.
Second, in the Gongguan (公館) area near National Taiwan University, a fenced-in smoking section received harsh criticism. The fixtures were dismantled at seven sites, costing about NT$149,000 each.
Third, sunshade structures in Xinyi District (信義) have drawn questions over their utility and cost.
On the day of the Shida inspection, reporters asked about an elderly man with a cane who fell on the MRT after support poles in the center of carriages were removed. Chiang returned to his refrain of “we will review and improve accordingly.”
The playbook of “build first, fix later,” “install first, dismantle later” and “review only after something goes wrong” naturally leads to backlash from residents over a lack of planning.
Chiang has also been promoting a policy of providing “fresh milk for every child.” Starting in April last year, Taipei elementary-school and kindergarten students could redeem one milk product a week. At the end of August, it was extended to junior-high students, benefiting about 289,000 children.
However, Tainan was already providing students with dairy products, up to three times a week at one point, as early as 2024, in line with a central government policy. Taipei is by no means the first to pursue such a policy.
Policies should be judged based on coverage, frequency and how long it lasts, not who blows their trumpet the loudest.
Chiang’s insecurity over his political record manifests when the form outweighs the substance, producing the absurd sight of a mayor crouching by the roadside to touch the pavement.
Strong municipal governance is not about daily photo ops. Residents know for themselves whether the roads are safe. People waiting for a bus know whether the bus shelter keeps out the rain. MRT riders know whether there is nothing to hold on to.
A mayor does not build a political record through staged photo ops. Rather than pointing at the street and proclaiming it a political achievement, why not fix the facilities plagued with problems?
Elliot Yao is a reviewer.

Vanguard to expedite Singapore fab
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:24 UTC
01:40:24 KST

Foundry service provider Vanguard International Semiconductor Corp (世界先進) said it is fast-tracking the timeline for its second fab in Singapore, after holding a grand opening ceremony for its first 12-inch wafer fab yesterday.
The new fab, operated by VisionPower Semiconductor Manufacturing Co Pte Ltd (VSMC), a joint venture between Vanguard and NXP Semiconductors NV, will support process technologies ranging from 130 nanometer to 40 nanometer for mixed-signal, power management, analog and interposer applications. An interposer is a critical component used in advanced chip-on-wafer-on-substrate packaging, the company said.
As robust artificial intelligence (AI) demand squeezes non-AI manufacturing capacity, the demand for specialty node chips “has gone through the roof,” Vanguard and VSMC chairman Fang Leuh (方略) said.
Photo: CNA
That has caused a chip supply crunch, which is expected to persist for a long time, he said.
“We really should have just built both fabs at the same time,” Fang said, adding that there has been additional chip demand from customers.
VSMC held a groundbreaking ceremony for the first fab in December 2024.
As the fab’s phase 1 capacity is entirely allocated, additional demand will be accommodated in phase 2 expansion, he said.
However, the company would not rush a decision, he said, after being asked if the expansion plan would be finalized by the end of this year.
To support such a capital-intensive 12-inch fab project, the company is carefully structuring its financial strategy and evaluating future product applications and technology portfolios, including 28-nanometer or 22-nanometer technologies, Fang said.
The company is evaluating whether to develop 28-nanometer or 22-nanometer technologies internally or license them, as licensing provides a faster route to scale production, he said.
More than 10 customers have visited the Singapore site and discussed their future demand and capacity requirements, he said.
Regarding debate about a slowdown in AI investment, he said that AI’s trajectory is “unstoppable and irreversible,” and that a future slowdown in growth would not leave foundry capacity idle.
Progress at the VSMC fab has exceeded expectations, Fang said.
Risk production is likely to commence in the next quarter, maintaining the timeline for mass production in the first quarter of next year, he said.
The fab has the potential to break even earlier than anticipated, with full capacity utilization projected ahead of the 2029 schedule, he said.
The fab is expected to produce about 44,000 12-inch wafers per month, and create about 1,600 jobs, the company said.
“The opening of this new fab represents a long-term commitment to strengthening the global semiconductor ecosystem, enhancing supply chain resilience and creating the capacity needed to support the technologies that will define our future,” NXP CEO Rafael Sotomayor said yesterday.
The facility would serve not only as a catalyst for innovation, but also as a catalyst for developing the industry’s next generation of engineering talent, creating opportunities for skills development and contributing to Singapore’s growing semiconductor ecosystem, Sotomayor said.
The investment in the VSMC fab is one of the most significant milestones in NXP’s history, he said, adding that it is also the largest investment NXP has made since its acquisition of Freescale in 2015.

Dead passenger found on bus days after boarding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:19 UTC
01:40:19 KST

A man was found dead on a bus in New Taipei City on Sunday, several days after he boarded, and the bus operator has been fined, authorities said.
The Taipei City Government on Sunday said that after an initial investigation of the incident, its Public Transportation Office has fined the operator, Sindian Bus, NT$30,000.
Sindian Bus issued a statement on the same day, saying that at about 7am that day, a passenger who boarded in New Taipei City’s Sindian District (新店) reported to the driver that a man on the bus appeared to be unconscious.
Photo: Lin Cheng-hung, Taipei Times
The driver called the police and emergency service.
The New Taipei City Police Department’s Sindian Precinct said in a statement that when authorities arrived on the scene, it was clear that the man was dead.
A forensic examination found no signs of trauma and ruled out foul play for the time being, police said, adding that the Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office has ordered an autopsy to determine the cause of death.
The man, surnamed Kao (高), was later identified.
Sources said he used to conduct business in China before returning to Taiwan several years ago after being diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease.
He lived with his 88-year-old father in New Taipei City’s Shenkeng District (深坑), who cared for him on a daily basis, they said.
On Wednesday last week, Kao’s father took him to Taipei’s Wanfang Hospital for a follow-up appointment, they said.
After the appointment, the two were preparing to take a bus home when the father briefly turned away and realized his son was gone.
On Saturday, the father reported to police that Kao was missing, prompting a search.
Police on Sunday said their initial investigation found that Kao had boarded the bus at about 8:40pm on Thursday at the Qingtan Parking Lot stop in Sindian.
The bus, which runs in Taipei and New Taipei City, returned to its terminal in Sindian at about 10:30pm on Thursday, with the man still aboard, police said.
Surveillance footage showed that the bus remained at the terminal until Sunday morning, when it departed at 6:45am with the same driver, surnamed Chen (陳), police said.
Sindian Bus president Kao Tsan-huang (高燦煌) said in the statement that video footage from inside the bus showed the driver looking back on Thursday night before getting off and closing the door at the terminal, but failed to notice the man.
The bus did not resume service again until Sunday morning, because of the Mid-Autumn Festival holiday, which began on Friday, he said.
Chen only learned that the man was still on the bus after the passenger reported the incident on Sunday morning, he added.
The company will cooperate with the police investigation and enhance training for its drivers to ensure that they check the buses properly before parking them at the end of the day, Kao Tsan-huang said.
Chen has been suspended from driving duties for failing to follow the proper procedure for clearing the bus, Sindian Bus said.
In addition, he might have suffered some trauma as a result of the incident and should not be on driving duty right now, the company said.
The bus will be safe to ride when it resumes service, as it will be thoroughly cleaned and disinfected, Kao Tsan-huang said.
Kuo Chien-chen (郭建辰), an official at the Taipei Public Transportation Office, on Sunday said that under his office’s regulations, bus operators are required to train their drivers to clear their buses properly at the end of their service routes.
The office has fined Sindian Bus NT$30,000 for failing to fulfill its managerial responsibilities in connection with the incident, Kuo said, adding that the penalty was imposed in accordance with the Highway Act (公路法).

Arms sales vital to ‘T-Dome’: source
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:18 UTC
01:40:18 KST

The long-delayed US$14 billion arms sale that Washington put on hold prior to US President Donald Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) last week is closely tied to Taiwan’s plans for developing a layered air-defense network known as “T-Dome,” sources said.
The package is expected to include hundreds of Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (PAC-3 MSE) units, nine National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile Systems (NASAMS) and an Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS).
Taiwan has sought to expand its missile stockpiles to potentially counter Chinese ballistic missiles and advanced military aircraft. The PAC-3 is primarily designed to intercept high-threat targets, such as ballistic and cruise missiles during their terminal phase.
The NASAMS units would provide medium and low-altitude air defense against cruise missiles, drones and aircraft. The units can use AIM-9X and AIM-120 air-to-air missiles carried by Taiwan’s fighter aircraft, providing logistical advantages.
Other reported components include the Lower Tier Air and Missile Defense Sensor, which provides 360° detection of aircraft and missiles, and the IBCS, which integrates different radars and interceptors so that targets can be engaged by the most suitable air-defense system. Both systems would be key components of the integrated “T-Dome” network.
Taiwan has already purchased three NASAMS units and 123 extended-range Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missiles from the US, as well as 102 PAC-3 MSEs.
The National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology is also producing Tien Kung III (天弓三, Sky Bow III) surface-to-air missiles and a mobile air-defense system based on the Tien Chien II (天劍二, Sky Sword II) missile, with both programs reaching mass-production milestones this year.
If the US$14 billion package includes the expected additional PAC-3 MSEs, NASAMS units and the IBCS, it would expand the density and integration of Taiwan’s layered air defenses, building on the Sky Bow III, Chiang Kung (強弓, Strong Bow), NASAMS and Sky Sword II systems, sources said.
US lawmakers and retired military officers have been urging the Trump administration to formally notify the US Congress of the package as soon as possible.
It received preliminary congressional approval in January.
A senior Taiwanese official familiar with US-Taiwan arms sales on Friday said that delays could have significant consequences, as defense manufacturers are facing heavy demand and limited production capacity.
Under the US Foreign Military Sales process, the US Department of State must formally notify Congress before detailed negotiations can begin. Taiwan and the US would then sign a letter of offer and acceptance, after which Taiwan would make an initial payment and the US military could place orders with defense contractors.
Manufacturers generally do not reserve production capacity for Taiwan until a formal contract is in place, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Advanced missiles and radar systems are also produced in batches, meaning that missing a scheduled production window could push an order into a later production run, they said.
Demand has been further driven by the war in Ukraine and NATO members competing for limited production capacity, the official said, adding that a delay in placing Taiwan’s orders could potentially extend well beyond the initial delay.
US senators Thom Tillis and Elissa Slotkin, cochairs of the Senate Taiwan Caucus, have said that continued delays could create disrupt Taiwan’s budget planning and efforts to raise its defense spending to 5 percent of GDP.
US officials and retired military officers have also said that most of the systems in the package are not urgently needed for current US military inventories.
They have urged the White House to approve the sale rather than use it as leverage in US-China negotiations, warning that delays could leave gaps in Taiwan’s air-defense capabilities.

Getting real about birth incentives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:16 UTC
01:40:16 KST

To address the nation’s declining birthrate and encourage young people to marry and have children, the government is planning to extend statutory marriage leave for workers from eight days to 14, subsidizing employers for the six additional days of wages.
An extra six days of marriage leave is welcome, but as a policy designed to encourage marriage and having children, is it truly a meaningful incentive? The issue is not just about whether young people can afford to marry and have children, but about whether they even want to. There are three main reasons for this.
First, young people are far less concerned with how much marriage leave they get than they are with what comes next. Housing prices and rents are high, while wages struggle to keep pace with the cost of living.
Once a couple has children, they begin racking up housing, childcare and education expenses. If both parents work, who looks after the children? If one takes time off work, what happens to their career and the family’s income?
Marriage leave lasts two weeks, but the marriage might last 50 years, and raising a child is a responsibility lasting two decades. Put side by side, and the chasm between the policy and the problem becomes obvious.
The second issue goes deeper than money: Family values are changing. The education system and society have long been placing increasing emphasis on individual autonomy, rights and self-fulfillment.
These are values worth cherishing, but in teaching the next generation to prioritize “what I want” over “who am I willing to take responsibility for?”, settling down goes from a shared project of building a life together into a cost-benefit analysis.
When marriage is seen as sacrificing a person’s freedom, having children as meaning a lower quality of life and family responsibilities as a burden, subsidies alone are unlikely to rekindle the desire to build a family.
The third issue is most critical for the government: young people’s confidence in the future. When a person is willing to marry and have children, it means they believe tomorrow is worth looking forward to, and that society is worth bringing children into.
Population policy is ultimately a policy of confidence. If people know that a lifetime of hard work might still not be enough to afford a home; if the gap between their earnings and the cost of living remains a constant source of anxiety; and if new subsidies are rolled out without a stable outlook on housing, employment, childcare and long-term prospects, then the government loses that confidence.
Childcare allowances, daycare subsidies, parental leave, rental subsidies, housing for newlyweds and families, and increased marriage leave — this string of policies makes it appear that the government is doing a great deal, but the number of births continues to decline. Quantity does not guarantee effectiveness; providing more subsidies does not mean the core problem has been addressed.
The low birthrate is a structural issue concerning the country’s future. The impact would be felt not only in school enrollment, but also in the workforce, industry, tax revenues, healthcare, long-term care and military staffing.
In this birthrate crisis, what Taiwan truly needs to save is an entire generation’s hopes for marriage, their sense of connection to family and their confidence in the nation’s collective future. When young people no longer believe in tomorrow, can six extra days of marriage leave truly bring about the next generation?
Voyu Poiconu is an adjunct lecturer at Meiho University and former deputy minister of the Council of Indigenous Peoples.
Translated by Gilda Knox Streader
