Small public schools in rural areas are set to receive more state support as falling numbers of children put some schools at risk of closing.
The government is allocating 500 million DKK through 2030 to support small schools and slow further closures.
Minister for Economic and Interior Affairs Pia Olsen Dyhr from the Socialist People’s Party, is presenting the plan today at a visit to a school in Toksværd in Næstved Municipality, according to TV2 ØST.
“A school is a gathering point for parents, teachers, and students, and they help create local life and connection in our rural districts,” Dyhr said.
The initiative follows a commitment in the government’s platform from June to prevent a new wave of school closures. Small public schools in rural areas are also expected to receive greater financial support and more freedom.
One school facing possible closure is Vesterlandsskolen’s branch in Hyllinge. Only fifty-four students attend this school, and Næstved Municipality’s administration has proposed ending teaching and after-school care there from August 1, 2027.
Closing the branch would save 7.53 million DKK annually from 2028. The proposal has not been approved, and the city council is expected to adopt its budget on October 6.
School board chair Karina Wolan said additional state funding could help keep the Hyllinge branch open.
“If it means that the school can be allowed to exist, that would be wonderful,” she said.
It remains unclear how the 500 million DKK will be distributed, which municipalities will qualify and whether the funding is included in the government’s previously announced five billion DKK annual investment in children, daycare, schools and leisure.
Social Affairs Minister Monika Rubin of the Moderates says the government wants more freedom to change Denmark’s disability system after withdrawing from a political agreement reached two years ago.
The framework agreement was signed in May 2024 by the government and Liberal Alliance, the Conservative People’s Party and the Social Liberal Party. It was not a formal political settlement with special rules governing withdrawal.
“With the framework agreement, one had bound oneself in a way that made it more difficult than it needs to be to cooperate broadly across the Folketing,” Rubin said, referring to Denmark’s parliament.
“The original agreement has outlived its potential,” she added.
When the deal was reached, then-Social Affairs Minister Pernille Rosenkrantz-Theil of the Social Democrats described it as a “completely new chapter in Danish disability policy” and the “first major agreement in the disability area ever.”
Rubin’s Moderates also supported the agreement at the time.
Rubin now says she will work on initiatives involving “fundamental changes to the disability area,” with more trust, structure and coordination of professional expertise around people with disabilities.
The decision drew different responses from other parties.
Katrine Daugaard, social affairs spokesperson for Liberal Alliance, a Danish liberal party, accused Rubin of “running away from an agreement.” She said ending it risks “more uniform, mediocre public services, less specialization, and less freedom of choice.”
Torsten Gejl, political spokesperson for the Alternative, a Danish green party that was not part of the agreement, welcomed the decision.
“The framework agreement for disability, which has tightened the finances in the disability area and made people with disabilities feel like a cost-cutting exercise, was suddenly dropped this evening. That is fantastic,” Gejl wrote on X.

Congo politician beaten to death after urging Ebola prevention on radio, party says
Sept 28 - A senior member of Congo's ruling party was beaten to death after taking part in a radio programme to raise awareness about the Ebola outbreak, a party representative said on Monday.
• The incident happened on Sunday in Butembo, North Kivu province, which has recently become a hotspot in the ongoing Ebola outbreak.
• Marie-Celestin Karondwa, acting president of the UDPS party's federal executive committee in Butembo and a party spokesperson, was attacked by residents of his neighbourhood after appearing on a radio show during which he promoted Ebola prevention measures, the UDPS federation in Butembo said in a statement.
• The party said the attackers beat him, looted his belongings and set his house on fire. It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack, how many were involved or what motivated it. But the party said Karondwa was "an innocent victim for having defended the party's position on the existence of the Ebola virus disease (...) and the threat it poses to the population."
• Karondwa later died from his injuries, the party said.
• The mayor of Butembo did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
• The incident is the latest in a series of attacks on Ebola response teams, underscoring persistent mistrust among the population.
• On Saturday, armed men attacked a hand-washing checkpoint in nearby Beni territory, killing at least one person and wounding several others, a local civil society group reported.
• The outbreak, declared on May 15, has infected 8,067 people and killed 3,901, according to government data released on Monday. REUTERS

Israeli strikes kill at least two people in Gaza, officials say
CAIRO, Sept 28 - Israeli strikes killed at least two Palestinians and wounded several others on Monday in two separate attacks in the Gaza Strip, health officials in the enclave said.
A woman was killed and her husband and others were wounded in one Israeli strike on the rooftop of their building in Gaza City, medics said. Another strike killed a woman and wounded others in central Gaza's Nuseirat refugee camp, they added.
The Israeli military said it struck a militant in Nuseirat, without giving further details. It did not immediately comment on the reported strike in Gaza City.
Palestinian authorities say more than 73,000 people have been killed in Israel's assault on Gaza, launched after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel in October 2023.
A US-brokered ceasefire agreed last year calls for the eventual reconstruction of the territory, but little progress has been made as negotiators have failed to agree terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops. Israeli airstrikes have continued.
At least 1,400 Palestinians, mostly civilians, have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire took effect, according to the territory's health officials, while the Israeli military says four Israeli soldiers have been killed.
Israel and Hamas trade blame over responsibility for violations of the ceasefire agreement. REUTERS

US, Iran set to hold separate talks with mediators on Monday or Tuesday, official says
Sept 28 - Qatari mediators are likely to hold separate talks with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi in New York and with the US side on Monday or Tuesday, an official briefed on the negotiations told Reuters, in a fresh push to end the war.
The talks are expected to focus on an amended version of a seven-day proposal that Iran presented last week on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Araqchi remains in New York after attending the General Assembly. It was not immediately clear who would represent the US side in the talks with mediators.
Iran's semi-official ISNA news agency later confirmed that Araqchi would meet the mediators in the US on Monday morning, New York time.
The two sides will "examine the latest proposals and views regarding the current situation", ISNA added.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei told state media later on Monday that Araqchi's stay in New York had not been extended and that the foreign minister would return to Tehran according to his original schedule.
Baghaei made no comment on the talks with mediators.
TRUMP HAS FLAGGED FURTHER TALKS THIS WEEK
Iran's seven-day plan envisages an end to all hostilities in Iran and Lebanon, the unfreezing of billions of dollars' worth of Iranian assets, an end to sanctions on Iranian oil and the lifting of the US blockade on Iranian ports.
Tehran would then allow the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and the two sides would also resume talks on Iran's nuclear programme.
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he had rejected Iran's proposal, saying Tehran wanted a swift agreement because of the crippling economic pressure it is under.
However, he also told Axios on Sunday that he expected US negotiators to engage in further talks this week.
Araqchi said on Sunday that mediators had not formally conveyed a US rejection to Tehran and that Iran was awaiting Washington's definitive position before deciding its next steps.
"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met," he said on Sunday, adding that only a negotiated solution could resolve the impasse. REUTERS

Scientists just discovered what coffee really does to your gut and brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:37:05 UTC
22:37:05 KST

Scientists just discovered what coffee really does to your gut and brain
- Date:
- September 28, 2026
- Source:
- University College Cork
- Summary:
- A new study suggests coffee may influence mood and brain function by changing the activity of microbes in the gut. Both caffeinated and decaf coffee were linked to lower stress, depression, and impulsivity, while also producing measurable changes in gut bacteria and metabolites. Decaf was associated with better learning and memory, while caffeinated coffee appeared to reduce anxiety and improve attention.
- Share:
Coffee may affect far more than alertness. New research suggests that both regular and decaffeinated coffee can alter the gut microbiome and may influence mood, stress, memory, and attention through the gut brain connection.
Scientists at APC Microbiome Ireland, a research center at University College Cork, investigated in detail how coffee may influence communication between the digestive system and the brain.
The study published in Nature Communications and sponsored by the Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee (ISIC), found that both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee were associated with changes in the gut microbiome as well as differences in mood and stress.
How Coffee May Affect the Gut-Brain Connection
Scientists have long studied coffee for possible effects on digestion, mood, and overall health, but exactly how these effects arise has remained less clear.
The new research focused on the microbiota-gut-brain axis, the two-way communication system linking microorganisms in the digestive tract with the brain. Signals can travel between the gut and brain through immune activity, hormones, nerves, and chemical compounds produced by microbes.
Researchers examined 31 regular coffee drinkers and 31 people who did not normally drink coffee. Participants completed psychological assessments and kept records of caffeine intake and diet. Researchers also collected stool and urine samples to track changes in gut microbes, metabolism, mood, and perceived stress.
For the study, 'Coffee drinkers' were set as those who regularly consume 3-5 cups of coffee a day, defined by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) as a safe and moderate amount for most people.
What Happened When Coffee Was Removed
The regular coffee drinkers first stopped consuming coffee for two weeks. During that period, participants repeatedly completed psychological assessments and provided stool and urine samples.
When coffee drinkers stopped drinking coffee, researchers observed substantial shifts in their gut metabolite profiles compared with people who did not normally consume coffee. Metabolites are small molecules produced or altered during metabolism, including compounds created by gut microbes as they process food and other substances.
Coffee was then reintroduced without participants knowing whether they were receiving caffeinated or decaffeinated coffee. Half received decaf, while the other half received caffeinated coffee.
After coffee returned to their diets, both groups reported lower perceived stress, depression and impulsivity scores. The findings suggest that some of coffee's effects on mood may not depend entirely on caffeine.
Coffee Was Linked to Changes in Gut Bacteria
Researchers also found differences in several types of gut bacteria.
Bacteria, such as 'Eggertella sp.' or 'Cryptobacterium curtum', were more abundant among coffee drinkers than non-coffee drinkers. 'Eggertella sp' is thought to contribute to acid secretion in the stomach and intestines, while 'Cryptobacterium curtum' may participate in bile acid production.
Both processes could potentially help create an intestinal environment that discourages certain harmful bacteria and infections.
Researchers also observed higher levels of 'Firmicutes' bacteria, a broad group of microbes that has previously been associated with positive emotions in females.
Decaf and Caffeinated Coffee Showed Different Effects
One of the most intriguing findings was that caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee did not appear to affect participants in exactly the same way.
Improved learning and memory were observed only among participants drinking decaffeinated coffee. That finding suggests that substances other than caffeine may contribute to some of coffee's effects on cognition.
Coffee contains thousands of chemical compounds, including polyphenols. These plant derived substances can act as antioxidants and can also interact with gut microbes, potentially influencing metabolism and other biological processes.
Caffeinated coffee, meanwhile, was associated with reduced feelings of anxiety as well as improved vigilance and attention. Caffeine was also linked to a reduced risk of inflammation.
Because the study involved a relatively small number of participants, the findings do not establish that coffee directly causes these changes in mood, cognition, or gut health. However, they provide new clues about the biological pathways that could help explain associations reported in earlier coffee research.
Coffee Is More Than Caffeine
Corresponding author of the study, Professor John Cryan, Principal Investigator at APC Microbiome Ireland, University College Cork, commented: "Public interest in gut health has risen hugely. The relationship between digestive and mental health is also increasingly being better understood, but the mechanisms behind coffee's effects on this gut-brain axis have remained unclear.
"Our findings reveal the microbiome and neurological responses to coffee, as well as their potential long-term benefits for a healthier microbiome. Coffee may modify what microbes do collectively, and what metabolites they use. As the public continues to think about dietary changes for the right digestive balance, coffee has the potential to also be harnessed as a further intervention as part of a healthy balanced diet."
The findings add to growing evidence that coffee should not be viewed simply as a source of caffeine. Its many other components may interact with the microbiome, metabolism, and nervous system in different ways.
"Coffee is more than just caffeine -- it's a complex dietary factor that interacts with our gut microbes, our metabolism, and even our emotional well-being," said Professor Cryan. "Our findings suggest that coffee, whether caffeinated or decaffeinated, can influence health in distinct but complementary ways."
Story Source:
Materials provided by University College Cork. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

- Serena Boscaini, Thomaz F. S. Bastiaanssen, Gerard M. Moloney, Federica Bergamo, Laila Zeraik, Caroline O’Leary, Aimone Ferri, Maha Irfan, Maaike van der Rhee, Thaïs I. F. Lee Asks Trump to Help Revive North Korea Talks During New York Trip
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:36:00 UTC
22:36:00 KST

South Korean President Lee Jae-myung asked U.S. President Donald Trump to help restart talks between the United States and North Korea in an unannounced meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly on September 22, according to the Blue House, the presidential office of South Korea. The Blue House also said that Trump reaffirmed his willingness to engage with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
The talks were arranged at the last minute. In the 30-minute meeting. Lee asked Trump to create a breakthrough amid almost no direct contact between the two Koreas. The two leaders also agreed to communicate closely as “peacemakers and pacemakers,” according to the Blue House.
Trump has been courting Kim since August, when he scaled back a major joint military exercise with South Korea. A day later, he said Kim had responded to his request for dialogue, calling the exchange very positive without offering details. Trump has since signaled he hopes to meet Kim before the end of the year – possibly during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, this November.
Yet North Korea denied any direct contact in a statement by Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of Kim Jong Un. She described the relationship between the two leaders as “excellent” while insisting that Washington had not changed its hostile policy. She also said North Korea was not impressed by the reduction in scale of the South Korea-U.S. joint exercises, calling it “unworthy of comment.”
Lee had made the case for reopening dialogue earlier on September 22 in an address to the General Assembly. In the speech, Lee said he hoped to see the long-suspended dialogue between North Korea and the United States resume without delay. He also added that his administration would lay the groundwork for talks among the parties aimed at formally ending the Korean War.
On North Korean weapons, Lee outlined a sequence that would begin with a halt to further advances in North Korean nuclear and missile capabilities. Then reductions would follow over the medium term, with the ultimate goal of a Korean Peninsula free of nuclear weapons. Lee credited Trump with creating a hard-won opportunity for change and pledged to act as a “pacemaker” for peace.
The speech came a day after the foreign ministers of South Korea, the U.S., and Japan reaffirmed their commitment to the complete denuclearization of North Korea in a joint statement issued on the sidelines of the same General Assembly session. The statement also urged Pyongyang to return to talks.
North Korean Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui denounced the joint statement on September 24, declaring in a message carried by state media that the will of her country to keep nuclear weapons through all ages was “irreversible.”
Beyond North Korea, in their brief meeting Lee and Trump took up alliance issues such as nuclear-powered submarines and the transfer of wartime operational control of South Korean forces from the U.S. Rights to enrich uranium and reprocess spent nuclear fuel, along with shipbuilding cooperation, also came up. Both leaders also welcomed progress on investment projects between the two countries. The Industry Ministry had briefed lawmakers on a $22.3 billion gas-fired power plant in Texas, which Seoul confirmed as the first project under a $200 billion strategic investment package. Under the trade deal, South Korea has pledged to invest $350 billion in the United States, including $150 billion set aside for shipbuilding.
While in New York, Lee also met U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres to review Korean Peninsula issues and cooperation between South Korea and the United Nations. In a separate meeting, he held talks with Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on energy cooperation amid disruptions linked to the Strait of Hormuz.
On September 23, Lee addressed the Korea Investment Summit in New York. He pledged to double semiconductor production capacity within five years and pointed to the shipbuilding cooperation covered in his meeting with Trump the day before.
Meanwhile, North Korea has said it tested a new weapon on September 20. That day, the South Korean military detected two short-range ballistic missile launches and assessed their flight distances at about 450 and 600 kilometers. Photos released by North Korea, however, showed a flight distance of 908.2 kilometers.
The North Korean delegation skipped the General Assembly address delivered by Lee. Two North Korean diplomats had attended the speech given by Trump earlier that day.
The U.N. General Assembly also overlapped with a summit between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington, during the first visit to the U.S. capital by Xi in more than a decade. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the two sides agreed to extend their trade truce by two months, to January 10. The White House later said China and the United States had reached consensus on recommendations for more favorable tariff treatment for $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction.
Each side also referred to the Korean Peninsula in its account of the talks. According to Washington, the two leaders discussed global concerns including Russia, North Korea, and Iran. Chinese state media reported that the leaders exchanged views on the Korean Peninsula, the Middle East, and the war in Ukraine. Neither side gave details of what was said about North Korea.
After his trip to New York, Lee paid a state visit to Mexico. Lee and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum adopted a joint action plan for 2026 to 2030 and signed 17 cooperation documents covering areas from trade and critical minerals to aerospace and defense.

Punjab's election drug debate has old players in new roles: BJP, Congress attack as AAP defends its record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:31:57 UTC
22:31:57 KST

NEW DELHI: "The sarpanch is also responsible for my death. I had questioned Cheema about drugs. My son takes drugs. My house was sold. I don't have anything and finally now I have consumed poison. The problem of drugs has not been solved anywhere in Punjab."Those were among the last recorded words of Gulzar Singh, a 47-year-old Dalit man from Dirba in Sangrur district, before his death. His family alleged that he had been pushed to the edge after questioning Punjab finance minister Harpal Singh Cheema about the easy availability of drugs in the area.Gulzar died, but his words reverberated across poll-bound Punjab. The BJP, Congress and Shiromani Akali Dal trained their guns on the Bhagwant Mann government, accusing it of failing to control the drug menace. AAP hit back, questioning their own records in power.Drugs have shadowed election after election in the state. Captain Amarinder Singh went into the 2017 polls promising to break the backbone of the drug trade within four weeks. Five years later, AAP sought votes with its own promise of eliminating the menace within months.
Now, with Punjab headed for another assembly election in 2027, drugs are again moving to the centre of the conversation.Only the roles have changed.AAP, which once attacked Congress and the SAD-BJP government from the outside, now has nearly five years in office to defend. Congress wants to use AAP's old promises against it. And the BJP, still trying to expand its footprint in Punjab, has launched perhaps its biggest statewide campaign yet around the issue.
BJP takes the drug battle on the road
Leading the opposition charge is the BJP, which has the weakest presence in the state as of now, but is making the strongest pitch for power.The Punjab BJP, on September 18, launched its 13-day 'Nasha Mukt Yatra' to turn its anti-drug campaign into a statewide political roadshow ahead of the 2027 assembly elections. The party divided its campaign into four yatras covering nearly 4,000 km and all 117 assembly constituencies.The campaign will end on September 30, with Union home minister Amit Shah likely to address the concluding rally. All the top BJP leaders including Union ministers and party chief ministers from other states have joined the campaign against drugs in Punjab.
BJP leader Anurag Thakur said the state has to be made 'Aam Aadmi Party Mukt' for turning it into 'Nasha Mukt'
Yet the BJP has a political history to answer for too. For 10 years, from 2007 to 2017, it shared power with the Shiromani Akali Dal, the period AAP repeatedly points to whenever its record on drugs is questioned.
From four weeks to three months: Punjab's many deadlines
Ahead of the 2017 election, Amarinder Singh's four-week promise became one of the defining messages of the Congress campaign. He later clarified that his pledge was about breaking the backbone of the drug supply chain rather than completely eliminating every trace of drugs within a month.By 2022, the roles had changed. AAP was the challenger and Arvind Kejriwal and other party leaders promised quick action, speaking of tackling the menace within three to four months of forming the government.The BJP has done its homework well. It knows that the drug menace in Punjab is deep-rooted and hence has sought a timeframe of two years to eradicate it. However, Union minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan has claimed that the BJP will destroy and eliminate the entire drug network within six months if voted to power in the state.Therein lies Punjab's problem: Congress cannot remind AAP about its three-month promise without being reminded of its own four-week vow. BJP cannot attack AAP without being taken back to its decade in government with SAD.Almost every party pointing fingers today has a past of its own to explain.
Congress, SAD join the attack
The Congress narrative on the drug menace seems to have been lost in the face of BJP’s high-decibel anti-drug campaign. The party, which for a long time was struggling to set its own house in order amid infighting, has done little till now to capitalise on the alleged failures of the AAP government to tackle the drug menace.The first big Congress show on the ground was only after Sachin Pilot took charge as state incharge and managed to get the rival state unit factions on one stage to protest against Punjab minister Cheema over the suicide of Gulzar.
Punjab finance minister blamed BJP-SAD for the drug menace in the state,
Pilot said: “If someone raises their voice against drugs, they face such attacks. I believe the government can go to any extent to suppress and conceal these voices. There are two sets of laws in the country, one for ministers and another for the common man. This cannot go on. I feel the government is completely on the back foot regarding the issue of drugs.”He then turned to AAP's pre-2022 promise: “The Aam Aadmi Party had promised in Punjab that they would eliminate the drug menace within three months of forming the government. They stand completely exposed. I sense a stir for change in Punjab, and change will happen.”Leader of opposition Partap Singh Bajwa has blamed both the AAP-led state government and the BJP-led Union government for turning the state's drug crisis into a political blame game instead of dismantling the drug supply chain.“Bhagwant Mann cannot wash his hands of responsibility by talking about cross-border, the BSF and Mundra Port. At the same time, the BJP cannot absolve itself by blaming Punjab while the international border, ports and the national drug-trafficking network fall within areas where the Union government has a critical responsibility. Punjab's youth need action, not a Mann-Modi blame-game,” Bajwa said.
Channi hits out at AAP govt
The Congress challenge is daunting. While on the one hand it has to target the AAP government’s failures, on the other, it also has to prevent the BJP from running away with the anti-drug fight initiative.SAD faces much the same problem. Bikram Singh Majithia recently took a jibe at the Punjab government when he said: “Under AAP's regime, delivery of drugs is faster than that of food.”Bathinda MP Harsimrat Kaur Badal has also appealed to women in Punjab to unite and launch an ‘andolan’ to free the state from the drug menace, including through ‘thikri pehra’, a community policing practice in which people guard their localities during emergencies.
Bathinda MP Harsimrat Kaur Badal has appealed to women in Punjab to unite and launch an 'andolan'
AAP hits back: What about the years before 2022?
AAP's response is to ask its rivals to look backwards before judging the Mann government.Punjab minister Cheema, who is at the centre of the row over Gulzar’s suicide, shifted the blame to the BJP and the SAD.“The BJP should look at its own record. The drug menace intensified during the 10 years of the SAD-BJP government from 2007 to 2017. It was during that period that terms such as 'chitta' and 'smack' became widely associated with Punjab, with countless young lives being destroyed by addiction,” Cheema said.Countering the BJP offensive, AAP national convenor Arvind Kejriwal has alleged that the majority of narcotics entering the country originate from Bharatiya Janata Party-ruled states and major maritime entry points controlled by the Centre.Kejriwal alleged: “Today, 80% of the drugs are coming from BJP-ruled states - Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana, UP, Delhi. Has the BJP failed to stop the drug trade in its own states, or does it not want to stop it? Their government has been in power in Gujarat for thirty years, and the highest drug trade is there. Drugs enter India through Mundra Port, and stopping that is the responsibility of the central BJP government.”Bhagwant Mann, meanwhile, has launched the ‘Soorma’ campaign to honour drug-rehabilitated people with specially crafted ‘Soorma’ rings and T-shirts. The chief minister said the initiative aimed to transform recovered drug victims into “Ambassadors of Hope”, who will lead the fight against addiction at the grassroots.
Beyond the blame game, what do numbers say
The Mann government has numbers with which to defend itself.Punjab Police says its ‘Yudh Nashean Virudh’ campaign has resulted in tens of thousands of cases and arrests. More recent state figures put the tally since March 2025 at 61,824 FIRs, 81,433 arrests and 3,918 kg of heroin seized.AAP presents the numbers as evidence that the state machinery is finally going hard after the networks. Its opponents turn the argument around: if such large quantities are still being seized and so many people are still being arrested, how deeply rooted does the trade remain?High seizures can show a crackdown is working but they can also show the scale of the problem being confronted.The government says its strategy now goes beyond policing. It has expanded treatment and rehabilitation under ‘Yudh Nashean Virudh’, with 547 OOAT centres, 219 de-addiction centres and 91 rehabilitation centres, besides programmes involving schools and local communities.
For AAP, this forms the other half of its defence: the battle against drugs cannot be measured only through FIRs and seizures but also through treatment and rehabilitation.
Punjab has seen this cycle before.
In 2017, anger over drugs was directed largely at the SAD-BJP government and Congress promised quick action. By 2022, Congress was on the defensive and AAP used the same issue to argue that Punjab's traditional parties had failed. In 2027, AAP is the incumbent being asked many of the questions it once asked others.The slogans have changed and the roles have reversed, but the question has survived different governments and different deadlines: after so many promises to make Punjab drug-free, why is the state heading into yet another election talking about the same problem?

Moscow's forces pounded apartment buildings, offices, data centers and a building of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine in downtown Kyiv in a brazen daytime attack.
CBS News' Aidan Stretch was forced to take shelter again due to more incoming Russian weapons not long after he arrived Monday at the scene of the strike on the science academy.
The attacks followed a week of diplomatic efforts at the United Nations to get traction for negotiations on ending Moscow's full-scale invasion that began 4½ years ago.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov indicated Monday that the chances of making speedy headway on forging a peace settlement were bleak after recent Ukrainian attacks, including during recent parliamentary elections in Russia.
"Ukraine will have to pay a price for the actions that have taken place in recent months," Peskov told reporters. "That is happening right now."
On Saturday, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said in a fiery speech to the U.N. General Assembly that "Europe is doing everything it can to thwart peace talks in which the Trump administration is interested," seeking, as Moscow has done throughout the war, to portray a rift within the NATO alliance.
Russian drone attacks across eastern Ukraine
Russian drone attacks on the Kyiv region killed four people and wounded eight, officials said.
A woman was killed in a Russian strike on Kyiv's Shevchenkivskyi district on Monday afternoon, the Kyiv city military administration said. The strike hit the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, the latest cultural landmark in the capital to be damaged. Russian forces also hit a pharmaceutical company and gas stations in Kyiv.
One drone struck an office center in central Dnipro during working hours Monday, killing three people and wounding at least 12, local authorities said.
A Russian strike on a nine-story apartment building in the northeast city of Kharkiv wounded 43 people, including 11 children, Mayor Ihor Terekhov said.
Four people, including two teenage girls, were hurt when a Russian drone struck a residential area in northern Ukraine's Chernihiv region on Sunday evening, said Viacheslav Chaus, head of the regional military administration.
Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces struck two data centers in Kyiv, as well as gas stations in the Ukrainian capital. A distribution hub belonging to the Nova Poshta postal service was struck in the southern city of Odesa, it said.
The Russian military also hit a cargo ship in the Black Sea and another one in the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk, the ministry said. The strikes aim to curb Ukraine's grain exports, though they may also create food shortages in countries that rely on Ukrainian imports.
The Russian aerial attacks regularly hit civilian areas. Moscow claims it targets only military-related sites.
Ukraine claims small gains along entrenched front lines
Battlefield positions have changed little since last year, in part because swarms of drones severely restrict troop movements, but Kyiv's forces launched a recent offensive, code-named Operation Vivaldi, on part of the 800-mile front line.
Ukraine's Third Army Corps said Monday it had recaptured another 20 square miles from the Russians, bringing the total to 68 square miles since the offensive began several months ago.
The corps said that in order to break through Russian defenses, it converted Soviet-era BTR-60 armored personnel carriers into kamikaze vehicles that blew up the strongest Russian fortifications. The operation has also used ground robots to attack Russian positions.
The claimed breakthroughs came in the Donetsk region of eastern Ukraine, which the bigger Russian army has been trying in vain to conquer.
Russian officials made no immediate comment on the Ukrainian claim.
Russia's Defense Ministry, meanwhile, said Russian troops captured the villages of Novovodiane in the Donetsk region and Ulanove in the northern Sumy region.
It was not possible to independently verify the claims.
Zelenskyy said long-range strikes on Russian soil hit two defense plants in the Tula and Voronezh regions and oil facilities in the Krasnodar region, all in southern and western Russia.
Ukraine's long-range drones have repeatedly targeted Russian fuel depots and industrial plants that are a mainstay of Moscow's economy and war effort.
Ukrainian drone attacks overnight started fires at three infrastructure facilities in Russia's Krasnodar region, local emergency officials said Monday, without identifying the locations.
Russia's Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 254 Ukrainian drones overnight.

Tehran gallery traces capital’s past, explores future of smart tourism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:21:27 UTC
22:21:27 KST

Tehran gallery traces capital’s past, explores future of smart tourism
TEHRAN – A new gallery in Tehran is taking visitors on a journey through the capital’s political, social, cultural and artistic history while using digital technology and artificial intelligence to offer a glimpse of how tourism in the city could evolve in the future.
The “Stories of Tehran” gallery opened at the Kushk-e Bagh-e Honar cultural complex in the Abbasabad Cultural and Tourism Zone on Sunday, coinciding with World Tourism Day and Tehran Week. The exhibition runs from September 27 to October 8 under this year’s World Tourism Day theme, “Digital Agenda and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to Redesign Tourism.”
The gallery brings together historical maps, illustrated timelines, infographics, photographs and interactive features, to name a few, to present different chapters of Tehran’s history, from its early development and eventual selection as Iran’s capital to its political and social transformations in the modern era.
Among the subjects presented are some of the city’s earliest known developments, its old plane trees, food culture, historic buildings and major political and cultural events. A section also documents damage inflicted on historic buildings and cultural spaces during the recent war with the US and the Israeli regime.
Seyyed Mohammad-Hossein Hejazi, managing director of the Abbasabad Cultural and Tourism Zone, said the event was designed to introduce Tehran’s tourism attractions and present the city through its past and future.
“Unfortunately, Tehran has mostly been viewed as a transit city in recent years rather than a final destination for tourists,” he told reporters.
Hejazi said the exhibition was part of broader efforts to introduce the capital’s attractions from different perspectives and strengthen its position as a tourism destination.
Digitalization is also being incorporated into plans for tourism services in the Abbasabad zone. Hejazi said Tehran Municipality’s “Shahrzad” application had been linked to a planned tourism card for the Abbasabad area.
The card, which has not yet been launched, is modeled partly on systems such as the Istanbulkart and Dubai Pass, he said. It is expected to eventually provide access to a range of services, including public transportation, museums, recreational facilities and tourism and leisure attractions.
Hejazi said the Abbasabad area had been selected as a pilot site for the initiative and that a trial could potentially begin in the coming months.
The “Stories of Tehran” concept itself dates back to the COVID-19 pandemic, when international tourism came to a halt. According to Alireza Moghaddam-Nia, director of tourism at the Abbasabad zone, the area at the time sought to provide virtual journeys through Tehran by drawing on the knowledge and experiences of tour guides, tourism businesses and other industry stakeholders.
The exhibition’s central timeline stretches across the gallery walls and traces major events in Tehran from the Safavid and Qajar periods to contemporary history. Historical maps of the old city are also eye-catching.
Visitors can hear stories about the city and interact with replicas and toys associated with old Tehran. The exhibition also incorporates elements of the city’s natural heritage, including its long-lived trees, rather than focusing solely on monuments and historical events.
One of the main features is the use of artificial intelligence and digital technology to create interactive tourism experiences. Visitors can take virtual tours of countless locations across Tehran and use a QR-code-based service to create photographs of themselves against images of the city from different periods.
The organizers say the idea is to combine digital tools with physical and immersive experiences rather than allow technology to replace direct engagement with destinations.
“The technology can facilitate tourism services and the travel experience, but it should not replace the tourist’s real experience,” Sara Mirzaei, deputy head of tourism and recreation at the Abbasabad Cultural and Tourism Zone, said.
She cited emerging tools such as smart glasses capable of translation and content generation as examples of technologies that could make travel easier.
The exhibition also looks at the history of the 560-hectare Abbasabad area, which today contains a number of Tehran’s major cultural, tourism and recreational facilities, including the Tabiat Bridge, Ab-o-Atash Park, Mina Dome, Bagh-e Honar, Book Garden and the Museum of the Islamic Revolution and Sacred Defense.
According to Mirzaei, the transformation of the area into a cultural and tourism zone followed years of planning and efforts to determine an appropriate future for the site. The exhibition traces that history and highlights how the area eventually developed into one of Tehran’s major cultural and recreational destinations.
The organizers say the gallery is partly intended to challenge the perception of Tehran as merely a transit point for tourists.
The exhibition also contains a distinctive element looking far beyond the present: a mailbox for letters addressed to Tehran’s mayor in the year 1450 in the Iranian calendar, equivalent to 2071–72.
Visitors are invited to write down their hopes, expectations and ideas for the future of Tehran and place them in the mailbox. The box will be sealed after the exhibition and preserved for opening in 1450.
Mirzaei described the idea as a paradox of the digital age. At a time when physical correspondence has largely given way to email and messaging applications, visitors are being invited to put their thoughts on paper and entrust them to the future.
The juxtaposition is deliberate: an exhibition centered on artificial intelligence and digital tourism has created space for one of the oldest forms of communication, a handwritten letter.
The broader program accompanying the exhibition includes educational panels, specialist workshops and film screenings focusing on smart tourism, tourism platforms, historical urban landscapes, safe travel and new technologies. Other programs comprise a screening of a documentary about the Omidvar brothers, the famed Iranian globetrotters, a workshop on rediscovering Iran and sessions on the role of emerging tourism technologies in developing smart urban economies.
The Abbasabad Cultural and Tourism Zone, described by its organizers as a major green and recreational hub in the capital, is also seeking to strengthen its international tourism profile.

Hong Kong’s checkpoints are expected to handle about 7.44 million passenger trips over mainland China’s National Day “golden week” break, while people movements are anticipated to peak this weekend.
The Immigration Department said on Monday that the figure would include inbound and outbound trips by Hongkongers and visitors travelling via the city’s sea, land and air control points between October 1 and 7.
The department also said it anticipated that the most popular control points would be those at Lo Wu, the Lok Ma Chau Spur line and Shenzhen Bay, but added that none of the city’s checkpoints would have their service hours extended.
Authorities earlier said they expected the city would welcome 1.29 million mainland visitors over the break. Last year’s figure reached 1.4 million thanks to a longer holiday period of eight days that included the Mid-Autumn Festival.

Nvidia said Monday it has authorized an additional $150 billion to its share buyback program, taking its total to $235 billion, amid record spending on artificial intelligence.
The chip giant said it marks the largest share repurchase authorization increase in history. It expects to complete the total remaining buyback program through fiscal 2028.
Nvidia produces the most advanced chips used for AI and has been a huge beneficiary of the boom in spending on the infrastructure needed to power the tech.

Huang earlier this month said Nvidia would double the number of chips it sells in 2027.
Alongside making the leading chips for AI — graphics processing units — including its Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems, the company produces a variety of additional semiconductors. That includes central processors, or CPUs, switch chips, chips for optical networking, chips for laptops, Jetson chips for robots and cars, and the chip inside Nintendo's Switch 2 gaming console.
"I think we're going through the largest infrastructure build-out in human history, and we have the benefit of being a very central part of that," Huang told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Monday.
"We're going to generate a lot of cash in the coming years, and every single year, as we generate more cash, we'd like to be able to return it back to shareholders," he said.

2026-09-28
21:07:02 CST
22:07:02 KST

ZAGREB, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- The Croatian government on Monday announced new fuel prices, raising the price of Eurosuper while lowering the price of diesel.
Eurosuper 95 will rise by 2 cents to 1.76 euros (about 2.01 U.S. dollars) per liter, while the price of Eurodiesel will drop by 5 cents to 1.86 euros (about 2.11 U.S. dollars) per liter. Blue diesel for farmers and fishermen will also drop and will cost 1.42 euros (about 1.62 U.S. dollars) per liter.
The new prices include government subsidies. Without them, they would be higher.
Under Croatia's fuel price system, the government sets temporary ceilings on retail prices, and stations cannot charge more than the limit. The caps are revised every week to follow changes in the global oil market, with the aim of protecting consumers and the wider economy from sudden price spikes.
Global oil prices have fluctuated in recent months amid the crisis in the Middle East, raising concerns over supply and pushing up energy costs worldwide.
The price of blue diesel in Croatia has almost doubled since the beginning of the year, putting additional pressure on farmers and fishermen. Rising fuel prices have also pushed up inflation in Croatia. According to the Croatian Bureau of Statistics, annual inflation stood at 4.2 percent in August. Energy prices rose 17.6 percent year-on-year. ■

21:06:57 CST

KINSHASA, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have surpassed 8,000, the DRC health authorities said Monday, as the World Health Organization (WHO) warned that the outbreak remains large, geographically expanding and marked by sustained transmission.
As of Saturday, the country had recorded 8,067 confirmed cases, including 3,901 deaths, with a case fatality rate of 48.4 percent, according to the latest government situation report released on Monday. A total of 2,070 patients have recovered.
In its latest Disease Outbreak News published Friday, the WHO said the number of new cases reported each day remained high, while transmission intensity varied considerably across affected provinces and health zones.
"The continuously high case fatality ratio, and especially the continuous high rate of deaths occurring in communities, highlights the seriousness of the disease and the persistent challenges in timely case detection and access to early and adequate patient care," the WHO said.
Ituri Province remains the epicenter of the outbreak, but transmission patterns continue to diverge. Incidence in Ituri had declined gradually from a mid-August peak, while North Kivu Province saw a substantial rise that reached its highest reported level in mid-September, according to the WHO. Sustained transmission also continues in Haut-Uele Province, while renewed transmission activity has been reported in Tshopo Province.
The outbreak has now affected 63 health zones across seven provinces. The WHO said the latest geographic expansion, including newly affected areas in Sud-Ubangi and Haut-Uele, had increased the risk of cross-border transmission.
Since it was declared in May, the outbreak has evolved into the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the DRC and the second-largest Ebola outbreak globally, after the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic. ■

HELSINKI, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Andreas Norlen of the Moderate Party was re-elected speaker of parliament on Monday as the newly elected Riksdag, Sweden's parliament, convened for the first time following this month's general elections.
Norlen won 200 votes in a secret ballot, defeating the Social Democratic Party's candidate Johanna Haraldsson, who received 146 votes.
The Moderate Party had nominated Norlen for another term, with the Sweden Democrats, the Christian Democrats and the Liberal Party backing his candidacy. The Left Party also announced ahead of the vote that it would support Norlen, citing his experience as speaker and in overseeing government-formation talks.
The Social Democratic Party requested a secret ballot and nominated Haraldsson, a lawmaker from southern Sweden's Jonkoping County, as their candidate.
Norlen, who has served as speaker since 2018, will now continue to oversee the process of forming Sweden's next government.
Earlier on Monday, the Social Democratic Party leader and former Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson announced that she would return the exploratory mandate she received from Norlen on Sept. 18 to explore the possibility of forming a new government.
Andersson said the Left Party's decision to support Norlen had created what she described as a new parliamentary constellation and that she currently saw no conditions for forming a government herself.
The Left Party rejected the suggestion that its support for Norlen amounted to a political alliance with the Moderate Party, saying the decision was based on his experience as speaker.
Sweden held its parliamentary election on Sept. 13. The Social Democratic Party, Left Party, Green Party and Centre Party won a combined 176 seats in the 349-seat parliament, while the Moderate Party, Sweden Democrats, Christian Democrats and the Liberal Party secured 173 seats.
Outgoing Prime Minister and Moderate Party leader Ulf Kristersson tendered his resignation following the election. Under Sweden's constitutional system, the speaker consults the parties and proposes a candidate for prime minister. ■

SpaceX’s Starship lifts off in make-or-break orbital test flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:06:27 UTC
22:06:27 KST

SpaceX’s Starship is on a mission to prove itself. The largest rocket ever built lifted off from the company’s Starbase facility in South Texas on Monday at 8:49 A.M. EDT, soaring toward space atop its giant Super Heavy booster. This test flight—the 14th fully integrated launch—was more than just another Starship shakedown: it marked the first time the enormous spacecraft has propelled itself into orbit around Earth.
The first orbital flight puts Starship over its biggest hurdle yet in SpaceX’s race to make the vehicle its new workhorse for space launches, replacing the wildly successful Falcon 9. Yet issues along the way—the flight was meant to last hours longer than it did—served as a potent reminder of just how audacious SpaceX’s hopes for Starship really are—and how far the company must go to build a robust, reliable orbital transportation system.
Flight 14’s vehicle is the third-generation version of Starship, standing about 124 meters (407 feet) tall when stacked with its Super Heavy booster. That first stage, Booster 21, powered the vehicle upward using 33 Raptor 3 engines. After stage separation, Booster 21 performed a controlled return and splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Meanwhile, Starship accelerated toward orbit. About 25 minutes after liftoff, it reignited one of its three sea-level Raptor engines to raise and circularize its trajectory. (The ship also carries three vacuum-rated Raptor engines for in-space maneuvers.) Incredibly, SpaceX seemed unsure as to whether to push ahead to orbit, calling off that part of the test for a brief moment before deciding to go for orbit minutes later.
At that point, Starship became an orbital spacecraft. The vehicle reached an altitude of roughly 275 kilometers. Along the way, it deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites—the first operational payloads to be carried to orbit by Starship. Three of those satellites also beamed back imagery of Starship’s heat shield, which must remain intact to ensure the spacecraft doesn’t break apart and burn up during reentry.
SpaceX had originally planned a 10-hour mission that would see Starship orbit the globe at least six times, but a little over an hour and a half into the flight, SpaceX made the call to bring Starship back to Earth early. Starship performed a deorbit burn at approximately 11 A.M. EDT and re-entered Earth’s atmosphere at around 11:40 A.M. The ship performed a controlled splashdown in the Pacific Ocean at 11:58 A.M.
A test of SpaceX’s grand vision
Starship occupies an unusual place in the history of rocketry. Unlike all previous launch systems, it’s designed to be fully reusable: both the Super Heavy booster and the Starship spacecraft would be recovered and flown repeatedly in normal operations.
Intended to carry both crew and cargo, Starship is the linchpin of SpaceX’s grand vision of launching a million data center satellites into orbit and separately sending astronauts to the moon and, eventually, to Mars.
That radical vision has depended on a chain of technological achievements: entering orbit, deploying payloads, surviving reentry, making pinpoint landings and achieving smooth recoveries—and then repeating the sequence flawlessly, again and again, to reach the frequency of flights necessary to make Starship’s economics work.
Today’s flight did not prove all of those things—and nor was it supposed to. Neither the Starship or booster attempted a tower catch (that may happen during the next test flight, according to SpaceX), and Flight 14 didn’t demonstrate any of the daunting orbital propellant transfers required for missions to the moon or Mars.
For more than three years, Starship’s development has been defined by a series of spectacular successes and failures, accruing incremental progress in between. The fourth flight, in 2024, demonstrated controlled splashdowns of both stages. Flight 5 saw the first-ever tower catch—a dramatic recovery of a Super Heavy booster using the launch tower’s mechanical arms. Later launches introduced major vehicle upgrades, including the current third-generation Starship. Flights 12 and 13 successfully tested this new generation, although the booster on Flight 13 was lost during landing.
A major failure during Flight 14 wouldn’t have doomed SpaceX’s plans for Starship—but it would have complicated them. The company uses a “test to failure” philosophy, pushing its systems to their limits to identify problems. Flight 14 didn’t deliver on all its aims—it was supposed to orbit Earth at least six times—but the fact that it deployed its payload and got in and out of orbit safely nonetheless could minimize any tinkering before the next test.
To the moon and beyond
Of all Starship’s promises, the most notable may be the vehicle’s role in NASA’s Artemis program to return astronauts to the moon. The space agency has selected a version of Starship as one of two potential Human Landing Systems (HLS) for Artemis. Under the current plan, SpaceX is developing Starship HLS for Artemis III—a low-Earth orbit test mission in 2027—and for a crewed lunar landing, the Artemis IV mission, in 2028.
That version of Starship must be refueled in Earth orbit via a succession of tanker flights by other Starships before heading to the moon. The Starship would then depart Earth orbit, travel to lunar orbit and rendezvous with astronauts there for a down-and-back foray to the moon’s surface. NASA’s inspector general has said this will require more than 10 tanker flights, with the first refueling beginning more than 200 days before the crewed mission.
That is a wildly ambitious plan. And it means the largely successful nature of today’s orbital test is not merely be good news for SpaceX. It could also reduce one of the fundamental uncertainties hanging over NASA’s lunar plans, adding credibility to the space agency’s controversial Artemis architecture.
NASA’s inspector general also concluded earlier this year that Starship HLS is behind schedule for future Artemis missions, warning that further technical problems could spiral into greater delays for the entire program. This no doubt contributed to NASA’s decision to shift an actual crewed landing from Artemis III to Artemis IV, and it reinforces the space agency’s choice to also pursue Blue Origin’s Blue Moon vehicle as another Human Landing System, creating some redundancy in the lunar architecture.
But after Blue Moon’s ride to space, Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket, suffered a catastrophic explosion on the launch pad during preflight testing in late May of this year, the status of this second option for Artemis lunar missions is also in question.
This makes it hard to understate NASA’s reliance on Starship—and hence on a successful Flight 14—for keeping Artemis on schedule.

SpaceX’s Starship makes orbital debut deploying Starlinks before early ending
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:03:05 UTC
22:03:05 KST

SpaceX’s Starship makes orbital debut deploying Starlinks before early ending
TEXAS - SpaceX’s next-generation Starship rocket reached orbit for the first time despite an unexpected engine shutdown mid-flight on Sept 28 and deployed the first batch of new Starlink satellites, but the mission was cut short and ended with a controlled and fiery touchdown in the Pacific.
The uncrewed 40-story-tall vehicle, consisting of a Super Heavy booster rocket topped by the main upper-stage Starship vessel, thundered off its launch pad from SpaceX’s Starbase complex along the Gulf of Mexico near Brownsville.
The mission was scheduled to last 10 hours, but was reduced to three hours after the engine problem. Launching from Texas, it was the rocket’s 14th flight since 2023, as Elon Musk’s company plans to put the vehicle into routine use starting later this year.
The Super Heavy booster lofted the Starship upper stage into space before returning itself to Gulf waters for an engine-controlled splashdown, following hard landings for the booster on two previous missions.
Upon reaching space, one of Starship’s three main engines shut down earlier than planned, a development that led SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot to announce on the company’s live stream of the mission that the craft would be unable to reach orbit.
“The team has made the call not to commit to orbit,” Huot said.
But Huot reversed course minutes later after an update from engineers confirmed that the craft could still attempt an engine firing that would boost it into orbit, which Starship successfully did minutes later.
Once in orbit, Starship began deploying 26 next-generation Starlink satellites one by one at a planned altitude of roughly 269 km.
Starship, built to launch SpaceX’s Starlink satellites more frequently and carry future NASA missions to the moon, was expected to complete six Earth orbits during a 10-hour voyage — its longest yet — before splashing down in the Pacific Ocean west of Chile.
Reaching orbit, a primary benchmark for any new rocket designed to deliver payloads to space, has been a long-delayed feat for Starship, which Musk once predicted would be achieved in 2022, to be followed by satellite deployments in 2023.
Since 2023, however, all 13 of Starship’s previous test flights have been limited to suborbital space, despite a nearly decade-long development campaign that has cost SpaceX more than $15 billion to date. Musk has said he envisions ultimately flying hundreds or thousands of Starships a year, a launch pace unprecedented in the space industry.
Test mission with real payload
The voyage on Sept 28 technically counts as the 14th test flight of Starship. But it is nonetheless carrying the group of new Starlink internet satellites potentially worth millions of dollars, the first orbital payload for Starship.
Analysts estimate the launch on Sept 28 of SpaceX’s new V3 Starlink satellites equals hundreds of millions of dollars in projected revenue for the company’s Starlink unit, based on the network's added customer capacity - underscoring Starship's fundamental role in serving the company's profit nucleus.
According to SpaceX, the V3 Starlink satellites on the mission on Sept 28 can handle 10 times more data than their predecessor V2 mini-sats that the company has been launching 20 or 30 at a time on its workhorse Falcon 9 rockets.
Seeking to build out his broadband satellite constellation at a faster pace, Musk wants to launch the higher-capacity V3s in batches of 60 per launch once Starship goes into routine operation, a goal he now aims to reach late in 2026.
Starship’s planned orbital debut also comes three months after SpaceX went public with a record-shattering IPO in June that made it the sixth-biggest US company by value and turned Musk, who founded the company in 2002, into the world's first trillionaire.
Much of SpaceX’s market worth and continued investor confidence in the company — valued at $2 trillion as of Sept 25's close — rides on the success of Starship, which was designed as the world's first fully reusable spacecraft.
The silver-coloured, multi-finned rocket ship will be key to achieving Musk’s ambitions of slashing launch costs, vastly expanding his Starlink business and deploying thousands of orbital AI data centres to space.
Starship is also set to play a pivotal role in NASA’s Artemis programme, which aims to return astronauts to the moon’s surface for the first time since 1972 and build a long-term lunar presence as a stepping stone to eventual human exploration of Mars.
As a measure of Starship’s integral place in SpaceX’s corporate future, investors wiped roughly US$100 billion off SpaceX’s market value after test flight 13 was aborted at the last second in July. The flight ultimately got off the ground five days later.
Surviving the return to Earth
One critical objective for Starship’s 14th outing will be surviving its return flight to Earth, starting with the deorbital firing of one Raptor engine while in space and precisely angling the vehicle for atmospheric re-entry.
The spacecraft’s final controlled descent is designed to culminate with a thruster manoeuvre to flip the vehicle vertically so that it hits the sea in a nose-up position. While future missions call for Starship to execute a similar touchdown on land back in Texas, no recovery of the spacecraft is planned for its latest flight, contrary to Musk’s previous hopes. In run for Brazil's presidency, Flavio Bolsonaro tests staying power of his father's legacy

In run for Brazil's presidency, Flavio Bolsonaro tests staying power of his father's legacy
SAO PAULO, Sept 28 - From the bare-walled, 12-square-meter cell where he was serving a 27-year sentence for a failed coup plot, former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro passed his most prized asset to his eldest son: his blessing to follow in his political footsteps in 2026.
"Let's go, it's you," Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the main right-wing candidate in the October 4 presidential election, remembers his father telling him in late 2025, over the rattle of the cell's air-conditioning unit.
The younger Bolsonaro immediately accepted the mission: "He was humiliated and convicted because the system did not want him in public life," he told Reuters last December, soon after announcing his candidacy for the presidency.
The two men now have a chance to exact revenge on the politicians, judges and special interests they blame for driving Jair Bolsonaro from public life and ending his far-right, populist makeover of Latin America's largest economy.
The 45-year-old senator is polling neck and neck with leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who has long been one of the region's most powerful figures and is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term.
The strength of Bolsonaro's bid, and the loyalty of the right-wing electorate to the former president, have turned Brazil into a test case for a belief embraced by many on the left around the world: that prosecuting and imprisoning a populist leader can contain the movement he or she built.
Carlos Melo, a professor of politics at Sao Paulo's Insper institution, said that former President Bolsonaro may be the most vocal figurehead of a movement that has long existed in Brazil and worldwide.
"The far-right goes beyond Bolsonaro," he added.
'IT HAD TO BE A BOLSONARO'
The competitiveness of the younger Bolsonaro's bid for power came as a surprise to many.
Unlike his brothers, he had faced corruption allegations, including leading an alleged kickback scheme that prosecutors said benefited relatives of Adriano da Nobrega, a former police officer accused of heading a gang of hired killers.
Of the former president's three eldest sons, the senator was also the least combative, softening the edge that was central to his father's rise and presenting himself as a "more centered Bolsonaro."
The announcement of his candidacy rattled markets, with bankers alternating between high-level meetings and cautious distance for much of the campaign.
Other conservative parties were skeptical, too, with some right-wing candidates announcing their own bids for the presidency.
For months, Flavio Bolsonaro tried and failed to convince others to join his ticket, ultimately settling on a little-known lawmaker from his own Liberal Party as his running mate.
"There was an initial lack of communication, owing perhaps to Flavio's first presidential run," said conservative Senator Tereza Cristina, a prominent agribusiness leader who was prevented from accepting the role of Bolsonaro's running mate by her party's leadership.
Still, Liberal Party loyalists seemed confident of their choice.
"It had to be a Bolsonaro," Valdemar Costa Neto, the head of the Liberal Party, told Reuters.
GLOBAL CONSERVATIVE EMBRACE
Despite the initial sour welcome at home, Senator Bolsonaro's bid was quickly embraced by the global conservative movement, which is eager to see Brazil join the regional right-wing wave that has brought Argentina's Javier Milei, El Salvador's Nayib Bukele and Ecuador's Daniel Noboa to power.
Senator Bolsonaro has followed the same playbook as many of those Latin American right-wing populists, uniting conservative factions around Christian traditionalism, free-market economics, and a fierce hostility to the left.
He is pledging to cut taxes and embark on an aggressive fiscal adjustment to lower long-term borrowing costs in Brazil. The platform has pleased the business community and investors, though economists say the proposals are short on specifics.
"Flavio sees a broader global realignment at stake and wants to be part of it," said Paulo Kramer, a political scientist and former campaign adviser to Jair Bolsonaro.
With the help of his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who was removed from his position as a member of the Brazilian Congress after he moved to the US, Flavio Bolsonaro managed at the end of May to get a meeting with US President Donald Trump, who described him as "a smart young man who loves his country, Brazil, very much!"
During his first term in the White House, Trump established a close political and personal friendship with Jair Bolsonaro. Flavio Bolsonaro's attempt to rekindle that alliance, however, has left many Brazilians cold.
His meeting with Trump was preceded by Washington's announcement of steep tariffs on Brazilian imports, giving Lula an opportunity to brand Flavio and Eduardo Bolsonaro as "traitors."
Polls showed Brazilians blamed the Bolsonaros more than Lula for the tariffs, which were imposed in July.
"I don't think President Trump has helped Flavio at all," said Thomas Shannon, who served as a U.S. ambassador to Brazil during the Obama administration. "I think that was more harmful to Flavio."
DARK HORSE
Having overcome the initial skepticism over his candidacy, Senator Bolsonaro's campaign faced its biggest blow in May, after an investigation revealed he had asked a disgraced banker, who was accused of leading a multibillion-dollar fraud scheme, for money to fund a Hollywood biopic of Jair Bolsonaro.
Production contracts outlined $12 million in transfers from a fund connected to the banker, Daniel Vorcaro, to a U.S. fund managed by an attorney representing Eduardo Bolsonaro.
After first denying involvement, Flavio Bolsonaro admitted that the banker had funded the movie, but maintained there was no wrongdoing, merely "a private sponsorship, with no strings attached."
The revelation, however, triggered swift backlash. The senator saw his support drop in polls and some of his allies turned openly critical. Romeu Zema, a businessman who is also running for the presidency, called it "a slap in the face."
Newly unsealed court records revealed that the Federal Police in July had opened an investigation into Flavio Bolsonaro for corruption, money laundering, and illicit capital flight linked to the movie project.
He dismissed the probe as a "political hit job" and has since recovered in the polls with less than two weeks to go before the first round of voting. A second round will be held on October 25 if no candidate wins a simple majority. If Bolsonaro wins, he would be sworn in some four years after thousands of supporters of his father rampaged through Congress, the Supreme Court and the presidential offices, smashing windows, furniture and artwork in the worst attack on state institutions since Brazil's return to democracy in the 1980s.
The prospect of a Bolsonaro returning to the Planalto Palace in Brasilia where presidents carry out their duties is raising the possibility of fresh institutional clashes.
If elected, Flavio Bolsonaro would likely move quickly to undo two legal blows to his family: his father's house arrest in Brasilia and Eduardo Bolsonaro's conviction for coercion related to a U.S. lobbying campaign that prosecutors said sought to pressure Brazilian Supreme Court justices not to convict the former president.
Freeing his father is Flavio Bolsonaro's main goal, something the presidential candidate alluded to during an Independence Day rally earlier this month.
"I ask God for the opportunity to walk up the ramp of Planalto Palace next year alongside President Jair Messias Bolsonaro, so that he may place the presidential sash across my chest," he said. REUTERS

How adults feel about their ADHD depends heavily on their specific symptoms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:00:42 UTC
22:00:42 KST

A new study published in the Journal of Attention Disorders suggests that how adults feel about their attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder depends on their specific symptoms. Researchers found that individuals with higher levels of hyperactive and impulsive symptoms tend to view their condition more positively, while those with primarily inattentive symptoms are less likely to see their diagnosis as an advantage. These findings highlight the diverse ways people experience and interpret their neurodevelopmental differences.
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, commonly known as ADHD, is a condition that begins in childhood and often continues into adulthood. The diagnosis is based on two main categories of symptoms. The first is inattention, which involves difficulty focusing, sustaining attention, or staying organized. The second category is hyperactivity and impulsivity, characterized by excessive physical movement, restlessness, or acting without thinking. For many years, medical and psychological research focused heavily on the negative impacts of these symptoms, such as difficulties in school, struggles with emotional regulation, and challenges in relationships.
Recently, the rise of the neurodiversity movement has encouraged scientists to look at the other side of the coin. Earlier qualitative studies gathered personal stories showing that people with ADHD often identify real strengths and silver linings in their condition. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that adults diagnosed with ADHD reported experiencing notable personal strengths, identifying positive themes like high energy, unconventional thinking, and a drive for novelty. Similarly, a 2018 interview-based study revealed that many adults with ADHD identify distinct personal strengths and resilience linked directly to their diagnosis.
This qualitative foundation sparked recent efforts to study these positives numerically. A 2024 study took early steps to measure these strengths, finding that people with more ADHD traits in the general population also scored higher on traits like cognitive flexibility and sensory processing sensitivity. The new research, led by Gili Katabi of Tel-Aviv University, builds on this momentum by creating a formal scale to measure positive attitudes toward ADHD. The authors wanted to test whether these positive feelings depend on whether someone’s symptoms are mostly hyperactive or mostly inattentive.
To explore this, the researchers developed the Positive Attitudes Toward ADHD Scale. This questionnaire was designed to capture how individuals perceive the positive aspects of their own condition, based on themes from previous interviews like creativity, dynamic energy, and resilience. Participants rated their agreement with various statements on a five-point scale. The team then recruited three distinct groups of adults with ADHD to test the scale and see how scores related to symptom types.
The first sample included 84 young adults in Israel with formal ADHD diagnoses who completed the questionnaires in a laboratory setting. This initial group helped the researchers confirm that the new scale was reliable and captured a wide range of attitudes. The second sample involved 125 adults in Israel who also participated in the lab. For this group, the researchers conducted structured clinical interviews by phone to verify that the participants still met the criteria for ADHD at the time of testing, while excluding those with heavy alcohol or cannabis use.
The third sample was an online group of 126 English-speaking adults residing in 24 different countries. These participants provided detailed written information about their diagnosis and treatment history to confirm their status. Across all three groups, participants filled out the new attitude scale alongside a widely used checklist that measures the frequency of their inattentive and hyperactive/impulsive symptoms over the past six months.
When analyzing the results, the researchers found that more frequent ADHD symptoms overall were associated with more favorable attitudes toward the condition. However, breaking the symptoms down into the two main categories painted a more detailed picture. Across all three samples, a higher frequency of hyperactive and impulsive symptoms strongly predicted more positive attitudes toward having ADHD.
In contrast, inattention symptoms showed a very different pattern. Higher levels of inattention tended to associate with less positive attitudes toward the condition, though this negative association was not statistically significant across every sample. The researchers also ran a follow-up test with 35 participants from the second sample to measure their general life satisfaction. They found that the link between hyperactive symptoms and positive attitudes remained distinct, indicating that the new scale was capturing specific feelings about ADHD rather than just a generally happy outlook on life.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that young adult hyperactivity and impulsivity predicted higher relationship and job satisfaction later in life. Together, this body of research suggests that the physical and mental energy associated with hyperactivity might foster traits like curiosity and enthusiasm that people learn to appreciate over time.
There are a few things to keep in mind about these findings. The new scale relies entirely on self-reporting, meaning it captures how people feel about their own condition, not objective measurements of their abilities. Endorsing statements about creativity or flexibility does not necessarily mean a person would score higher on a behavioral test of divergent thinking. The study focuses on subjective opinions, which are important for understanding self-esteem and coping, but are separate from observable advantages.
Another detail to consider is the potential for reporting biases based on how society views different symptoms. Hyperactive and impulsive traits might be easier to reframe in a positive light, such as viewing restlessness as boundless energy. Inattentive traits, like spacing out or forgetting things, might feel less socially acceptable and harder to spin positively. Additionally, the researchers noted that their scale did not include questions about hyperfocus, a common experience where people with ADHD become intensely absorbed in tasks they find interesting, which might have skewed the results away from the inattentive dimension.
Future studies could incorporate reports from friends or family members to provide a more rounded view of how these traits manifest in daily life. Scientists might also test whether these contrasting attitudes exist in children and adolescents, or if they are unique to adults who have had more time to adapt to their neurodevelopmental differences.
The study, “ADHD Individuals’ Positivity About Their Condition Varies by Their Levels of Hyperactivity/Impulsivity Versus Inattention Symptoms,” was authored by Gili Katabi, Merav Huss, Steve Lukito, Tycho J. Dekkers, Edmund Sonuga-Barke, and Nitzan Shahar.
