Dogmatic beliefs about sex and gender are linked to authoritarianism on both the left and the right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:00:33 UTC
19:00:33 KST

A new study published in Archives of Sexual Behavior indicates that rigid, dogmatic thinking about sex and gender exists on both ends of the political spectrum. The research suggests that while viewing gender as strictly binary and fixed is tied to conservative authoritarianism, believing gender is fluid and nonbinary is similarly associated with progressive authoritarianism.
In the social sciences, “sex” generally refers to biological characteristics like chromosomes and anatomy, while “gender” describes an individual’s psychological identity and social role. People tend to hold differing beliefs about how these two concepts interact. Some view sex and gender as firmly binary and permanently fixed at birth, viewing male and female as the only options. Others see gender as a spectrum that can change and operates independently of biological sex.
Previous research investigating the psychology behind these views has often linked a strictly binary perspective to right-wing authoritarianism. For instance, a 2021 study found that people who strongly favor submitting to traditional societal authorities also tend to hold rigid beliefs about traditional gender roles. This body of work painted a picture of conservative ideology as a primary driver of dogmatic views on gender.
“We found that, to date, there have been several empirical studies regarding the relationship between right-wing authoritarianism and beliefs regarding whether human sex or gender are binary or not,” Alex Bertrams, a researcher at the University of Bern, told PsyPost. “However, what had been completely absent until now were studies examining how sex/gender beliefs are related to left-wing authoritarianism.”
However, separate psychological research points out that authoritarian tendencies can also occur on the political left. A 2020 study established a model of left-wing authoritarianism, noting a specific urge among some progressives to aggressively enforce unconventional norms. This aligns with a study covered by PsyPost in 2025, which identified anti-conventionalism as a distinct component of left-wing authoritarian beliefs, characterized by a demand for political homogeneity and the absolute rejection of conservative values.
Bertrams and Ann Krispenz conducted the new study to connect these two lines of research, suspecting that authoritarianism plays a role in modern gender debates regardless of which side someone takes. “In addition, we noticed that certain ideological circles (also within universities) label those beliefs toward sex and gender which do not align with their own progressive views as ‘authoritarian’ or even ‘fascist,'” the researchers said. “However, certain morally overbearing forms of advocacy for progressive sex/gender beliefs may also be authoritarian – but left-wing authoritarian.”
The research team set out to test whether an anti-conventional, progressive view of gender is just as linked to left-wing authoritarianism as traditional gender views are to right-wing authoritarianism. “It is not a secret that the social sciences, including psychology, are ideologically biased these days by progressive views,” they added. “Part of our motivation was the desire to counteract this questionable situation, even if only a little, by conducting respective empirical research. In our view, it is not an appropriate role for publicly funded universities to one-sidedly provide material for the rhetorical manipulation of the population.”
To investigate this, the researchers conducted two separate online surveys. In the first study, they recruited 1,431 adults from the United States. Participants answered questions to measure their beliefs about sex and gender on a continuous scale, and they also answered a simple question about whether there are only two genders. In this sample, 57 percent stated there are only two genders, and 43 percent stated there are more than two.
The participants also completed psychological assessments measuring two specific types of authoritarianism. The first was right-wing authoritarian conventionalism, which is the desire to force everyone in society to comply with traditional moral standards. The second was left-wing authoritarian anti-conventionalism, which is the desire to force everyone to adopt progressive values while treating conservative views as inherently immoral.
The researchers found a strong relationship between the participants’ gender beliefs and their authoritarian tendencies. Believing that gender is binary and fixed was strongly associated with right-wing conventionalism. Believing that gender is nonbinary and changeable was strongly associated with left-wing anti-conventionalism. These relationships remained robust even after the researchers accounted for demographic differences like age, income, and general political orientation.
“We generally found strong associations between the sex/gender beliefs and the investigated forms of left- and right-wing authoritarianism,” the researchers noted. “Given the conceptual proximity of the sex/gender beliefs on the one hand and the ideological underpinnings of these authoritarianism forms on the other hand, this was not particularly surprising. After all, our goal was not to investigate something particularly sensational but something obvious for the purpose of filling a gap in research that had not been addressed until now.”
In the second study, the researchers recruited 1,390 adults from the United Kingdom to see if the pattern held in a different culture. They used the same measures for gender beliefs, right-wing conventionalism, and left-wing anti-conventionalism. In this British sample, 68 percent of participants endorsed a binary view of gender, and 32 percent endorsed a nonbinary view.
This second study also measured additional authoritarian traits, including social dominance orientation, right-wing aggression, left-wing anti-hierarchical aggression, and the desire for top-down censorship. The findings mirrored the first study, showing that binary beliefs were strongly linked to right-wing conventionalism and nonbinary beliefs were strongly linked to left-wing anti-conventionalism. The researchers noted that conventionalism and anti-conventionalism were the strongest predictors of gender beliefs, standing out above the other authoritarian traits like aggression or the desire for censorship.
This replication across datasets was a key part of the team’s methodology. “In contrast to many psychological studies conducted to date, our study (including the hypotheses as well as the methodology and data analysis) was pre-registered and adheres to open science standards,” they explained. “In addition, our study includes two independent samples from different countries, meaning that the findings from the first sample were replicated in a second sample.”
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2020, which found that right-leaning ideology is strongly linked to holding rigid, binary beliefs about sex and gender. The new research adds depth to this by demonstrating a parallel relationship on the political left, while looking specifically at right-wing authoritarian conventionalism rather than general political conservatism.
“From our perspective, our study can help to counter misleading rhetoric,” the researchers noted. “If certain people label a particular belief about sex and gender as the viewpoint of (right-wing) authoritarians—and in doing so imply that their own position is therefore the only correct option—one can counter this viewpoint by citing our study results which contradict this characterization. Our findings suggest that very different, even contradicting, views on sex and gender can be held by authoritarian individuals on the left and the right. It is therefore inappropriate to make a one-sided association between a particular sex/gender belief and authoritarianism.”
As with all research, there are a few caveats to consider. The study measured correlations, meaning it cannot determine whether holding a specific gender belief makes someone more authoritarian, or if naturally authoritarian people just gravitate toward strict rules about gender. The researchers also caution against assuming that any specific belief about gender is inherently authoritarian on its own.
Many people hold binary or nonbinary views on gender without having any desire to force those views on others. The study simply indicates that people who do possess highly controlling, authoritarian personalities tend to attach themselves strongly to these distinct gender ideologies. “Whatever one believes about the binary or non-binary nature of sex and gender and whether or not people can freely determine their own sex and gender, one can also express and advocate for the respective view in a non-authoritarian way,” the researchers clarified.
Future work will need to explore whether these patterns appear in countries outside the United States and the United Kingdom, and whether deeper personality traits like narcissism help explain why some people adopt highly authoritarian approaches to gender debates. “Our research is not specifically focused on sex/gender beliefs, but rather on the diverse phenomena that could be explained by the dark-ego-vehicle principle,” the researchers said.
“According to this approach, individuals with dark (e.g., narcissistic or psychopathic) personalities tend to use ideologies and activism as vehicles to satisfy their dark needs (e.g., expressing supposed moral superiority over others, acting out aggression at protests),” they explained.
“We have already found some evidence that authoritarianism may be useful for dark personalities in this regard,” they continued. “In a study that was just published, we also found evidence that ideologically completely opposed stances may be useful vehicles for dark personalities. In this new study, antagonistic narcissism was associated with abortion-related radicalization intention, that is, the intention to also use illegal and violent means.”
This willingness to use extreme tactics was present regardless of the cause. “The key point is that this was true for both the individuals of the pro-choice as well as the pro-life group,” the researchers noted. “We believe that political activism on sex/gender issues is also a useful way to investigate the dark-ego-vehicle principle in terms of opposing ideological perspectives in future studies.”
The study, “Sex/Gender Beliefs are Strongly Related to Either Right‑Wing Authoritarian Conventionalism or Left‑Wing Authoritarian Anti‑Conventionalism,” was authored by Alex Bertrams and Ann Krispenz.

Money Reveals What Kind of Friend You Are
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:00:06 UTC
19:00:06 KST

There is a scene in season two of Friends I think about often. Rachel, Phoebe, and Joey, who have low-paying jobs, decide to have a serious conversation with their more wealthy friends —Ross, Monica, and Chandler—about struggling to pay for expensive group dinners and concert tickets.
Ross says he never thinks about money, prompting Rachel’s famous line, “That’s because you have it!”
Even though this scene aired in 1995, the same dynamic continues to play out in friendships in 2026.
Last year, my friend wanted to have a birthday dinner at Carbone in London, an Italian restaurant that is arguably more famous for celebrity sightings than its actual food. My friend works full-time at a national magazine, whereas I’m a freelancer. Everyone else cancelled on her birthday, so it was just the two of us. I felt bad for her, so I didn’t mind spending $75 on food. But a few months later, when it was time to plan my birthday, I couldn’t imagine asking any of my friends to spend the same amount on me just to visit a fancy restaurant. It felt like an extortionate amount of money. It felt tone deaf and entitled. So I hosted a house party instead and asked everyone to bring pizza.
Another friend recently ranted to me about how she has spent more than $10,000 over the last year attending destination weddings and bachelorette parties. And while she is, of course, ultimately responsible for her decision to oblige, she has also noticed that the financial pressure to participate in expensive wedding culture tends to breed unnecessary, quiet resentment among her friends. This pattern is painfully, but subtly, common.
Money can shape friendships and also reveal people’s values. The wealth gap between friends doesn’t necessarily cause dramatic fights or resentment. More often, it shows up in the small decisions: where you eat, which holidays you can afford, whether you can join a last-minute night out, or whether suggesting an expensive activity feels embarrassing in the first place.
And unlike romantic relationships, where finances are often explicitly discussed, friends rarely sit down and talk about the fact that one person earns significantly more than another. Instead, the person with less money can become the one who compromises or simply starts opting out.
The way we handle money with our friends reveals a lot about our values, particularly when there is a significant wealth gap. Someone who can comfortably spend lavishly on a dinner, holiday, or birthday celebration may not realize that they're effectively asking a friend with less disposable income to make a significant financial sacrifice to participate.
The problem is widespread. Too often people go into debt in order to attend a friend’s bachelorette. Then there’s Venmo ghosting where people avoid repaying their friends after a shared bill. When friends repeatedly avoid paying someone back, the problem is that one person is comfortable making another person carry the financial burden.
Money and conversations around money are taboo in our society, says psychotherapist Silvia Dutchevici, a licensed clinical social worker. “In my practice, I’ve seen patients share their most intense fears and sexual desires with little reservation, and then become visibly uncomfortable when asked about their salary, or naming the amount of a bonus or raise.” Think about it: how many of us actually know how much money our friends have or the salaries they make?
Money, it turns out, is never just money. It’s a modern measurement of traits like freedom, prestige, power, and control. Our society implicitly and explicitly sends the message that money is equivalent to worth. “Neoliberal ideology tells us that financial success is the result of hard work, and that poverty is a personal failure rather than a systemic problem,” points out Dutchevici. When two friends have very different financial circumstances, acknowledging the gap can feel like saying something about who is more deserving, or who is less hard working.
Both sides can carry shame. The friend with less money may feel judged or inadequate. Meanwhile, many affluent people also carry a deep shame around wealth, feel undeserving of it, and hide their financial means. “I once worked with a woman set to inherit millions who felt she couldn’t accept it until she had proved her worth by earning her own,” says Dutchevici.
It is interesting to witness how wealth inequality is reshaping friendships, particularly as the cost of living continues to rise and people in the same social circles can have wildly different disposable incomes. Many of my friends have had their parents buy them houses, so their entire salary is spent on holidays, shopping, and frivolous hobbies. My paycheck, in contrast, goes towards rent and covering my basic needs. This inherently changes how we spend our days.
There is an emotional side of the friendship wealth divide, too: the guilt of saying no, the shame of admitting you can’t afford something, the resentment that can build when one friend gets to choose the restaurant or holiday, and the awkwardness of accepting that in the face of a high price tag. All of these pressures have led me to believe that friendship requires more financial negotiation than it once did.
We need new etiquette around money in friendship. What does it look like to make plans that don’t automatically exclude the least wealthy person in the group? Can friends with very different incomes maintain genuine equality? What happens when one person’s idea of a casual dinner is another person’s weekly food budget?
These conversations don’t have to be complicated. Last week, my friend who works in radiology picked a sushi restaurant with a $40 per-person menu. “Is $40 okay for you? We can go somewhere else if not,” she said in a casual tone on the phone. I appreciated her thoughtfulness and conscientiousness. The end result: a closer friendship and no resentment.
Friendship has its own financial morality. Being a good friend means being conscious of what your choices cost other people, not assuming everyone can afford your lifestyle, paying people back without being chased, and being willing to compromise.
The wealth gap simply makes those values much more visible. And money reveals how we treat the people we claim to care about.

AI Agents Are About to Flood the Workforce. No One’s Ready for It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

In the coming months, hundreds of thousands of brand-new coworkers will be entering the workforce. You’ll learn their names and recognize their profile pictures. They’ll get added to your email chains and Slack channels. They’ll become chiefs of staff, engineers, and marketing gurus.
But these coworkers aren’t human: They are all artificial intelligence agents.
The rise of AI agents—systems, based on large language models, designed to complete tasks autonomously—has launched a tsunami of companies selling the services of digital employees. These agents are supposed to be the perfect worker bees: available 24/7, never complaining, and providing superhuman intelligence.
Yet there has been curiously little discussion of what these agents are like as actual coworkers. Julie Bedard, a Boston Consulting Group partner, noticed the murky nature of how people talked about AI at work three years ago, as rapid adoption of ChatGPT convinced executives the technology could bring exponential improvements in productivity.
“People didn't have language for it,” Bedard tells WIRED. “Is it a tool? Is it a teammate? Is it a colleague? Is it a coworker?”
When platforms such as Microsoft’s Copilot and Google’s Gemini for Workspace launched in 2023, they were marketed primarily as tools for employees. But in January, when Bedard and colleagues polled 1,261 managers, 22 percent said their organizations had added AI agents to corporate org charts. Bedard said that this percentage is likely to grow as dozens of startups offer up the services of AI employees and big tech companies hype their autonomous agents. In June, for example, Microsoft launched “Scout,” an agent built to complete tasks like rescheduling meetings and drafting emails.
“Your company essentially hires your assistant,” Omar Shahine, the corporate vice president of Microsoft Scout, said when the agent launched. “The whole point of having a personal assistant is that they're working when you're not working.”
The success of AI agents depends not only on their ability to provide financial returns, but also to work harmoniously alongside the existing workforce. That means companies have crafted agents that boast the benefits of AI, packaged in a human-like bundle of traits to encourage employees to anthropomorphize their new colleagues.
“People start to really respect the agent and form strong attachments," says Dhruv Amin, cofounder of Anything, a vibe coding startup that entered the AI coworker market in August with a platform called Skydive. “They'll talk about it like humans.”
Skydive’s agents “aren’t chatbots or workflows,” but coworkers, with their own names, roles, and cloud computers. They work across Slack, email, iMessage, and more. Each is represented by a Muppet-esque avatar, which Amin described as “close to human, but definitely not human.” They have names often related to their roles; Canary, for instance, monitors production 24/7.
“We think it's important to personify them a little bit,” Amin says, “because most people still don't know what a real agent is.”
Christine Wendell, CEO of Pronto Housing and an early Skydive adopter, uses agents for a laundry list of busy work: writing contracts, scheduling meetings, sending follow-ups emails to customers. Her agents are, essentially, perfect employees.
But how are they as coworkers? Skydive agents not only embed in every form of workplace communication, they continually evolve to match coworkers’ communication styles, requests, and corrections. In other words, they become better and better at fitting in with their actual coworkers. When Pronto’s engineering team began using a coding agent, Wendell noticed that employees started saying that they “worked with Alice”—the agent—on a project.
Yet part of the agents’ appeal is that they are not human. Beyond their limitless work ethic, they also exist outside of office politics or professional neuroses. When “Bob,” the agent serving as Wendell’s chief of staff, errantly listed all the details of Wendell’s calendar in a Slack channel, she didn’t feel the need to sugarcoat her swift correction.
“I'm definitely very aware that it's not human,” Wendell says. “I dump on them in a way I wouldn't do to a human, because it would not be polite.”
AI coworkers are entering the job market just as agents are increasingly infiltrating our personal lives. While Silicon Valley has been using agents such as Open Claw and Instinct for months to complete annoying tasks, Meta’s newly launched Muse aims to push personal AI agents into the mainstream.
Muse, like Skydive’s muppets, is represented by a cute and fuzzy little avatar. In the words of WIRED senior writer Reece Rogers, the user experience is something “like texting a friend with task requests—the AI agent acknowledges messages with a thumbs-up emoji and gets to work in the background.” By using existing relationships as a blueprint, these agents—whether they’re AI coworkers or, like Muse, “built for everyone”—offer a shortcut to understanding how to use them.
Anthromorphizing AI comes with specific risks in a work context. Research from Bedard and her colleagues at BCG found that, when managers were told work was completed by an AI employee, they caught 18 percent fewer errors than when told it came from an AI tool. Agents also don’t necessarily fit in the same boxes as human employees, Bedard says, in their abilities or their weaknesses.
“Companies are just starting to wrap their heads around what guardrails” are even applicable, Bedard says.
People forming deep emotional connections with AI is nothing new; people have been dating chatbot companions for years at this point. Even in the workplace, AI tools have sparked some curious reactions. Last year, Henry Blodget—the founder of my former employer, Business Insider—wrote a blog about building a team of digital subordinates, and having a “human response” to the headshot of a particularly attractive AI colleague.
“After a few decades in the human workplace, I’ve learned that sharing certain human thoughts at work is almost always a bad idea,” Blodget wrote. “But did the same rules apply to AI colleagues and native-AI workplaces?”
Sarah Franklin, the CEO of HR company Lattice, has more existential concerns. Lattice added digital employees to the org chart two years ago, before the concept had fully entered the mainstream. Franklin emphasizes that Lattice uses this model to encourage accountability—not to encourage workers to treat AI colleagues as if they were human.
Franklin sees such anthropomorphizing as a strategy by tech companies to get users hooked on their services, unable to resist the dopamine trigger of an emotional connection. While this can help companies build an active user base, Franklin believes it may have detrimental neurological and behavioral repercussions for the human workforce.
“We have these models that have consumed all human knowledge, and are so proud to have these multitrillion valuations—but are potentially destroying humanity,” Franklin says. “It is very scary. And what is the purpose? Is the purpose to put people out of work?”

More than $200 million spent fighting and supporting billionaire tax measure, and more to come

- Opponents of California’s proposed one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets and measures designed to block it have raised $187 million, compared with $32 million for supporters.
- Proposition 40’s supporters say the tax would offset looming federal healthcare cuts; opponents argue it threatens the state’s budget and economy.
- Likely voters are divided: 45% said they support the billionaire tax and 42% oppose it.
Opponents of the billionaire tax on the November ballot have vastly outraised the proposal’s supporters, with the anti-Proposition 40 effort and the backers of two other ballot measures crafted to nullify it raising $187 million compared to the $32 million raised by boosters of the wealth tax, according to campaign finance documents filed with the state.
The reports, filed Thursday, account for donations through Sept. 19 and do not include several million dollars that have poured into campaign coffers in recent days. The numbers are expected to vastly increase before the Nov. 3 election.
The bulk of the money raised by the proponents of Proposition 40, which would enact a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires’ assets, appears to have been spent on gathering signatures to qualify the measure for the November ballot. The campaign had only $207,000 in the bank, according to the latest campaign finance reports.
A leader of the union that crafted the proposal accused wealthy Californians who are spending heavily against the measure of lying to voters. The measure is designed to offset $100 billion in impending federal healthcare funding cuts expected to impacts millions of Californians.
“The billionaires take and take — tax break after tax break — and now they’re spending that money to deceive voters and avoid paying their fair share,” said Suzanne Jimenez, the chief of staff of the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. “Voters want their money back from the billionaires and want local emergency rooms to stay open. California does not need more tax breaks for billionaires. California needs emergency rooms for patients, hospitals that stay open, and healthcare people can access and afford.”
Opponents of the billionaire tax argue that it would do more harm than good.
“The more Californians learn, the more they see Proposition 40 for what it is — a harmful tax scheme that permanently damages the state’s budget and economy with zero accountability or safeguards to ensure funding actually improves care or lowers costs for patients,” said California Medical Assn. President Dr. René Bravo, the leader of one of the groups opposing the billionaire tax.
Proposition 41 would nullify the billionaire tax if, in the event that both measures are approved, it receives more “yes” votes. Proposition 41 would prohibit any new state tax from being excluded from a voter-approved cap that restricts how much tax revenue the state can spend each year.
“Californians deserve better results for their hard-earned tax dollars,” said Molly Weedn, a spokesperson for the Proposition 41 campaign.
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on personal property, intellectual property, retirement accounts and other assets, and would limit situations in which a ballot measure or state lawmakers can impose or raise taxes retroactively — both of which are essential parts of Proposition 40. If both measures pass and Proposition 42 receives more “yes” votes, it would nullify the wealth tax.
Here is a list of some of the billionaires who’ve made moves to leave California.
The proposed billionaire tax has divided California Democrats, with Gov. Gavin Newsom opposing it while the state Democratic party supports it.
In recent polling, a majority of likely voters did not support any of the three proposals.
While 45% of likely voters supported the billionaire tax, 42% opposed it, according to a poll released Friday by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies and co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times. Voters also are torn about the two ballot measures designed to nullify it.
September LA Times/Berkeley poll on statewide propositions
The other measure receiving great attention, Proposition 39, which would require voters to show government-issued ID to cast ballots, faces a similar financial disparity. Opponents to the measure have raised $39.3 million compared to $15.6 million garnered by supporters.
Fifty-two percent of likely California voters oppose the voter ID proposal, while 39% support it and 9% are undecided, according to the Berkeley poll.
In the race to replace Newsom, Democratic former Biden cabinet member Xavier Becerra has raised $35.8 million, while his GOP rival, conservative strategist and television commentator Steve Hilton, has raised $22.3 million.
Becerra remains the front-runner in the governor’s race, which is not surprising since Democratic voters outnumber Republicans nearly 2 to 1. In last week’s Berkeley poll, the Democrat had the support of 58% of likely voters, while 33% backed the Republican.

California donors have funded both sides of Democrats' primary battles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

California donors have funded both sides of Democrats’ primary battles
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Californians have given more to far-left candidates and their moderate opponents than donors from any other state.
- California donors helped fund the Senate primary victories of progressives Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota.
WASHINGTON — California is sometimes described as the ATM of Democratic politics.
That’s certainly been the case in the most divisive Democratic races this year.
Donors from California have given more to far-left candidates and their moderate opponents in congressional races and U.S. Senate contests than donors from any other state — more than $17 million combined, according to a Times analysis of the most recently available campaign finance filings.
More of that money — nearly $11 million — went to more progressive candidates. That giving came from more than 95,000 individual donors, which was more than double the number of California donors who gave to their more moderate opponents. That includes 18,000 donors who gave to both progressive and moderate candidates.
There was a geographic divide in giving by Californians. The largest share of cash to progressive candidates came from donors in the Bay Area, while the largest share of financial backing to moderate candidates came from donors in the Los Angeles area.
The Times looked at competitive races outside California in which one of the candidates had been endorsed by either the Justice Democrats or the Democratic Socialists of America, or DSA, as well as key Senate races in Michigan, Minnesota, Florida and Maine that featured a stark ideological divide between top Democratic contenders.
Although these races represent a small fraction of the electoral contests across the country, they were the races in which the future ideological direction of the Democratic Party was most fiercely contested.
Maine Democrats are calling for Republican Sen. Susan Collins to account for a report that alleged she was the target of a federal investigation over campaign contributions
Progressive candidates fared better in the majority of these contests.
California donors helped fund the Senate primary victories of progressives Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota — second only to in-state donors in providing cash to each of those candidates.
Progressive House candidates such as Melat Kiros in Colorado and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York were able to defeat more moderate incumbents with heavy support from California donors.
Their efforts weren’t always successful, however.
Former Rep. Cori Bush raked in more cash from California donors than in-state supporters in her bid to unseat incumbent Rep. Wesley Bell in Missouri’s 1st Congressional District, the seat she had held previously. But Bell easily cruised to victory in this year’s primary.
And then there was Graham Platner.
California donors gave nearly $2.5 million to his Senate campaign in Maine before he withdrew after he was accused of sexual assault by a former girlfriend. He has denied the accusation.
The Times analysis looked at direct contributions to campaigns, which are capped at $7,000 per election cycle. It did not include contributions to party committees or independent committees that could also be spending in these races. The analysis included both bigger contributions required to be disclosed by campaigns as well as small-dollar contributions through the Democratic fundraising platform ActBlue.
Flipping the script
Progressive donors said they were motivated to give to candidates who would shake up the Democratic Party’s status quo.
“The Democratic Party has to understand that they can’t keep doing the same thing,” said Rehan Alvi, a real estate investor in El Dorado Hills.
He gave the maximum allowable to support the campaigns of El-Sayed and Bush, and also supported Junaid Ahmed’s failed primary bid in the Illinois 8th Congressional District, as well as Platner’s campaign.
Harry Saddler, a retired designer who lives in San Francisco, said that the state of the party is “enraging.”
“That leads me to think about people who can actually flip the script,” he said.
Saddler has written checks to a number of more progressive candidates, including Flanagan, Chevalier, Ahmed and Nida Allam, who lost her primary bid to unseat incumbent Rep. Valerie Foushee in North Carolina’s 4th Congressional District, though he has also supported some moderate candidates in other races he sees as crucial to Democrats chances at retaking control of one or both chambers of Congress.
That pragmatic approach is part of the reason Joshua Saltman said he has supported a number of moderate candidates.
“The reality of the map is that if Democrats are going to retake the House, it’s not just winning super blue districts,” said Saltman, a former entertainment industry lawyer who now runs a Broadway music festival.
The dispute stands to heighten voters’ economic worries and add to the GOP’s political challenge in dead-heat races, analysts say.
Saltman said that he considers himself to be a more moderate Democrat and is also inclined to give to moderate candidates who he believes “get a little less love” from other donors, particularly in California.
He has written checks to Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed in Michigan; Rep. Angie Craig, who lost to Flanagan in Minnesota; Bell in Missouri and Gov. Janet Mills in Maine, who was Platner’s main competition in the Democratic primary before dropping out of the race.
Alan Burye, a retired accountant who lives just outside San Diego, said he prefers more moderate candidates because he thinks they are more productive politicians.
“The ones who are out on the edges, like Bernie Sanders, really don’t get much done,” Burye said.
He cut checks to Craig in Minnesota and Stevens in Michigan.
Israel’s impact
American support for Israel — in the wake of wars in Gaza and Iran — has been a major point of division among more progressive and moderate candidates and is a key fault line among many donors.
Progressive candidates have been increasingly critical of the actions and influence of the Israeli government as the public, broadly, has adopted a more negative view of the Israeli government.
Politicians who have drawn support in the past from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, have been a particular target of progressive challengers.
“The problem with the Democratic Party is that they’re all just beholden to AIPAC and to corporate interests,” said Alvi, the real estate investor in El Dorado Hills. “I want a candidate who has the courage to speak.”
In Michigan, El-Sayed described AIPAC’s support of Stevens, his moderate opponent, as “legalized bribery.”
El-Sayed has made no secret of his criticism of American foreign aid for Israel and said that he “doesn’t believe in ethno-states” in response to a question in the summer about whether he supports the right of Israel to exist.
El-Sayed’s comments and similar sentiments expressed by other more progressive candidates are part of the reason some donors have given to moderate candidates.
“I feel that people who fundamentally aren’t big fans of Israel aren’t necessarily people I want to give money to,” said Saltman, who gave to Stevens.
Saltman, who was born in Michigan, said that he would still vote for El-Sayed if he lived in the state.
Other donors said they were inspired to give to moderate candidates because of concern that anti-Israel rhetoric could veer into attacks on Jews more broadly.
Los Angeles investor Steve Emerson said his motivation in writing checks to moderate Democrats such as Stevens is “to fight antisemitism.”
El-Sayed, for his part, said in the summer that his criticism of Israel is about foreign policy, not Jewish people.
“Judaism and the Jewish people are a light onto the world,” he said.

Paternity is poetical
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
25 minute listen
Here’s an old story, often told. In Book 6 of the Iliad, Hector – dressed splendidly in bronze armour and a helmet with a horsehair crest – bids farewell to his wife Andromache. She begs him not to return to battle and hands him their newborn son. Hector raises the boy into the air, says a short prayer, and hands him back. ‘Go home, attend to your own handiwork / at loom and spindle,’ he commands, in Robert Fitzgerald’s translation: ‘As for the war, / that is for men.’
Hector is a father in the heroic mode, and his parenting style has long been irresistible to artists and writers. Few were shocked when the painter Paul Gauguin left his wife and five children in Denmark to pursue fame and art in Paris, then Tahiti. Such distance, they say, is good for a child. ‘The father, from his distance, supports, protects, nourishes his child,’ wrote D H Lawrence in 1922: ‘and it is ultimately on the remote but powerful father-love that the infant rests.’ Distance is equally necessary for the father who seeks to make art. ‘There is no more sombre enemy of good art than the pram in the hall,’ wrote Cyril Connolly in Enemies of Promise (1938).
This is a deeply self-serving story, of course. It’s nice for the male poet not to have to change diapers. But the argument that unsullied privacy is essential to creativity is tenacious. It surfaces when Virginia Woolf writes that ‘a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction.’ Contemporary feminists have continued to respond to this archetype of generativity. In Jenny Offill’s novel Dept. of Speculation (2014), for example, the narrator vows never to marry but to become ‘an art monster instead’.
But what if domesticity – and specifically parenthood – is in fact generative for artists? What if the cliché of solitary male creativity got it wrong? We may begin with one nursing poet. In his poem ‘Frost at Midnight’, written in the winter of 1797, Samuel Taylor Coleridge pictures himself at home in his cottage on a frosty night. The owls cry outside and the frost rings the trees and he is alone, ‘save that at my side / My cradled infant slumbers peacefully.’ He addresses his infant son:
         Dear Babe, that sleepest cradled by my side,
Whose gentle breathings, heard in this deep calm,
Fill up the intersperséd vacancies
And momentary pauses of the thought!
He is transported to memories of his own childhood, and then his hopes for his son’s future.
‘Frost at Midnight’ is a poem about caring, in both senses of the word: caring for and caring about. As such, it is a surprising poem about domestic labour, which has invited comment from scholars. ‘What is truly radical about “Frost at Midnight” is Coleridge’s self-representation as a father in the traditional maternal posture of watching over a sleeping baby,’ notes Jonathan Bate. What Bate calls ‘the traditional maternal posture’ is what Hector calls ‘your own handiwork / at loom and spindle’. But perhaps it is not so radical to picture a poet who is equally involved in the work of parenting. Perhaps it is precisely fatherhood that made Coleridge a poet.
What makes ‘Frost at Midnight’ significant in Coleridge’s career is that it represents the crest of the much longer wave of his stylistic development. It is not just a great poem – it is the poem within which he becomes a great poet, and his growth as a poet can be tracked neatly against his experience of becoming a father.
Coleridge was far from home when his son was born. A lost revolutionary, he was always trying to save or at least improve the world, and he was preaching in Birmingham when word came by letter: Hartley, born to his wife Sara, on 19 September 1796. He met the news with shock and a trio of sonnets. ‘My o’erwhelmed Heart / Trembled, & vacant tears stream’d down my face,’ he wrote in the first of these. He sent this to a friend, and it was published only in 1847, after his death. He wrote another on the journey home, and here imagines that he might arrive to terrible news: ‘when I reach my door, / If heavy looks should tell me thou art dead …’ They are not charming poems, but repressed; so guarded even when apparently tender, as if he is trying out how he feels in the set form of an Italian sonnet. ‘When I saw it on its mother’s arm, / And hanging at her bosom,’ he confesses in the last of these sonnets: ‘Then I was thrill’d and melted.’ This is a cautious, half-convincing expression of fatherly love. A few days later, he wrote to a friend: ‘in truth, I have seen handsomer babies in my lifetime.’
‘Kubla Khan’, ‘Christabel’, ‘The Rime of the Ancient Mariner’ were all begun or completed within 18 months of his son’s birth
Because Coleridge narrated his moods, and wrote letters that turned into poems, he permits us to reconstruct a detailed timeline of his changing feelings towards his son. Later, it will be an unhappy story, and Hartley will live an unhappy life, but at first it did not seem to be going that way. By December 1796, Coleridge was planning to move his family to a thatched cottage in the village of Nether Stowey in Somerset. He wrote to a friend with enthusiasm: ‘I mean to work very hard as Cook, Butler, Scullion, Shoe-cleaner, occasional Nurse.’ He turned out to love nursing. By the start of February, he was writing to another friend: ‘You would smile to see my eye rolling up to the ceiling in a Lyric fury, and on my knee a Diaper pinned, to warm.’ This moment – of writing while nursing, of diapers and poetic inspiration – is the genesis of ‘Frost at Midnight’.
The creation of the father is also the creation of the poet. In the spring of 1797, Coleridge was writing 50 lines of blank verse a day. He began to develop his ‘conversation poems’, which drew from his letters to friends and family: their language is intimate, domestic; their topics often autobiographical. Towards the end of that year, he turned to what are now called his ‘mystery poems’, and are those for which he is most celebrated: ‘Kubla Khan’, ‘Christabel’, ‘The Rime of the Ancient Mariner’, all of which were begun or completed within 18 months of Hartley’s birth.
This was a moment of golden invention, and Coleridge knew that something had changed. Years later, in his rambling autobiography Biographia Literaria (1817), he recalled the transformation. ‘I retired to a cottage in Somersetshire,’ he wrote, and:
Here I found myself all afloat. Doubts rushed in … The fontal truths of natural religion and the books of Revelation alike contributed to the flood; and it was long ere my ark touched on an Ararat, and rested.
It is a biblical scene and a beautiful crisis, and suddenly all is both new and old.
‘Frost at Midnight’ was written over the winter of 1797 and completed by February 1798. It is highly structured. Coleridge’s biographer Richard Holmes calls it a ‘curve of memory and prophecy’, and, in four parts and carefully measured blank verse, it moves gently between the present moment, his own past and his hopes for the future. He thinks back to church bells – ‘the poor man’s only music’ – heard when he was a boy, and is filled with gladness that, while his own boyhood was spent in a great city, his sleeping son:
       shalt wander like a breeze
By lakes and sandy shores, beneath the crags
Of ancient mountain.
The poem ends with a blessing: ‘all seasons shall be sweet to thee.’
A man becomes a father and a poetic revolution follows. Not always, but often enough. Percy Shelley’s son William was born in January 1816. According to his biographer, also Richard Holmes, ‘after 1816: no other Romantic writer learned, and changed, and developed his art so swiftly.’ A century later, William Carlos Williams began what his biographer Paul Mariani describes as his ‘poem of initiation, his early crossing, his coming to some sort of terms at last with his own imperfect, vibrant world’ when his wife was pregnant. Their son was born in January 1914, and the poem was published that spring. Eighty per cent of the men who have won the Nobel Prize in Literature or the Pulitzer Prize for poetry were fathers. Celebrated philosophers, on the other hand, tend to be childless.
There are other ways to narrate poetic breakthroughs, of course. Coleridge’s development as a poet is often recounted – most powerfully by Adam Nicolson, in The Making of Poetry (2019) – as bound up with his friendship with Wordsworth, so that the two men together pioneered what we now think of as Romanticism. A pattern is not a recipe, and each of these examples has its own complications in the granular details. But the pattern is substantial enough – and counterintuitive enough – to be worth remarking upon. It is also supported by recent developments in neuroscience. As a field, neuroscience has been transformed by neuroimaging technologies: particularly functional MRIs, developed in the early 1990s, which permit researchers to track brain activity by measuring changes in blood flow. This has led to notable insights in two research fields: into creativity, and into fatherhood. Strikingly, the two may be linked.
Cognitive scientists distinguish between what are popularly known as Type-1 and Type-2 mental processes. The first are quick, unconscious, associative thoughts, while the second are slower, deliberate and conscious, mediated by the frontal lobe and executive control network. A 2020 study put EEG beanies on the heads of 32 jazz guitarists and asked them to improvise riffs while their brain activity was scanned. ‘Higher-quality improvisations were associated with predominantly posterior left-hemisphere activity,’ the study found, while ‘lower-quality improvisations were associated with right temporo-parietal and fronto-polar activity.’ This suggests that the creative process takes place – or takes place best – in the automatic and unconscious left posterior part of the brain, sometimes described as the ‘default’ system, rather than the more conscious, deliberative ‘control’ system.
The brain assists new fathers by encouraging the perception that fatherhood is meaningful
This feels like commonsense to anyone who has experienced states of creative ‘flow’, say. But it has specific consequences for our understanding of art as a process. Artistic creation is marked by activation of the medial prefrontal cortex and by deactivation of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. A 2015 study of 30 poets found similar patterns of activity. The poets at work showed increased activity in the inferior front gyrus, left middle temporal gyrus, and superior temporal sulcus as well as in ‘mesial temporal areas, including the parahippocampal gyrus, hippocampus, and amygdala bilaterally and subcortical areas in the left hemisphere.’ These are the areas associated not just with language, but with memory and improvisation. In a 2020 study, published in Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience, expectant fathers who were played 30-second clips of infant cries interspersed with white noise responded to the infant cries ‘with increased activation in bilateral areas of the temporal lobe involved in processing speech sounds and social and emotional stimuli.’ Heightened activity within the temporal lobe is marked in both new fathers and poets.
While specific areas are activated at specific moments, it is key to see the brain as a network, and to trace patterns of connectivity between the regions. Both of these studies of creativity – of the guitarists, and of the poets – had a second step. The jazz guitarists were divided between experts and novices; and the poets, who were also compared by level of experience, were scanned twice, once while writing, then again while revising their poems. One characteristic of the experts is that they more effectively suspended the cognitive control mediated by the executive network; in the case of the revising poets, this was then re-engaged. The two processes are working together. David Rosen of Drexel University in Philadelphia, who led the study of the jazz guitarists, emphasises the importance of connectivity between the default and executive networks, which are both implicated in neuroscientific studies of creativity. He writes: ‘Increased connectivity across these networks may enable creative performance in a variety of domains, including music improvisation and creative writing.’
The clinical psychologist Darby Saxbe has surveyed recent developments in the scientific analysis of neurological – as well as hormonal and physical – changes in new fathers. In her book Dad Brain: The New Science of Fatherhood and How It Shapes Men’s Lives (2026), she points out that new fathers’ brains lose volume, for example, and this is chiefly in the cortex. ‘The cortex thinks ahead, makes sense of the world, and navigates our complex social lives,’ she explains. Meanwhile, the ‘cognitive and mentalising work’ that goes into fatherhood is indicated by the changing patterns of connectivity between different regions of the brain. Saxbe studies family relationships at the University of Southern California. Discussing a study by a junior researcher in her lab on how fathers experience a new sense of meaning, she notes that those fathers who reported an increased sense of purpose and meaning in their lives across the transition to fatherhood ‘had increased connections within the temporal poles, which are key components of the mentalising network, and the right hippocampus.’ This is pragmatic, Saxbe suggests: the brain assists new fathers by encouraging the perception that fatherhood is meaningful.
Such assistance can play out in surprising ways, and with surprising consequences. A study of the transition to fatherhood by Anthony G Vaccaro and colleagues at the University of Southern California, published in the journal Emotion in 2025, emphasises the impact of ‘resting-state connectivity between default mode and limbic networks’. It suggests that:
Functional connections between these networks may facilitate the integration of affective aspects of the environment with a sense of self and autobiographical memory, facilitating meaning-making throughout emotionally complex times.
This increased connectivity enhances the feeling of being closely attuned to the environment, and draws upon memories to help the self navigate and understand the present.
Again and again, the research points to intensified cerebral connectivity, and suggests that such changes take place regardless of biological relationship. A fascinating 2014 study conducted by Ruth Feldman and Eyal Abraham and their colleagues in Israel found the familiar patterns of response in homosexual male couples raising infants who had either been adopted or born through surrogacy. Summarising the study, Saxbe wrote that the homosexual fathers performing the primary caregiver role ‘showed amygdala activation similar to the primary caregiver moms and mentalising network activation similar to the secondary caregiver dads, as well as stronger connectivity between those two parts of the brain.’ The process of becoming a father – quite literally, thinking your way into it – is itself a creative act, driven by time, proximity and a sense of responsibility.
Neuroscientists tend to shy away from making direct and causal claims about the brain’s activity. They prefer the language of association, so that a brain region is described as being associated with certain habits or tendencies. That brain activity might lead to explicit changes in a poet’s style is necessarily speculative.
And yet: the shifting emphases and patterns described in neuroscientific studies of the brains of new fathers are echoed in the distinctive elements of Coleridge’s remade style: his assertion of autobiographical memory and its resonance in the present; his attention to his child and sense that his own identity is formed anew; his heightened creativity evident in what we might sentimentally see as a new openness. Perhaps we can use the neuroscience to read the poetry, and the poetry to read the neuroscience, in a kind of new longitudinal study, which returns us to the familiar poetic record and in it finds new forms.
Let’s take the example of confessional poetry, emerging as a group project in the late 1950s’ United States. The key characteristics of this new style – domestic details, departure from traditional poetic decorum – are shared by several poets, including W D Snodgrass and Sylvia Plath. In her essay ‘What Was Confessional Poetry?’ (1993), Diane Wood Middlebrook observes that the original four confessional poets were all recent parents of daughters when they had their poetic breakthroughs. She includes Robert Lowell and Anne Sexton as well as Snodgrass and Plath, but another candidate for the group is John Berryman, who was already a celebrated poet by March 1957, when his son Paul was born. Over the following 18 months, Berryman suffered, he said, from ‘an inability to stop writing verse’, and he remade his style and produced a great rush of the curious, brilliant poems later called his ‘Dream Songs’.
These poems are no longer in set, regular patterns. Harriet was born at the start of January 1957
Of the group, Robert Lowell is perhaps the purest example of a father poet – because of his enormous skill, and the drama of his life, and because the change in his own style is so stark. At first, Lowell wrote like this:
I saw the spiders marching through the air,
Swimming from tree to tree that mildewed day
In latter August when the hay…
And like this:
When we were children our papas were stout
And colorless as seaweed or the floats
At anchor off New Bedford. We were shut
In gardens where our brassy sailor coats …
The two poems quoted here are taken from his collection Lord Weary’s Castle (1946), which was published when he was 29. Young Lowell loved rhyme. He later told an interviewer that he wrote his first poems unrhymed and then put the rhymes in after, like an obedient schoolboy doing his homework. Of the 42 poems in the collection, only one doesn’t rhyme completely and this has a complex system of repeated words at the line ends. Beneath the rhymes steps a cautious measure or rhythm. Try saying ‘I saw the spiders marching through the air’ aloud, or even tapping along: the 10 syllables and five balanced feet of iambic pentameter. Lowell followed this collection with a set of dramatic monologues in rhymed iambic pentameter, sometimes known as heroic couplets, published in 1951. He was taking form seriously.
Then, after the birth of his daughter Harriet in 1957, he wrote like this:
Given a year,
I walked on the roof of the West Street Jail, a short
enclosure like my school soccer court,
and saw the Hudson River once a day.
And like this, addressing his young daughter while shaving:
Dearest, I cannot loiter here
in lather like a polar bear.
These two poems are from Life Studies (1959). If they rhyme – and many don’t – it is in a sneaky, cat-like way. The line-lengths vary; these poems are no longer in set, regular patterns. Harriet was born at the start of January 1957. At the end of that year, Lowell sent a handful of new poems to his old friend William Carlos Williams with a note: ‘At forty I’ve written my first unmeasured verse.’
He offers the intimate details of a turbulent emotional life, all bound in elegant, beautiful poems that duck in and out of traditional poetic forms
Lowell knew that Life Studies was different. He explained to an acquaintance: ‘It’s all quite a different style, uses a lot of free verse, is intelligible to anyone on the surface, and heavily and directly autobiographical.’ This is a good definition of what soon became known as ‘confessional poetry’, arguably the dominant mode of US poetry of the second half of the 20th century, and which was first named in a review of Life Studies. Lowell’s volume won the National Book Award and has been celebrated ever since. Lowell himself saw the breakthrough in a humbler register. As he went on in his letter: it was only now, in ‘the years of my second marriage, and the birth of my daughter, that I have written to my mind what I really have had to say.’
What is wonderful about Lowell’s poetry from Life Studies on is the jumble of life and art. He offers the intimate, often tender, sometimes shocking details of a turbulent emotional life, all bound in elegant, beautiful poems that duck in and out of traditional poetic forms. A new set of materials alongside a new sense of poetic form: that mix is the characteristic of Lowell’s breakthrough. It is played out when he talks about his daughter and equally is the core of poems far removed from her.
For him, all had changed. ‘I’m really mad about my little daughter’ Lowell wrote to the poet Elizabeth Bishop, shortly after Harriet’s birth, ‘and feel as though I had been up to now lacking some prime faculty: eyesight, hearing, reason.’ He wrote to another poet, Adrienne Rich, in November 1960. This letter – from a poet to a poet – was filled with gossip about operas and writerly encouragement, but it is also a letter from one new parent to another, and to amuse her he breaks off: ‘interruption: Harriet has just come with her toy telephone.’ Harriet and her toys were for Lowell a brilliant, productive interruption: she prompted him to change his style. He now found himself, he went on, living in and writing from a ‘queer jumbled world’.
‘Parenting involves heightened emotional and cognitive demands,’ observes the study led by Vaccaro: ‘further emphasising the brain’s role in integrating diverse experiences into a coherent sense of purpose.’ Here is T S Eliot, who was not a father, defining the poet’s task in 1921: ‘When a poet’s mind is perfectly equipped for its work, it is constantly amalgamating disparate experience.’ The coincidence of language here points to an idea that we have often overlooked: that fatherhood and artistic creation are not antagonistic but congenial; that becoming a father might, quite simply, improve a new father’s poems.
But not only poems. Because poems are short and often time-stamped, they make legible the changing way a father may look upon and respond to the deep changes of fatherhood. The same forces are surely powerful, if harder to trace, in creative work by parents more widely, and echo across our cultural moment. We live, in the West, in an age of sensitive dads, dad jokes, and dad dancing: all signs of a cultural revaluation of fatherhood, freed from the stigma of patriarchy. The consequences are political as well as poetic. In The Argonauts (2015), Maggie Nelson powerfully describes the imaginative work and possibility of artistic freedom that come with parenthood, quoting the feminist thinker Susan Fraiman’s call for ‘the decline of the domestic as a separate, inherently female sphere and the vindication of domesticity as an ethic, an affect, an aesthetic, and a public.’ The poetry of fatherhood may take a thousand forms: the tender strangeness of Coleridge, the jumpy brightness of Lowell, the moving and original memoirs and novels by contemporary poets and writers including Ben Lerner and Jack Underwood as well as Nelson. But for each, the material entanglement of creativity and parenthood is a prompt, not a hindrance, to wild new work.

160-million-year-old proteins show surprising power against superbugs

160-million-year-old proteins show surprising power against superbugs
Scientists revived 160-million-year-old antimicrobial proteins that could inspire new weapons against antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
- Date:
- September 28, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oregon
- Summary:
- Scientists resurrected antimicrobial peptides from mammals that lived millions of years ago and found that some were more potent against drug-resistant bacteria than modern human versions. These evolutionary relics could provide new clues for designing treatments as antibiotic resistance becomes an increasingly serious threat.
- Share:
University of Oregon biologists have brought prehistoric proteins back to life, reconstructing molecules that date back as far as 160 million years and naturally attack microbes. The revived proteins could provide scientists with new ideas for treating antibiotic resistant infections, which have become a major global health challenge.
The work, described in a paper published in PLOS Biology on Aug. 25, traced the evolutionary history of peptides, short fragments of proteins, back to the earliest placental mammals. This broad group includes humans and nearly all mammals living today. Laboratory experiments showed that some reconstructed peptides from extinct ancestors were more effective against drug resistant bacteria than some versions found in modern species.
These long lost biological defenses could give researchers useful starting points for developing treatments that complement or replace antibiotics that no longer work, according to Matt Barber, senior author of the study and an evolutionary biologist at the UO College of Arts and Sciences.
"For anybody who studies pathogenic bacteria, it's always in the back of our minds that antibiotics are one of the most important breakthroughs in medicine in the 20th century," Barber said. "But bacteria are, and have been for a long time, evolving resistance to them."
He continued: "We're definitely interested in whether by resurrecting or engineering some enhanced antimicrobial peptides, we could use these as therapeutics down the road."
Tracing an Ancient Antimicrobial Defense
About 160 million years ago, near the end of the Jurassic Period, the common ancestor of all placental mammals, whose young develop in the womb, appeared. Around that same time, lactoferrin, the protein at the center of Barber's research, also emerged.
Lactoferrin is an immune protein present in almost every body fluid except blood, including breast milk, tears, saliva, snot, and intestinal mucus. One of its primary jobs is to keep iron away from pathogens. Bacteria inside the body depend on iron, but lactoferrin binds tightly to the element, making it much harder for microbes to access.
Lactoferrin also carries its own direct defense against pathogens. It contains an antimicrobial peptide capable of damaging bacterial membranes, creating holes that can rupture the cells.
"Antimicrobial peptides are a key part of the body's first line of defense," said Titas Sil, lead author of the paper and a doctoral student in Barber's lab. "They can target a broad range of pathogens, and due to their potency, scientists have been trying to synthesize a variety for therapeutic uses."
Close relatives of lactoferrin do not share this bacteria killing ability. That suggests the trait appeared sometime after lactoferrin emerged during mammalian evolution. To determine when the ability developed and how it changed over time, the team retraced lactoferrin's evolutionary history and reconstructed versions belonging to its extinct ancestors.
For Barber, that evolutionary record offers a natural archive of biological experiments that could help researchers develop new medical tools.
"Evolution is essentially a billions-year-old science experiment, right?" he said.
"We're seeing the results of what worked and what didn't work. Looking at how traits are naturally produced and selected through evolution, you can get information that could be useful for designing new antimicrobial tools."
Rebuilding Proteins From 160 Million Years Ago
To recreate the extinct antimicrobial peptide, Sil began by comparing lactoferrin gene sequences from living species such as humans and cows. She then mapped the evolutionary relationships among those sequences and used statistical methods to estimate the most likely genetic sequences carried by their common ancestors, extending the reconstruction back roughly 160 million years.
The advanced method is known as ancestral sequence reconstruction, which was pioneered by Joseph Thornton, a former UO scientist whose old laboratory space is now occupied by Barber's group.
Sil synthesized the predicted genes and used cells to produce the reconstructed ancient proteins. She then tested them against several pathogens linked to human disease, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, and Streptococcus.
The oldest resurrected antimicrobial peptides were able to disrupt bacterial membranes, but the bacteria apparently repaired the damage and survived exposure to the peptides. Versions reconstructed from more recent mammalian ancestors, dating back a few million years, became progressively more effective. In some cases, they performed better than the corresponding modern human peptides.
One Mutation Produced a Major Change
Researchers traced much of that increased potency to a remarkably small structural difference. A single mutation in the chain of amino acids, the protein "building blocks," was enough to make the antimicrobial peptide substantially more effective.
"What was surprising and unexpected was how small changes in these domains could have such large effects," Barber said. "There have been clinical trials using derivatives of human lactoferrin peptides to treat infections. But there were several instances where (Sil) showed that you don't need a lot of changes for evolution to enhance the activity of these peptides beyond the human versions."
Barber and Sil caution that resurrected antimicrobial peptides are unlikely to become new medicines anytime soon. Unlike conventional antibiotics, these peptides are less structurally stable and are rapidly broken down inside the body.
Even so, reconstructing their evolutionary history could reveal useful strategies for designing future treatments. By learning how antimicrobial peptides changed over millions of years, researchers may be able to create new approaches that make it harder for pathogens to develop resistance.
"Similar to antibiotics, pathogens are going to be able to evolve against antimicrobial peptides," he said. "But if we understand and can anticipate how they become resistant to these molecules, we can hopefully find better ways to target them or develop combination treatments that better avoid resistance."
This research was funded by the National Institutes of Health.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Oregon. Original written by Leila Okahata. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Titas Sil, Caitlin H. Kowalski, Sierra Scamfer, Natalie Copeland, Matthew F. Barber. Retracing the origin and evolution of a cryptic antimicrobial peptide within mammalian lactoferrin. PLOS Biology, 2026; 24 (8): e3003932 DOI: 10.1371/journal.pbio.3003932

Kremlin says Ukraine is now 'paying the price' for its own attacks on Russia

On Friday, Putin said Moscow had been ready to resume negotiations with Kyiv after September's parliamentary election in Russia, but complained about Ukraine launching a big attack on Moscow during the vote, about what he said was its targeting if polling stations, and about its drone attack on St Petersburg during a major economic forum there in June.

formafantasma joins santa maria novella as creative directors after eight centuries of history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:56:33 UTC
18:56:33 KST

Formafantasma has been appointed Creative Director of Officina Profumo-Farmaceutica di Santa Maria Novella, bringing Andrea Trimarchi and Simone Farresin into one of Florence’s longest-running institutions. Founded in 1221 from the medicinal herb cultivation and preparations of Dominican friars, Santa Maria Novella has spent more than eight centuries turning botanical knowledge into fragrances, body products and preparations for the home. Apparently, there was still room for a new creative director.
The collaboration will see Formafantasma work across products, packaging, communication, retail spaces and events, in dialogue with Santa Maria Novella’s internal team and specialists from different disciplines. Rather than approaching the appointment as an exercise in visual reinvention, the studio describes the product itself — its quality, materials and the expertise behind its production — as the starting point.
heritage becomes the starting point for a new chapter | all images courtesy of Santa Maria Novella
EIGHT CENTURIES OF MATERIAL KNOWLEDGE
For Formafantasma, the attraction appears to lie precisely in the weight of what is already there. Santa Maria Novella’s identity has developed through the accumulation of ingredients, formulations, techniques, objects and spaces, with knowledge transmitted and adjusted over generations. The studio sees this continuity not simply as heritage to preserve, but as material to question: what survives, what transforms and how an institution with roots in the 13th century continues to operate in the present.
That position aligns naturally with Trimarchi and Farresin’s interest in the histories carried by materials and systems of production. Their role at Santa Maria Novella will therefore be less about imposing a single recognizable aesthetic than examining how the company’s many expressions can speak more coherently to one another — from what sits inside a bottle to the box around it and the space in which someone eventually picks it up.
the collaboration builds on more than eight centuries of history
SANTA MARIA NOVELLA WITHOUT THE REBRAND
Crucially, Formafantasma says its intention is not to redefine Santa Maria Novella through a new image. Instead, the studio wants to understand what has allowed the Officina to remain relevant since 1221 and use those conditions to inform its next chapter. That means looking at how its history is communicated, how new products are conceived and how physical spaces, objects and visual language can develop without reducing eight centuries to a particularly tasteful moodboard.
‘Their role will be that of curators, attentive to the knowledge the Officina has safeguarded for eight centuries,’ Santa Maria Novella says, pointing to Formafantasma’s multidisciplinary practice across product, space, research and exhibition design. The first results of the collaboration have yet to be revealed, but the brief is already unusually clear: no clean slate, no heritage frozen behind glass, and plenty of history to work with.

Man sets himself on fire at Copenhagen immigration agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:55:36 UTC
18:55:36 KST

A man set himself on fire Monday at the Danish Agency for International Recruitment and Integration in Copenhagen, police said.
The incident took place at the agency’s offices on Carl Jacobsens Vej in Valby. Copenhagen Police received the report at 10:12 a.m. and sent a large response to the scene.
“He set himself on fire inside. A quick-thinking employee managed to put him out, but he is in a lot of pain,” Copenhagen Police duty officer Dyre Sønnicksen said.
The man was taken to Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen’s main hospital, where he is being treated for his injuries. Shortly before noon, police said he was no longer in life-threatening condition but remained under treatment.
Several people witnessed the incident.
“There were a number of witnesses who are very shocked,” Sønnicksen said.
Police said the witnesses would receive crisis support.
It is not yet known what led the man to harm himself or why he went to the agency to do so. His relatives have been informed.
Police said there were no immediate signs that a criminal act had taken place. No one else was injured.
The Danish Agency for International Recruitment and Integration, known as SIRI, handles a range of matters involving foreign nationals in Denmark, including residence and work permits.
The agency confirmed the incident on its website and said the man had acted alone and that the case involved self-harm.
It said the situation was under control and was being handled in cooperation with police and crisis psychologists.
SIRI’s citizen service center on Carl Jacobsens Vej will remain closed for the rest of the day because of the incident. People whose appointments were canceled will receive new appointments, the agency said.

2026-09-28
09:55:30 UTC
18:55:30 KST

Eight Danish municipalities did not meet the required staffing ratio in kindergartens in 2025, according to figures published Monday by Statistics Denmark.
The municipalities are Ringsted, Odder, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Struer, Brønderslev, Rebild and Thisted.
Under the political requirement, there must be at least one pedagogical staff member for every six children in kindergartens. In 2024, 14 municipalities failed to meet the requirement.
The trade union BUPL, which represents pedagogues working in Danish children’s institutions, noted that more municipalities now meet the requirement than before.
“Staffing ratios have improved, and that is an important first step to ensure the quality in our daycare institutions,” BUPL chairperson Elisa Rimpler said.
“But we are not at the finish line at all when it comes to giving children the quality they are entitled to.”
Since 2024, there has also been a requirement of at least one employee for every three children in nurseries.
Five municipalities failed to meet that requirement last year: Bornholm, Holstebro, Ikast-Brande, Thisted and Rebild.
Rimpler said the figures were not good enough and called on municipalities to increase their efforts.
“There is a need to build on top of this, because in many places the staffing ratios on paper are experienced as very far from reality,” she said.
“Both because managers, long-term sick employees, and pedagogues employed to support individual children are counted, and because many of the extra employees do not have the necessary professional qualifications.”
According to BUPL, the law does not require the employees counted in the staffing ratios to have professional training.
The union said the share of pedagogues among staff was 57% in 2019, compared with 50.6% last year.
Children, Elderly and Housing Minister Jacob Mark of the Socialist People’s Party, SF, said it was serious when municipalities failed to meet the legal requirement.
He said the minimum staffing ratios were working because more nurseries and kindergartens were getting more staff around children and nationwide cuts to staffing had stopped.
“But, as I also see, there are eight municipalities that do not meet the minimum staffing ratios. That is completely unacceptable. I am going to intervene against that,” the minister said.
Mark also criticized the practice of counting managers and long-term sick employees in the staffing figures. He said managers are not with children all the time, while long-term sick employees are not with them at all.
According to Mark, municipalities “just” need to hire more pedagogical staff.
The minister said he will send a letter to the eight municipalities that do not meet the requirements. The same municipalities will also face scrutiny from Ankestyrelsen, Denmark’s public authority for supervising municipalities and other public bodies.
Ankestyrelsen can impose a range of sanctions after assessing why a municipality is not complying with the law, including advisory opinions and fines.
“Now they have had four years. Now they must reach the finish line with those minimum staffing ratios,” Mark said.
