Rod Stewart to bring final tour to Copenhagen in June 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
09:55:18 UTC
18:55:18 KST

British singer Rod Stewart will perform at Royal Arena in Copenhagen on 6 June 2027 as part of his “The Final Encore” tour, concert promoter Live Nation Denmark said in a press release.
The 81-year-old singer said the time has come to end his career on the road.
“After more than six decades, ‘The Final Encore’ will without doubt be my last tour,” Stewart said.
“I have sung the music I love since I was 19 years old, and I have had the privilege of taking it around the entire world to all of you. It has given me a life that is far more fantastic than I could ever have imagined,” he said.
Stewart had to interrupt his “One Last Time” tour in August this year after having a stent inserted into a coronary artery, according to a statement from his representative reported by CNN.
A stent is used to keep a narrowed coronary artery open, including in cases where the artery has been affected by atherosclerosis.
Stewart began making music as a teenager. His career took off in the late 1960s, when he became a member of several rock bands, including The Jeff Beck Group and The Faces.
He released his first solo album, “An Old Raincoat Won’t Ever Let You Down,” in 1969.
His major breakthrough as a solo artist came in 1971 with “Every Picture Tells a Story,” which included the song “Maggie May.”
Another of his best-known songs is “Da Ya Think I’m Sexy?” from his ninth solo album, “Blondes Have More Fun,” released in 1978.
Stewart is also known for recording his own versions of songs by other artists, including Cat Stevens’ “The First Cut Is the Deepest,” Van Morrison’s “Have I Told You Lately” and the Sutherland Brothers’ “Sailing.”
His latest album so far, “Swing Fever,” was released in 2024 in collaboration with pianist and composer Jools Holland.
“The Final Encore” will begin in Dublin on 23 April and end in Hannover, Germany, on 24 July.
Fewer trains are running between Ringsted and Slagelse until 8 p.m. Monday after an overhead wire fell near Sorø Station, according to DSB, Denmark’s national rail operator.
Passengers may also face longer travel times between the two stations.
DSB told Ritzau that trains are still able to run on one track despite the damaged overhead wire.
Around 50 rail replacement buses have been ordered to operate between Ringsted, Sorø and Slagelse. The first buses have already started running.
DSB has also sent staff to the stations in Slagelse and Ringsted to help passengers affected by cancellations and delays.
Banedanmark, the state agency responsible for Denmark’s rail infrastructure, is at the site and working to repair the fault.
At 2:51 p.m., DSB’s traffic information showed that the company was unable to operate all scheduled trains between the regions.
InterCityLyn and InterCity services between Copenhagen and Esbjerg are still running, but passengers should expect longer travel times.
DSB is advising travelers to check the journey planner before traveling.
Øresund Bridge to close for 3 hours Thursday evening
The Øresund Bridge will close to all car traffic in both directions Thursday evening as Danish and Swedish authorities carry out a major emergency response exercise, Copenhagen Police said.
The closure will last from 8 p.m. until 11:15 p.m. on October 1.
The exercise will include a scenario involving an accident in one of the tunnel tubes, Copenhagen Police told Ritzau in a written response.
Emergency vehicles will be visible on the bridge during the exercise.
Chief Police Inspector Peter Dahl of Copenhagen Police stressed that the operation is planned and that there is “no danger.”
“It is important for safety on the link that the authorities regularly conduct exercises so that we are as well prepared as possible if a serious situation should arise,” Dahl said.
Copenhagen Police will issue an update through Politi Update, the Danish police public information service, when the bridge reopens Thursday evening.
“We therefore hope for road users’ understanding, and as soon as the exercise is completed, we will reopen the bridge to traffic again,” Dahl said.
Copenhagen Police said smaller exercises are regularly carried out in cooperation with Swedish authorities, while larger full-scale exercises such as Thursday’s are held less frequently.
Five British citizens arrested near RAF Fairford suspected of preparing terror attack
Five men arrested Sunday morning near the RAF Fairford airbase are all British citizens from London and are in their early or mid-20s, British counter-terrorism police said Monday.
Police have previously said the five are suspected of preparing a terrorist attack.
A “very complex and extensive operation” remains underway, according to counter-terrorism police.
“This is an extremely complex and extensive operation involving local and national police authorities, the Ministry of Defence, and local authorities, working together to advance the investigation and provide support to the local community,” Vicki Evans, a deputy assistant commissioner in counter-terrorism policing, told the BBC.
Evans said the operation had caused disruption for local residents but said it was “first and foremost in the interest of their own safety.”
RAF Fairford is used by the US military.
US President Donald Trump said Sunday that the arrested men were “looking to do great damage.”
“We had them under observation for a long time,” Trump told journalists Sunday afternoon, according to the German news agency dpa.
According to Reuters, the British government has previously allowed the US military to use the airbase for attacks on Iranian missile installations used in strikes on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
In July, Britain said its armed forces were ready to protect the country against any attack after Iran’s Revolutionary Guard warned Britain against allowing US bombers to take off from RAF Fairford.
Speculation spread in the media and online Sunday about a possible Iranian role in the suspected terror plans.
Iran’s embassy in London rejected what it called “unfounded and malicious speculation” Monday, saying Iran had no involvement with the five arrested men.
Such speculation “serves no other purpose than to fuel the anti-Iran propaganda in Britain,” the embassy said in a post on X.
British police have not mentioned any possible connection between Iran and the arrested men, according to Reuters, and have urged people not to spread rumors or speculation.
EU foreign policy chief: EU struggles to reach 2030 defense goal
Europe must sharply increase the pace of its military buildup if it is to meet its goal of being able to defend itself by 2030, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Monday.
“Europe needs to rearm faster and more effectively if we are to achieve the 2030 goal,” Kallas said at a press conference following a meeting of EU defense ministers in Brussels.
The ministers discussed the first annual report on the EU’s defense readiness. The report, which has not yet been published, is intended to assess whether Europe is on track to become capable of standing on its own militarily by 2030.
Kallas indicated that the findings were not encouraging.
“Europe needs decisive changes in the scale and speed of investments in defense, innovation, and industrial capability,” she said.
Her comments come as intelligence services in several EU countries warn of an increasing threat from Russia.
Last week, Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service, known as FE, published an assessment saying it could no longer rule out a Russian invasion of a NATO country, although it considered such a scenario unlikely. The assessment also said Russia was expected to intensify and escalate its hybrid warfare against NATO and the West in the coming months.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats has repeatedly pushed for Europe to be capable of defending itself by 2030.
Denmark has also launched a major military buildup with support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament. The country is expected to reach NATO’s target of spending 3.5% of gross domestic product on defense this year.
Other European countries are not increasing their capabilities at the same pace, however, a gap that was also apparent at Monday’s meeting.
According to Kallas, no EU country came forward ready to send Patriot air defense missiles to Ukraine. The systems are Ukraine’s most effective defense against Russia’s heavy ballistic missiles.
Despite continued Russian missile attacks that kill civilians and damage key infrastructure, no EU country is currently prepared or able to send the requested missiles for Ukraine’s air defense.
Kallas also pressed EU countries to provide the warships they had promised for the bloc’s Aspides mission in the Middle East.
She said the mission needs at least 10 ships to operate and meet its objectives. EU countries were unable to provide the required number at Monday’s meeting, although Kallas said two member states were discussing whether they could provide additional naval vessels at a later stage.
The European Court of Auditors has previously warned in a separate report that the EU is not on track to meet its 2030 defense-readiness goal.
According to the court, years of underinvestment have left Europe with insufficient ammunition and missile stockpiles, long production times, dependence on suppliers outside the EU and logistical bottlenecks.
A man set himself on fire Monday at the Danish Agency for International Recruitment and Integration in Copenhagen, police said.
The incident took place at the agency’s offices on Carl Jacobsens Vej in Valby. Copenhagen Police received the report at 10:12 a.m. and sent a large response to the scene.
“He set himself on fire inside. A quick-thinking employee managed to put him out, but he is in a lot of pain,” Copenhagen Police duty officer Dyre Sønnicksen said.
The man was taken to Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen’s main hospital, where he is being treated for his injuries. Shortly before noon, police said he was no longer in life-threatening condition but remained under treatment.
Several people witnessed the incident.
“There were a number of witnesses who are very shocked,” Sønnicksen said.
Police said the witnesses would receive crisis support.
It is not yet known what led the man to harm himself or why he went to the agency to do so. His relatives have been informed.
Police said there were no immediate signs that a criminal act had taken place. No one else was injured.
The Danish Agency for International Recruitment and Integration, known as SIRI, handles a range of matters involving foreign nationals in Denmark, including residence and work permits.
The agency confirmed the incident on its website and said the man had acted alone and that the case involved self-harm.
It said the situation was under control and was being handled in cooperation with police and crisis psychologists.
SIRI’s citizen service center on Carl Jacobsens Vej will remain closed for the rest of the day because of the incident. People whose appointments were canceled will receive new appointments, the agency said.

A 31-year-old man has been charged with assault after a Swedish man was punched during a World Cup viewing event at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen on 30 June.
The Swedish man, who was 32, died three days later, on 3 July, according to the Copenhagen Police prosecution service.
The 31-year-old has been charged under section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers ordinary assault.
According to prosecutors, the man struck the Swedish man with a powerful punch from a clenched fist to the left side of his head or neck.
The blow caused, among other injuries, a rupture of an artery, which led to the Swedish man’s death.
The 31-year-old is also charged with throwing two beer cans toward a group of people that included the Swedish man. Another person was hit by one of the cans.
Because the accused has previously been convicted of assault, the case also includes section 247 of the Penal Code. Under that provision, a sentence can be increased by up to half.
The prosecutor in the case has previously said the 31-year-old faces a prison sentence of between eight and 10 months.
That is considerably shorter than a sentence under section 245, which covers aggravated assault and can also apply when a victim dies as a result of an assault.
In this case, prosecutors have charged the man only under the ordinary assault provision.
Criminal law expert Lotte Helms, an assistant professor at the University of Southern Denmark, previously explained to Ritzau that a single punch with a fist will normally fall under section 244.
“A punch with a fist will as a starting point be 244, but I cannot rule out that it could fall under 245 if, for example, one has specifically gone after hitting the neck in a specific way,” she said in July.
“But it will always be a specific and individual assessment, and in the end it is the courts that assess it,” she said.
The 31-year-old is a Danish citizen. During an earlier court hearing, he said he came to Denmark from Congo when he was four months old.
The case will be heard at the Copenhagen City Court on 7 October.
Denmark could face more Russian espionage, influence operations and sabotage if Russia intensifies its hybrid war, the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, PET, says.
The warning comes in a press release Thursday, following a new threat assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
PET says the expected increase concerns both the scope and nature of Russian espionage, influence and sabotage.
In Denmark, PET has observed “an increased Russian willingness to take risks and concrete planning and preparation of sabotage”, according to the assessment.
The threat of increased sabotage is particularly directed at companies in the defense industry and other organizations with a direct connection to military support for Ukraine.
The warning also applies to possible sabotage and increased espionage targeting what PET describes as “critical infrastructure and other functions vital to society”.
PET, which handles Denmark’s domestic security, says the threat picture has become more “serious and complex”.
PET does not provide details about specific countermeasures. The intelligence service says, however, that it “together with the police is implementing the necessary security measures”.
Dansk Industri, DI, the Confederation of Danish Industry and Denmark’s main employers’ and business association, says companies need to pay attention to their security.
This applies both to physical security and cybersecurity, according to Rasmus Anderskouv, DI’s deputy director for societal security and emergency preparedness.
“Hybrid attacks against Denmark and Danish companies are unfortunately a new normal that we have to relate to,” he said in a press release.
DI describes the situation as serious and calls for closer cooperation between public authorities and the business sector.
Statens Museum for Kunst, Denmark’s national gallery in Copenhagen, is planning an “ambitious transformation project” aimed at making its collection accessible to more people.
The museum, known as SMK, said the project will include renovations and an “architectural rethinking” of its building on Sølvgade, which opened in 1896.
The project is financed by foundation donations totaling 70.5 million kroner. This includes 15 million kroner from Den A.P. Møllerske Støttefond and 8 million kroner from Ny Carlsbergfondet.
The renovation will respect the original architecture and existing buildings, according to SMK.
It will allow the museum to display more of its approximately 200,000 works. SMK plans to bring artworks back from castles and ministries, along with works that have rarely or never been shown at the museum.
The first phase of the new collection exhibitions will focus on European art from the 1300s to the 1800s.
About half of the works displayed in this section will have never or rarely been shown at SMK. They will include “Susanna in the Bath” by Dutch artist Godefridus Schalcken.
“We want to create a museum where more people experience that art concerns them, and that the collection is something they have a share in,” director Astrid la Cour said.
The project will also focus on helping visitors find their way through the museum, improving physical accessibility and highlighting the historical qualities of the original museum building, designed by architect Vilhelm Dahlerup.
The new exhibitions will open in stages between 2027 and 2029.
Each stage will focus on one of the museum’s three main collection areas: European art, Danish and Nordic art, and Danish and international art.
The second phase will focus on Danish and Nordic art from 1750 to 1900. Among the works to be displayed is August Jerndorff’s “Portrait of Marie Oppermann” from 1894.

Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months, with attacks becoming more frequent and potentially having greater consequences for affected countries, according to a new assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
The assessment is being presented Thursday at a press conference at Kastellet in Copenhagen.
FE says the increased threat could include destructive cyberattacks with serious consequences for critical societal functions, as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus, a member of the Social Democrats, said the situation was serious.
“The situation is serious, and we take it seriously,” Bruus said.
“That is why we are standing here today. We are presenting the assessment because having as much openness as possible is important,” he said.
FE also assesses that there is a “low, but increasing risk” that Russia could launch a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia.
“It is unlikely that Russia will initiate an actual invasion of a NATO country, but we cannot rule it out,” FE chief Thomas Ahrenkiel said.
Ahrenkiel said it was new that FE could no longer rule out such an invasion.
According to the assessment, Russia would need at least six months to prepare for an actual invasion of a NATO country.
Bruus stressed that the assessment does not concern a possible military attack on Denmark.
“One is not talking about military attacks on the Kingdom of Denmark” in the assessment, he said.
Chief of Defence Michael Hyldgaard, who also attended the press conference, said the Danish military is adapting to the assessment.
“We will fight and win with what we have, and those we fight alongside. That is our task. That is what we are preparing for. We are ready for that – regardless of the threat,” Hyldgaard said.
The assessment does not concern Greenland or the Faroe Islands, according to the information presented at the press conference.
The new assessment comes just over a week after a Russian frigate fired flares at a Danish helicopter in international waters off Gedser.
Ahrenkiel described the incident as “unprofessional behavior” by Russian soldiers aboard the frigate.
“It is also our impression that such risky behavior was not sanctioned by the Russian military leadership,” he said.
People in Italy can expect around 11 more years without health-related limitations than people in Denmark, according to figures from the EU’s statistical office, Eurostat.
The figures cover healthy life years across the 27 EU countries. Danes have 62.4 healthy life years, while Italy ranks highest at 73.4.
Healthy life years measure the number of years a person can expect to live without limitations in daily life because of health. Eurostat’s indicator is based on people’s own assessment of their health.
Denmark ranks below 18 other countries in the figures.
Neighboring Sweden and Norway also rank above Denmark, with 67.5 and 64.8 healthy life years respectively.
Diabetes Association calls for greater focus on prevention
The Diabetes Association has described the Danish figures as a “health alarm.”
“Because the figures show that we in Denmark have dragged our feet for too long when it comes to health promotion and preventing chronic illnesses such as type 2 diabetes, which is growing explosively,” the association’s CEO, Claus Richter, said in a press release.
The Eurostat figures cover 2024. It is the first year in which Denmark’s figures have been calculated using the same method as the rest of the EU.
Life expectancy in Denmark has increased year by year. But Richter said the figures show that Danes are living longer “but not better.”
He attributed this in part to a health care system that prioritizes treatment over health promotion and prevention.
He also pointed to what he described as an outdated financial silo mentality, in which an expense in one area “can rarely be justified” by gains in another.
“It is a tragedy for each individual, but also for our society. Illness pulls many thousands of full-time equivalent jobs out of the workforce. Therefore, there is a need for a paradigm shift where we view prevention and health promotion as an investment – not an expense,” he said.
The Diabetes Association is proposing that Denmark set a national target for healthy life years in legislation.
Its vision for 2045 is for Denmark to be among the European countries with the highest number of healthy life years.
Among its proposals is the creation of a Health Economics Council that would assess and prioritize preventive measures based on their long-term value.
The Diabetes Association is due to present the proposal Thursday morning at a health policy debate at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketinget.
Denmark’s wolf population has grown to 77, an increase of 28 from the previous monitoring year, according to a new count by Aarhus University and the Natural History Museum Aarhus.
The figures are included in a memo from the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment.
The population is approaching a size at which it may become possible to regulate the predator, Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said in comments to DR and TV 2.
The ministry will now count the wolves individually. It expects that the results will allow Denmark to “demonstrate to the EU that the wolf has a favorable conservation status.”
“Then we can begin hunting, and we should,” Rabjerg Madsen told DR.
According to the Danish Nature Agency, a species has a favorable conservation status when its population development shows that it can maintain itself in the long term.
Wolves have been protected under the EU Habitats Directive since 1992. The directive “prohibits deliberate killing.”
In Denmark, the protection is implemented through the Hunting and Game Management Act, which prohibits hunting or capturing wolves. Shooting a wolf can result in a fine or imprisonment for up to two years.
However, the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment can grant permission to regulate, meaning shoot, an individual wolf in special circumstances.
The authorities can grant permission if there is no other solution and the action does not threaten the wolf’s natural range.
This can include cases involving “public health, safety, and security, or to prevent serious damage to livestock and other forms of property.”
An exemption can also be granted if a wolf “lacks an instinctive shyness towards humans.”
The 77 wolves are spread across 11 packs, which have produced a total of 61 pups this year. There are also two pairs of wolves and two lone male wolves in Denmark.
They have been identified in at least 15 locations, all in Jutland, from Løgumkloster in Southern Jutland to the northernmost part of Northern Jutland.
Wolves may also be present in three additional locations, but further investigations are needed to confirm this.
Without “human persecution,” the Danish wolf population is expected to continue growing.
The wolf returned to Denmark from Germany in 2012 after being absent from the country for almost 200 years.
A new resident has arrived among the leopards at Copenhagen Zoo after an Amur leopard gave birth to a cub last week.
The zoo announced the birth in a press release.
The Amur leopard is “the rarest subspecies of leopard,” according to zoological director Mads Berthelsen.
“Even though the species is experiencing slight growth, there are still only around 110 individuals in the wild,” he said in the press release.
Amur leopards generally live alone in the wild. The newborn cub is still small and blind, however, and is completely dependent on its mother.
The mother spends most of her time with the cub and only leaves for short periods, including to find food.
Because of this, zookeepers are keeping their distance for now. They are monitoring the cub’s development by listening for sounds from the stable.
Zoo visitors will also have to wait before they can see the cub.
“The first weeks are about giving the mother and the cub as much peace as possible. We expect it will take about two months – maybe a little longer – before the cub begins to come out enough that guests can have the opportunity to experience it,” Berthelsen said.
In addition to the approximately 110 Amur leopards known to live in the wild, 93 males and 97 females are kept in zoos around the world, according to the international zoological database Zims.
Only one Amur leopard cub has been registered in the database over the past 12 months, Copenhagen Zoo said.
This does not necessarily mean the animals are having difficulty breeding, Berthelsen said.
“We are increasingly seeing that zoos choose not to let their animals breed because they are concerned about what to do with any surplus offspring,” he said.
The Amur leopard lives mainly in the Primorye region of southeastern Russia. In summer, temperatures in the large forest area can reach 40 degrees Celsius, while winter temperatures can fall below minus 30 degrees.
Cold cuts, filter coffee, chocolate and olive oil were among the products that became cheaper in Denmark in September, according to a monthly analysis by food price monitoring service Madprisluppen.
Overall shelf prices were slightly lower than in August, with the decline most noticeable at discount chains Lidl, 365discount, Rema 1000 and Netto.
Online supermarket Nemlig.com has also lowered prices because it matches the prices of nearly 400 products sold by Rema 1000.
“The cheapest baskets have become cheaper, and the distance from the cheapest to the most expensive basket has grown larger,” Madprisluppen commercial manager Lars Smidt said.
Consumers now pay 27 percent more for the most expensive shopping basket than for the cheapest, with Lidl and Rema 1000 offering the lowest-priced baskets, according to Smidt.
Lidl began cutting prices on a range of products in May as part of its permanent low-price program. Rema 1000, Netto and 365discount soon followed.
A survey conducted by analysis institute Norstat for Lidl found that seven in 10 Danes know about the permanent low-price concept and have bought products at permanent low prices. More than half said they prefer stores with permanent low prices to stores offering frequent special deals.
Lidl Denmark purchasing director Peer Sandtner said the chain now has permanent low prices on more than 300 products.
Smidt said it remains uncertain whether grocery prices will continue falling across supermarket chains. Higher oil and gasoline prices could eventually affect food prices, he said.

The updated defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. does not introduce new restrictions on how the American military can use its bases in Greenland, according to Danish government officials.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Greenland’s head of government signed the agreement with the U.S. in New York on Tuesday.
The agreement largely confirms rights granted under a 1951 defense deal, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates said.
“But subtracting that, the agreement is an opportunity for the US to establish itself with a military footprint in Greenland, as they already can,” Rasmussen said.
One restriction remains unchanged: nuclear weapons are prohibited in Greenland.
The issue has historical significance. In 1957, Danish Prime Minister H.C. Hansen secretly allowed the U.S. to keep nuclear weapons in Greenland. In 1968, a U.S. B-52 bomber carrying hydrogen bombs crashed near Thule, causing radioactive contamination.
Denmark and the U.S. subsequently agreed that nuclear weapons could not be kept in Greenland.
Rasmussen said the new agreement does not give the U.S. greater military access than it already had.
“The important thing for us is that our nuclear policy is intact, and that in this context we do not give the US any greater access than they actually had beforehand,” he said.
The agreement also introduces stricter requirements for the U.S. to protect Greenland’s environment. American military bases have previously caused pollution affecting local communities.
Before the updated agreement can take effect, it must be approved by Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament, and Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.

The security and defense agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark is based on all three parties being members of NATO, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Tuesday evening.
“If the USA withdraws from the agreement, it thus no longer applies,” Frederiksen said after the agreement was signed.
“It is a very clear premise for this agreement that the countries that have signed the agreement are in NATO. All three countries are now,” she said.

Some 363,600 people who receive prescription allergy medication in Denmark will need to renew their prescriptions if they want to continue receiving a subsidy.
The Danish Medicines Agency announced the changes following a new decision on subsidies for prescription allergy medicines.
Under the new rules, subsidies for some medicines will only be available to specific patient groups, while other patients will no longer be eligible for a subsidy.
If a patient is no longer eligible for a subsidy for their current medicine, they can ask their doctor for a prescription for another medicine with the same effect that is eligible for a subsidy.
Patients who experience side effects or cannot use an alternative for other reasons can have their doctor apply for an individual subsidy.
The changes affect various nasal sprays, eye drops, tablets and capsules, according to the Danish Medicines Agency.
Patients who can use an alternative will no longer be able to receive a subsidy for medicines including Allergone, Altifex, Benadryl, Beconase and Benarhin once the changes take effect on February 1, 2027.
Around 750,000 people in Denmark receive prescription allergy medication. The Danish Medicines Agency encourages patients to check its website to see whether they are affected.
The decision follows a recommendation from the Reimbursement Committee, which advises the Danish Medicines Agency on medicine subsidies.
Deciding which medicines should receive subsidies is part of the Danish Medicines Agency’s routine work.

There appears to be broad political support in Denmark for a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States.
The agreement, signed Tuesday in New York by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump, must now go through approval procedures in Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut, and the Folketing, Denmark’s national parliament.
The agreement is intended to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The signing took place at the United Nations headquarters during the U.N. General Assembly.
Trump has repeatedly expressed a desire for the United States to own Greenland, citing national and international security concerns. His statements led to a prolonged diplomatic crisis between the United States, Denmark and Greenland.
Several Danish political parties have welcomed the agreement, including Venstre, the Conservative Party, the Red-Green Alliance and the Denmark Democrats.
Venstre’s chairman, Troels Lund Poulsen, described the agreement as “an extraordinarily good agreement.”
Poulsen was defense minister in the former SVM government, a coalition between the Social Democrats, Venstre and the Moderates, and played a significant role in the negotiations with the Trump administration.
“It is a joyful day for Greenland, Denmark, the Realm, and for the cooperation with the USA in the future,” he told TV 2 on Tuesday.
When Frederiksen held a press conference for Danish media in New York, she gave particular thanks to Poulsen for his efforts. Poulsen described it as “beautiful” that the agreement had become a reality.
The Conservative Party’s chairman, Mona Juul, also praised the agreement on Facebook.
“An agreement has been reached. And that is unequivocally good. Therefore, I would also like to praise the enormous political and diplomatic work that preceded the agreement,” she wrote.
The Denmark Democrats’ chairman, Inger Støjberg, also expressed support.
“It is an agreement we can be proud of, because it both emphasizes our sovereignty and cements NATO’s presence,” she told TV 2 on Tuesday, referring to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
The Red-Green Alliance, a party that supports the government in parliament, also backed the agreement.
“It is an agreement that does not in any way alter Danish sovereignty. An agreement that Greenland signs with Denmark and the USA. They have stayed within the red lines,” the party’s Greenland spokesperson, Trine Pertou Mach, told Jyllands-Posten on Tuesday.
The agreement will enter into force only after the necessary parliamentary procedures have been completed.

Minister for Economic and Interior Affairs Pia Olsen Dyhr from the Socialist People’s Party, is presenting the plan today at a visit to a school in Toksværd in Næstved Municipality, according to TV2 ØST.

Chinese shoulder-fired anti-aircraft missiles appear in Russian service
Unknown

- Russian state TV footage shows a Russian air defense unit with unmarked shoulder-fired missiles resembling China's QW-18A and QW-19, Militarnyi reported.
- The launchers were filmed with a mobile fire group of the 51st Air Defense Division in the Rostov region.
Russian air defense troops appear to be using Chinese-designed shoulder-fired anti-aircraft missiles, according to an analysis by Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi of footage aired on Russian state television.
The launchers were shown during an exercise by a mobile fire group of Russia’s 51st Air Defense Division in the Rostov region, in a segment broadcast by the state channel Rossiya 1 and shared on X by the account TheDeadDistrict. Mobile fire groups are small teams, often riding in pickup trucks, that Russia uses to hunt Ukrainian drones with machine guns and short-range missiles.
The soldiers in the report called the weapon “Iva.” But the launcher does not match any man-portable air defense system, or MANPADS, known to be in Russian service, Militarnyi reported Sept. 28. Russia’s own shoulder-fired missiles in current use include the Igla-S and the newer Verba.
Militarnyi said the launcher most closely resembles Iran’s Misagh-3 and China’s QW-18A and QW-19. Neither the launchers nor the missiles shown on camera carried any visible markings, which the outlet said could point to an effort to hide where they came from.
A closer look at the footage favors a Chinese origin, according to Militarnyi. The Russian launchers have an extra fitting on the front section that does not appear in available photos of the Iranian Misagh-3. The outlet did not rule out that it could be a newer Iranian version, but said no photos of Misagh launchers with that feature have been published. Militarnyi said it could not determine whether the system is a QW-18 or a QW-19. China’s state-owned CASIC showed the QW-19 at the DSA 2024 defense exhibition in Kuala Lumpur.
The weapons may have reached Russia through Iran, Militarnyi said. Tehran buys Chinese arms, including shoulder-fired missiles, and in July 2026 reports emerged that an Iranian deal with China covers up to 400 MANPADS, including the QW-12 and FN-16, at an estimated cost of $60 million to $70 million. Iran’s Misagh family is itself derived from China’s QW series, and Pakistan builds a similar missile under the name Anza-2.
Militarnyi said Russia’s use of foreign-made shoulder-fired missiles may indicate that its own industry cannot produce enough to meet the military’s needs. Mobile fire groups have become a main line of defense against the long-range drones Ukraine sends against Russian refineries, airfields and weapons plants, which increases demand for short-range missiles.
Ukraine has previously said it confirmed Chinese supplies of gunpowder and artillery systems to Russia, and Ukrainian intelligence services believe military cooperation between the two countries includes producing Chinese-designed weapons inside Russia. China has repeatedly said it does not supply lethal weapons to either side in the war.

Asian Games | Feature: 18-year-old Yan Ziyi throws her way into a new era
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
17:41:09 CST
18:41:09 KST

by sportswriters Cao Yibo, Yue Chenxing, Wang Qinou
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- With a roar, Yan Ziyi sent her javelin flying into the rainy night sky in Nagoya.
The crowd gasped as the big screen showed 70.46 meters, a result that secured the 18-year-old the women's javelin title at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Sunday.
The throw, on Yan's Asian Games debut, broke the Games record by 4.37 meters. The previous mark of 66.09 meters was set by Chinese athlete Liu Shiying at the 2018 Jakarta Games.
It was also Yan's only throw of the final. She passed on her remaining five attempts, and nobody else came close. Olympic champion Haruka Kitaguchi of Japan took silver with 62.70 meters.
"I didn't expect to finish it with one throw. My plan was just to make my first two throws count," she said in the mixed zone, with tears still in her eyes.
The tears had a reason. Two weeks earlier, at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest, Yan threw 68.05 meters on her first attempt before withdrawing with a foot injury. Kitaguchi passed her with 68.92 meters to take the title.
Yan said she felt she had let people down. After claiming victory at the Asian Games, she said the weight was finally gone.
"I'm actually a pretty calm person. I don't show my feelings much," Yan said.
She has nothing but respect for Kitaguchi, a rival she has faced many times. Yan said she watches and learns from the Japanese star and feels more admiration than pressure.
"I can't say I'm stronger, because we are all chasing each other," Yan said. "Everyone is a target for me to chase."
Yan's journey began in a primary school PE class. After she once threw a softball farther than her classmates, a coach put her on the field team. At sports school, she started with the shot put before switching to the javelin.
People often call Yan a javelin prodigy, but she does not fully agree.
The road was not always smooth. "At the beginning it was really tiring, and I thought about giving up. But I stuck with it," Yan told Xinhua.
"Having talent isn't enough. I have to train so that my talent can show," she added.
Her body keeps changing, and so must her training. As she grows taller and heavier, she has to keep working on her run-up speed and adjusting her technique. Training, she noted, is not simply about repetition. "Learning new moves and new ways to train" is something she enjoys.
Age restrictions once kept Yan out of some senior international events. She said the wait gave her time to sharpen her technique and gain experience.
The results followed quickly. In 2024, Yan threw 64.28 meters at a national grand prix, setting a world U20 record. She won the U20 World Championships the same year.
In 2025, she threw 65.89 meters at the national championships despite carrying an injury. It was the fourth time she had broken the world U20 record.
In May this year, she threw 71.74 meters on her first attempt at the Diamond League meeting in Xiamen, breaking the Asian and world U20 records. It was also the second-best throw in women's javelin history, just 54 centimeters short of Barbora Spotakova's world record of 72.28 meters set in 2008.
Yan kept winning. Xiamen, Oslo, Paris and Monaco all went her way, with each winning throw exceeding 67 meters. In September, she came from behind in Brussels to win the Diamond League final and claim the season title.
Yan is now ranked No. 1 in the world. After her Monaco victory, the Diamond League posted a comment in all capital letters on social media: "ABSOLUTE DOMINATION."
Back in 2024, at 16 and too young for the Paris Olympics, Yan told Xinhua with a smile: "In the future, let's start a new era that belongs to me."
Two years later, that line sounds less like a wish and more like a plan.
"I can start a new era, because I'm still young. I have more time and more chances," she said.
Yan remains modest when the conversation turns to Chinese shot put great Gong Lijiao. "I don't think I can compare myself to her. She's a role model for me. I still have to keep learning from her and chasing what she's achieved," Yan said.
Yan's next targets are already clear: the world championships in Beijing, followed by the Olympics the year after.
"I plan to save the new record for the world championships in Beijing," Yan said after Sunday's competition. "So stay tuned for that." ■

Full text: Address by Chinese Vice President Han Zheng at general debate of 81st session of UN General Assembly
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
17:41:04 CST
18:41:04 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Vice President Han Zheng delivered a speech on Saturday at the general debate of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA).
The following is the full text of the speech:
Statement by H.E. Han Zheng
Vice President of the People's Republic of China
At the General Debate of the 81st Session of
The United Nations General Assembly
New York, September 26, 2026
Mr. President,
Colleagues,
The world is witnessing intertwined changes and turbulence, protracted geopolitical conflicts, widening development gaps and a growing number of global challenges. Five years ago, at the 76th Session of the UN General Assembly, President Xi Jinping put forward the Global Development Initiative. Since then, he has proposed the Global Security Initiative, the Global Civilization Initiative and the Global Governance Initiative. These initiatives provide strategic guidance for building a community with a shared future for humanity. At a time when countries of the world find their future so closely linked, more and more of them want to join hands to shoulder the historic mission of addressing difficulties and challenges, and advancing the well-being of all humanity. With this in mind, I propose that we take the following four steps.
First, we should safeguard the postwar international order and foster lasting peace based on common security. The world wants peace, not war. The international system centered on the UN and the international order underpinned by international law that emerged after World War II must be upheld. We should turn into action the vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative, and sustainable security, and reject the Cold War mindset and bloc confrontation. We should settle differences and disputes through dialogue and consultation, and oppose unilateral military actions that violate the UN Charter and circumvent Security Council authorization. Major countries shoulder special responsibilities for safeguarding international peace and security, and they should take the lead in complying with rules, upholding rule of law and doing what's right.
China holds that the sovereignty and security of countries in the Middle East including the Gulf should be respected, international industrial and supply chains should be kept stable and unimpeded, and global trade should be safeguarded. China calls for advancing the governance of the West Bank and the post-conflict reconstruction of Gaza in accordance with the principle of the Palestinians governing Palestine. It also calls for bringing the Palestinian question back onto the right track of the two-state solution at an early date. On Ukraine, President Xi Jinping has put forward four points on what must be done, which are the fundamental guidance for China in playing a continued, constructive role in its own way for achieving a political settlement of the crisis. China urges the relevant country to immediately stop using threat of force against Cuba and immediately and completely lift the blockade and sanctions against Cuba.
Second, we should address the global development predicament and promote prosperity for all through openness and cooperation. We should keep development at the center of the international agenda, and jointly forge a global development partnership based on unity and equality and that is balanced and inclusive. It is important to give priority to key areas including poverty reduction, food security and energy transition, step up resource input, and increase support for countries in the Global South. Developed countries should honor their commitment to development financing and climate financing. The international community should also build consensus and pool strengths to formulate the post-2030 global development agenda. Facing a new scientific and technological revolution and industrial transformation, especially the dynamic development of artificial intelligence, we should take a people-centered approach and develop AI for the positive and for good, narrow the digital divide, and promote development that is universally beneficial.
Both history and reality prove that countries can hardly achieve development without an open and cooperative international environment. Protectionism produces no winners; building walls, erecting barriers, decoupling and cutting off supply chains disrupt global industrial and supply chains and harm the interests of all parties. We must firmly safeguard the WTO-centered, rules-based multilateral trading system, build an open world economy, jointly foster and strengthen new growth drivers, and see that economic globalization is inclusive and delivers benefits to all.
Third, we should advance exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations and rebuild unity and mutual trust through communication and dialogue. Diversity has created splendor in the world. Condescension and a self-centered mindset have no place in the interactions among different cultures. Promoting mutual respect, solidarity and harmonious coexistence is the right approach to take. We need to use the UN platform to boost international people-to-people exchanges, and take the celebration of the International Day for Dialogue Among Civilizations as an occasion to promote mutual understanding and amity among all peoples and the common development of diverse civilizations. We should reject ideological prejudice, and respect the development paths and social systems decided on independently by the people of all countries. We should deepen the sharing of governance practices and jointly explore ways to tackle challenges facing our times.
Fourth, we should stay committed to multilateralism and take steps to safeguard fairness and justice. Multilateralism is the choice made by humanity after going through scourges, and fairness and justice are the joint pursuit of the people of all countries. China holds that all countries, big or small, are equal members of the international community, and that world affairs should be handled by all through consultation, and rule of law, fairness and justice in international affairs should be jointly upheld. Countries should join forces and act together to safeguard the UN and make it stronger. China supports the UN in reforming and improving itself. It should advance the UN 80 Initiative and enhance the performance of its bodies rather than merely cut its budgets and mandates. It should effectively address global challenges including climate change and public health security, improve governance rules in such areas as cyberspace, outer space and polar regions, and truly increase the representation and voice of the Global South.
China pays high tribute to Secretary General Antonio Guterres who will complete his term soon. China supports the election, in accordance with the UN Charter, of a new secretary general who honors the UN Charter, has exceptional capability, upholds integrity and fairness, and demonstrates courage and dedication.
Mr. President,
Colleagues,
On October 25, 1971, right here in this august hall, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 2758 at its 26th Session with an overwhelming majority, by which the UNGA decided to restore all the rights of the People's Republic of China in the UN and recognize the representatives of the Government of the People's Republic of China as the only legitimate representatives of China to the UN. This is of profound and far-reaching significance for both China and the world.
Over the past 55 years, China has been a stabilizing force in times of volatility. China is firmly committed to pursuing peaceful development, and has the best track record on peace and security among major countries. It is the largest contributor of peacekeepers among the permanent members of the UN Security Council. It also took the initiative that led to the issuance of the first joint statement of the leaders of the five nuclear-weapon states on preventing nuclear war. China has been a main engine driving common development. China has created two miracles at home, namely, fast economic growth and long-term social stability, and it has, over many years, contributed around 30 percent to global growth. China has joined hands with more than three fourths of the countries in the world in pursuing high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, it has mobilized over 23 billion U.S. dollars and carried out more than 2,000 projects under the Global Development Initiative, and it has granted zero-tariff status to all the African countries and least developed countries having diplomatic relations with it to empower the Global South in pursuing modernization. China has been a progressive force in an era of change. China has always spoken up for the Global South, stood up for the legitimate rights and interests of developing countries, and continued to work toward a more just and equitable global governance system. In October, China will host the Global Governance Forum in the Xiong'an New Area. You are welcome to attend the forum and join the discussion about the way forward in global governance.
Mr. President,
Colleagues,
No matter how the international dynamics evolve, China remains unchanged in its pursuit of peace and development, in its dedication to safeguarding fairness and justice, and in its commitment to multilateralism. China will join hands with all other countries to build a community with a shared future for humanity and make the world a better place for all of us. Thank you. ■

SAN FRANCISCO, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Steve Hoffman, CEO of Silicon Valley-based startup incubator Founders Space, said he remains optimistic about China-U.S. economic and trade cooperation, citing the two economies' complementary strengths and broad potential for collaboration in artificial intelligence (AI) and other emerging technologies.
In a recent interview with Xinhua, Hoffman said he sees particularly strong potential for cooperation in AI.
During Chinese President Xi Jinping's just-concluded state visit to the United States, the two sides agreed to establish China-U.S. AI dialogue to exchange views on AI-related risks and benefits, with the next round to be held in November. A communication channel for AI-related incidents will also be set up.
"As CEO of Founders Space and someone deeply involved in AI, I see President Xi Jinping's visit as an important step forward," Hoffman said. "I was encouraged that AI was discussed at the presidential level."
"At Founders Space, I have always believed that cross-border collaboration drives the most transformative breakthroughs, and the progress made between the United States and China on AI is a vital step forward," he said.
"Establishing formal channels to manage high-stakes risks proves both nations recognize AI safety as a shared global responsibility rather than a zero-sum game," he added.
Hoffman noted that competition between China and the United States does not have to preclude cooperation, adding that the two countries could work together in areas such as AI safety, scientific research, open-source AI and responsible AI deployment.
"The United States and China will have a major role in shaping the future of technology, so continued dialogue and cooperation are important," Hoffman said.
He also pointed to the potential for cooperation between Chinese and American entrepreneurs, saying their different strengths can create opportunities that would be difficult to develop within either market alone and lead to "genuine win-win outcomes."
"The most successful collaborations are never one-sided," Hoffman said. "They happen when each side understands what the other side needs and then finds a structure where both can succeed."
"Innovation is increasingly global," he said. "Trying to force innovation back inside national borders would be extremely difficult and, in many cases, counterproductive."
In his work advising large companies on AI strategy, Hoffman said he has seen some companies turn to Chinese open-source models to maintain greater control over their data.
"Open models also allow entrepreneurs, researchers, and smaller companies to participate in the AI revolution," he said.
Looking ahead, Hoffman said China and the United States could continue working together in areas of shared interest, including AI safety, scientific research, climate change and global economic stability.
"That is ultimately what I want to see more of: practical cooperation that turns differences into new opportunities for both sides," Hoffman said. ■

====================================================================================================

Across China: French scholar in pursuit of century-old cultural imprints in coconut carvings
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
17:40:54 CST
18:40:54 KST

HAIKOU, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Roland Bourdeix, a French researcher devoted to coconut genetics for over two decades, has chosen to bring his cherished collections back to China for restoration, seeking the origins of the century-old cultural exchanges centered on coconut carvings.
The scholar has visited more than 40 tropical countries for his research. He regards the coconut tree as the "tree of life" and believes that coconut shell carving stands out as one of the most exquisite forms among the material and symbolic cultures derived from it.
Aiming to build a coconut-themed ecological museum, Bourdeix has collected a large number of rare ancient coconut carvings from around the world over the past 25 years, including a batch of Chinese coconut carvings dating back to the Qing Dynasty (1644-1911) that were exported to Europe about a century ago.
Since the 19th century, Chinese coconut carvings have been sold to Europe and Southeast Asia as souvenirs or diplomatic gifts via southern Chinese cities of Guangzhou and Macao. Some of these works were subsequently passed down through generations in European families.
When Bourdeix discovered that some of the collections had cracked or been damaged over time, he decided to bring them back to south China's Hainan Province for restoration rather than having them repaired locally in Europe.
He explained that this is not merely about restoring the artifacts, but also a cultural journey back to their origin, expecting his efforts to draw greater public attention to the culture of coconut carving.
A traditional carving art using coconut shells, coconut wood and other materials, coconut carving is mainly practiced in Hainan. Records of Hainan coconut carvings date back to as early as the Tang Dynasty (618-907), and the carvings were presented as treasures to the imperial court during the Ming and Qing dynasties.
Hainan coconut carving was included in the national intangible cultural heritage list in 2008.
In 2025, the province launched a three-year action plan to systematically promote the inheritance and innovation of coconut carvings.
Coordinated by the provincial coconut industry association, Qiongtai Normal University in the province undertook the restoration.
Wu Mingju, a national intangible cultural heritage inheritor of coconut carving and a teacher of coconut carving courses at the university, immediately identified the works' age and craftsmanship features upon seeing them.
"Most of them feature Chinese mythological figures, and although the appearance is flawed, the complete lineage of traditional craftsmanship is still evident," he said.
Zhang Bidi, a coconut carving artist with the industry association, introduced a comprehensive restoration plan: bonding broken parts with epoxy resin, meticulously repairing and carving along the original grain with chisels, and grinding and filling damaged fragments with coconut material of the same type.
The artisans consulted with Bourdeix and confirmed every detail of the restoration. A shared understanding of craftsmanship that transcended language and culture soon established full mutual trust between the two sides.
Recalling his encounter with Wu, the Frenchman said that despite their different cultural backgrounds, he regarded Wu as a brother, and that both were driven by the same passion, curiosity and love for multiculturalism.
They discussed restoration techniques, their personal collections and ways to promote coconut carving, and agreed to co-author academic papers and jointly participate in the museum's construction that Bourdeix is preparing in France.
"The coconut carvings' journey witnessed another reconnection of a cultural bond that transcends remote mountains and seas," said Gao Yiping, a professor at the university's school of fine arts.
In recent years, cultural and creative products that integrate coconut carvings with trendy brands have repeatedly won popularity in the domestic market, showcasing the strong vitality of traditional craftsmanship in modern times, according to the professor.
Bourdeix believes the open platform of the Hainan Free Trade Port (FTP) is providing a broader space for coconut carvings to reach the global stage.
He expects Chinese coconut-carving culture to reach more parts of the world and for the country's coconut research resources to be further integrated into the international academic network.
Hainan FTP began island-wide special customs operations on Dec. 18, 2025. In the first half of 2026, Hainan recorded 1.603 million inbound and outbound passenger trips, including 883,000 by foreign nationals. ■

High-speed rail line through mountainous central China region opens to traffic
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
17:40:53 CST
18:40:53 KST

The first train of Yichang-Xingshan high-speed railway, G6888, is pictured ahead of its departure from Xingshan Railway Station in Xingshan County, central China's Hubei Province, Sept. 28, 2026. The 101-kilometer Yichang-Xingshan high-speed railway officially entered service on Monday. The railway, with a designed speed of 350 kilometers per hour, is an important part of the country's high-speed rail network. (Xinhua/Wang Zichen)
WUHAN, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- The Yichang-Xingshan high-speed railway line in central China's Hubei Province began service on Monday, facilitating tourism, industrial development and rural revitalization in the mountainous region, according to China Railway Wuhan Bureau Group Co., Ltd., its operator.
Traversing the Daba Mountains, the 101-km line with a design speed of 350 km per hour connects China's two major high-speed railway arteries, namely the Shanghai-Chongqing-Chengdu line and the Zhengzhou-Chongqing line.
Shang Zejin, chief designer of the railway, said the construction process faced multiple challenges posed by complex geological conditions, including deep-buried tunnels, high in-situ stress, high gas concentrations and karst formations.
Designers and constructors applied numerous new technologies and construction techniques to tackle these problems. Of the total length, bridges and tunnels account for more than 94 percent of the line, Shang said.
Opened shortly before China's National Day holiday, the railway is expected to boost tourist flows between major cities including Wuhan, Zhengzhou and Chongqing, as well as iconic attractions such as the Three Gorges region along the Yangtze River, unleashing renewed economic momentum for the central region.
Ma Rong, deputy director of the passenger transport department of China Railway Wuhan Bureau Group Co., Ltd., said the railway line will cut travel time and improve services, providing solid support for high-quality development in adjacent regions.
China has built the world's largest high-speed railway network. By the end of 2025, the total length of operating railways in the country had reached 165,000 km, including over 50,000 km of high-speed rail.
Under national plans, China's high-speed rail network is projected to reach 70,000 km by 2035. ■

TOKYO, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- China maintained its dominance in diving at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games by winning both 1m springboard gold medals here on Monday.
Lin Shan and Long Yiping finished 1-2 in the women's 1m springboard. Li scored 263.05 points for gold, while Long finished second with 254.25. South Korea's Kim Su-ji took bronze with 245.05.
Although Lin remained consistent throughout the five rounds, she said she was not fully satisfied with her performance.
"Although the result is quite good, I am not very satisfied with the process," Lin said. "I didn't show my strengths. Each dive was stable, but not elegant or refined enough."
Lin said her strengths usually lie in her lines and entries, but neither had been perfectly executed on Monday.
"I have to set high standards for myself. If I don't demand enough of myself, I can't reach the world's top level," she said.
Lin, who won silver at the Hangzhou Asian Games in 2023, said reaching the top of the podium after several years of hard work gave her further motivation. "After all these years, I've come this far, and my results have improved. I need to be more determined and keep moving forward," she said.
For Long, who was making her Asian Games debut, a mistake on her fourth dive cost her valuable points. Her 107C earned only 33.00 points, leaving her eighth in that round.
"It was more regret than disappointment, because I lost too many points on that dive," Long said. "But this is something I can adjust in training. That dive has already passed, so I was more focused on doing the upcoming one well."
Long bounced back with a strong final dive, scoring 57.20 points for her 5333D.
"I was very excited to take part in the Asian Games. The venue and environment here are excellent. As for my performance, I still have some shortcomings that give me more areas to improve in training," she said.
Long said she hopes to compete at more international events and work toward the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games.
In the men's 1m springboard, Wang Zongyuan added another gold for China with 442.75 points, well ahead of South Korea's Kim Yeong-nam, who scored 373.30. China's Liu Chengzan took bronze with 361.45.
Wang led from the opening dive and topped the standings in four of the six rounds. His highest score came on his fourth dive, a 405B, which earned 81.60 points.
Despite successfully defending his title, Wang said there was still room for improvement.
"I'm very happy to stand on the top of the podium and successfully defend my title from the Hangzhou Asian Games," Wang said. "But there were still many shortcomings throughout the competition, and I'll work on them in training."
Wang said he had not fully settled into his competition rhythm in the opening rounds.
"Maybe it was the first two dives. I didn't immediately enter the competition mode or reach the right level of excitement. I was distracted a little," he said. "Fortunately, I gradually found my competition rhythm in the later rounds."
Liu, making his Asian Games debut, made a costly mistake on his third dive, a 205C, scoring just 36.00 points and dropping to fourth after the round. He recovered with 73.60 points on his fourth dive and eventually secured bronze.
"I'm definitely not satisfied. To be honest, today's performance was quite far from the level I showed in training," Liu said.
After the mistake, Liu said he tried not to dwell on it. "Once I made the mistake, I told myself not to think about that dive anymore and to focus on the dives ahead. There were still opportunities, so I just wanted to slowly make up the points," he said.
Looking ahead to Tuesday's 3m springboard competition, Wang said he would focus on himself.
"My goal hasn't changed. I hope to do my best tomorrow," he said. "The biggest challenge is still myself." ■

He said the organisation would also raise issues related to floods, Kaziranga and other local concerns.“All the student and youth-centric issues that the youth of Assam have been struggling with for a long time, we will work on all of them in the coming time. We will definitely go to other Northeast states. We have received a very good response, a very good support,” Ranka said.The CJP leaders were detained on Sunday shortly before the organisation's first regional volunteers' meeting in Guwahati was scheduled to begin near the Assam Secretariat.The organisation said several senior leaders and Assam-based volunteers, including Ranka, Ankit Bhardwaj and Prem Aakash, were taken to a police facility. Reports said around 30 CJP workers were detained.The CJP had described the gathering as a peaceful meeting on private property. Assam Police has not publicly provided a detailed explanation for the detentions, according to the information available.
CJP to begin nationwide protest from Oct 2
Ranka also said that CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke had initially planned to travel to Assam following the detentions but would now focus on preparations for the organisation's proposed October 2 protest over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and its demand for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.“Abhijit's plan was based on our arrest yesterday. But as I've been released, Abhijit is not coming. He is busy preparing for the protest planned for October 2nd regarding SIR and Gyanesh Kumar's resignation,” Ranka told reporters.On the demand for Kumar's resignation, Ranka said the organisation would launch a nationwide protest from October 2.“It will happen now. For 48 hours, the ball was in Gyanesh Kumar's court. Now the ball is in CJP's court. We'll start our nationwide protest from 2nd October, and we won't back down until Ganeshkumar resigns,” he added.Ranka also alleged that more than 13 crore people had been removed from electoral rolls and questioned the process of electoral boundary redrawing in Assam. These claims were made by Ranka and CJP and have not been independently established.
The remarks come amid a wider political dispute over the functioning of the Election Commission and the SIR exercise. An Indian Express report cited by CJP said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised objections on multiple occasions over SIR-related decisions.
The Election Commission has rejected allegations of internal disagreement and maintained that decisions concerning SIR were taken with the “unanimous approval of the Commission.” The detentions came after the leadership of Akhil Gogoi-led Raijor Dal met CJP leaders, including Ranka, in Guwahati.

Economic Watch: China's industrial profits retain double-digit growth via high-tech, new growth drivers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
17:40:16 CST
18:40:16 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- China's industrial profits maintained double-digit growth in the first eight months of 2026, driven by rapid expansion of high-tech manufacturing and new growth drivers, official figures showed on Monday.
Profits of industrial firms above designated size increased 15.7 percent year on year during the first eight months of 2026, according to National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) data.
These industrial firms with an annual main business revenue of at least 20 million yuan (about 2.97 million U.S. dollars) saw their combined profits reach 5.27 trillion yuan in the January-August period.
In August alone, profits of major industrial firms grew 4.2 percent year on year, the NBS noted.
Yu Weining, an NBS statistician, attributed this relatively fast profit growth to the steady advance of industrial production and a widened increase in industrial product prices.
Earlier data revealed that the country's industrial output rose 5.3 percent in the first eight months of the year, while the producer price index, which measures costs of goods at the factory gate, climbed 3.8 percent year on year in August.
Yu highlighted the electronic sector as the main pillar supporting industrial growth, with profits surging 110 percent year on year, contributing 62 percent to the overall profit growth of industrial firms.
"The accelerated expansion of new technology applications, represented by artificial intelligence, has driven the expansion of demand in related fields, propelling swift profit growth in the electronics industry," Yu said.
Yu noted that rising chip demand driven by emerging scenarios such as new energy vehicles, the Internet of Things and computing power centers had boosted profits in the optoelectronic device manufacturing and semiconductor discrete device manufacturing industries by 72 percent and 51.8 percent, respectively.
High-tech manufacturing played a prominent role in driving growth. During the January-August period, profits of high-tech manufacturing firms above designated size soared 54.7 percent year on year, 39 percentage points higher than the overall growth rate.
Profits of raw material manufacturing jumped 47.3 percent year on year in the January-August period, contributing 6.2 percentage points to the overall profit growth. Higher international crude oil and non-ferrous metals prices, meanwhile, helped lift chemical and non-ferrous metals profits in this period, while petroleum processing recovered from making losses to generating profits.
Industrial firms' unit costs continued to decline in the January-August period, with cost per 100 yuan of operating revenue down 0.41 yuan year on year, while the profit margin on operating revenue rose 0.44 percentage points to 5.66 percent, reflecting improved cost control and profitability.
China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) highlights the development of a modern industrial system anchored by advanced manufacturing. The country will move to upgrade traditional sectors to the mid-to-high end of the value chain, nurture emerging industries, and make forward-looking plans for industries of the future, according to this development blueprint.
Looking ahead, Yu said efforts should be made to expand domestic demand, optimize supply, accelerate the shift from old growth drivers to new ones, and promote the sustained development of the industrial economy with new and improved quality. ■

A glimpse of Yuanyang Hani Terraces in SW China's Yunnan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
17:40:16 CST
18:40:16 KST

Villagers harvest rice in Aichun Village of Yuanyang County in Honghe Hani and Yi Autonomous Prefecture, southwest China's Yunnan Province, Sept. 21, 2026.
Listed as a World Cultural Heritage Site, a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System, and a World Heritage Irrigation Structure, the Yuanyang Hani Terraces vividly demonstrate China's ecological wisdom of "harmonious coexistence between humans and nature." Today, the millennia-old mountain farming in the terraced fields is taking on a new look.
The terraces are nestled in the Ailao Mountains along the southern bank of the Red River in Yunnan. For centuries, fragmented plots, steep slopes and narrow paths had forced farmers to carry rice sacks on their backs or with horses. Today, drones can transport grain directly from paddy edges to village rooftops, reducing transport costs and shortening the transport time from 40 minutes to less than 10 minutes.
New planting technologies are also easing farmers' workloads. A degradable paper-film embedded seeding and fixed-point planting technology developed by the School of Agriculture of Yunnan University has been applied in Niujiaozhai Town of Yuanyang County, allowing farmers to complete a full day's transplanting work in two to three hours. Local agricultural authorities have also improved rice varieties and introduced rice-fish-duck farming to raise household incomes.
While new technologies support farming, the ancient terraces still rely on the participation of local people, who maintain and repair ditches to keep water supplies stable and prevent terraces from being abandoned.
To protect the terraces, it is critical to let farmers share the fruits of economic development. Cooperatives here have boosted sales of local red rice via e-commerce and distributed profit dividends to farmers. Azheke Village, nestled in the heart of the terraces, has embraced a unique approach to tourism development. Villagers have contributed resources such as terraces, houses and traditional ways of life, creating a model of collective participation and shared prosperity.
The improved livelihoods have drawn young rural migrants back home. In Duoyishu Village alone, over 80 homestays are now in operation, with more than 100 returning youths working in tourism, catering and transport sectors.
In Yuanyang, the annual rice harvest now means far more than a good crop. It embodies a dynamic balance between ancient heritage protection and modern development, ensuring that the millennia-old terraces stay cultivated, local communities stay prosperous, and the unique farming legacy endures for generations.
