US tech firm charged over secret Russian ownership sold tools to European police
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:40:43 UTC
12:40:43 KST

BRUSSELS — A U.S.-based data-extraction firm accused of being secretly run from Russia has worked on EU-backed projects and sold its services to European law enforcement agencies, according to documents seen by POLITICO.
The U.S. Justice Department last week charged Oxygen Forensics — officially headquartered in Virginia — of concealing that it was actually owned and operated by Russians. The company develops and sells powerful software capable of extracting and analyzing information from smartphones and computers, a process known as "digital forensics."
According to public records reviewed by POLITICO, Oxygen was used in at least two EU-funded projects aimed at improving how electronic evidence is collected, processed and shared in criminal investigations.
Advertisement
The first project, EVIDENCE, (European Informatics Data Exchange Framework for Courts and Evidence), which received more than €1.9 million in EU funding between 2014 and 2016, listed Oxygen Forensics among the companies consulted on how Europe could better handle and exchange digital criminal evidence. That placed the company in a wider network that included EU police agency Europol, judicial cooperation agency Eurojust and the European Anti-Fraud Office's digital forensics unit.
The second project, INSPECTr, backed under Horizon 2020, an EU research and innovation funding arm, was designed to help European police bring together and analyze digital evidence collected using different tools. It built software that could take evidence extracted with Oxygen Forensics and make it easier for investigators using other systems to access and analyze it.
Although both of those EU-backed projects were launched well before Russia’s February 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine and subsequent European sanctions, INSEPCTr continued to operate until 2023. Oxygen also currently remains listed on the websites of both projects. On its own now-defunct website, Oxygen Forensics had listed the European Commission as a client.
A Commission spokesperson stressed that Oxygen Forensics was not a member of either consortium, "and hence did not receive funding under these projects from the Commission." The spokesperson, who was granted anonymity to speak freely about a sensitive topic, said EU-funded projects are subject to strict eligibility and ethics standards, and "since the beginning of the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine, Russian-based entities cannot participate in Horizon Europe projects in any capacity."
Sister company's FSB link
More recently, after its involvement with the EU-backed projects, Oxygen's products have been accredited and purchased by multiple national police agencies across Europe, including those in Germany, Spain, Italy and Poland, according to notices in the EU tender database.
A statement published Wednesday by the U.S. Justice Department found Oxygen Forensic's software was developed and managed by a team in Russia under the direction of Russian national Oleg Sergeyevich Davydov, but purported to be led by Lee Reiber, a 55-year-old native of Boise, Idaho. An affidavit filed with the complaint says Oxygen Forensics was in contact with the U.S. Department of War and several parts of the Department of Homeland Security, including the Secret Service, its digital-forensics training institute, Homeland Security Investigations and the department's internal watchdog.
Advertisement
Reiber has since been arrested in the U.S. Davydov was arrested Sunday at London's Heathrow Airport as he prepared to board a flight to Istanbul, according to a statement by the Justice Department. Lawyers for the two men did not respond to POLITICO's request for comment.
Representatives for Oxygen Forensics did not respond to requests for comment either. In the meantime, the company's website has been seized by the U.S. government.
Prosecutors allege that after Washington imposed sanctions on Russia in 2022, Oxygen's Russian owners concealed both their ownership and the continued development of the company's software in Russia. The five Russians behind Oxygen Forensics also controlled a Russian sister company, MKO Systems, that sold the same underlying technology to the Russian Security Service (FSB) and the country's Interior Ministry.
The Justice Department complaint does not allege that Oxygen's software contained malicious code or that the company used it to gain unauthorized access to customers' systems or data. U.S. investigators did, however, seize corporate bank accounts, 57 domains and other cyber infrastructure they said was "used in furtherance of the alleged acts."
Used across Europe
Oxygen's footprint extends beyond the Commission-backed research projects. The French investigative news organization, Disclose, found its surveillance software was supplied to Moroccan authorities under an EU-funded border-management program for the Maghreb. As well as financing the purchase of the software, the EU also funded training courses led by employees of Oxygen Forensics for Moroccan police.
The company has listed major European law-enforcement bodies among its customers.
Advertisement
In Hungary, a government procurement document shows that the Hungarian police signed an IT contract in Dec. 2024 with Oxygen Forensics worth 10.14 million Hungarian forints (€27,000) which ran through Dec. 2025.
In Italy, an April 2026 technical brief issued by the Public Prosecutor's Office in the Sardinian city of Sassari explicitly lists Oxygen Forensics among the recognized systems that judicial police can use to extract and analyze data from mobile devices.
And in Spain, a 2026 study on digital analysis of WhatsApp on Android and Apple smartphones was produced by a National Police inspector accredited by Oxygen Forensics and involved in training police investigators in digital analysis.
Law enforcement agencies in Romania and Latvia also bought its software, as recently as September.
None of the national police agencies involved responded to requests for comment.
Natalia Krapiva, senior legal counsel at digital rights group Access Now, said civil society organizations had warned for years about Oxygen Forensics' Russian ownership and development links, which she said have now been corroborated by the U.S. case.
"If in fact Russian-made software designed for the FSB and Investigative Committee was used for handling EU Commission criminal evidence database, it raises a serious possibility of sensitive information being compromised and accessed by Russian authorities," Krapiva said.
"We call on the EU and every government using these tools to suspend them and fully investigate how a Russian-owned company spent a decade inside Western law enforcement."

Malaysian durian industry eyes China market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:33:56 UTC
12:33:56 KST

Malaysia is pushing to take durian, whose powerful smell delights its lovers and repels its haters, beyond its roadside stalls and family orchards, particularly targeting the Chinese market.
Devotees savour durian like wine. 
For the Malaysian ones, the taste of their rich and creamy flesh varies widely across types. 
Some are prized for their sweet custard and fruity notes, others for a hint of bitterness, an alcohol tinge or even a peanut butter flavour.
Malaysians' efforts to elevate the industry can be found in the capital, Kuala Lumpur, at a centre devoted exclusively to the fruit and the growing variety of products made from it.
At the Kuala Lumpur Durian Experience Centre, near the landmark Petronas Twin Towers, visitors venture into a replica durian orchard to discover the fruit’s culture and history. 
In another room, a theatre show draws laughter. 
Downstairs, visitors enjoy platters and egg tarts crafted from it.
Launched this summer after an investment of nearly US$2 million, the two-story centre spans about 1,900 square metres and is open daily. 
Its durian shop welcomes guests from morning to midnight.
Its founder, Edison Ang, said the centre targets both local customers and tourists, especially those from China, the world's biggest durian importer. 
He said Chinese palates have long been influenced by Thai durian culture.
“What we actually hope for now is not to get people who don’t eat durian to start eating durian," he said. 
“Instead, we hope consumers who are already eating durian from other countries will switch to Malaysian durian.”
In 2025, China imported 1.87 million tonnes of fresh durian worth US$7.5 billion, with volume jumping over six times in the past decade.
Thailand’s earlier entry helped it secure over half that market by value in 2025. 
Malaysia, which began exporting fresh durian to China in 2024, was dwarfed. 
But for the first half of 2026, the value of China's fresh durian imports from Malaysia quadrupled compared with the same period last year, pointing to rapid growth.
Unlike their rivals, Malaysian growers typically do not harvest early, instead collecting only naturally ripened fruit caught in nets or ropes as they fall.
That’s the industry’s biggest advantage and also its biggest weakness, Ang said, as sellers have to race against time because the fruit’s shelf life is at most two to three days. (AP)

Taiwan ends 60-year men's athletics gold drought at Asian Games
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:30:49 UTC
12:30:49 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — High jumper Fu Chao-hsuan (傅兆玄) ended a 60-year wait for a men's athletics gold medal at the Asian Games on Sunday, clearing 2.25 meters to win the men's high jump.
The 23-year-old matched his season-best mark in a rain-soaked final in Nagoya. Fu and India's Sarvesh Kushare both cleared 2.25 meters, but Fu won the gold after clearing the height on his first attempt. Kushare needed two attempts, while South Korea's Woo Sang-hyeok (禹相赫) took bronze with 2.22 meters, per LTN.
Fu and Kushare subsequently failed three times at 2.28 meters, leaving Fu atop the standings. Fu said he had initially expected to finish second or third and was surprised to win gold. “I thought I might get third, and if I was lucky, second. I never expected to win the gold medal,” he said.
Fu also said he was deeply moved. “I hope I can go around the track and stay on the field longer,” he said.
The victory marked Taiwan's first Asian Games medal in men's high jump since Liao Hsueh-sung (廖學松) won bronze at the 1990 Beijing Games. It was also Taiwan's first Asian Games gold in a men's athletics event since Wu Ah-min (吳阿民) won the decathlon at the 1966 Bangkok Asian Games, per CNA.
Fu said his progress had been slow at times as he watched teammates improve and set national records while he struggled to improve his own performances. He credited his family and friends with helping him stay focused.
His mother was in Japan for the competition, marking the first time she had watched him compete at an international event in person. Fu said he felt he performed better when his family was in the stands.
Fu is set to receive NT$4.5 million under the National Glory Award system. He will also receive a bonus of NT$63,000 (US$2,000) from Taiwan Olympic Committee President Tsai Chia-fu (蔡家福) and NT$300,000 from Taiwan Athletics Association Chair Yeh Cheng-yen (葉政彥), per LTN.
Fu said he planned to share a significant portion of the prize money with his family as a way of thanking them for their support.

US releases product lists for US$30 billion China tariff deal

US releases product lists for $38 billion China tariff deal
- The US and China agreed to cut tariffs on about US$30 billion of imports each, focusing on non-sensitive goods like household products, toys, meat, and agricultural items to stabilise trade relations.
- The tariff relief covers US$60 billion in bilateral trade, with about 90% of products seeing reductions to most-favoured-nation rates, benefiting US agricultural exports and Chinese consumer goods.
- Both countries extended their trade truce to January 2026 and will set up a new Agricultural Working Group to boost US agricultural purchases, aiming to meet annual targets through 2028.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The US and China detailed a plan to cut tariffs on about US$30 billion (S$38 billion) of imports from each country, as the superpower rivals take steps to steady ties following a summit between leaders Donald Trump and Xi Jinping.
The list for goods entering the US contains 77 entries, including fireworks, household products, sporting equipment and toys, according to documents published by both governments.
They also listed 1,619 goods set to potentially enter China, such as meat, seafood, dairy products, grains, coal, timber and medical equipment.
The expected tariff relief for US$60 billion in bilateral trade was one of the most tangible outcomes of Xi’s state visit to Washington last week, even though the amount is a fraction of the US$415 billion in total goods exchanged between the world’s largest economies in 2025.
The two sides extended their trade truce until January as they pursue a broader agreement ahead of two more expected meetings between Trump and Xi in 2026.
With major disputes over export controls and Taiwan unresolved, non-sensitive trade has emerged as one area where agreements remain possible.
Shares of some Chinese appliance makers rose after details of the tariff cuts emerged, with Joyoung Co jumping by the 10 per cent limit in Shenzhen and Bear Electric Appliance up as much as 9.5 per cent.
China said the tariff reductions would take place simultaneously after fulfilling procedures required in domestic law.
“This arrangement will help to further stabilise China-US economic and trade relations and create favourable conditions for China’s exports of relevant products to the US,” the Chinese Commerce Ministry said.
About 90 per cent of the products covered by the reciprocal arrangement would have their tariffs reduced to most-favoured-nation rates, according to the statement.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer described the selected products as non-sensitive goods that could qualify for more favourable tariff treatment.
He said the recommendations would improve access for US agricultural products and medical devices while lowering barriers on Chinese household goods and toys.
“President Trump is unlocking improved market access for about 30 percent of US exports to China, while benefiting consumers with imports from China of household goods, toys, and other products that the United States generally does not import from other countries,” Greer said.
Beijing said tariffs on coal imported from the US would be included in the framework, a step it said would support Chinese purchases in 2027 and 2028.
The White House had previously said China agreed to import at least 10 million tonnes of coal from the US in 2027 and again in 2028.
Key grains including wheat, corn and sorghum are among the agricultural exports destined for a tariff cut.
That could help China make progress toward a goal to buy at least US$17 billion in US agricultural products annually through 2028, in addition to a commitment to buy 25 million tons of soybeans per year.
Progress towards the US$17 billion goal has been slow since it was announced by the Trump administration after the last leaders’ summit in May, with traders looking to potential tariff cuts from the meeting in Washington DC to spark a wave of new buying.
Agricultural purchases are often seen as the low hanging fruit of any trade deal between the US and China, less complicated than more sensitive issues such as chip technology or artificial intelligence.
A new Agricultural Working Group will be established between the two countries following the summit, according to China’s Commerce Ministry, with an inaugural meeting set to take place by the end of 2026. BLOOMBERG

Is the universe infinite? The answer gets weird fast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:18:42 UTC
12:18:42 KST

Is the universe infinite? The answer gets weird fast
- Date:
- September 27, 2026
- Source:
- Universe Today
- Summary:
- Measurements of ancient light from the cosmic microwave background suggest that the universe is remarkably flat. But that does not prove it is infinite, because the observable cosmos could be only a small patch of a much larger curved universe. Space could even be flat while wrapping around on itself in exotic ways.
- Share:
Earth has a finite surface. We can measure it, and if the planet itself were expanding, that surface area would increase over time. Surprisingly, our familiar planet also offers a useful way to think about something far harder to understand: what the universe might be like beyond the region we can observe.
The simplest assumption is that beyond our cosmic horizon, there is simply more universe. More stars. More galaxies. More AI-generated cat videos. It is similar to standing somewhere on Earth and assuming that beyond your visible horizon, there is still more Earth.
But how large is the entire universe, including everything beyond what we can see?
The frustrating answer is that we may never know.
The Limits of the Observable Universe
The boundary of the observable universe is not merely the farthest distance our telescopes can currently reach. It represents a deeper limit on what information can ever reach us. The universe contains a finite amount of information that can become accessible to us, even if we waited for an arbitrarily long time.
Beyond that boundary, we are left to infer and speculate.
One possibility is straightforward: the universe is infinite. Space simply continues forever with no endpoint.
But another possibility is that the universe is finite.
That immediately raises an obvious question. How can something be finite without having an edge?
Earth provides the answer.
The surface of our planet has a finite area, yet someone traveling along that surface never encounters a boundary where the ground suddenly ends. Yes, Earth has an edge if you leave its surface in the third dimension and head into outer space, but that misses the point. The two-dimensional surface itself is finite and has no border because it curves back around.
How Geometry Reveals Curvature
We do not need to leave Earth to prove that its surface is curved. Mathematics gives us several ways to detect curvature while remaining entirely on the surface.
Triangles provide one example. On a perfectly flat plane, the three interior angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. Thank you, Euclid.
But imagine drawing enormous lines between three widely separated cities on Earth. The resulting triangle would not behave like one drawn on a sheet of paper. Its interior angles would add up to more than 180 degrees because the surface beneath it is curved.
Parallel lines offer another clue. On a flat plane, parallel lines never meet. On a curved surface, however, lines that begin parallel can eventually converge.
Imagine that you and I begin at different points along the equator and travel straight north. Eventually, our paths meet at the North Pole. Neither of us turned toward the other. The surface of Earth curved beneath us.
Astronomers can perform similar geometric tests on the universe itself.
Ancient Light Tests the Shape of Space
One of the most powerful tools comes from the cosmic microwave background, or CMB.
This ancient radiation was released when the early universe cooled enough for light to travel freely through what had previously been a hot, dense plasma. Scientists understand much of the relevant plasma physics (we have a decent understanding of plasmas here on Earth), which allows them to predict what patterns should appear in this ancient glow.
Those predictions include tiny temperature variations scattered across the CMB.
And those variations are exactly what astronomers observe.
More importantly, scientists can calculate how large those temperature patches should appear. If space were strongly curved, the light traveling toward us across billions of light years would follow altered paths. That distortion would change the apparent size of the patterns.
Astronomers can therefore compare the observed size of the CMB features with the size predicted for different cosmic geometries.
The features appear at essentially the expected scale for flat space.
That is why scientists say the universe appears to be geometrically flat.
So is the mystery solved? Does a flat universe automatically mean an infinite universe?
Not quite.
Flat Does Not Necessarily Mean Infinite
Imagine trying to measure the curvature of Earth while confined to your own neighborhood. The area would look nearly flat. Small triangles would behave almost exactly as Euclid predicted, and short parallel paths would not noticeably converge.
The problem would not be that Earth is actually flat. Your measuring area would simply be too small compared with the size of the planet.
Something similar could be true of the universe.
Our measurements are limited to the observable cosmos. Within that enormous region, space appears extremely flat. But the universe outside our observable patch could be vastly larger.
It is therefore possible that the universe has curvature that becomes apparent only on scales much larger than we can access (I know that tens of billions of light-years isn't exactly tiny, but it is compared to how big the universe COULD be.)
If so, space might eventually curve back around itself.
In principle, that could mean traveling continuously in one direction would eventually return you to where you started, much as traveling around Earth can bring you back to your starting point.
In practice, the expansion of the universe places regions beyond our cosmic horizon permanently out of reach, so such a journey remains a theoretical thought experiment.
But things can get even stranger.
The Universe Could Be Flat and Still Wrap Around
A universe can be geometrically flat without being infinite in every direction.
To understand how, picture a flat sheet of paper. Draw triangles and parallel lines on it. Now bend the paper into a cylinder without stretching or tearing it.
Locally, the geometry remains flat. The triangles still behave like ordinary triangles, and the parallel lines still behave like parallel lines. Yet one direction now loops around.
This highlights the difference between geometry and topology.
Geometry describes properties such as curvature. Topology describes the broader way a space is connected.
The observable universe appears geometrically flat. But that does not automatically tell us whether one or more dimensions might wrap around and connect back to themselves while remaining locally flat.
Topology allows for some very strange possibilities.
A Mobius strip can be created by connecting the ends of a strip after introducing a twist. A Klein bottle can be thought of as another unusual connected surface. Cylinders, donuts, Mobius strips, and Klein bottles can all illustrate how spaces with locally flat geometry can have very different overall structures.
In three dimensions, mathematicians have identified 17 distinct topologies that can all remain geometrically flat. One particularly interesting example is Hantzsche Wendt space, which involves repeating structures related to hexagonal patterns.
Scientists Have Looked for Cosmic Loops
Astronomers have searched for evidence that the universe has a closed topology.
One strategy is to look for repeated patterns in the cosmic microwave background. Another is to search for galaxies that might appear in different places on opposite sides of the sky because their light has traveled through a universe that wraps around itself.
So far, researchers have found no convincing evidence that this happens.
Based on everything we can currently observe, the universe appears both geometrically flat and topologically simple. In other words, there is no detected sign that its dimensions loop back on themselves.
But once again, our cosmic horizon creates a fundamental limitation. If the scale of any such looping is larger than the observable universe, we may never be able to detect it.
That means we may never know with certainty whether the entire universe is infinite, finite, curved, or connected in some larger and stranger way.
And then there is the multiverse.
In some cosmological ideas, everything we call the universe, including regions far beyond our observable horizon, might be only one bubble among potentially countless others. Those bubbles could expand away from one another while new regions undergo their own Big Bang-like beginnings.
But that is probably enough cosmic geometry for one day.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Universe Today. Original written by Paul Sutter. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

The Islamabad Memorandum Returns to the Spotlight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:09:00 UTC
12:09:00 KST

The Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) that Pakistan helped negotiate between Iran and the U.S. in June and which had largely dropped out of public discussion in recent months is back in the news again. The renewed attention on the MoU, however, does not necessarily indicate a clear pathway toward a lasting de-escalation of the conflict. Rather, it signals a new high level of endorsement since its signing in June.
The Pakistan-mediated 14-point interim understanding that Washington and Tehran endorsed was intended to halt the armed hostilities, reopen the Strait of Hormuz and create space for broader talks on nuclear and other issues. Its recent return to high-level conversations during the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) summit in New York suggests that, despite repeated setbacks, the agreement still serves as the primary reference point for those seeking to prevent further escalation.
The latest references to the MoU emerged largely at meetings held on the sidelines of this year’s UNGA. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, speaking after discussions with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, stated that the entire Pakistani leadership remained united in its resolve to expedite the peace efforts outlined in the Islamabad MoU. Pezeshkian, for his part, reaffirmed that the memorandum remained “totally acceptable” to Iran and that Tehran was ready to take it forward. These remarks, delivered after weeks of relative quiet, signaled that both sides of the original mediation still viewed the document as a viable baseline for de-escalation.
Chinese President Xi Jinping added further weight to the MoU during his state visit to the United States last week. In talks with U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House, Xi expressed support for the U.S. and Iran returning to the June deal that was meant to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. He also said that both parties should resolve differences through dialogue and negotiation and reach a comprehensive agreement that included the nuclear issue.
Amid this renewed focus on the June agreement, President Xi’s intervention carried particular significance because it came amid broader discussions on global economic stability. The Chinese leader also noted that new economic and trade arrangements between Beijing and Washington represented positive news for the economies and peoples of both countries and for the world economy at large. By linking regional de-escalation to the condition of the global economy, Xi underscored that the prolonged crisis in West Asia carries costs that go far beyond the immediate theater of conflict.
While these high-level statements are important, developments on the ground indicate that negotiations have not gathered significant momentum. For instance, Iranian officials held three hours of talks with U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of UNGA. This was the first such contact since U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance met an Iranian delegation in Switzerland in June to advance the memorandum. The meeting itself produced no public breakthrough, but its occurrence after months of silence suggested that channels remain open.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi injected urgency into these latest conversations by stating that if the necessary conditions were met, the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days. He emphasized that the actions required of the U.S. are already contained in the MoU and that the choice now resides with Washington.
Meanwhile, Trump has rejected the Iranian proposal for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, with some reports indicating that the U.S. is planning another round of attacks on Iran after the upcoming midterm elections. Meanwhile, Iranian officials appear to have ignored Trump’s rhetoric, saying that they are waiting for an official response from mediators on the proposals under discussion within the Islamabad framework.
For Pakistan, the renewed focus on the MoU offers another opportunity to press for de-escalation between Iran and the U.S., especially since the agreement now has Xi’s explicit backing.
However, the stakes for Islamabad have grown considerably since June. Pakistan is no longer focused solely on salvaging the original understanding. The country’s policymakers are simultaneously attempting to help ease tensions between Yemen’s Houthis and Saudi Arabia as well as Iran and the U.S.
Last week, the military leadership from Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan convened under the joint Makkah defense pact to discuss urgent steps in support of the Saudis amid Houthi attacks. The three countries resolved to accelerate military cooperation, with Islamabad and Riyadh separately committing to joint efforts to confront threats to Saudi territory. This expanded mediation portfolio has arguably stretched Pakistan’s diplomatic capacity at a time when the original Iran-U.S. conflict has only broadened in scope.
Moreover, there are additional risks which can complicate the picture. For instance, Trump has reportedly hinted at the possibility of renewed military action against Iran even as de-escalation talks continue. Tehran has responded with warnings of new military surprises should it come under attack. Iranian officials have also cautioned that any future confrontation could extend the conflict into the Arabian Sea.
It is pertinent to mention that Pakistan possesses no enforcement mechanism within the Islamabad MoU. The country’s influence rests solely on the goodwill of the primary parties and the diplomatic capital it has accumulated through mediation efforts. As the war continues to stretch and new fronts are opening, there is a growing risk that the original understanding may be overtaken by events, which could put additional pressure on Islamabad’s carefully cultivated role as a regional mediator.
The Islamabad MoU has arguably returned to the diplomatic conversations not because its implementation is imminent, but because it remains the only structured framework both sides have formally accepted as part of a de-escalation mechanism.
Whether that framework can still function as a roadmap depends less on statements delivered in New York or Washington and more on the willingness of Iran and the U.S. to translate words into actions on the ground.
For Pakistan, the coming days will test whether its mediation capacity can keep pace with a conflict that continues to expand in both geography and complexity.

Putin is testing NATO on Norway’s remote Arctic islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:07:39 UTC
12:07:39 KST

BARENTSBURG, Norway — For the best part of a century, the biggest threat to the residents of Svalbard was polar bears. Increasingly, it now comes from Russia.
Fears are growing that Moscow could use the sprawling Arctic archipelago — a part of Norway with an unusual legal status — to test NATO militarily amid growing uncertainty over the U.S. commitment to European defense.
Allies suspect Russia of probing crucial undersea cables in the waters off Svalbard and staging military-style events that test the limits of the rules governing its presence there. As Russia ramps up hybrid attacks across Europe, Oslo is racing to boost its naval and surveillance capabilities to protect its northern flank, while local authorities on Svalbard are investing in critical infrastructure — and even have an evacuation plan in place.
Advertisement
“There is more tension in the Arctic and in the north, and of course also Svalbard is a part of that,” Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik told POLITICO. “We know that Russia ... uses a lot of ways to try to provoke or find ways to do hybrid threats.”
Despite its status as Norwegian territory, the archipelago's main island, Spitsbergen, is home to a Russian town.
“Russian leadership is highly unpredictable and more and more risk prone,” said Kari Aga Myklebost, a Russian history professor and Svalbard expert at Norway's Arctic University. “I wouldn't close out any scenario when it comes to the Kremlin's will to confront NATO.”
High North, high tension
For decades, Svalbard symbolized the Norwegian maxim “High North, low tension,” which saw efforts to build cooperation among Arctic countries, including Russia.
Beyond its remoteness — lying over 900 kilometers from mainland Norway — and its glacial temperatures, that was down to the archipelago's unique status. Under a 1920 international treaty, countries recognized Oslo’s sovereignty over the islands and in return gained resource exploitation rights — with the Soviets buying the town of Barentsburg to mine local coal deposits soon after.
Advertisement
The treaty also forbade any nation from using Svalbard for “warlike purposes” including the construction of naval bases and fortifications, but Norway does visit the archipelago with coast guard and military vessels.
At its Cold War peak, 2,400 Soviet citizens lived on Spitsbergen, the only populated island, making up around 70% of its population.
Moscow has little incentive to upend the treaty because it could rebound against its own interests. With Russia’s northwestern Kola Peninsula — home to two-thirds of its nuclear second-strike submarines — sitting around 1,000 kilometers away, “Russia has been cautious to avoid any kind of escalation,” Myklebost said.
A Soviet-era placard in Barentsburg. | Victor Jack/POLITICO
That makes it strategic for NATO, too. “In a military conflict … this is where the Russian submarines could enter the North Atlantic and hide at greater depths and pose a threat to NATO and the U.S.,” she argued.
Yet tensions have grown following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Moscow also began direct boat trips from Russia in 2024 and last year set up a chapter of the Russian Geographical Society, which is led by former Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu.
“We call them gray zone provocations,” Myklebost said. “It’s a very cost-efficient way of asserting Russian presence and … challenging Norway's jurisdiction.”
As a result, Norway’s intelligenceservices this year warned the Kremlin “aims to increase Russian scope for action in Svalbard.”
British, American and Norwegian forces this spring reportedly caught Russian vessels testing a secret subsea cable-cutting weapon off Svalbard’s coast.
Although Barentsburg’s coal reserves are dwindling, Moscow is not abandoning the town. Moscow provided state-owned Trust Arktikugol, which administers Barentsburg, with about 1.89 billion rubles (€20 million) in federal subsidies in 2025, according to its accounts.
Russia’s ambassador to Norway, Nikolay Korchunov, told POLITICO he wanted to see a “transformation of the economic activities” from coal to services in Barentsburg, and said Arktikugol was investing in maintaining the town.
Advertisement
Cranes and scaffolding adorn many of Barentsburg’s Soviet-era buildings, which lie scattered across a jagged hill facing the imposing snow-specked Vøringen glacier — a sign of Russia’s continued interest.
But “we are not questioning any sovereignty of Norway,” Korchunov insisted. “We stress the necessity and importance of fulfilling all the Svalbard Treaty,” he said, accusing Oslo of contributing to a “negative trend towards NATO militarization of entire Baltic-Arctic region.”
On thin ice
Vice Adm. Rune Andersen, the chief of the Norwegian Joint Headquarters, said his priority was “striking that balance between deterrence but maintaining stability” on Svalbard, and remaining “calm and collected” on hybrid threats.
Svalbard Deputy Governor Katharina Rise. | Victor Jack/POLITICO
But given the “risks” of escalation, the military is investing to reinforce its surveillance capabilities, he said, including launching three new maritime mapping satellites next year — alongside “a renewal of the navy and coast guard … to have a continuous presence” nearby.
NATO countries “are more often up in our waters,” said Sandvik, the minister. Defending Svalbard is also a part of NATO’s planning process, he said.
Advertisement
Locally, the strategy is to keep a lid on tensions. Svalbard’s Deputy Governor Katharina Rise said her office meets with Russia’s local consulate four times a year. “We have good and constructive dialogue,” she said. “It's our responsibility to secure the stability and … low tension here.”
Terje Aunevik, the mayor of Longyearbyen, the main Norwegian town on Spitsbergen, said authorities had plans in place to rapidly evacuate the settlement if tensions flare.
With just two subsea internet cables, one airport, one water reservoir and one diesel-run power plant in Longyearbyen that depends on imports, Aunevik said “major investments” are underway, including the construction of two new water reservoirs by around 2029. “We are quite vulnerable in that perspective,” he said.
Out in the cold
Up close, Barentsburg doesn’t look particularly threatening. Few locals venture outside the several dozen crumbling buildings. A plume of smoke escapes the aging coal plant and a lonely hammer-and-sickle Soviet flag flaps in the wind. Barentsburg feels like an abandoned relic of a bygone era.
Some of the recent hybrid activity is also down to a local push for attention from Moscow, said Arild Moe, a research professor and Russia expert at the Fridtjof Nansen Institute think tank. “They’re playing on nationalist strengths … to get priorities and to get finance.”
But Putin’s unpredictability and Trump's repeated wavering on NATO remain wild cards.
Anxiety is also palpable on Spitsbergen. In Barentsburg, “we don’t speak about [political] topics,” said a waitress from St. Petersburg who asked that her name not be used, while acknowledging locals fear a potential NATO-Russia war. “Of course this worries us,” she said.
“There is of course this constant chatter about if the Russian government wants to push a NATO member and Svalbard is the place where they would do it,” said Jonatan Svensson, an expedition guide who has lived in Longyearbyen for five years.
Jonatan Svenssson. | Victor Jack/POLITICO
To assuage those fears, NATO should consider air patrols over Svalbard, shift defensive air assets to the north of mainland Norway and hold joint exercises nearby, the two NATO diplomats said, provided Oslo agreed and the measures complied with the Svalbard Treaty.
However, so far NATO has no public plans to boost its naval or air presence around the islands. But some worry the alliance's current posture won't be enough to deter Moscow.
In theory, it would be “really easy” for Russia to occupy Svalbard, said Ståle Ulriksen, a lecturer at the Royal Norwegian Naval Academy, if it flew in special forces from northern Russia and seized the airport. However, he argued such a scenario is unlikely.
Yet Moscow wouldn’t need to launch a full occupation. According to Myklebost, the analyst, Russia could stage an emergency affecting its local citizens and send in crisis management forces, a move that may not clearly trigger NATO’s Article 5 mutual defense clause.
“A worst-case scenario is a situation where Moscow sees an opportunity to test NATO cohesion,” she said. “Maybe Norway's shouting for help from allies, and then you have Donald Trump saying: ‘No — we are not risking our good deals with Russia over this tiny island.’”

Another Lao Activist Vanishes in Thailand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
03:02:00 UTC
12:02:00 KST

In the early hours of September 15, Khieo Lapchanh, a 26-year-old Lao content creator, finished his shift at a restaurant in Thailand’s Samut Sakhon province and vanished. The following day, he was due at the Office of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) for his first asylum registration interview. He never arrived.
Khieo came to Thailand in 2019 and late last year began posting Facebook videos sharply critical of the Lao government. Within months, his Khiew Channel Facebook page had amassed some 159,000 followers. Among his targets was the Siphandone dynasty, whose hold on high office runs from former president Khamtay Siphandone to his son, Prime Minister Sonexay Siphandone, and his daughter, Vice President Viengthong Siphandone.
The backlash was swift. Khieo was doxxed, depicted in violent AI-manipulated content and subjected to death threats, including a $8,000 bounty on his life. Fearing for his safety after Lao officials twice visited his mother’s home, he withdrew from public activism. Silence, however, offered little protection.
A Familiar Pattern
Khieo is far from the first Lao dissident to vanish or die in Thailand while seeking UNHCR protection. In August 2019, Od Sayavong, a member of the Free Lao group, disappeared in Bangkok while awaiting resettlement to a third country, and Thai police concede that their investigation has made no progress. In May 2023, the body of Bounsuan Kitiyano, a UNHCR-recognized refugee and fellow Free Lao member, was found near the Lao border in Ubon Ratchathani province with three gunshot wounds. He had been planning to move to Australia, and no one has been held accountable for his killing.
The timing of these cases suggests that Lao authorities are closely monitoring activists’ engagement with UNHCR, and that they are prepared to use violence to stop their critics from reaching the safety of a third country.
These cases also expose Thailand’s failure to protect those seeking refuge within its borders. In a 2024 report, Human Rights Watch analyzed 25 cases of transnational repression in Thailand since the 2014 military coup, finding that refugees and asylum seekers have faced surveillance, violence, abductions, enforced disappearances, and forced returns facilitated by the Thai government. The report describes a “swap mart” in which foreign dissidents sheltering in Thailand are effectively traded for critics of the Thai government living abroad.
Thailand’s legal framework compounds this vulnerability. Because the country is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention, asylum seekers are treated as illegal immigrants and remain liable to deportation. In January 2022, another member of the Free Laos group, Khoukham Keomanivong, was arrested in Thailand for overstaying his visa (despite holding a UNHCR card) and only narrowly avoided deportation to Laos following intervention by civil society actors.
A Global Problem
Responsibility for Khieo’s disappearance does not rest with Laos, or Thailand, alone. On September 23, just eight days after Khieo disappeared, more than 130 U.N. human rights experts issued a joint statement urging states to prevent and combat transnational repression and calling for expedited asylum, resettlement and humanitarian visa processes for those at risk. They also warned that such repression is increasingly digital, deploying social media, spyware and malware.
The cross-border targeting of activists is part of a broader global democratic retreat in which many states are culpable. Freedom House reports that global freedom declined in 2025 for the 20th consecutive year, while CIVICUS finds that just 7 percent of the world’s population lives in countries with open or relatively open civic space. Laos fares poorly on both, scoring 13 out of 100 in Freedom House’s index and rated “closed” by CIVICUS. Nor does the threat to Lao activists end at Thailand’s borders. In June 2025, exiled activist Joseph Akaravong was stabbed in the throat and torso in Pau, France, in what the local prosecutor described as an attempted assassination.
China has long been identified as a force for authoritarian consolidation in Southeast Asia and it is the largest source of development assistance and investment in Laos. But China is not the only country with responsibility to bear. In 2025, after Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency set its sights on USAID, the Trump administration cancelled 83 percent of the agency’s programs. Human Rights Watch reports that safe houses for at-risk human rights defenders in authoritarian countries have closed as a result. Manushya, the organization supporting Khieo, had relied on U.S. government funding to run nine safe houses for activists from neighboring states, including Laos and Cambodia, and its founder warned that without that funding it could no longer protect activists facing transnational repression. The sector is now understaffed and under-resourced, leaving activists less safe. The United States must reinvest heavily in human rights protection in Southeast Asia, and other democracies must increase their funding.
The Real Story of 2026
On November 24, Laos is scheduled to graduate from least developed country status, a milestone that will no doubt be marked with much fanfare. Yet it must not be forgotten that the Lao People’s Revolutionary Party has ruled for five decades without organized opposition, independent civil society or independent media, and that since Sombath Somphone’s shocking abduction in 2012, there have been at least 10 murders or attempted murders of Lao activists. Any celebration of the country’s graduation must be accompanied by this story.
Another accompaniment to the graduation toasts is a recognition that young Laotians are no longer willing to remain silent about the lack of freedom and opportunity in their country. Each dissident killed or disappeared only deepens convictions that activism is necessary. The party may continue to silence individual critics, but others will continue to speak out – and those who do not confront the government directly are protesting with their feet. Freedom House notes that Laos’ economic crisis has prompted growing youth emigration, with Lao nationals now the largest group using Thailand’s formal labor migration channel; they now total 267,871, or 40 percent of the total, a figure that continues to rise. In one Xayaburi district, 1,039 of 5,632 high school students dropped out in a single year to find work, and the true number of young Lao leaving is considerably higher once irregular migrants are counted. Their departure is a protest against a government that is failing to offer them a future.
The final lesson of Khieo’s disappearance is one for Lao activists themselves: they must build stronger solidarity. In May, a prominent U.S.-based Lao activist posted a video stating that Khieo was alive and working at a restaurant in Thailand, and shortly before he vanished, it was circulating online once more. This is not the first time an activist has been exposed in this way. When Anousa “Jack” Luangsuphom was shot in Vientiane in 2023, his family initially reported him dead, fearing that the gunman would return if he learned Jack had survived. Within days, news that he was alive in hospital became public and was shared online by a fellow activist. Rivalries and egos among Lao activists only undermine their shared cause and leave everyone less safe. To succeed, they will need to work together.

            Lead Architect: Antonio G. Liñán
Text description provided by the architects. Young and old have one thing in common: they are defined by their relationship with time. People's relationship with time is ephemeral and fleeting. The architecture we propose seeks to improve conditions so that all inhabitants, with varying degrees of dependence on others and on a comfortable and pleasant environment, find themselves in the best possible conditions for time and space to merge into a single point, a Place where the world works better.

Israel says it has killed Oct 7 attacker who was filmed abducting couple
JERUSALEM – Israeli forces have killed a Palestinian militant who was filmed abducting a couple at a music festival during Hamas’s deadly attack on Oct 7, 2023, the military said on Sept 27.
Video footage widely circulated in the aftermath of the attack showed militants abducting Noa Argamani and her boyfriend Avinatan Or at the Nova music festival.
Argamani was rescued in June 2024 during an Israeli operation in the central Gaza Strip, while Or was released by Hamas in October 2025 as part of a ceasefire deal.
Israeli forces “struck in the Nuseirat area and eliminated the terrorist Saher Nidal Latfi Sakr, a terrorist operative affiliated with global jihadist organisations operating in the Gaza Strip”, the Israeli military said in a statement on Sept 27.
Sakr drove the motorcycle used to abduct Argamani and Or, according to the statement.
Hamas and allied factions killed at least 370 people and took 44 hostages at the Nova festival on Oct 7, 2023, according to Israeli figures. AFP

BEIJING, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- China, home to the world's largest high-speed rail network, opened four major high-speed railway sections to traffic on Monday, improving transport links across several regions.
The new sections connect Xiong'an in Hebei Province with Shangqiu in Henan Province, Xi'an with Ankang in Shaanxi Province, Yichang with Xingshan in Hubei Province, and Harbin with Yichun in Heilongjiang Province.
Spanning northern, northwestern, central and northeastern China, the new lines will facilitate travel for residents, improve regional connectivity and support economic development. ■

5 elderly residents die amid flu outbreak at southern Portugal care home
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:49:45 CST
11:49:45 KST

LISBON, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Five elderly residents have died at a care home in southern Portugal following an outbreak of influenza A, local health authorities said Sunday.
The Local Health Unit of Central Alentejo (ULSAC) said that its Multipurpose Emergency Service had received nine patients from the care home since Wednesday. Among these patients, three died, with laboratory tests confirming the virus in two of the deceased. Three others had been discharged from hospital, while three remain hospitalized, it added.
The three hospital deaths brought the total number of fatalities linked to the outbreak to five, following two earlier deaths at the care home.
The ULSAC public health department visited the care home in Estremoz, in the Evora district, on Thursday and has been conducting epidemiological surveillance, including monitoring compliance with infection control measures, hygiene protocols, isolation procedures and the use of personal protective equipment.
A follow-up visit on Sunday afternoon found no new cases or clinical deterioration among the remaining residents.
Portugal's Attorney General's Office confirmed that an inquiry had been opened into the deaths, with no suspects formally identified so far. ■

Sarah Brightman mourns Liu Huan, her Beijing Olympics duet partner, as "true gentleman"
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:49:36 CST
11:49:36 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Soprano Sarah Brightman has paid tribute to late Chinese singer Liu Huan, her duet partner at the 2008 Beijing Olympic Games, describing him as a "true gentleman."
Brightman said on her social media account, "I have been saddened to hear of the passing of the great Liu Huan, who I had the pleasure of singing with at the 2008 Beijing Olympic Games, performing the opening theme song, 'You and Me.'"
"He was an amazing talent and a true gentleman. He will be greatly missed."
Liu, one of China's most celebrated musicians, died of illness in Shanghai on Friday morning at the age of 63.
His most internationally recognized performance came at the opening ceremony of the 2008 Beijing Olympics, where he performed the theme song "You and Me" alongside Brightman before an audience of billions around the world.
A few years ago, Brightman told the Foreign Correspondents' Club of Japan (FCCJ) in Tokyo that it was an honor to be invited to sing with Liu before 91,000 spectators at Beijing's Bird's Nest stadium, describing the performance as "the highlight" of her career.
"It was such an honor," she said. "I think I was the only western artist to have performed on the opening show."
"In many ways, it was the highlight of my life. It was wonderful," she said.
Brightman has returned to China many times since the 2008 Olympics to hold concerts across the country. She and Liu also performed "You and Me" together again during her 2014 concert in Beijing. ■

Chinese yuan strengthens to 6.7399 against USD Monday
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
10:49:25 CST
11:49:25 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- The central parity rate of the Chinese currency renminbi, or the yuan, strengthened 90 pips to 6.7399 against the U.S. dollar Monday, according to the China Foreign Exchange Trade System.
In China's spot foreign exchange market, the yuan is allowed to rise or fall by 2 percent from the central parity rate each trading day.
The central parity rate of the yuan against the U.S. dollar is based on a weighted average of prices offered by market makers before the opening of the interbank market each business day. ■

Faulty road design can turn an everyday drive into a deadly crash.
NEW DELHI: Even seven years after a penal provision was introduced to hold road contractors, designers and road-owning agencies accountable for crashes caused by faulty road design, construction or maintenance resulting in death or disability of victims, not a single agency has been penalised so far under this provision of Motor Vehicles Act.Last week experts flagged this issue at a conference on the impact of amendments that govt made to the Motor Vehicles Act in 2019 while pointing out the need to carry out detailed and proper investigation into all serious crashes across all types of roads. However, there have been few instances where agencies and courts have pulled up road owning entities for failure on their part for serious crashes.
Only this year, govt increased the penalty for agencies found responsible in such cases by 50 times -- from earlier provision of up to Rs 1 lakh “fine” to up to Rs 50 lakh “penalty” through an amendment to Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act.While fines can be imposed by courts after trial, which is a lengthy process, penalties can be levied directly by administrative, regulatory, or governing authorities for non-compliance without a court trial. Sources said this change is likely to have its impact on govt authorities taking action against agencies responsible for poor design, construction and maintenance where these factors resulted in a serious crash.
Some officials of the state road owning agencies admitted that one of the biggest hurdles is establishing a direct causal link between a road engineering defect and a crash as in almost all cases multiple reasons contribute to accidents. This has resulted in accountability remaining confined largely to drivers, with agencies responsible for planning, constructing and maintaining roads escaping scrutiny.The MV Act amendments in 2019 specified that while imposing the fine, courts must consider the road’s design, expected traffic, applicable maintenance standards, the condition in which users could reasonably expect to find the road, whether the designated authority knew or should have known about the hazardous condition, and whether adequate warning signs had been displayed.

Scientists found a surprising driver of Alzheimer’s outside the brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
02:39:28 UTC
11:39:28 KST

Scientists found a surprising driver of Alzheimer’s outside the brain
A surprising immune pathway outside the brain may help drive Alzheimer’s-related damage, and blocking it dramatically protected mice from neurodegeneration.
- Date:
- September 27, 2026
- Source:
- WashU Medicine
- Summary:
- Scientists found that immune cells contributing to Alzheimer’s-related brain damage may be activated in lymph nodes outside the brain before traveling into the nervous system. Blocking this pathway in mice dramatically reduced neurodegeneration and preserved cognitive abilities, pointing to a potentially more accessible treatment target.
- Share:
Immune cells that usually defend the body by attacking infected or foreign cells appear in unusually high numbers in the brains of people with Alzheimer's disease and related conditions. Evidence suggests these cells contribute to neurodegeneration, but researchers have not known where they originate or what prompts them to gather in the brain.
A new study from Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis points to an unexpected source outside the brain. In experiments with mice, researchers found that T cells receive signals from lymph nodes that appear to prepare them to enter the brain and contribute to damage. When the scientists disrupted those signals, neurodegeneration was dramatically reduced.
The findings reveal a previously unrecognized immune pathway that may offer a way to slow or potentially halt damage associated with Alzheimer's disease and primary tauopathies. These disorders are marked by twisted accumulations of tau protein in the brain.
The study was published Sept. 3 in Nature Neuroscience.
An Alzheimer's Pathway Outside the Brain
David M. Holtzman, MD, the Barbara Burton and Reuben M. Morriss III Distinguished Professor in WashU Medicine's Department of Neurology and senior author of the study, said the discovery is especially intriguing because it identifies a disease related process that begins outside the brain. That could make it possible to target mechanisms that are easier to reach and better understood.
"One of the issues in developing treatments for neurological diseases is that you need to engineer your treatment so that it gets into the brain and past the blood-brain barrier, but we might not actually need to get the drugs into the central nervous system to mitigate neurodegeneration," Holtzman said. "There are lots of ways to manipulate T cells that have been studied extensively and that are approved treatments for other diseases, but many haven't yet been explored for neurodegenerative diseases."
Tracing T Cells Back to the Lymph Nodes
Holtzman's laboratory has played a leading role in investigating how the immune system contributes to neurodegenerative disease. In a previous study, the team showed that removing T cells from the brain prevented much of the neurodegeneration that normally develops in mice modeling the tau related damage seen in Alzheimer's disease and primary tauopathies.
The next question was where those immune cells came from and what caused them to move into the brain.
In the new study, Holtzman's team included Hao Hu, PhD, a postdoctoral fellow and the study's first author; co-senior author Jason Ulrich, PhD, a professor of neurology; and their collaborators.
Certain T cells rely on other immune cells, known as dendritic cells, to identify the molecular targets they should attack. Very few of the relevant dendritic cells, known as classical dendritic cells type 1 (cDC1), are found in the brain. Those that are present also do not appear to interact with the T cells that emerge after tau tangles develop.
That evidence suggested that both the dendritic cells and the T cell activation process were originating somewhere outside the brain.
Blocking Immune Signals Reduced Brain Damage
To test that possibility, the researchers eliminated dendritic cells from the lymph nodes and other locations in mice that would normally develop tau tangles and neurodegeneration.
The result was striking. Elevated numbers of T cells in the brain, particularly CD8 T cells, largely disappeared, along with the associated brain damage. Yet the amount of tau tangles in the brain did not change.
The mice also preserved their cognitive abilities. That finding suggests that suppressing T cell activity could potentially slow or reduce the cognitive decline associated with Alzheimer's disease, even when tau tangles remain present.
How Brain Damage May Trigger an Immune Attack
Researchers still do not know the exact signal that causes dendritic cells to activate the T cells.
Holtzman said one possibility is that damage caused by tau releases material from brain cells. That material may then travel to lymph nodes in the neck, where dendritic cells identify it and present it as a target for T cells.
The T cells could then be directed toward the brain, where their activity contributes to neurodegeneration.
A Potential New Route for Alzheimer's Treatment
Because this immune pathway operates outside the brain, it may provide several new therapeutic targets.
Holtzman's team is now testing whether interfering with dendritic cell activity in midlife, around the time tau tangles begin to emerge, can produce the same protection seen when the cells were blocked from birth in this study.
The researchers are also working to identify the specific signal that guides T cells toward the brain. If that signal can be determined, it could offer another way to prevent the immune cells from reaching brain tissue and contributing to damage.
"Until not that long ago, most people, including myself, did not think that the immune response was even involved in neurodegenerative diseases that are due to protein accumulation in the brain," Holtzman said. "That these dendritic cells are involved in neurodegenerative disease is exciting; we've shown they're important, and that they are a potential target for future therapy."
Story Source:
Materials provided by WashU Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Hao Hu, Peter Bor-Chian Lin, Carisa Zeng, Yongyi Li, Megan E. Bosch, Joshua T. Emmerson, Prabal Sharma, Ray A. Ohara, Wendy Dong, Tong Wu, Siling Du, Wenqing Gao, Hong Jiang, Liya Yuan, Xin Bao, Shasha Li, Anthony N. Vomund, Petra Erdmann-Gilmore, Yichen Gu, Miwei Hu, Jonathan Nulman, Timothy M. Miller, Wayne M. Yokoyama, Cheryl F. Lichti, Jeffrey Milbrandt, Richard J. Perrin, Jonathan Kipnis, Maxim N. Artyomov, Kenneth M. Murphy, Jason D. Ulrich, David M. Holtzman. Priming of CD8 T cells by peripheral dendritic cells exacerbates tau-mediated neurodegeneration. Nature Neuroscience, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41593-026-02427-5

The meeting is expected to approve the calendar of events under Pakistan’s presidency, leading up to the Council of Heads of State (CHS) summit for which Islamabad will soon send out invitations to the leaders of all member-states of the Eurasian bloc, including PM Narendra Modi.After joining the China-dominated grouping in 2017 as a full member, India has participated actively in various SCO mechanisms, with Modi representing India at the heads of state summits and external affairs minister S Jaishankar joining the heads of government meetings.Unlike with SAARC, India has ringfenced its involvement in SCO from outstanding bilateral differences with Pakistan, mainly the core issue of cross-border terrorism, while consistently reminding the Organisation that one of its original mandates was to fight terrorism, extremism and separatism. Government has backed SCO connectivity initiatives too but with the rider that these must respect sovereignty and territorial integrity of all States.India’s national coordinator Alok Dimri is expected to participate in the national coordinators’ meeting that will begin on Monday. Even without any substantive bilateral engagement for a decade, India and Pakistan have regularly seen their officials visiting each other’s country for SCO-related exercises and Jaishankar himself travelled to Pakistan in 2024 for the SCO heads of government meeting.
However, the key question remains – even if it’s too early to ask – whether Modi will attend the summit in Islamabad next year. The SAARC summit process remains blocked because of the PM’s reluctance to travel to Pakistan and, barring a dramatic change in the situation, the PM is unlikely to visit Islamabad.
According to Indian officials, any such change can only be effected by Islamabad through tangible and irreversible action against cross-border terrorism and UN-proscribed terror entities operating out of Pakistan. Government recently denied strongly that it is involved even in any track 2 dialogue with Islamabad.Pakistan had assumed presidency of the SCO at the Bishkek summit earlier this month. Debutant Bambase Conte threatened again shortly after the restart, forcing Tzolakis into action, before the Greek goalkeeper tipped away a curling Joshua Kimmich free kick.
Germany was warned in the 67th minute when Kimmich lost possession to Vangelis Pavlidis, who released Fotis Ioannidis, but the forward dragged his effort narrowly wide.
Greece made the host pay seven minutes later. Tzolis switched play across the German defense and Kourbelis found space on the edge of the area. His shot took a deflection off Kimmich and beat Alexander Nubel.
Klopp introduced Florian Wirtz and Jonathan Burkardt in search of an equalizer, but Germany struggled to break down the visitor in the closing stages.
"It wasn't an easy game. To be honest, we didn't do well enough," Germany defender Jonathan Tah said. "We had our chances but didn't take them. In the end, they made the most of their moments and scored the one they needed."
The result leaves Germany on one point from its opening two Group 2 matches, while Greece tops the group with six points.
Germany will host Serbia in Munich on October 1 before traveling to face Greece in Thessaloniki on October 4. ■

One day in Sāvatthī, a wealthy woman named Visākhā came to see the Buddha at midday, her hair and clothes still wet from the funeral of her granddaughter. Visākhā was the greatest of the Buddha’s lay patrons, a mother of many children and grandmother of many more, and she had loved the dead girl dearly. The Buddha asked her whether she would like to have as many children and grandchildren as there were people in the city. She said she would. He asked how many people died in Sāvatthī each day. Some days ten, she said, some days one; the city was never free of the dying. “Then would you ever be without wet hair and wet clothes?” No, she admitted. And the Buddha said:
The story is in the Udāna (8.8), one of the oldest collections in the Pali canon, and it is the kind of passage that makes people say Buddhism is against love. Read on its own, it seems to be: love brings grief, grief is suffering, and the whole point of the path is the end of suffering. But the same canon contains the Mettā Sutta, in which the Buddha tells his monks to cherish every living thing as a mother cherishes her only child, and to let boundless love fill the whole world “above, below and across.” And the tradition that grew from that canon produced the bodhisattva, a figure who vows to remain in the world of birth and death, for as long as space endures, until every being is free – the most extravagant ideal of love in the history of religion.
How can both be true? The answer is that Buddhism drew a line through the middle of what other traditions call love, and put one half on the side of the problem and the other on the side of the cure. This entry is about that line: where it runs, why it was drawn there, and what the different Buddhist schools built on either side of it.
Pali terms are used for the early tradition and Sanskrit for the Mahāyāna; words that have entered English (Buddha, nirvana, karma, sutra, bodhisattva, Zen) are left in their usual forms.

Love in Hinduism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Ask an English speaker what love is and they will struggle, partly because one word has to cover a parent’s tenderness, a lover’s passion, a friend’s loyalty and a saint’s devotion. Sanskrit never had this problem. It has separate words for all of these, and several more besides, and the Hindu traditions built distinct philosophies around each of them.
That is the first thing to know about love in Hinduism: there is no single doctrine, because there is no single Hinduism. The word covers three thousand years of texts, dozens of schools and many gods, and they do not agree about love any more than they agree about anything else. The second thing to know is that, out of this variety, one strand became dominant from roughly the seventh century onwards and has shaped Hindu religious life ever since. It is called bhakti – devotion – and its central claim is that the highest form of love, and the surest way to God, is to love God the way you would love a person: with longing, tenderness, jealousy, grief and joy.
This entry gives a map of the traditions and then focuses on bhakti, since that is where the Hindu philosophy of love is richest. Sanskrit terms are given in the standard scholarly spelling; well-known names (Krishna, Radha, Shiva, Vishnu) are left in their familiar English forms.
Daily Philosophy: Love in Islam
The Qur’an says that God loves and is loved, and Muslims have argued for fourteen centuries about what that means. This guide explains the key Arabic words, sets out the three main theories – the theologians’ love as obedience, the philosophers’ love as cosmic attraction, and the Sufis’ love as the secret of creation – and shows how the mystical tradition turned even Layla and Majnun into a parable of the soul. Part of our series on love in the world religions.
The words
Five terms recur throughout, and it helps to have them in view.
Kāma is desire, especially sensual and erotic desire, and also pleasure in general. It is personified as the god of love who shoots flower-arrows, but it is also, in the earliest texts, a cosmic force. Kāma is not sinful; it is one of the legitimate aims of human life. But it is self-directed – it seeks the satisfaction of the one who desires – and this becomes the crucial contrast.
Prema (or prīti) is love in the fuller sense: tender, selfless affection that seeks the good of the beloved. In devotional theology prema is the name for the highest love of God, the love that has burned away all desire for one’s own gratification.
Bhakti comes from a root meaning to share, to participate in, to belong to. It is usually translated “devotion,” and it means loving attachment to a personal God, expressed in worship, song, service and surrender. Bhakti is the relationship; prema is its perfected emotional content.

Love in Islam

In the year 878, in Baghdad, a Sufi named Abū ‘l-Ḥusayn al-Nūrī was put on trial for his life. Among the charges was that he had been heard to say “I passionately love God, and He passionately loves me.” The prosecutor’s objection was not that Nūrī loved God – every Muslim was supposed to do that – but that he had used the wrong word. The verb he chose, ʿashiqa, was the word for the love of a man for a woman: obsessive, bodily, unreasonable. To apply it to God was, in the prosecutor’s view, an indecency bordering on unbelief. Nūrī was acquitted, but the argument he started did not end. Over the next four centuries it produced one of the richest bodies of writing about love in any religious tradition.
That trial is a good way into the subject, because it shows two things at once. First, that love was never marginal in Islam: the disagreement was about how God is loved, not whether. Second, that the disagreement was real. Islam has a scripture that speaks of love in dozens of places, a law that regulates marriage and kinship, a rationalist theology that was nervous about attributing emotion to God, a philosophical tradition steeped in Plato and Aristotle, and a mystical movement that made love the answer to every question. They did not agree, and this entry maps their disagreements before following the mystical line, since that is where the Islamic philosophy of love went deepest.
Arabic and Persian terms are given in standard scholarly transliteration; familiar names and words (Muhammad, Qur’an, Sufi, Rumi, Mecca) are left in their usual English forms.
Daily Philosophy: Love in Hinduism
Hinduism has no single word for love – it has a dozen. This guide explains the main ones, surveys how the Vedas, Upaniṣads, Advaita and the Gītā treat love, and then focuses on bhakti, the devotional tradition that made love of God the heart of religious life. Part of our series on love in the world religions.
The words
Arabic distinguishes kinds of love as carefully as Sanskrit does, and the distinctions carry theological weight.
Ḥubb and its near-synonym maḥabba are the general words for love, from a root that also gives the word for a seed. This is the Qur’an’s word: God’s love for human beings and theirs for him are both ḥubb. It covers affection, attachment, preference and devotion, and it is morally neutral – one can have ḥubb for wealth or for God.
ʿIshq is passionate, excessive love: love that has become an affliction. Its root may be connected to a word for a creeping vine that strangles the tree it clings to. The Qur’an never uses it. It was the word of the love poets, and it became the word of the Sufis, precisely because it named a love that overwhelms the lover and cannot be controlled. Nūrī’s trial was about this word.

Virtue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

The word has a faintly musty smell. “Virtue” suggests Victorian sermons, chastity, and people who do not have much fun. It is not a word we reach for when we admire someone. We say they are kind, or brave, or have integrity – but we rarely say they are virtuous, and if we did, it would sound like a joke.
This is a historical accident, and a recent one. For most of the history of Western thought, from the fifth century BCE to the eighteenth century CE, virtue was not one moral idea among others. It was the moral idea – the central concept around which the whole of ethics was organised. The question philosophers asked was not “What should I do?” but “What kind of person should I be?”, and the answer was always given in terms of the virtues. Then, for roughly two centuries, the concept went into eclipse. Then, in the second half of the twentieth century, it came back. This entry tells that story and tries to say, at the end of it, what a virtue is.
The word
The Greek word is aretē, and its basic meaning is excellence – being outstandingly good at whatever it is you are for. The word is not specifically moral. A knife has aretē if it cuts well; a horse has aretē if it runs fast; an eye has aretē if it sees clearly. The aretē of a human being is whatever makes a human being excellent at being a human being.
The Latin translation, virtus, comes from vir, “man,” and originally meant something like manliness or valour – the qualities of a good soldier. It broadened, especially in Cicero, to cover the whole range of Greek aretē. Our word “virtue” inherits both, and older English still preserves the sense of excellence or power: a medicine has “virtues,” and something happens “by virtue of” a cause.
The point matters because the Greek concept is much wider, and much less prim, than the modern connotation. To ask about aretē is to ask what it is to be really, fully good at living. That is a question almost everyone finds interesting.
Before philosophy: Homer
In Homer, aretē belongs above all to the warrior. Achilles has it in abundance: strength, courage, skill in battle, a fierce sense of honour. It is competitive – to have aretē is to be better than others – and it is publicly displayed and publicly rewarded. But even in Homer the word is not confined to fighting. Penelope has aretē for her fidelity and cleverness, and Odysseus for his cunning and endurance as much as for his spear.
What Homer does not have is any thought that these excellences might conflict, or that the truly excellent person might have to give up glory for the sake of justice. That thought arrives with the philosophers.

Virtue Ethics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

A friend is in hospital. You visit. She is touched, and says so. “Don’t mention it,” you reply. “I worked out that visiting you would produce more overall happiness than anything else I could do this afternoon.” Or: “I recognised that I had a duty to visit, and I always do my duty.”
Something has gone badly wrong, and it is not that you did the wrong thing. You did the right thing. What is missing is you – the friend who visits because she cares about her friend, not because a theory told her to. The philosopher Michael Stocker used this example in 1976 to diagnose what he called the “schizophrenia” of modern ethical theories: they split what we ought to do from what a good person actually feels and wants. Virtue ethics is the attempt to put them back together.
This entry is about that attempt in its modern form. For the long history of the concept of virtue itself – from Homer through Aristotle and Aquinas to its eighteenth-century eclipse – see our separate entry on Virtue. Here we take up the story where that one leaves off: with the revival of virtue as the foundation of an ethical theory, the shape that theory has taken, and the arguments for and against it.
Daily Philosophy: Virtue
For two thousand years, ‘virtue’ was the central word in Western ethics – the name for whatever it is that makes a person good at being a person. Then it nearly disappeared, and then it came back. This entry traces the concept from Homer and Socrates through Plato, Aristotle, the Stoics and Aquinas to Hume, Kant and the twentieth-century revival, and asks what a virtue actually is.
What virtue ethics claims
Normative ethics – the part of philosophy that asks how we should live – is usually taught as a contest between three approaches. Consequentialism says that what matters is outcomes: the right act is the one that produces the best results. Deontology, in its Kantian form, says that what matters is duty: the right act is the one that conforms to the moral law, whatever the results. Virtue ethics says that what matters, first and foremost, is character: the fundamental moral question is not “What should I do?” but “What kind of person should I be?”, and the answer to the first question falls out of the answer to the second.
The point is one of priority. Every ethical theory talks about virtues; Kant wrote a whole Doctrine of Virtue, and Mill discusses it at length. What makes a theory a virtue ethics is that it treats virtue as basic and explains right action in terms of it, rather than the other way round. The Kantian defines a virtue as a disposition to do one’s duty; the utilitarian defines it as a trait that tends to produce happiness. The virtue ethicist reverses the direction of explanation: a right action is what a virtuous …
