NEW DELHI: Overall acreage of kharif (summer-sown) crops in the country declined by just over 1% this year compared with last year and while the dip was expected due to deficient monsoon rainfall this year, the sowing season still ended up recording higher than 'normal' (average of last five years) acreage. Though only marginally above the 'normal', it reflects tweaks in farmers' strategy if warning comes in advance.Latest acreage data shows total sown area at 1,107 lakh hectares (ha) as of Friday was 3 lakh ha more than 'normal' acreage (1,104 lakh ha) despite a cumulative deficit of 12% (June 1-Sept 26) in monsoon rainfall. In the same period in 2025, which recorded 8% more than normal (surplus) rainfall, total acreage was 1,121 lakh ha.The most popular kharif crop and one of the most water-intensive, paddy, reported a 3.6% decline in acreage compared with last year, but this was still 4.6% higher than the 'normal' acreage. Another guzzler, sugarcane, too reported higher acreage than its normal sown area, reflecting farmers' preference for crops which assure them of better returns, even as they had to depend on excessive use of groundwater, at the risk of high input cost.
The real test of what rainfall deficit will entail, however, may be reflected in the yield of these crops, first estimates for which will soon be released by the Union agriculture ministry. The output of pulses (mainly pigeon peas), oilseeds (mainly soybean and groundnut), cotton and coarse cereals (mainly bajra and maize) may be a real concern due to deficient and skewed distribution of rainfall in the 'monsoon core zone' - the large part of central India and Bihar which depend on seasonal rains for farming in absence of adequate irrigation coverage.
Floods in certain parts of Bihar and Assam, and drought in parts of Maharashtra and Karnataka may also negatively impact the overall output.Apprehending the impact of deficient monsoon rainfall on the rabi (winter-sown) crops due to low moisture content in the soil and shortage of water for irrigation, the agriculture ministry will discuss contingency measures at a two-day meet starting Monday.

Ismat Ara on India’s Crackdown on Love
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
01:38:00 UTC
10:38:00 KST

Love and marriage across religious and caste lines have always been frowned upon and forbidden in India. However, Hindu right-wing organizations have taken this to a new extreme by conjuring up a conspiracy theory they term “love jihad.” India is witnessing a systematic strategy being implemented by Hindutva activists to not just prevent Hindu women from marrying Muslim men but to malign the latter by ascribing to them sinister motives of enticing Hindu women with false promises of love and marriage for the sole purpose of converting them to Islam. Bharatiya Janata Party politicians have used the “love jihad” bogey to deepen Hindu anxieties and polarize society. BJP governments in several states have enacted anti-religious conversion laws. Meanwhile, right-wing goons have wreaked enormous havoc in the lives of young couples who dare to love across religious lines.
In her recent book, “Under a Saffron Sky: Inside India’s Crackdown on Love,” author Ismat Ara recounts the enormous stress and suffering that Hindu-Muslim couples experience. She draws attention to how the “love jihad” “myth” has come to “define an entire community.” In an interview with The Diplomat’s South Asia editor, Sudha Ramachandran, Ara pointed out that while an interfaith relationship is a private matter between two people, “within the ‘love jihad’ narrative, the Muslim man is reimagined as part of a larger, organized project to convert Hindu women, increase the Muslim population, and eventually alter the country’s demographic and religious character.”
What is “love jihad”?
“Love jihad” is the idea that Muslim men are deliberately targeting Hindu women for relationships and marriage in order to convert them to Islam, and that this is part of a larger organized conspiracy. It is an elaborate example of political myth-making and what happens when paranoia about “Muslim danger” enters the mass psyche.
While doing fieldwork for my recent book, “Under a Saffron Sky,” what interested me was not only whether individual cases of deception or coercion exist — they can, as they do in any relationship — but how these individual cases are transformed into evidence of a larger, vast conspiracy, one that comes to define an entire community. The leap from “a Muslim man deceiving a woman” to “Muslim men are conducting an organized campaign against Hindu women to take over this country” is the crucial political leap. When it becomes part of a larger conspiracy, the myth then becomes powerful enough to shape families, communities, police action, and even public policy, acquiring a life of its own, with its own set of myths.
There have been cases such as the 2023 Purola episode in Uttarakhand, where an alleged attempt to abduct a 14-year-old girl was quickly branded as “love jihad,” triggering communal protests and the exodus of Muslim families. The case later collapsed in court, with the girl and her uncle contradicting the initial police version. The minor also told the court that police had tutored her to make allegations against the accused, who were subsequently acquitted.
Could you share with us an example of what an interfaith couple undergoes when they are accused of “love jihad”?
Once people believe the myth of “love jihad,” real couples have to live with its consequences. One of the stories I reported from Uttar Pradesh is of a Hindu woman and a Muslim man who got married. After their nikah (wedding), when the couple went to the district magistrate’s office for their marriage registration, the man was shot in the head by two unidentified assailants right outside the government office in broad daylight. The couple wanted to register their marriage, make it official so no harm could touch them. But the woman saw her husband die before her eyes, minutes before that.
What made the story particularly chilling is the context. The couple had received warnings for weeks and months from local right-wing outfits and people opposed to the relationship and believed that once they had an official stamp from the government, no harm could touch their marriage. So, what began as a deeply personal decision, two people deciding to marry, gradually becomes something that others felt entitled to intervene in, threaten, and violently police.
In another example, from Gujarat, a state still scarred by the communal violence of 2002, a stamp vendor who had sold the couple their marriage stamps went on to call the woman’s family to inform them of their daughter’s “misdoings,” escalating the tension further.
In your book, you argue that “love jihad” is all about controlling women. Could you explain how?
One of the book’s main premises is that this is ultimately about controlling women, and that control operates across communities, although in very different ways. When a Hindu woman is told that she cannot choose her own partner because he belongs to another faith, her agency is being taken away. She is often treated as someone who has been deceived or brainwashed rather than as an adult capable of making a decision. But I also looked at Muslim women in the book. There is a case of a Muslim woman whose parents oppose her marriage because the man she has chosen was not just Hindu, but also belonged to a lower caste. The woman was told by her family that they might have considered a Hindu man — but only if he was upper caste. So, the policing of women’s choices isn’t confined to one community.
It’s an old story of women’s choices being made to represent the honor of an entire community, but what is distinctive about the “love jihad” campaign specifically is the way the Hindu woman has increasingly been made into a symbol, used as a tool, almost as the keeper of her entire community’s honor, purity, and demographic future. Her personal choices are seen as a collective threat. She is considered incapable of making her own decision, but in reality, her decision is powerful enough to threaten the demographic future of an entire community.
Article 21 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the right to life and personal liberty, which includes an individual’s freedom to choose whom they wish to marry. In reality, less than 3 percent of marriages in India are actually interfaith, so this has never been an easy choice. It has always meant navigating disapproving parents, nosy neighbors and hostile looks. But increasingly, crossing that boundary can also mean the police coming to your home. These single-digit marriages are framed as “dangerous” or as something that could alter India’s demography.
“Love jihad” is fundamentally a threat-based concept: it brings together anxieties around women, community honor and national security. But what about the real wars being fought by women? The opposite can be opportunity-based concepts, focusing on potential gains, growth, and positive outcomes rather than on “avoiding dangers or risks.” We must look at the basics that affect the majority of our country’s women, from the girl child being killed to girls not getting education or healthcare access.
Could you share with us how right-wing organizations mobilize and prevent interfaith marriages?
The “foot soldiers,” as well as organizations that work around “love jihad” cases, have multiple sources of information and multiple ways of mobilizing. Some maintain strong local networks; others are highly visible on the street, actively watching for such cases. In some places, they don’t even need to go looking. They have become such recognized “authorities” that people from neighboring areas approach them directly to report what they see as suspicious behavior, or word that a Muslim man is trying to “lure” a Hindu woman.
There are also rehabilitation programs aimed specifically at women, meant to remind them of their religious identity and, in the language of these organizations, to “correct” or undo the ideological influence they are believed to have absorbed from Muslim men. It is not one form of mobilization but many: surveillance, family pressure, public intervention, ideological programming, and street action. Together, they create an environment in which an interfaith relationship becomes something the wider community feels entitled to police.
The Special Marriage Act of 1954 was supposed to help interfaith couples marry. Why hasn’t it worked?
A law can create a legal route, but societal adoption of that route is equally important. The Special Marriage Act was meant to allow people of different faiths to marry without requiring either person to convert. But over the years, interfaith marriage has become increasingly politicized, particularly when it involves a Hindu woman and a Muslim man. The problem is that couples aren’t operating in a social vacuum. They have to navigate families, communities, local officials, and, increasingly now, political scrutiny. A legal provision cannot by itself remove the social stigma or the fear surrounding the choice. The Special Marriage Act exists, but the real question is whether people feel genuinely safe to use it. What do couples do when the law gives you a right, but the process through which you exercise that right can expose you to physical, mental, emotional and legal risks?
Allegations of “love jihad” are usually hurled at Muslim men marrying Hindu women. Are such allegations levelled against Muslim women marrying Hindu men?
Yes, there have been cases where Muslim women have faced similar allegations, particularly allegations that they were attempting to convert Hindu men through marriage. In Uttar Pradesh, for instance, there have been cases where criminal complaints under anti-conversion laws were filed against Muslim women and their male relatives, with families alleging that conversions were being orchestrated through the promise of marriage. In some cases, Muslim women have even been sent to custody in connection with such allegations. So, the idea of a Muslim woman being an agent of conversion is certainly present in some cases.
If religious conversions did not happen, would anxieties that fuel “love jihad” allegations reduce?
Conversion sits at the center of the “love jihad” narrative, but I don’t think its absence would make the deeper anxiety disappear. One thing that became clear to me while reporting these stories is that suspicion often exists even where no conversion has taken place at all. A Hindu woman simply being in a relationship with a Muslim man can be enough to trigger the allegation of “love jihad.” There has been no substantial body of cases establishing an organized “love jihad” conspiracy behind forced conversions. Individual cases of coercion or deception can occur, of course, and deserve to be investigated on their own merits, but that is a very different thing from proving a larger, organized conspiracy.
What happens, then, is that the political idea becomes much larger than the evidence behind it. I sometimes think of it like Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein’s monster: something that is created and then acquires a life of its own. The narrative begins to generate its own evidence. An interfaith relationship becomes suspicious because people have already been told what such a relationship means; the absence of conversion does not necessarily dispel the suspicion. So, conversion is important to the mythology, but it is not really the whole story. The deeper anxiety is about the crossing of community boundaries through intimacy and marriage. Who is allowed to love whom? What happens when a woman chooses a partner from another community? What religion will the children follow? Will the family retain its religious identity? And that is why I see “love jihad” as part of a larger politics of controlling women’s choices.
The policing of interfaith marriage exists across communities. Muslim women too can face enormous family and social pressure when they marry outside the community. But “love jihad” has given that anxiety a particularly powerful political vocabulary when the relationship is between a Hindu woman and a Muslim man.
The Christian Church in Kerala has also accused Muslims of “love jihad.” How similar is their campaign against interfaith marriage?
While there are similarities, there are also important differences. The similarity is in the underlying anxiety: the fear that women from one’s own religious community are being targeted by men from another community, and that such relationships could lead to conversion, loss of community identity, or demographic change. But the Christian discourse in Kerala has been more localized and has emerged from a very different social and political context, rooted largely in concerns within the Christian community about young women, interfaith relationships, and conversion.
The “love jihad” narrative in the wider Hindu nationalist discourse, on the other hand, has acquired a much larger political vocabulary. It has been linked not just to conversion and interfaith marriage, but also to concerns about demography, population growth, religious identity and, at times, national security. It has therefore travelled far beyond individual relationships and become part of a broader political narrative. These campaigns may emerge from different contexts, but they draw upon an older anxiety around women, sexuality and community boundaries.
So I would say the resemblance is real, but the scale, impact, context, and political consequences are different.
The Sangh Parivar’s “love jihad” campaign, you write, brings together several strands of its agenda, including national security. Could you explain?
The idea of “love jihad” draws together things that might otherwise seem unrelated: women’s sexuality, interfaith marriage, religious conversion, demography, Muslim identity, and national security. That is precisely what makes “love jihad” such a potent political idea in the larger Hindu nationalist discourse. An interfaith relationship begins as a private matter between two people, but within the “love jihad” narrative, the Muslim man is reimagined as part of a larger, organized project to convert Hindu women, increase the Muslim population, and eventually alter the country’s demographic and religious character.
There is a kind of escalation at work: first, the relationship is framed as a question of conversion; then conversion is linked to demography and Muslim population growth; and from there, the narrative is stretched to a much larger claim, a threat to the nation’s social and national fabric. That is where national security enters. Once an intimate relationship is recast as part of an organized threat, intervention starts to look like protection. Surveillance, police action, restrictions on marriage, mobilization against individual couples, even mob violence, all justified in the name of the larger public interest.

Assam Government Encroaches Into a World Heritage Site in India’s Northeast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
01:31:00 UTC
10:31:00 KST

Manas National Park in the northeast Indian state of Assam is in danger. The Assam government, which should be protecting this 1,176-acre World Heritage Site, has encroached on the park for several years.
Originally part of the North Kamrup Reserve Forest, the land under contention, which is spread over 9.3 sq km, was given on a 30-year lease to the Indian government for setting up a seed farm. After the lease expired in 2001, the area became part of the Manas National Park and Tiger Reserve, the Assam forest department said in a letter to the Bodoland Territorial Council (BTC) that governs this region.
In the letter, the Assam forest department pointed out that the BTC had leased the encroached land for cultivation. Sources claimed that local farmers are engaged in farming in the area, which is officially not permitted inside a wildlife sanctuary, national park or World Heritage Site. The letter made a case for its handover to the forest department. The forest department also urged the Assam government to convince the BTC to return the encroached area to the Assam forest department
The area that has been allegedly encroached by local farmers with the BTC’s consent is part of the Manas National Park’s core tiger and Bengal florican habitats. This falls in the Bhuyanpara Range of the park, which is also where the erstwhile government-owned Kokilabari Seed Farm was located.
Concerned about the encroachment and its devastating impact on the park, the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) has also been reminding the Assam government to initiate action over the past few years.
In a communique dated July 30, 2026, which was also posted on social media, the NTCA asked the chief secretary of the Assam government to “intervene” and facilitate the “handing over” of the encroached area to the Manas Tiger Reserve authorities. It also reminded the government that a directive on the issue had been sent on June 11, but the authority was “not aware about the progress made in the matter so far.”
Manas National Park was designated as a reserve forest in 1907 and declared a wildlife sanctuary in 1928. In 1973, it became India’s first tiger reserve. Spread across an area of 2,837 sq km, the park was the largest in the country. In 2004, the park secured another feather in its cap when BirdLife International, a global partnership of bird conservation organizations, identified it as an Important Bird Area. UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site in 1985. “Manas has exceptional importance within the Indian sub-continent’s protected areas, as one of the most significant remaining natural areas in the region, where sizeable populations of a large number of threatened species continue to survive,” UNESCO observed.
Manas faced several challenges in the 1980s and 1990s. It was adversely impacted by the powerful insurgency that swept Assam in the late 1980s. With a large area of the park becoming a no-go zone for officials, environmental activists and tourists, conservation efforts suffered a big blow.
Poaching of the one-horned rhino also grew in this period. The number of rhinos reportedly dwindled from around 100 in the late 1980s to zero by the time peace returned to the region in the mid-2000s. Wildlife researcher Anwaruddin Choudhury estimated in 1996 that over 80 percent of the park’s large mammals had also been decimated. In 1992, UNESCO’s World Heritage Convention declared that Manas was “in danger.”
A former official of the forest department told The Diplomat that Assam’s Bharatiya Janata Party-led government was apprehensive of a “backlash” from the BTC if the encroachment is cleared from the park. The Bodoland People’s Front (BPF), which rules the council, is also an ally in the BJP-led coalition government in Assam.
Meanwhile, the Gauhati High Court has issued orders to the Assam government and the BTC to prevent further encroachment in the park after activist Rohit Choudhury filed a Public Interest Litigation (PIL).
The encroachment of national parks lays bare the lackadaisical approach of the Assam government towards the conservation of forests and wildlife in the country. The government evicted illegal settlers from the World Heritage Site of Kaziranga National Park, also in Assam, in 2016, only after the Gauhati High Court intervened and issued orders.

Advertisement
Opinion
How Hong Kong is trying a new solution to its land value problem
After decades of lucrative land sales, can the city finally build a system in which the land itself creates economic value?
3-MIN READ3-MIN
1
 Listen
Dr Ken Ip is an assistant professor specialising in business innovation and entrepreneurship at Saint Francis University, Hong Kong. 
When Hong Kong’s first chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, announced his housing plan in 1997, the ambition was extraordinary. The government would produce at least 85,000 flats a year across the public and private sectors, and raise the home ownership rate to 70 per cent. The idea was simple. Build more homes, make housing more affordable and allow more families to own a piece of Hong Kong. Then history intervened.
The Asian financial crisis struck. Property prices collapsed. The economy weakened. The 85,000-flat target quickly became politically toxic, and the government retreated. Nearly three decades later, Hong Kong is still wrestling with the same dilemma: how much land can the government release without destabilising the value of the land already in the system? That is the uncomfortable question behind the Northern Metropolis today.
Rising land and property values can generate government revenue and household wealth, but they also make it harder for younger generations to enter the housing market. Hong Kong took this model to an extreme.

To live with joy, a person’s attention needs to be open and free. When it is open and free, it…
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
01:23:00 UTC
10:23:00 KST

To live with joy, a person’s attention needs to be open and free. When it is open and free, it becomes possible to see need and how it must be addressed, and it is by meeting need that joy is created. Conversely, attachment to particular intentions limits the range of attention, causing need to be ignored, which then produces suffering.
The experience of suffering is an indicator that attachment is present, and liberation from suffering is possible only by releasing attachment. Attachment is released through the awareness developed from open and free attention to experience, but it is attachment itself that causes attention to become limited and narrow.
The only feasible solution to this problem is to make a conscious effort to loosen attention until the awareness is developed to keep it loose. But loosening attention from the objects of attachment first requires the ability to loosen it in general. It is necessary to develop the skill of letting go of the many thoughts, feelings, memories, ideas, and so on that arise throughout ordinary life.

'Use lowest effective dose of Nsaids': Fresh advisory on kidney risks of painkiller abuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
00:54:39 UTC
09:54:39 KST

Health Ministry warns against misuse of painkillers, antibiotics over kidney disease risk.
NEW DELHI: Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has issued a fresh advisory on rational consumption of painkillers and antibiotics, in view of their repeated use, without proper medical advice, putting people at the risk of kidney complications and other adverse effects.The drug regulator's circular says non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (Nsaids) and antibiotics are prescription medicines under Drugs and Cosmetics Rules and should be used only when clinically indicated, at the appropriate dose and duration and under medical supervision. It has asked people not to take Nsaids, commonly used as painkillers, repeatedly or for a prolonged period without advice.
Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation has also cautioned against self-medication with antibiotics and advised people with existing kidney disease or other risk factors for renal impairment to inform their doctor before taking Nsaids.Prof Sandeep Mahajan, nephrologist at AIIMS, said unregulated and prolonged use of painkillers can accelerate the decline in kidney function. "All prescription medicines should be taken under the supervision of a qualified physician, with the prescribed dose and duration strictly followed."CDSCO has advised doctors to use the lowest effective dose of Nsaids for the shortest appropriate duration, with extra caution in patients at risk of kidney injury. This comes against the backdrop of a substantial chronic kidney disease burden in India. A 2025 review of community-based studies estimated pooled chronic kidney disease prevalence at 13.24%, although estimates varied widely across regions and studies.

Balakot to Sindoor, India gave befitting reply: PM Modi on Pakistan terror

Unknown Publisher

PM Modi’s stern message to Pakistan: ‘Time for sponsoring terror to go unpunished is long gone’
NEW DELHI: In a stern message to Pakistan, PM Modi said on Sunday the time when its role in sponsoring terror attacks on India would go unpunished is long gone, and his govt has made it clear with its actions, including Op Sindoor, that terrorists will be given a befitting response for their sinister designs against India.Modi's message came in his 'Mann ki Baat' broadcast as India marks the 10th anniversary of the surgical strikes on terror hideouts in Pakistan on Sept 28-29, 2016. "The world was astonished to see the manner in which our brave soldiers crossed the LoC to take action against terror. The strike demonstrated a new aspect of India's counter-terror policy. It was our decisive response to long-standing pain India had endured," he said.
"Over the past decade, from Balakot airstrike to Op Sindoor, India has repeatedly sent out a clear message: if terrorists dare to cast an evil eye on India, they will be met with a befitting response."
'Zero-tolerance terror policy has borne results'
Contrasting his government's targeted action against Pakistan to the approach of the previous Congress-led UPA govt, PM Narendra Modi said serial blasts had once become a common occurrence in the country. On Sept 13, 2008, serial blasts rocked Delhi and, just a few weeks later, the Mumbai terror attack stunned the country, the PM said.
Demands for action against Pakistan following every terror attack used to be made then but were ignored. "Today, India pursues a zero-tolerance policy against terrorism, and we are witnessing the results of that," he said.During Op Sindoor, the Modi govt also unveiled a tougher national security doctrine, declaring that any future terror attack will be treated as an act of war. Trump offered to sell arms to China, US ambassador says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
00:23:00 UTC
09:23:00 KST

Trump offered to sell arms to China, US ambassador says
Edward Wong
- President Trump offered to sell US weapons to China during Xi Jinping's visit, an unusual move given China is seen as America's main rival.
- The US government denies any plans for arms sales to China, citing legal prohibitions and concerns over China's military growth and regional threats.
- Trump has delayed a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan, using it as a negotiation tool with China, despite bipartisan pressure to proceed with the sale.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump has asked Chinese President Xi Jinping whether he would like to buy US weapons, David Perdue, the US ambassador to China said in a television interview on Sept 27.
“President Trump continues to say, ‘Hey, we sell arms to other people around the world,’” Perdue said on Fox News Sunday, while discussing the state visit by Xi to Washington last week.
“He actually asked President Xi if he would like to buy some at one point.”
Perdue did not give further details and did not reveal Xi’s reply.
An admission that the US president offered to sell arms to China is extraordinary.
China is considered by most US policymakers and legislators of both parties to be the greatest military, economic and diplomatic rival of the United States – the only real challenger to the US as a superpower.
When asked for comment, the White House said through a US official that the United States had no plans to sell arms to China.
The State Department said in a statement that “US law prohibits arms sales to China, and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China”.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
China has the world’s fastest-growing military, and for decades US officials across administrations, including in the current one, have warned of a potential military clash between the two nuclear-armed powers in the Asia-Pacific region, particularly over the island of Taiwan or China’s aggressive actions in territory claimed by US allies in the South and East China Seas.
Chinese defence companies, with the approval of the Chinese government, are supporting adversaries of the US, including Iran and Russia, by selling them dual-use equipment and satellite imagery, as well as planning the secret export of weapons, according to US officials.
The US has imposed sanctions on some Chinese companies.
The US has been the dominant military power in the Asia-Pacific region, but that strength is fading relative to China’s, especially as the Trump administration diverts resources from the region for use in its war against Iran.
In recent years, the US defence industry has also struggled to manufacture weapons systems at a rate considered sufficient for global needs by US officials.
“If there was any ambiguity about whether President Trump views China as a security threat, this disclosure by @USAmbChina Perdue puts the question to rest,” Ryan Hass, a former career diplomat and White House national security official who is director of the China Centre at the Brookings Institution, wrote on social media platform X.
“Trump’s offer to sell weapons to China will be unsettling to American partners at the pointy edge of China’s spear,” he added.
Those partners include the Philippines, Japan and Taiwan, the de facto independent island and democracy that the Chinese Communist Party seeks to rule.
Trump has been withholding a US$14 billion (S$17.9 billion) sale of weapons to Taiwan, even though the US government has been required by law since 1979 to send arms of a defensive nature to the island.
The latest arms package was put together by State Department officials and was approved by congressional leaders early in 2026, but has since languished at the department, The New York Times reported. Senators sent a bipartisan letter in May to Trump urging him to move forward with the sale.
On Sept 23, hours before Xi arrived in Washington, four Republican senators led by Senator Mitch McConnell of Kentucky sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth asking for the same thing.
They also pressed the two men to allocate US$300 million in aid for purchasing arms that Congress had already approved for Taiwan, as well as US$1 billion for the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative, a US defence programme.
When a Fox News interviewer asked Perdue on Sept 27 about the widespread concerns over withheld weapons sales and military aid to Taiwan, Perdue pointed out that Trump had approved US$11 billion in arms sales to Taiwan in 2025. And he said “there are continuing conversations about other sales. He and President Xi talk about that every time they get together”.
It was then that Perdue said Trump had argued that the US sells arms to “other people around the world” and offered such sales to Xi.
China has said Xi has told Trump that he opposes the US selling weapons to Taiwan.
In May, after leaving a Beijing summit with Xi, Trump told reporters he had discussed Taiwan arms sales with Xi “in great detail”.
Such conversations – the existence of which Perdue underscored in his remarks Sept 27 – are a violation of a 1982 document in which the US agreed to broaden its support of Taiwan; one of the assurances said Washington “has not agreed to consult” China on arms sales to Taiwan.
When asked in May about that commitment, Trump replied: “Well, I think the 1980s is a long way. That’s a big, far distance.”
In a Fox News interview recorded in May while he was in Beijing, Trump said he was holding back Taiwan arms sales because it was a “very good negotiating chip” with China.
After the summit last week, Trump said he and Xi did not talk much about Taiwan. “Right now, it’s fine,” he said. “It’s just moving along.” NYTIMES

Indonesia’s 3% deficit cap: guardrail or growth barrier?
As lawmakers weigh lifting the statutory deficit ceiling, economists warn of downgrades and higher borrowing costs
Supporters argue that greater room to borrow and spend would let Southeast Asia’s largest economy invest its way towards Prabowo’s target of 8 per cent annual growth by 2029. Economists counter that weakening the rule could push up borrowing costs and dent investor confidence.

            Lead Architects: Zhang Ming, Zhang Zi, Shen Jie, Wang Xunan
Text description provided by the architects. Yuelang Road is located in the core area of Qianjiang Century City, Hangzhou, surrounded by six high-density commercial and office towers. Before renewal, this approximately 330-meter internal street primarily served office commuting, garage access, temporary parking and building logistics. Motor vehicles, bicycles, pedestrians and loading activities competed within the limited road space, while the building frontage spaces on both sides were fragmented by fences, planting, level changes and varied paving. The result was a commercial-office backstreet dominated by movement, with little space to pause. The design brings the roadway, pedestrian spaces and building frontage areas on both sides into a coordinated renewal framework. By relocating surface parking, reorganizing the street section, opening the building frontages, and introducing seating, outdoor dining and public activity spaces, it gradually establishes a continuous pedestrian and public-space system. At the same time, drawing on Yuelang Road's existing metropolitan nightscape, the design uses lunar phases as a recurring motif across structures, lighting and street furniture, making room for rest, outdoor dining, social interaction and nighttime activity alongside everyday circulation.

South Africa Rocked by 3 Mass Shootings: What to Know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
00:00:00 UTC
09:00:00 KST

South African police have launched manhunts after three mass shootings killed at least 32 people.
Police were searching for suspects early Monday after separate shootings took place over the weekend in impoverished townships, including Wedela in West Rand District outside Johannesburg, Lwandle in Western Cape, and Khayelitsha in Western Cape.
“Violence and criminality continues to spread in our country,” President Cyril Ramaphosa said on Sunday. “This is the level of criminality that we must bring down, and our security forces are now going to continue pulling out all stops. It cannot go on like this.” He pledged stronger action by security forces to reduce violent crime in the country.
The shootings came amid a recent spate of mass shootings and other killings that have alarmed South Africans. Authorities have linked some of the attacks to criminal gangs fighting over territory or illicit businesses like illegal mining, drug trafficking, and extortion. South African police define a mass shooting as a single attack that results in three or more people shot.
In March, Ramaphosa deployed soldiers to support police as part of a yearlong operation against gang violence and illegal mining, including operations around Johannesburg. The President described organized crime as the most immediate threat to the country’s democracy and economic development. Some observers, however, noted that the deployment was an overdue attempt to address the police’s failure to keep communities, especially in poorer townships, safe.
Wedela shooting kills 18
Eighteen people were killed and more than a dozen wounded in a shooting in the township of Wedela on Saturday night.
Police said eight men opened fire on patrons drinking outside a tavern at around 9:30 p.m. local time, before entering the bar and “shooting at patrons inside.” The perpetrators allegedly searched some patrons and stole cellphones before escaping in two unidentified vehicles. The attackers allegedly carried pistols and AK-47 rifles.
Two vehicles were also burnt during the attack.
Seventeen people died at the scene, including 13 men and four women. Police identified two of the deceased victims as South Africans and another two as Lesotho nationals. Fifteen injured victims were transported to hospital for treatment, with several in critical condition.
Another victim died in hospital, police said on Monday, bringing the death toll to 18.
Gauteng Deputy Police Commissioner Fred Kekana said police had a clear picture of the suspects and their names, according to local media reports. He did not publicly identify the suspects.
Kekana said police are investigating the attack as possible retaliation for an August shooting at the same tavern that killed one person and wounded another. One of those killed was wanted in connection with the earlier shooting, he said.
Gunmen kill 10 in Lwandle
Ten people were shot and killed at a nighttime entertainment venue in Lwandle, a township on the outskirts of Cape Town, that began at around 1:46 a.m. local time on Sunday.
Police said gunmen entered an entertainment venue selling grilled meat and fired at patrons. Five victims died at the scene and five after being transported to medical facilities. At least 11 others were wounded.
Police have launched a manhunt for the suspects, with no arrests announced as of Monday morning. Western Cape Police Commissioner Sizakhele Dyantyi pointed to “business rivalry” as a possible motive for the attack.
“People are buying alcohol maybe at cheaper places and they come and drink in this place. But we are still investigating that,” Dyantyi said. Police said they increased deployments in the area after the shooting.
Police said the deceased victims would be publicly identified only after relatives were informed.
Four killed in Khayelitsha
Police are investigating the murder of four people in Khayelitsha, a township in Cape Town, on Saturday.
Police responded to reports of a shooting at around 7:15 p.m. local time, and found three men dead with multiple gunshot wounds. Two of the victims were found inside a stationary vehicle and the third beside it. A fourth victim who sustained gunshot wounds died upon arrival at a medical facility, police said.
No suspects had been identified or arrested, police said on Sunday morning.
Organized crime drives mass shootings in poorest areas
South Africa is confronting a spate of mass shootings that has affected some of the country’s poorest communities, even as violent crime declined nationally this year. Contact crime, which includes violence or threats against people, between April and June fell 2.3% compared with the same period in 2025, while murders declined 5.9%.
But the country still has among the highest homicide rates in the world. In the same three months, 5,427 people were killed, averaging roughly 60 murders a day, according to police data.
Organized crime researchers have raised alarm about the rise in mass shootings. Julian Rademeyer, an adviser for the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, told the Newzroom Afrika broadcaster that the organization has tracked 41 mass killings resulting in around 196 deaths since January. The Associated Press counted seven mass shootings that had drawn national headlines since December 2025, six of which involved multiple gunmen.
The country’s poorest communities bear the brunt of the violence. After a mass shooting in June that killed 12 people in an informal settlement of shacks in Johannesburg, the AP reported that many of the country’s impoverished townships have inadequate lighting, slow police responses, and a lack of security. Those townships at times border affluent suburbs with armed private security controls and substantially lower violent crime rates, highlighting the country’s deep economic divide.
There are also more than 2 million illegal guns in the country despite strict gun ownership regulations, according to civil society groups. Allegations of police corruption have also undermined public trust: allegations that top police officials were colluding with organized criminals prompted Ramaphosa to announce a national investigation last year into police corruption, which has led to more than a dozen arrests of senior officers.
Illegal mining gangs are also a notorious problem in Johannesburg, and often establish their bases in poorer areas with lower policing. The government said last year that illegal mining had cost South Africa more than $3 billion in 2024. Last month, residents in Wedela reportedly described living in fear of rival illegal mining gangs in the area.
On Tuesday night, three gunmen opened fire at a house where around 14 people were gathered for a party in KwaMakhutha, south of the city of Durban. The shooting killed 12 people, including a woman believed to be pregnant. Following the attack, KwaZulu-Natal premier Thami Ntuli raised concerns about illegal guns and drugs in the area, noting that residents hear gunshots every night.

Houthis say Saudi strikes on Yemen’s Taiz leave dozens of casualties
SANAA, Yemen – Saudi air strikes on Taiz in south-west Yemen caused dozens of casualties in an area controlled by the Houthis, the Iran-backed group said on Sept 27, as fighting escalated further after a truce broke down.
The Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree accused Saudi Arabia of launching two air raids that hit a market on the outskirts of the city, saying nearly 50 people were killed or wounded without specifying the exact breakdown.
The spokesman said blood was “unjustly and aggressively spilled” in a statement posted online, vowing there would be consequences for the attack.
Earlier, the group’s Al-Masirah TV channel said a strike killed seven people and wounded 40 more at a market in Taiz, minutes after reporting that a Saudi fighter jet had targeted the area.
In a subsequent statement, the channel, citing the Houthis’ health ministry, said that five children were among those wounded.
Multiple Houthi sources later told AFP that nearly 30 fighters from the group were killed in the series of strikes, while eight civilians died.
The city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s civil war.
Images broadcast by Al-Masirah showed vehicles with blown-out windows as well as damaged warehouses, where goods were covered in a thick layer of dust.
Following several years of relative calm, Yemen’s war reignited in July, against the backdrop of the widening Middle East war.
The country is one of the poorest in the world and remains gripped by a vast humanitarian crisis.
Fighting intensified in September as the Houthis launched a lightning offensive that saw them seize Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast, including the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital shipping lane.
The Houthis have in parallel launched a blockade on Saudi energy exports, already choked off by Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
On Sept 26, Saudi Arabia said it intercepted two Houthi drones that were heading in the direction of the capital Riyadh.
Riyadh schools adopt remote learning for a week
Schools in Riyadh announced on Sept 27 that they would be shifting to remote learning for a week, without giving a reason, according to messages sent to parents and seen by AFP.
“We have just been informed by Saudi authorities that schools must remain closed all week,” read two separate messages seen by AFP.
There was no official reason given but the move comes amid heightened tensions in the Gulf and near-daily attacks aimed at Saudi Arabia by Iran-backed Houthi fighters in Yemen.
“When a decision affects an entire school community for a full week, families deserve clear communication and transparency about the reasons behind it,” one Riyadh parent, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told AFP.
“It’s a last-minute decision. We have no clue what’s happening,” a Lebanese expatriate living in Riyadh added.
Late on Sept 27, some schools indicated that they would be returning to in-person learning the next day.
Saudi officials have not officially commented publicly on the closures or on any order to return to in-person learning this week.
Yemen’s war erupted in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa from the Saudi-backed government, before going on to take control of vast swaths of the country’s north.
Riyadh intervened in the war the following year at the head of an international coalition.
Despite Saudi backing, Yemen’s government forces have been unable to repel the latest Houthi offensive. AFP

A dog-walker in Cirencester, who did not want to give his name, said his wife had been “worried about threats to Fairford”.
So the news “was like her nightmares have come true”, said the man.
Residents said the airbase is generally quiet apart from a major annual airshow that brings visitors from several countries.
“It’s no trouble at all,” said the dog walker about living near the base. “But actually using it as a bomber base is a bit worrying.”
“Normally, RAF Fairford is very quiet but at the moment, with Epic Fury, that’s changed,” local councillor Tristan Wilkinson told AFP, referring to the US military codename for its attacks on Iran.
“The local community and the authorities have had greater vigilance around the base”, in recent months, Wilkinson added.
The interior ministry has previously accused Iran and Russia of using proxies to carry out criminal activities on their behalf on British territory.
“I mean, with everything that’s been going on, with the activity around the airbase, something like that is bound to happen,” said 21-year-old Victor Compton.
“The effects of war reach into the safest parts of the world,” added the university student, saying it was a “bit of a reality check”. AFP

Under Burnham, Investment Screening Remains Hard to Predict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

Under Burnham, Investment Screening Remains Hard to Predict
There is uncertainty over what capabilities a sovereignty-minded government decides Britain must control.
Starmer Years: Conflicting Impulses
Since Labour took office in July 2024, UK investment screening has sat between two conflicting impulses: stronger appetite to protect the UK’s strategic and national security interests, and greater pressure to attract inward investment.
Policy like the National Security Strategy (NSS) and Defence Industrial Strategy established the strongest links yet between economic security and national security. The NSS and Strategic Defence Review identified China as a persistent geostrategic challenge. And since President Trump’s re-election, political concern over dependence on US technology and infrastructure has grown.
The Government also agreed to update the sectors of focus under the National Security and Investment Act (NS&I Act), subject to secondary legislation. The changes will bring the water sector into the mandatory notification regime, establish standalone schedules for critical minerals and semiconductors, and clarify areas including, data infrastructure and sensitive government data.
The period also saw steps from the Treasury and other ‘prosperity’ departments to encourage inward investment, particularly from China. This included efforts to reduce the risk thresholds applied to some sectors to support investment decisions, albeit maintaining a cautious approach in the most sensitive. We also saw the Government direct the Competition and Markets Authority to prioritise investment and growth in related competition law, manifesting in June 2026 revised draft guidance noting the positive effect of mergers for innovation and R&D which the European Commission has recognised as important for strategic sectors like defence.
A Stable Regime
Small wonder, the conflict delivered continuity in the latest NS&I Act report (the Government’s 2025–26 annual tally of trends in investment screening), with outcomes over the last four years, and the overall intent of the Act.
It is clear the regime remains selective, rather than becoming more or less permissive. Numbers of deals notified under the Act fluctuate, but the proportion subjected to detailed scrutiny has barely moved. Of notified acquisitions reviewed – the so-called ‘marginal’ (difficult) cases ‘called in’ for further scrutiny – rates were 4.4% in 2025–26, 4.5% in 2024–25, and 4.4% during 2023–24. The latest year produced nine final orders, only one prohibiting a transaction (Chinese-backed Versarien/BIMT), compared to one, zero, and five in years back to 2022.
Defence, military and dual-use, advanced materials, semiconductors, critical suppliers to Government and data- and data-infrastructure related activities feature heavily amongst cases escalated in all years.
As Britain’s geopolitics and conception of strategic sovereignty changes, so too will the companies, technologies and foreign dependencies that officials and ministers judge too important to leave uncontrolled
The same three acquirer countries of origin also dominate the marginal caseload. The percentages move a bit, but UK, Chinese and US-associated acquirers consistently dominate; they accounted for 52%, 30% and 23% of call-ins in 2025–26 respectively (acquirers can have more than one origin, and acquisitions more than one acquirer, so percentages can exceed 100%). China therefore continues to attract disproportionate scrutiny, consistent with China remaining a severe strategic challenge for the UK. But this has always been a ‘cases, not countries’ regime: UK and allied acquirers’ transactions are remedied where risks justify it.
The Government demonstrates repeatedly it is seeking to manage three broad security harms, which include disruption or dependency affecting critical infrastructure; risk of degradation of UK defence, intelligence or security capabilities and supply chains; and transfers of capabilities aiding a potential adversary.
Beneath those strategic harms, the same practical concerns recur, reflecting a broad range of equities going far beyond traditional ‘national security’.
- These can include loss of assured UK access to strategically important capabilities. QDI/Oxford Nanoscience was, in 2025, required to maintain manufacture and supply from the UK; similar concerns were evident in Epiris/Sepura in 2022 and materially in the David Brown/Stellex case in 2023.
- Transfer and loss of IP, know-how and R&D capability is another concern. UK Delin (buying Agile Analog) and Mubadala (investing in graphene experts Paragraf) have this year effectively been ordered to safeguard vital IP in the UK. The Pulsic/Super Orange HK semiconductor design automation deal saw this risk first managed in 2022.
- Access to sensitive data and systems is acted on consistently. In your author’s assessment this year’s (Irish-US) Taoglas/SFL Mobile Radio case appears to require that sensitive UK customer communications data is not harvested extra-territorially, but we first saw data protection in Electricity North West/Redrock in 2022.
- Lastly, harm to wider ecosystems is a consistent concern. IonQ was this year ordered to keep Oxford Ionics’ trapped-ion quantum hardware in the UK, because it is foundational to future UK quantum computing success. Looking back, Nexperia/Newport Wafer Fab (2022) saw the government identify future compound semiconductor capability across the UK as at risk through Newport’s place within the ecosystem.
Similar threat vectors, beyond majority acquisitions, are also consistently controlled.
- The regime has addressed joint ventures, for example by Vodafone/Hutchison 3G; in 2025 Versarien/BIMT applied the same logic to a risk that graphene know-how could leave for China.
- The Act has addressed ‘minority influence’ risks, or access and control disproportionate to ownership share, starting with (now defunct) Reaction Engines in 2022.
- ‘Cumulative risk’, in other words, whether an acquirer acquires increasingly significant positions in sectors in the UK and abroad, first surfaced most strikingly when HMG forced Nexperia to divest most of Newport Wafer Fab. Chinese-owned Nexperia was already operating silicon semi fabs in Manchester and across Europe.
- And lastly, what can be thought of as ‘sleeper risk’, or where an entity’s presence may cause a harm in future, has been a recurring theme, whether in the Newport Wafer Fab case, or the Liverpool–Pinggao energy research centre (2024). This proposed ringfencing to mitigate risk to the university’s wider research and IP.
These patterns are not simply retrospective readings of cleared cases and published orders. The Government has been clear about what it is seeking to protect from the start. Further clarity was added by the May 2024 statement on use of the call-in power and consultation on the Notifiable Acquisition Regulations (NARs) in 2025.
Where the mix of marginal cases has changed, investor behaviour probably shifted more than any Government direction. Data over four years shows transactions abandoned after encountering complexity mid-process have fallen by more than half (11 in 2022–23, to four last year). Former colleagues describe how increasing work on research protection and greenfield investment may indicate threat actors moving ‘outside’ the Act. Ascribing deterrence to the Act may be a step too far but is consistent with investors adapting.
The Burnham Government – Continuity and Change?
Against this mature background, we can expect some change in outcomes under the Burnham Government – but perhaps not from the sources onlookers may expect.
The standout move so far has been administrative: the transfer of the Investment Security Unit (ISU) from the Cabinet Office to the new Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST), and the Business Secretary, Jonathan Reynolds.
This will not make investment screening more ‘pro-business’. The regime is already favourable to business: 99%+ of transactions are approved. And transaction volumes and risk patterns ultimately drive what balance can be struck.
Rather, this move reflects bureaucratic considerations, including a desire to rationalise the centre of government. Whether or not it will be successful, it certainly creates some administrative challenges. Ethical walls will need to separate the ISU’s statutory decision-making under the NS&I Act from other parts of BIST responsible for promoting investment and sector growth. There is also likely to be disruption as the ISU establishes its new reporting arrangements and appoints a new Director.
The Government is likely to respond to political pressure to demonstrate that investment screening supports business, rather than deters it. Reducing unnecessary delays for lower-risk transactions will be addressed by staffing and reforms to the NARs. Mechanisms to speed ‘crowding in’ of private investment are addressing opportunities of ‘Trusted Capital’; this could conceivably see whitelists, with investment and economic security teams collaborating in their development. But this would largely formalise existing practice rather than representing some fundamental departure.
Most important is that whilst the Government will not cast aside the protection of critical infrastructure, strategic capabilities and economic resilience, it is set to take place within a new, much stronger ‘regional revival’ and a national sovereignty evolution of Starmer’s industrial strategy foundations, with heightened emphasis on British procurement. This will involve reindustrialisation via strengthened critical sectors such as defence, AI and advanced technologies, steel, energy, food and farming – especially outside the Southeast. The Burnham government is also dialling up focus on British technological sovereignty, especially from the US.
Sovereignty Matters
Bigger changes will arise from how the shifting context affects pursuit and protection of these goals. Shifting geopolitical, technological, industrial and investment trends create, on the one hand, new opportunities for the UK to advance economic, industrial, technological and security strength. On the other hand, those opportunities, and the threats posed by shifting geopolitics, technology and industrial power of other countries, evolve the very definitions of the sectors and competences the Government perceives it needs ‘in house’, and where it can safely, and even desirably, internationalise.
Consider how the Government might deal with three looming issues:
‘Europeanisation’ of defence supply chains. Defence and dual-use sectors are ‘jewels in the crown’ for the UK. However, defence ecosystems in eastern and northern European nations are benefiting from particularly large increases in Government spending, boosting confidence for private capital and merger and acquisition activity. The EU and major EU economies are also using foreign direct investment (FDI) and policy to bolster (and defend) sovereign capabilities. UK acquirers may face a tilted playing field coming from the outside, a concern which the Prime Minister raised with French President Macron on 3 September. One consequence may be greater scrutiny of European acquisitions of strategic UK capabilities, to preserve reciprocal interdependence. UK decision makers have voiced this concern to us.
The US in the UK. The US remains the number one source of FDI in the UK economy. However, precedents unthinkable even two years ago are being established. Political and procurement scrutiny of reliance on US suppliers in sensitive public services has intensified, with Palantir the most visible example. The UK is pursuing a more sovereign AI tech stack with a £500 million fund. The Government and Bank of England are backing a new UK retail payments infrastructure that could reduce reliance on Visa and Mastercard. US investment in the UK energy and data infrastructure nexus is another area where questions are now being asked.
US concerns over allied technology dependencies. US pressure over 5G and Huawei through the late 2010s brought out into the open US ability to shape the decision environment for UK ministers. The launch of the 6G ‘call to action’, alongside tightening restrictions on foreign technologies such as Chinese humanoid robotics, are early warning signs of further pressure on allies to limit Chinese market access and technological dependencies.
It is too early to say what the outcome of these pressures will be. But it seems safe to say they, and many others, will evolve the desirable ‘balance of UK control’ across sectors. In your author’s experience in risk assessment, the hardest judgement was where to draw the line: when does foreign control become excessive, particularly when assessing industrial strategy and the future?
Looking Ahead
The NS&I Act regime is unlikely to become materially more or less permissive under Burnham. But broad continuity should not be mistaken for predictability in its outcomes in marginal cases. The ‘next frontier’ of uncertainty under the Act is likely the Government’s changing view of acceptable foreign control across strategically important ecosystems. As Britain’s geopolitics and conception of strategic sovereignty changes, so too will the companies, technologies and foreign dependencies that officials and ministers judge too important to leave uncontrolled.
Continuity lies in the fact that what this means for deal risk will vary sector-by-sector, case-by-case. Investors and businesses will need to be unusually attuned to policy, technology, industry and geopolitical shifts around their value propositions.
NS&I risk can no longer be treated as a clearance exercise at the end of a transaction: whether a deal reinforces or weakens capabilities the UK increasingly regards as sovereign will shape its prospects from the outset.

Some companies are already adding contractual protections in the event a pause on diesel shipments overseas prevents deliveries to foreign buyers, people with knowledge of the situation told Bloomberg News on Sept 25.
In the event of a ban, US diesel prices would be widely expected to plummet, at least in the short run.
A halt would leave America’s allies, including Brazil and Britain, urgently needing to secure fuel. BLOOMBERG

People in strained relationships show somewhat higher preference for hearing lies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-27
22:00:40 UTC
07:00:40 KST

A study in Poland asked participants whether they preferred their partner to lie or tell the truth. Results showed that people less satisfied with their relationship tended to show a somewhat greater preference for hearing lies, both prosocial and egoistic. They also tended to perceive blatant truth as more harmful. The paper was published in The Journal of Social Psychology.
Honesty is widely regarded as a foundation of healthy romantic relationships. It is widely believed to support trust, commitment, and relationship satisfaction. At the same time, people do not always view complete truthfulness as the best response when honesty is likely to cause unnecessary emotional pain.
Prosocial lies, which are intended to benefit another person rather than the liar, are often judged more favorably than selfish deception. In romantic relationships, such lies can sometimes protect a partner’s feelings, preserve self-esteem, and help maintain harmony. They may also support positive illusions, in which partners view themselves, each other, or their relationship somewhat more favorably than objective reality would justify.
These positive beliefs can promote optimism, reduce conflict, and contribute to relationship satisfaction, particularly when they reinforce a sense of security and connection. Emotional resilience—the ability to adapt and recover from stress or adversity—may influence whether people prefer difficult truths or more reassuring forms of communication, with less resilient individuals potentially finding harsh information more difficult to manage.
The Theory of Resilience and Relational Load suggests that supportive and validating interactions help build emotional reserves that allow couples to cope more effectively with stress. From this perspective, occasional prosocial dishonesty can sometimes function as a protective form of communication, although it creates an ongoing tension between the values of honesty, kindness, and relationship stability.
Study authors Sebastian Wnęk and Katarzyna Cantarero conducted a study aiming to examine the relationship between relationship satisfaction, emotional resilience, and the preference for prosocial lies. They hypothesized that higher relationship satisfaction is associated with a greater preference for hearing prosocial lies, and a lower preference for hearing egoistic lies (lies told primarily to benefit the liar). They also expected individuals with lower emotional resilience to show a greater preference for hearing prosocial lies.
Study participants were 672 residents of Poland who had been in a romantic relationship for at least one year, recruited from a research panel. 336 of them were women. Their average age was 46 years. For their participation, they received points that could be exchanged for various goods such as headsets or flash drives.
Participants were first shown six stories that described different scenarios involving themselves and their partner. In three of these scenarios, the partner had the option to lie egoistically or tell the truth, while in the other three, the partner could tell a prosocial lie, or the truth.
Participants’ task was to choose which option they would prefer to hear from their partner (the lie offered in the scenario or the truth) in each scenario. After this, they completed assessments of relationship satisfaction (the Relationship Assessment Scale), emotional resilience (the Brief Resilience Scale), closeness, perceived importance of truth, perceptions of how blatant truth affects a romantic relationship, conflict avoidance, and whether participants would lie prosocially to their partner.
The results showed that participants preferred prosocial lies more than egoistic lies. Participants who showed a higher preference for lies, both prosocial and egoistic, tended to be somewhat less satisfied with their relationships and to perceive truth as more harmful. They also saw themselves as more likely to tell a prosocial lie to their partner, and showed a lower preference for the truth. Participants with a higher preference for egoistic lies tended to see themselves as somewhat less close to their partner.
The study authors tested a statistical model proposing that lower relationship satisfaction might make individuals perceive blatant truth as more harmful, leading to a higher preference for hearing prosocial lies. The results showed that such a dynamic is possible.
This model also supported the notion that the relationship between relationship satisfaction and the perception of blatant truth as harmful might depend on emotional resilience. It turned out that in individuals with high emotional resilience, the strength of the association between low relationship satisfaction and perception of blatant truth as harmful was stronger than in individuals with low emotional resilience.
“Taken together, our research not only offers a useful material that can be used in future studies that focus on deception, but also underscores the complexity of prosocial lying in romantic relationships. While prosocial lies are often viewed as more acceptable than egoistic lies, their use appears to be nevertheless undesired in satisfied romantic relationships. However, when satisfaction is low and individuals perceive truth-telling as potentially harmful, they may prefer positive illusions to honest communication,” the study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific knowledge about romantic relationships. However, it should be noted that the design of the study does not allow any causal inferences to be derived from the results.
The paper, “If I cannot bounce back easily, can I handle the truth? Satisfaction in romantic relationships, resilience and preference towards prosocial lies,” was authored by Sebastian Wnęk and Katarzyna Cantarero.

First Copenhagen China Festival brings Mid-Autumn charm to Danish capital

Performers perform Wu Opera during the first Copenhagen China Festival at Copenhagen City Hall Square in Copenhagen, Denmark, Sept. 27, 2026. Drums, lion dances, opera movements and the aroma of Chinese food filled Copenhagen's City Hall Square on Sunday as the first Copenhagen China Festival was held in celebration of the Mid-Autumn Festival.(Photo by Liu Zhichao/Xinhua)
COPENHAGEN, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Drums, lion dances, opera movements and the aroma of Chinese food filled Copenhagen's City Hall Square on Sunday as the first Copenhagen China Festival was held in celebration of the Mid-Autumn Festival.
Organized by the China Cultural Center in Copenhagen and other partners, the event, under the theme "Mid-Autumn in Poetry," turned one of the Danish capital's busiest public squares into an open-air stage for Chinese culture, featuring performances, food and hands-on cultural activities.
The program opened with a lion dance and a street parade, followed by a series of stage performances by Chinese arts groups, schools and cultural organizations from across Denmark.
A highlight of the day was Wu Opera, a traditional Chinese theatrical form listed as part of China's national intangible cultural heritage. Performers from Zhejiang presented excerpts including "Three Fights Against the White Bone Demon," bringing to the stage the expressive singing, stylized movements and martial elements of Chinese opera.
The festival also featured tai chi, Peking Opera, music ensembles, dance performances and a Mid-Autumn poetry dialogue, offering local audiences a glimpse of both traditional and contemporary Chinese cultural expressions.
Food was another attraction. Visitors watched hand-pulled noodle demonstrations and tasted Chinese specialties, including mooncakes, a symbolic food of the Mid-Autumn Festival associated with family reunion and sharing.
Interactive booths invited visitors to try Chinese calligraphy, learn about tea culture, explore traditional crafts and take part in a quiz on Chinese culture. ■

Vucic resigns as president of Serbia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
05:58:33 CST
06:58:33 KST

Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic speaks during a press conference in Belgrade, Serbia, Sept. 27, 2026. Aleksandar Vucic signed and submitted his resignation on Sunday, stepping down as president. (Photo by Predrag Milosavljevic/Xinhua)
BELGRADE, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic signed and submitted his resignation on Sunday, stepping down as president.
"I am now signing the text that reads as follows: 'Pursuant to Article 116, paragraph 5 of the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia, I submit my resignation from the office of President of the Republic.'...Ana, this goes to the Parliament, and tomorrow you go to the handover," said Vucic.
Under Serbia's Constitution and Law on the president, the president's term ends when the written resignation is formally received by the National Assembly, without requiring approval. The Speaker of the National Assembly Ana Brnabic then assumes presidential duties for up to three months and must call a presidential election within that period.
Vucic also said he would take part in the snap parliamentary elections scheduled on Oct. 25 as an ordinary citizen.
The Serbian parliament was dissolved on Sept. 9. Under the Constitution, a dissolved parliament has limited powers, while the government continues to perform its duties until a new government is formed.
On Sept. 5, the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) nominated Vucic as head of its electoral list and its candidate for prime minister in the upcoming snap parliamentary elections.
Following the Oct. 25 elections, the process of forming a new government will begin. The acting president, after consulting representatives of the elected electoral lists, proposes a prime minister candidate to the National Assembly. The candidate then presents the government's program and cabinet members, which must be approved by a majority of all lawmakers.
Vucic, born in Belgrade in 1970, had served as defense minister, first deputy prime minister and prime minister. He was elected president in 2017 and re-elected in 2022. Under the Constitution, the presidential term is five years, with a maximum of two terms for any individual. ■

Syria begins transit of gasoline to Iraq via Banias oil terminal
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
05:58:17 CST
06:58:17 KST

Vessels are pictured off the coast of Banias, Tartous province, western Syria, Sept. 27, 2026. The Syrian Petroleum Company (SPC) has begun transporting gasoline supplied for Iraq through the Banias oil terminal under a three-month renewable agreement, as regional energy flows face disruption from instability around the Strait of Hormuz, Syria's state news agency SANA reported Sunday. (Str/Xinhua)
DAMASCUS, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- The Syrian Petroleum Company (SPC) has begun transporting gasoline supplied for Iraq through the Banias oil terminal under a three-month renewable agreement, as regional energy flows face disruption from instability around the Strait of Hormuz, Syria's state news agency SANA reported Sunday.
Ahmed Qabbaji, deputy executive president for transportation and storage at the company, said the operation began Thursday with an initial batch of 57 tanker trucks, with plans to increase capacity to around 200 trucks per day traveling to Iraq through the al-Tanf border crossing between Syria and Iraq.
According to media reports, Iraq's State Organization for Marketing of Oil signed a contract with Qatar's UCC to supply Iraq with improved gasoline via road tankers from Banias. The operation is carried out under a transit contract between the SPC and the Qatari company.
Qabbaji said UCC is purchasing the gasoline from several international sources, while the Syrian side handles its transportation in return for transit fees.
Ten fuel tankers are currently at sea as part of the operation, two of which have already unloaded into the SPC's storage facilities in Banias, he said.
The company has prepared loading areas and eight loading bays capable of filling eight tanker trucks simultaneously, with unloading and loading operations continuing around the clock.
Qabbaji said the transit operation would generate revenue for both the company and the Syrian state while strengthening Syria's role as a regional corridor for imports, exports and energy transportation.
He added that gasoline and fuel oil are currently being transported through the al-Tanf crossing, while other border crossings could be used for different products. Plans are also under consideration to expand transit operations to other commodities.
Separately, between 1,000 and 1,200 tanker trucks carrying Iraqi oil are currently moving through Syrian territory each day, according to Qabbaji, with volumes varying depending on weather and transportation conditions.
Qabbaji also said work is underway to prepare the Arab Gas Pipeline up to the Syrian-Jordanian border and a branch toward Lebanon, which is expected to be ready within about 15 days to transport gas to Lebanon once the necessary preparations are completed.
The developments come as Syria seeks to revive its energy and transit infrastructure and capitalize on its geographical position linking Iraq and the Gulf region with Mediterranean ports.
The country's economy has shown signs of recovery after years of conflict and isolation. The International Monetary Fund said in August that Syria's economy began recovering in 2025 and projected growth of more than 10 percent in 2026, supported partly by the country's gradual reintegration into regional and global economies. ■
